To that god whom they call the All, whom they call the one who desires, whom they call the giver and the receiver—to those Agnis, let this be offered.
To you, whom the thirteen Bhauvanas and the five Mānavas have recognized in their minds as the Hotṛ priest—to him who bestows luster, fame, and pleasant truth; to those Agnis, let this be offered.
To the one whose food is the bull, whose food is the cow, the ordainer with Soma upon his back, to those Agnis headed by Vaiśvānara, let this be offered.

To those who move along the sky, the earth, and the intermediate space, who follow the lightning, who are within the quarters, or who are within the wind—to all those fires, let this offering be made. We invoke Savitṛ of the golden hands, Indra, Bṛhaspati, Varuṇa, Mitra, Agni, the All-gods, and the Aṅgirases; may they pacify this flesh-eating fire.
Pacified is the flesh-eating fire, pacified is the one who destroys men; and furthermore, that which causes universal consumption—that flesh-eater I have extinguished.
Those mountains whose backs are Soma, the waters that flow upon their surfaces, Vāta, Parjanya, and Agni—they all have extinguished the flesh-eater.
May the great splendor and wide fame of the elephant spread forth—that which was produced from the body of Aditi. All the gods and Aditi, being of one accord, have bestowed this upon me.

May Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra, and Rudra take heed; may the all-sustaining gods anoint me with splendor. With that splendor by which the elephant came into being, with which the king among men [shines], and with which the gods attained divinity in the beginning—with that splendor, O Agni, make me radiant today.

Whatever splendor is yours, O Jātavedas, that arises from the oblation—as great as the splendor of the sun and as great as the splendor of the elephant of Asura—so much splendor may the Aśvins, adorned with lotus-garlands, bestow upon me.
As far as the four quarters extend, as far as the eye reaches, so much sensory power (indriya) may come to me; let that splendor of the elephant enter into me.
For the elephant has become the preeminent dweller among well-seated beasts; with his fortune and splendor, I sprinkle myself.
That by which you have become barren—that we destroy from you. This [cause] we place far away from you, elsewhere than you.
May a male embryo enter your womb like an arrow into a quiver; may a heroic son be born here for you, ten months old.
Give birth to a male child, and may a male be born after him. May you be the mother of sons—of those already born and those whom you shall bring forth.
By means of those excellent seeds which bulls produce, may you find a son; as such, be a prolific milch-cow.
I prepare for you that which belongs to Prajāpati; let the embryo enter your womb. O woman, may you find a son who shall be auspicious to you, and may you be auspicious to him.

Those divine herbs whose father is heaven, whose mother is earth, and whose root is the ocean—may those herbs aid you, O son, for the sake of knowledge. The herbs are full of milk; full of milk is my speech. And so, from those that are full of milk, I bring [this medicine] by the thousands. I know the one who made the grain full of milk in abundance. We invoke that god whose name is *Saṃbhṛtvan*, whoever he may be in the house of the non-sacrificer.
May these five directions and the five human tribes bring here abundance, like rivers bringing their curse upon the rain.
Draw forth the inexhaustible spring that flows in a hundred streams and a thousand streams! Even so, let this grain of ours flow in a thousand streams and be inexhaustible!
O you with a hundred hands, gather it together; O you with a thousand hands, scatter it abroad! Bring about here the increase of what has been done and what is yet to be done!
The Gandharvas have three measures, and the housewife has four; with that which among them is most full, we touch you.
Upoha and Samūha are your two attendants, O Prajāpati; may they bring here abundance, great prosperity, and inexhaustible wealth.
Let Uttuda prick you; do not be stiff in your own bed. With that arrow of Desire which is terrible, I pierce you in the heart.
Having made well-straightened that arrow whose feathers are longing, whose barb is desire, and whose nock is volition, let Kāma pierce you in the heart.

That well-bent arrow of Kāma which dries up the spleen, the east-winged, the burning—one with that I pierce you in the heart. Pierced by the burning pain, you shall become dry; crawl toward her! Soft, free from anger, entirely devoted, speaking kindly, and faithful—such a one I seek for you from the mother and from the father. So that you may be according to my will and may follow my mind.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, pierce through her heart and thoughts; then, depriving her of will, bring her under my control.

O gods who dwell in this eastern quarter, you whose name is "Spears"—Agni is your arrow. Be gracious to us, speak for us, homage to you, svāhā to you! O gods who dwell in this southern quarter, you whose name is "Seekers"—Desire is your arrow. Be gracious to us, speak for us, homage to you, svāhā to you!

O gods who are in this western quarter, you whose name is Vairājas, may your waters be your arrows; be gracious to us, speak for us, homage to you, svāhā to you! O gods who are in this northern quarter, you whose name is Pravidhyantas, may your wind be your arrows; be gracious to us, speak for us, homage to you, svāhā to you!
O gods named Nilmipas who abide in this fixed quarter, the plants are your arrows; may you be gracious to us, may you speak in our favor; homage to you, to you svāhā!
O gods named Avasvants who abide in this upward quarter, Bṛhaspati is your arrow; may you be gracious to us, may you speak in our favor; homage to you, to you svāhā!

The eastern direction has Agni as its overlord, Asita as its protector, and the Ādityas as its arrows. Homage to them, the overlords; homage to the protectors; homage to the arrows; let there be homage to these! Whosoever hates us, and whomsoever we hate—him we place within your jaws.

The southern direction has Indra as its overlord; the cross-lined snake is its guardian; the ancestors are its arrows. To them be homage! To the overlords be homage! To the guardians be homage! To the arrows be homage! Let there be homage to these! Whosoever hates us and whomsoever we hate, him we place within your jaws.

The western quarter has Varuṇa as its overlord, the viper as its guardian, and food as its arrows. Homage to them, the overlords; homage to the guardians; homage to the arrows; let there be homage to these! Whosoever hates us and whomsoever we hate, him we place within the jaws of you [all].

The northern quarter has Soma as its overlord, the Svaja as its protector, and the thunderbolt as its arrows. Homage to them, the overlords; homage to the protectors; homage to the arrows; let there be homage to these! Whosoever hates us, and whomsoever we hate, him we place within your jaws.

The fixed quarter has Viṣṇu as its overlord; Kalmāṣagrīva is its protector; plants are its arrows. Homage to them, the overlords; homage to the protectors; homage to the arrows; let there be homage to these! Whosoever hates us, and whomsoever we hate—him we place within your jaws.

The upward direction has Bṛhaspati as its overlord, Śvitra as its protector, and raindrops as its arrows. Homage to them, the overlords; homage to the protectors; homage to the arrows; let there be homage to these! Whosoever hates us, and whomsoever we hate—him we place within the jaws of you [arrows].

This one has become united with each single creation, where the creators of beings released the cows of every form. Where she who is born without a season gives birth, she, the hissing and the glowing one, destroys the cattle.

This [female spirit], having become a flesh-eater and a devourer, destroys the cattle. One should give her to a Brahmin; thus she will be pleasant and auspicious. Be auspicious toward men, auspicious toward cows and horses; be auspicious toward this entire field, and be auspicious to us here.
Here is nourishment, here is sap; here become the most thousandfold in gain. O self-restraining one, cause cattle to thrive!

Where those of good heart and well-doing rejoice, having cast off disease from their own bodies—to that world the self-restraining one has gone. May she not harm our men and our cattle! Where there is the world of those of good heart and well-doing who have offered the *agnihotra*—to that world the self-restraining one has gone. May she not harm our men and our cattle!

Of that which kings divide—the sixteenth part of one’s sacrifices and charitable works—those who sit in Yama’s assembly [take]. Therefore, the white-footed sheep, when given as *svadhā*, releases [the giver] from that;
it fulfills all desires, being present, prevailing, and manifesting. The white-footed sheep, given for the fulfillment of intention, does not fail.
He who gives a white-footed sheep, equal to the world, ascends to heaven where no tax is levied by the weak against the stronger.

The giver of a five-cake white-footed sheep, equal to the world, lives on inexhaustibly in the world of the ancestors. The giver of a five-cake white-footed sheep, equal to the world, lives on inexhaustibly in the world of the Sun and Moon.
Like a stream, he does not fail; like the ocean, his greatness is water. Like two gods dwelling together, the one with white feet does not fail.
Who has given this to whom? Desire has given it to desire. Desire is the giver; desire is the receiver. Desire has entered the ocean. With desire I receive you; O Desire, this is yours.
May the Earth receive you, as does this great intermediate space. Having received [this] with my breath, my self, and my progeny, may I not come to ruin.
I create for you a state of heart-felt unity, concord, and freedom from enmity. Cherish one another as the cow cherishes her newborn calf.
Let the son be devoted to his father and be at one with his mother. Let the wife speak to her husband words that are honey-sweet and auspicious.
Let not brother hate brother, nor sister sister. Becoming harmonious and bound by a common vow, speak your words with goodness.
That by which the gods do not depart nor do they hate one another—that we establish as a sacred formulation (*brahman*) in your house, a means of mutual recognition for all men.
O elders, full of wisdom, do not be divided; acting in harmony and moving together as companions, speaking kindly to one another—come! I make you all turn toward one another with a single mind.

Common is the water-trough for you, common is your share of food; with a single yoke-thong I bind you all together. United, worship Agni, as spokes surround the hub. I make you all turn toward one another, of one mind, with a single impulse, through this bond of union. Like gods guarding immortality, may there be goodwill for you every evening and morning.
O gods, be free from old age; O Agni, be free from ill-will. May I be free from all evil, free from disease, and united with long life.
May Pavamāna drive away [sickness] with distress; may Śakra drive it away with evil-doing. May I be separated from every evil, separated from consumption, and united with long life.
May the domestic animals be separated from those of the wild; may the waters flow away from thirst. May I be separated from every evil, separated from consumption, and united with long life.
May heaven and earth depart from here for me; may the paths go apart in every direction. May I be separated from every evil, separated from consumption, and united with long life.

"Tvaṣṭṛ yokes the bridal procession for his daughter"—thus this entire world moves apart. May I be separated from all evil, separated from consumption; may Agni restore my vital breaths, he who is joined with the moon through life-force. May I be separated from all evil, separated from consumption; may I be united with life-force. With life-force, the gods have sent forth the sun, whose strength is universal. May I be separated from all evil, separated from consumption; may I be united with life-force.

O long-lived ones, you who have made life long, live by means of breath; do not die! May I be separated from all evil, separated from consumption, and united with life! O breath, through breath, become one who possesses breath; remain right here, do not die! May I be separated from all evil, separated from consumption, and united with life!
Up with life, up with longevity, up with the essence of the plants! May I be separated from all evil, separated from consumption, and united with life!
Through the rain of Parjanya, we have risen up as immortals. May I be separated from all evil, separated from consumption, and united with long life.
The Brahman, first born in the east, the radiant Vena, has revealed it from the boundary. He, its lowest and highest manifestations, has disclosed the womb of both the existent and the non-existent.

Let this royal lady, the mother of the fathers, go forth at the head, she who stands firm in the world for the first-born. For him, let them prepare this radiant, serpent-like oblation, this heated milk, for the first nourisher.

He who was born knowing his kinship proclaims all the generations of the gods. From the midst of the sacred word (*brahman*), he drew forth the sacred word; from below and above, he established himself over the self-sustaining powers (*svadhās*).

For he knows [all] of the earth, standing firm in the cosmic order (*ṛta*); he has propped up the two great worlds for their security. Great when born, he propped apart the vast heaven and the earthly dwelling-place, the mid-air.
From the base of the earth, Bṛhaspati, the sovereign lord among the gods, has reached the summit of his birth. When the bright day was born from the light, then may the inspired singers shine forth.
Now indeed Kāvya stirs that ancient majesty of the great god; he was born together with many, having slept in the loosened eastern half.

He who with reverence shall approach Atharvan, the father, the kinsman of the gods, Bṛhaspati—may he be like you, the progenitor of all, the wise one, the self-dependent god who cannot be deceived. He who bestows life and bestows strength, whose command all obey, whose command the gods obey; he who rules over his bipeds and his quadrupeds—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
He who by his majesty became the sole king of the breathing and blinking world; whose shadow is immortality and whose [other] shadow is death—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
Upon whom the two shouting worlds depend, upon whom the two trembling worlds call out in fear; whose path is that which measures out the mid-air—what god shall we worship with our oblation?
He to whom belong the vast sky and the great earth, to whom belongs that wide intermediate space; he by whose majesty yonder sun is spread abroad—what god shall we worship with our oblation?
He whose greatness is all the snowy mountains, and of whom they say the ocean is the flow; whose arms are these quarters of space—what god shall we worship with our oblation?

In the beginning, the waters bore all things, conceiving the embryo, immortal and knowing the Eternal Law (*ṛta*). Upon those divine waters the God was established. To what God shall we offer worship with our oblation?

In the beginning, the Golden Embryo (*hiraṇyagarbha*) came into being; once born, he was the sole Lord of all that exists. He sustained the earth and the heavens. To what God shall we offer worship with our oblation? The waters, giving birth to their calf, brought forth the embryo in the beginning. And as it was being born, its membrane was golden. To what God shall we offer worship with our oblation?
Three have stepped forth from here: the tiger, the man, and the wolf. For the rivers flow separately; separately stands the divine tree of the forest; separately shall the enemies bow down.

Let the wolf go by a distant path, and let the thief likewise go by the farthest way. Let the toothed rope go beyond; let the malevolent one flee far away. O tiger, we crush both your eyes and your mouth, and then all twenty of your claws.
We crush first the tusked tiger; then the thief, then the serpent, then the sorcerer, and then the wolf.
Whoever comes today as a thief departs ground to pieces. May he go by the ruin of his own paths; may Indra slay him with his thunderbolt.
Blasted are the teeth of the beast, and its ribs are shattered. Let the leather thong be broken for you, and let the hare-beast fall low.
That which is restraint is not separation; that which is separation is not restraint. Born of Indra, born of Soma, you are the Atharvanic [charm] that rends the tiger.
You whom the Gandharva dug for Varuṇa, whose brilliance is immortal— that very herb we now dig up, the stimulator of the male organ.

Up has Dawn risen; up has Sūrya risen; up has this word of mine arisen. Let Prajāpati, the bull, spring upward with vigorous strength, so that as you grow, you may consume [the seed] like something heated. From that, let this herb make you even more vigorous.
Upward now the vigor of the plants, the essences of the bulls—O Indra, bestow upon this manly one the virility of heroes, O Lord of the body!

You are the first-born sap of the waters and likewise of the lords of the forest; you are the brother of Soma, and you are the virile power of the arrow. Today, O Agni; today, O Savitṛ; today, O Goddess Sarasvatī; today, O Brahmaṇaspati, draw taut his bowstring like a bow!

I stretch out your fetters like a bowstring upon a bow; stride forth like a deer toward a red bull, never growing weary. Whatever vital strengths belong to the horse, the mule, the goat, and the ram, and those of the bull—bestow them all upon this man who has control over his body.
The bull with a thousand horns who rose up from the ocean—with that powerful one, we lull the people to sleep.
The wind does not blow across the earth, nor does anyone see anything; cause all women and dogs to sleep, O Indra’s companion, as you wander.
Women who lie on couches, women who lie on beds, women who ride in litters, and those women who possess auspicious fragrances—all of them we cause to sleep.
Moving, moving, I have seized it; I have seized sight and breath. I have seized all the limbs at the deep end of the nights.
Whoever sits, whoever moves, and whoever looks about while standing—of them we close the eyes, just as this dwelling house is closed.
Let the mother sleep, let the father sleep, let the dog sleep, let the lord of the household sleep. Let her kinsmen sleep; let these people around her sleep.
By means of the power of sleep, put all people to sleep! Put others to sleep until the sun rises; let me remain awake until the dawn. Like Indra, may I be unharmed and undecaying.

The Brāhmaṇa was born first, ten-headed and ten-mouthed; he drank the Soma first and rendered the poison powerless. As far as heaven and earth extend in breadth, as far as the seven rivers have spread out—from here I have uttered that speech which destroys poison.

The fair-winged Garuḍa first swallowed you, O poison. You did not intoxicate him, nor did you wound him; rather, you became food for him—even for him who placed you upon his five-fingered bow from its very curve. From the shaft of the Apaskambha, I have uttered the poison away. From the shaft, I have uttered the poison away; from the ointment and from the feather-case; from the butt, the horn, and the barb, I have uttered the poison away. From the shaft, I have uttered the poison away; from the ointment and from the feather-case; from the butt, the horn, and the barb, I have uttered the poison away.
Painless is your shaft, O poison; painless, too, is your venom. And painless is the bow of the painless tree; painless, O painless one, is yours.

Those who crushed it, those who chewed it, those who swallowed it, and those who released it—all of them have been rendered impotent; the mountain, the source of the poison, has been made impotent. Impotent are your diggers; you yourself, O herb, are impotent. Impotent is that mountain and peak from which this poison was born.
This warding-off power resides in Varaṇāvati; there the nectar of immortality was poured. With that, I ward off your poison.
Tasteless is the poison of the east, tasteless is that of the north; and this poison of the lower region is rendered powerless by the *karambha* porridge.
Having made the *karambha*, [I ward off] the Tiryam, Pībaspāka, and Udārathi. O you of evil teeth, he whom you have indeed devoured out of hunger shall not cause you harm.
We cause your intoxication, O Intoxicating One, to fall like an arrow; we steady you with our word as you rush forward like a boiling cauldron.

Like a village surrounded [by a wall], we establish you with our word. Stand firm like a tree on its base; do not break, even though you are dug up by a spade. They have purchased you with winnowing-baskets, with spears, and with skins. You are bought, O herb; do not break, even though you are dug up by a spade. May those who were the first to perform these deeds for you—those who were unattainable—do no harm to our heroes here. I place this before you.

Having become manifest among beings, he bestows milk; he has become the sovereign lord of all beings. Death performs his *rājasūya* sacrifice; may that King grant his approval for this. Go forward, do not be averse;
you are fierce, wise, and the slayer of rivals. Ascend, O increaser of friends; the gods have spoken in favor of you.

All have honored him as he stood firm; clothed in splendor, he moves with his own radiance. That is the great name of the Bull, the Asura; assuming all forms, he has taken his stand among the immortals.
O tiger, stride upon the tiger-skin; traverse the great quarters. Let all the people desire you, and the celestial waters rich in milk.
Those celestial waters that rejoice with their milk in the intermediate space or upon the earth—with the splendor of all those waters, I sprinkle you.
The celestial waters, rich in milk, have sprinkled you with splendor, so that you may be a multiplier of friends; even so shall Savitṛ make you.

Embracing the tiger, they urge on the lion for great good fortune; like the well-formed ones [urging] the sea, they groom the leopard standing within the waters. Come, O living one! You are the protector of the mountain, the axle-pin of the earth. Given by all the gods, you are a fence for the sake of life. You are the protection of men, the protection of cattle; you stand as the protection for horses and swift steeds.
And you, O ointment, are a protection on all sides, a destroyer of demons. You know the way to immortality, and you are the sustenance for life, as well as the yellow remedy.

O ointment, as you glide over limb after limb, joint after joint, you drive away the wasting disease like a fierce warrior stationed in the midst [of the fray]. Neither a curse, nor sorcery, nor consuming fever reaches him; neither does the *viṣkandha* afflict the one who wears you, O ointment.
From evil incantations, from bad dreams, from misdeeds, and from impurity; from the fierce eye of the malevolent—protect us from that, O ointment!

Knowing this, O ointment, I shall speak the truth and not falsehood: may I win back the horse, the cow, and my own self, O man! Fever, consumption, and the serpent—these three are the slaves of the ointment. The highest of mountains, named Trikakuḍ, is your father.

The ointment born of the three-peaked mountain, produced from the Himavat, which crushes all sorcerers and all female sorceresses—whether you are called Traikakuda or whether you are called Yāmana, both your names are auspicious; by them, O Ointment, protect us!
Born from the wind, from the atmosphere, from lightning, and from light—may that conch-shell born of gold, the *kṛśana* gem, protect us from distress.
You who were born foremost from the luminous realms, from the ocean—having struck down the *rakṣas* demons and the devourers with the conch-shell, may we overcome them.
With the conch-shell, [we ward off] sickness and lack of vision; with the conch-shell, the *sadānvās*. May the conch-shell, the universal healer, the *kṛśana* gem, protect us from distress.
Born in heaven, born from the ocean, brought forth from the river—may that conch-shell born of gold, the jewel that prolongs our life, protect us.

Born from the ocean, the jewel born from Vṛtra, the maker of light—he shall protect us on all sides from the weapons of gods and asuras. You are the one among golden things; you were born from Soma. You are beautiful to behold in the chariot; you are radiant in the quiver. May he extend our lifespans.

The seed of the gods became gold; it moves endowed with life within the waters. That I bind upon you for long life, for luster, for strength, for longevity lasting a hundred autumns. May the descendant of Kṛśanu protect you.
The ox has supported the earth and the sky; the ox has supported the wide mid-air. The ox has supported the six broad quarters; the ox has entered the entire world.
The ox is Indra; he looks out upon all creatures. The powerful one measures out the three paths. Milking the past and the future, he carries out all the ordinances of the gods.
Indra, once born among men, moves as the heated cauldron, glowing intensely. He who knows the ox and would not eat of it shall fare like one with good offspring in a desert.

The ox yields milk in the world of the righteous; Pavamāna causes him to swell from the front. Parjanya is his streams, the Maruts his udder; sacrifice is his milk, and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is his milking.

He who rules over our sacrifice—the Lord of the Sacrifice—is neither the sacrifice itself, nor is his giver the master, nor is the receiver the master. Tell us of that Gharma which is all-conquering, all-sustaining, and the maker of all; which of the four-footed [beings] it is.

By that means by which the gods ascended to heaven, leaving behind the body at the navel of immortality—by that may we go to the world of the well-done, through the vow of the Gharma and through austerity, seeking glory.

Indra by his form, Agni by his vehicle, Prajāpati, Parameṣṭhin, and Virāj stepped upon Viśvānara; he stepped upon Vaiśvānara; he stepped upon the cow that does not fail (*anaduhi*). He made it firm; he held it steady.

This is the middle of the ox where this vehicle is placed. So much is its extent forward as is its extent backward when properly arranged. He who knows the milkings of the ox, the seven that follow one another, attains offspring and the world—so the Seven Seers know.
Treading upon exhaustion with his feet, drawing forth nourishment with his shanks, the ox and the plowman go toward the watery meadow through their toil.

Twelve indeed are these nights of the vow said to belong to Prajāpati; he who knows the sacred formulation (*brahman*) regarding them truly knows the vow of the ox. He yields milk in the evening, he yields milk in the morning, and he yields milk throughout the midday. We know those milkings of his that come together, which follow one after another.
You are the healer; you are the healer of the broken bone. Heal this, O Arundhatī!

Whatever of yours is injured, whatever is shattered, and whatever of yours is crushed within your body—may Dhātṛ restore that with auspiciousness, joint by joint. May your marrow be united with marrow, and may your joint be joined with joint. May what is torn away from your flesh be healed, and may your bone grow back together.
Let the marrow be joined with the marrow; let the skin grow together with the skin. Let your blood grow upon the bone; let the flesh grow together with the flesh.
Join the hair with the hair; join the skin with the skin. Let your blood rise up to the bone; mend what is broken, O herb!
Arise, go forth, run forward! The chariot has good wheels, good fellies, and a good nave; stand firm upon it, upright.

If the spear, having fallen, has pierced him, or if the hurled stone has struck him down—just as a craftsman sets together the parts of a chariot, joint by joint, O Rbhus, so do you mend him. O Gods, you raise up again that which has been cast down; O Gods, you restore to life again the man who has become like a stone.
These two winds blow from the ocean and from afar: may one breathe strength upon you, and may the other blow away whatever is disease.
O Vāta, blow hither the medicine; O Vāta, blow away whatever malady there is, for you, the all-healing one, move as the messenger of the gods.

May the gods protect this man; may the hosts of Maruts protect him; may all beings protect him, so that he may be free from affliction. I have come to you with healing remedies and with means for safety. I have brought you powerful vigor; I drive away your wasting disease. This hand of mine is blessed; this hand of mine is even more blessed. This hand of mine possesses all medicines; this is the one whose touch is auspicious.
With these two hands, which have ten branches, and with the tongue, the forerunner of speech—with those two hands that cause no harm, we touch you.

For the Unborn was born from the heat (śoka) of Agni; he beheld his progenitor in the beginning. By him the gods attained godhood in the beginning; by him the worthy ones ascended to the heights. Step forth with Agni toward the firmament, bearing the fire-pan (ukhā) in your hands. Having gone to the back of heaven, to the light, unite yourselves with the gods.

From the back of the earth I have ascended to the intermediate space; from the intermediate space I have ascended to heaven. From the back of the firmament, from heaven, I have gone to the light of *svar*. Those going to *svar* do not look back; they ascend to heaven and the two worlds (*rodasī*), they who, being well-knowing, have spread the sacrifice that flows in every direction. O Agni, go forward as the first among the deities, the eye of gods and of men. Desiring to sacrifice, in harmony with the Bhr̥gus, may the sacrificers go safely to *svar*.
I purify the unborn one with milk and ghee—the divine, well-winged, milk-drinking, vast one. Through him may we go to the world of the well-done, ascending to the light, toward the highest firmament.
With five fingers and a ladle, draw out this five-fold rice-oblation. Place the head of the unborn one in the eastern direction; place his right side in the southern direction.

Place his buttock in the western direction; place his northern flank in the northern direction. Place the back of the Unborn One in the upward direction; place his belly in the fixed direction, and his middle in the midst of the intermediate space.

The goat is cooked; clothe it with its cooked skin, it which is gathered with all its limbs and possesses every form. Arise from here toward the highest firmament; stand firm in the quarters with your four feet.
Let the cloud-bearing intermediate directions rise up together; let the clouds driven by the wind come together. May the lowing waters of the great bellowing, cloud-borne bull satisfy the earth.

May the powerful, bounteous ones look upon us; may the essences of the waters unite with the plants. May the outpourings of rain glorify the earth; may plants of every form spring forth separately. Look upon the singing clouds; let the torrents of water surge forth separately. May the outpourings of rain glorify the earth; may plants of every form spring forth separately.
O Parjanya, let the Marut hosts, sounding with their roar, sing unto you separately. Let the streams of the raining one pour down upon the earth.
Rise up from the ocean, O Maruts! Let the brilliant light cause the cloud to fly upward. May the lowing waters satisfy the earth, like the bellowing of a great, roaring, thundering bull.
Roar toward us, thunder, and strike the ocean; O Parjanya, drench the earth with milk. Let the abundant rain released by you come forth; let the swift-moving, thirsty one go to his rest.
May the bounteous ones protect you, as well as the springs and the non-venomous serpents. Set in motion by the Maruts, may the clouds rain down upon the earth.
Let every quarter flash with lightning; let the winds blow from every direction. Let the clouds, driven forth by the Maruts, gather over the earth.
May the waters, the lightning, the cloud, and the rain protect you together, O bounteous ones—both the springs and the serpents. Let the clouds, driven forth by the Maruts, flow over the earth.
May Agni of the waters, in harmony with his own bodies, he who has become the lord of plants—he, Jātavedas, may he win rain for us: the breath of life and immortality from heaven for all creatures.

Prajāpati, driving forth the waters from the ocean and the flood, causes the sea to swell. May the seed of the potent horse swell; come hither, O steed, with this thundering roar. Pouring out the waters, our father the Asura, let the gargling sounds resound; release the downward-flowing waters, O Varuṇa. Let the frogs with spotted arms croak along the pools—those who, like Brahmins observing a vow, lay dormant for a year. Stirred by Parjanya, the frogs have uttered their voice.
Speak out, O female frog; speak toward the rain, O *tāduri*. Swim in the middle of the lake, having spread out your four feet.
*Khaṇva khā3i khaima khā3i*—in the middle, O *tāduri*. Win the rain, O fathers; seek the mind of the Maruts.

Draw up the great reservoir; pour it forth. Let there be lightning, let the wind blow. Let the rain-clouds, released in many ways, extend the sacrifice; let the plants be full of joy. Their mighty overseer beholds them as if from close at hand. He who thinks he moves in secret while walking—O Gods, they know all this.
Whether one stands, walks, or deceives; whether one moves in hiding or goes on a journey; when two sit together and whisper a counsel, King Varuṇa, the third, knows it.
And this earth belongs to King Varuṇa, and yonder vast sky with its distant ends; even the two oceans are the belly of Varuṇa, and he is hidden even in this small amount of water.
Even he who should glide beyond the sky to the farthest distance shall not be released from King Varuṇa. His spies move forth from heaven; with their thousand eyes, they look out across this earth.
King Varuṇa beholds all that which is between the two worlds and that which is beyond. He has counted the very blinks of men; he fixes them down like a gambler laying out the dice.
Those snares of yours, O Varuṇa, seven times seven, which stand spread out in three ways, fierce—let them all cut the one who speaks untruth, but let them release him who speaks the truth.

Bind him with a hundred snares, O Varuṇa! Let him who speaks untruth not escape you, O Beholder of Men! Let this wretch remain with his belly hanging down, like a leather bag being cut away. That Varuṇa who belongs to our own people, that Varuṇa who belongs to strangers, that Varuṇa who is to be addressed at home, that Varuṇa who is to be addressed abroad; that Varuṇa who is divine, and that Varuṇa who is human—with all those snares of yours, I bind you, O [Name], son of [Name] and descendant of [Name]. I point them all out to you.
We take hold of you, the sovereign of healing remedies, for the sake of victory. O herb, you have performed a feat of a thousandfold power for the sake of all.
You who conquer truly, who ward off curses, who are triumphant, and who returns again—I have summoned all the herbs; may they carry us across from here.
She who cursed with a curse, she who laid upon [him] evil and folly, she who undertook to seize the offspring for the sake of stealing the essence—let her devour her own child.

With that *kṛtyā* which they fashioned for you in an unbaked vessel, which they fashioned in blue-and-red [clay], the *kṛtyā* which they fashioned in raw flesh—with that *kṛtyā* do thou slay the one by whom the *kṛtyā* was made.
Bad dreams, a miserable life, demons, the monstrous, and all ill-named, evil-speaking witches—we cause them to perish away from us.

Hunger as Māra, thirst as Māra, childlessness, and lack of offspring—O Apāmārga, by means of you we wipe all that away. Thirst as Māra, hunger as Māra, and furthermore, defeat at dice—O Apāmārga, by means of you we wipe all that away. Apāmārga is the one sole ruler among all plants; with it we wipe away what has settled upon you, so that you may go about free from disease.
The light is equal to the sun; day and night are alike. I make this true for my protection: let the sorceresses be powerless.

O Gods, may he who, having fashioned a magical spell (*kṛtyā*), carries it to the house of one who knows not, fall headlong upon him like a calf to its mother. He who, having committed evil at home, seeks to slay another with it—when that [spell] is burnt up, may many stones crackle loudly over it.

O thou of a thousand abodes, with thy shadow, strike down the Viśikhās and the Vigrīvās. For him who has performed a *kṛtyā* against thee, O lover of the beloved, take away his dear one. By means of this herb, I have rendered all *kṛtyās* powerless—those which they have wrought in the field, those in the cattle, or those in thy men.
He who performed it was unable to complete it; he has shattered his foot and his toe. May he do us good, while he brings torment upon himself.
May the Apāmārga plant wipe away the *kṣetriya* disease and whatever curse there is; may it drive away the sorceresses and all the *arāyī* demons.

Having wiped away the sorcerers and all the *arāyī* demons—O Apāmārga, through you we wipe away all that. You are the maker of enmity, and you are the maker of kinship; like a reed in the rainy season, cut down the offspring of those who perform magic spells.
You have been consecrated by the Brahmin Kaṇva Nārṣada. You advance like a brilliant army; there is no fear where you arrive, O Herb.
You go at the head of the plants, illuminating them as if with light. You are the protector of the simple-minded, and you are the slayer of the Rākṣasa.
When the gods formerly drove away the Asuras with you, from that time forth, O Herb, you were born as Apāmārga.
Splitting into a hundred branches, your father is named Vibhindu; split him apart who assails us from the west.
That which arose from the non-existent earth—that vast expanse—truly smokes it out from there; let it strike back at the doer.
For you have come forth facing us, you whose fruit is directed toward us. Ward off from me all curses; keep the deadly weapon far away.
Protect me with a hundredfold, guard me with a thousandfold! O Indra, Lord of plants, may the fierce one bestow vigor upon you.
She looks hither, she looks thither, she looks afar; she looks upon heaven, the mid-air, and the earth—she, the Goddess, beholds all that.

The three heavens, the three earths, and these six directions separately—through you, O divine herb, may I behold all beings. You are indeed the pupil of that divine, well-winged bird. You have ascended the earth like a weary bride mounting her vehicle. The thousand-eyed god placed you in my right hand; through you, I see everything, both the Śūdra and the Ārya.

Reveal your forms; do not hide yourself away. O thousand-eyed one, look out for the *kimīdin*s! Show me the sorcerers (*yātudhāna*), show me the female sorcerers (*yātudhānī*); show me all the *piśāca*s—thus do I grasp you, O herb!
You are the eye of Kaśyapa and of the four-eyed bitch. Do not let the *piśāca* pass you by, like the sun gliding through the rift in the clouds.
I have seized the sorcerer and the Kimīdin from every side; by means of that, I see everything—both the Śūdra and the Ārya.
Show that piśāca who flies through the intermediate space, who glides across the sky, and who considers the earth his refuge.
The cows have come and performed a blessing; let them sit in the cow-pen and find delight with us. May they be here, prolific and many-colored, yielding their milk for Indra through many dawns.

Indra bestows gifts upon the sacrificer and the singer; he gives them up and does not steal back what is his own. Increasing his wealth ever more and more, he establishes the one devoted to the gods upon his unbroken field.

They are not lost; no thief can harm them; no enemy’s distress dares to attack them. With those cows by which one worships the gods and gives gifts, the master of the herd dwells together with them for a long time. No dust-raising horse overtakes them, nor do they ever go toward a place of slaughter. Following the wide-striding, fearless man, the cows of that mortal sacrificer roam about.

Cows are fortune; cows Indra desires for me; cows are the first draught of Soma. These cows that exist, O people—they are Indra. With my heart and with my mind, I desire Indra. O cows, you make even the emaciated fat; you make even the unlovely beautiful to look upon. You make the house auspicious, O you of auspicious speech; your great vitality is proclaimed in the assemblies.

May you be rich in offspring, grazing on lush pasture, radiant, and drinking pure waters at a good watering-place. Let no thief nor any who speaks evil have power over you; may the missile of Rudra pass you by.

O Indra, make this my *kṣatriya* prosper; make him the sole bull among the people. Strike down all his enemies and subject them to him. Grant him preeminence over those who come after; include him in the village, in horses, and in cattle. Exclude from these whomsoever is his enemy. Let him be the height of all lordships, O Indra, and let him be king; subject every foe to him. Let him be the master of wealth among riches; let him be the lord of the people and their king. O Indra, bestow great splendors upon him, and render his enemy devoid of splendor.

For him may Heaven and Earth milk forth abundant wealth, like two milch-cows yielding the *gharma* oblation. May this king become dear to Indra, dear to the cows, dear to the plants, and dear to the cattle.
I yoke for you Indra, the victorious one, by whom men conquer and are never defeated. May he make you the sole bull among the people and the highest among kings of men.

You shall be superior; your rivals, O King, and whoever are your adversaries, shall be inferior. As the sole bull with Indra as your ally, having conquered, bring back the possessions of those who act as enemies.

With the face of a lion, devour all the tribes; with the face of a tiger, drive away our enemies. O Indra, sole bull and our friend, having conquered, seize the possessions of those who act as foes. I meditate upon Agni, the first, the wise one, whom the people of the five tribes kindle in many ways. Entering into every tribe, we implore him: may he deliver us from distress. Just as you carry the oblation, O Jātavedas, and just as you arrange the sacrifice with full knowledge, so bring to us the favor of the gods; may he deliver us from distress.

I praise Agni, who is most effective in every journey, the best performer of every rite, the one who shares in the portion, the slayer of demons, the increaser of sacrifice, and the one invoked with clarified butter;
may he deliver us from distress. We invoke the well-born Jātavedas, the pervasive Vaiśvānara Agni, the bearer of oblations; may he deliver us from distress.

By which the seers displayed their power, by which they overcame the magic powers of the Asuras; with that Agni by which Indra conquered the Paṇis—may he deliver us from distress. By which the gods discovered immortality, by which they made the plants full of sweetness; with which the gods brought forth the light of heaven—may he deliver us from distress. In whose direction all this shines, whatever has been born and whatever is yet to be born, exclusively his; I praise Agni, and in my need I call upon him repeatedly—may he deliver us from distress.

We meditate upon Indra; ever indeed do we meditate upon him. These hymns have come to me, [hymns] of the slayer of Vṛtra. May he who comes to the invocation of the donor who performs good deeds deliver us from distress.

He who has mighty arms among the fierce ones, who has swiftly shattered the strength of the Dānavas, by whom the rivers were won and by whom the cattle—may he deliver us from distress. He who is the bull, the protector of men, the finder of light, for whom the pressing-stones proclaim his manly power, whose sacrifice is most exhilarating with its seven priests—may he deliver us from distress.

He for whom the barren cows, the bulls, and the oxen are prepared, for whom the sacrificial posts are set up by the knower of heaven; he for whom the bright Soma flows, purified as a sacred prayer—may he deliver us from distress.
He whose favor the Soma-pressers desire, whom they invoke as the wielder of the arrow in the quest for cattle; in whom the hymn rests, in whom the vital power resides—may he deliver us from distress.
He who was born first for the performance of deeds, whose heroic might was recognized as the foremost; by whom the raised thunderbolt assailed the serpent—may he deliver us from distress.

He who leads from battle to combat, the master who brings together both kinds of prosperity—I praise Indra, seeking protection I call upon him; may he deliver us from distress. We meditate upon the ordinances of Vāyu and Savitṛ, you two who enter into embodied beings and who guard them, you who have become the encompassers of the universe; may you two deliver us from distress.
Whose breadth is measured by the earthly realms, by whom the mid-air and the firmament are fixed, and whom no one has ever reached even as far as the horizon—may you two deliver us from distress.
In your vow the people settle; when you have risen, O wondrously radiant one, they stir forth. You two, Vāyu and Savitṛ, protect all beings; as such, deliver us from distress.
Drive away from here, O Vāyu and Savitṛ, evil-doing; drive away the demons and the *śimidā* disease. For you two endow [all things] with vigor and with strength; as such, deliver us from distress.
May Savitṛ and Vāyu send forth for me wealth, nourishment, and personal skill that is most auspicious. Bestow upon us here great freedom from disease; as such, deliver us from distress.

O Savitṛ and Vāyu, you two grant us favor for our aid; you exhilarate the great and intoxicating [Soma]. Turn hither and bestow upon us the downward flow of wealth; may those two release us from distress. May the most excellent blessings rest upon the dwelling place of the two gods. I praise the god Savitṛ and Vāyu; may those two release us from distress. I honor you two, O Heaven and Earth, the bountiful and harmonious ones, who have spread yourselves through immeasurable leagues. For you have become the foundation of all treasures; may you two release us from distress.
For you two have become the foundations of the Vasus, O goddesses, exalted, fortunate, and far-reaching. O Heaven and Earth, be gracious to me; may you two release us from distress.
I invoke the two who are free from heat, well-heated, vast, profound, and worthy of homage by the seers. O Heaven and Earth, be gracious to me; may you two release us from distress.
You who bear immortality, you who bear the oblations, you who bear the rivers and the human beings—O Heaven and Earth, be gracious to me; may you two release us from distress.
O Heaven and Earth, you who sustain the rays of light, you who support the lords of the forest, and within whom all beings dwell—be gracious to me; deliver us from distress.

You who satisfy [all] with honey and with clarified butter, without whom nothing at all can be accomplished—be gracious to me; deliver us from distress. Whatever burns me here, whether it was done by human agency or by fate—I praise Heaven and Earth, seeking protection; I call upon you repeatedly; deliver us from distress.

I call to mind the Maruts; may they speak for me and protect this strength in the contest for booty. Like swift and well-governed horses, I have invoked them for aid; may they deliver us from distress.
They who always open the inexhaustible spring and pour their essence into the plants—I place those Maruts, whose mother is Pṛśni, before me;

may they deliver us from distress. O sages, you who send forth the milk of the cows, the sap of the plants, and the speed of the horses—may the Maruts be powerful for us and gracious; may they deliver us from distress.
They carry the waters from the ocean up to heaven; they pour them down from heaven upon the earth. May those Maruts who move about as lords through the waters release us from distress.

Those who satisfy [the world] with sweet wine, those who with clarified butter, or those who mix strength with fat—may those Maruts who, as lords through the waters, cause rain to fall, release us from distress.

O Maruts, if this has been done by us through the Marut-host, or if, O Gods, it has been done by us through the divine power, such as it is—O Vasus, you alone have the power to remedy it; may they release us from distress.

Sharp is their face, renowned and powerful is the host of Maruts, fierce in battles. Seeking protection, I praise the Maruts; I call upon them repeatedly: may they release us from distress. I honor you two, Śarva and Bhava; take heed of this, you by whose command all that shines forth here exists. You who rule over these bipeds and these quadrupeds—release us from distress. Those whom one fears whether near or even far away, those who are known as the swiftest among the wielders of arrows, you who rule over these bipeds and these quadrupeds—release us from distress.

I invoke here the two thousand-eyed slayers of Vṛtra; praising the two fierce ones who range over distant pastures, I approach them. You two who rule over his bipeds and his quadrupeds—deliver us from distress!
You two who seized many things together in the beginning and have spread your brilliance among the people—you who rule over his bipeds and his quadrupeds—deliver us from distress!
From the blow of whom no one escapes, neither among the gods nor among men—you who rule over his bipeds and his quadrupeds—deliver us from distress!

O fierce ones, hurl your thunderbolt upon that sorcerer who performs witchcraft, the root-destroyer, the Yātudhāna! O you two who have power over his bipeds and his quadrupeds, deliver us from distress! Speak for us, O fierce ones, in the battles; strike with your thunderbolt against the Kimīdin! I praise Bhava and Śarva, seeking protection I cry out to them: deliver us from distress! I acknowledge you, Mitra and Varuṇa, increasers of Truth, who are of one mind and who drive away the deceitful; you protect the truthful man in battles: deliver us from distress!

O you two who are conscious, you who drive away those who act with malice—O truthful ones, you aid the one who possesses truth in battles; O you two who look upon men, you who go to the brown juice, deliver us from distress.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, you who aid Aṅgiras, Agastya, Jamadagni, and Atri; you who aid Kaśyapa and Vasiṣṭha, deliver us from distress. O Mitra and Varuṇa, you who aid Śyāvāśva, Vādhryaśva, Purumīḍha, and Atri; you who aid Vimada and Saptavadhri, deliver us from distress.

O Varuṇa and Mitra, you who protect Bharadvāja, you who protect Gaviṣṭhira, Viśvāmitra, and Kutsa; you who protect Kakṣīvat and Kaṇva—may those two deliver us from distress. O Mitra and Varuṇa, you who protect Medhātithi, you who protect Triśoka and Uśanas Kāvya; you who protect Gotama and Mudgala—may those two deliver us from distress.

Whose chariot, with its straight reins and true path, pursues and strikes down him who acts deceptively—I praise Mitra and Varuṇa; seeking protection, I cry out to them: may they two deliver us from distress. I move with the Rudras and the Vasus; I am with the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas. I sustain both Mitra and Varuṇa; I [sustain] Indra and Agni, and I both Aśvins.

I am the sovereign ruler, the gatherer of treasures, the conscious one, the first among those worthy of sacrifice. The gods have distributed me in many places, establishing me in many stations and causing me to enter into many forms.
I myself declare this, which is pleasing to both gods and men: whomsoever I desire, him I make fierce; him I make a Brahman, him a seer, him a man of great wisdom.
He eats the food through me who sees, who breathes, and who hears what is spoken; they dwell near me without perceiving it. Listen, O famous one! This pure truth I declare to you.
I bend the bow for Rudra, so that his arrow may strike the hater of sacred knowledge; I stir up conflict among the people; I have entered heaven and earth.
I bear the crushing Soma, and I bear Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, and Bhaga. I bestow riches upon the one who offers oblations, providing excellent protection for the sacrificer who presses the juice.

I bring forth the Father upon the summit of this world; my source is within the waters, in the midst of the ocean. From there I spread out through all beings, and with my highest point I touch even yonder sky.

I alone blow forth like the wind, setting all worlds in motion; beyond the sky and beyond this earth, I have become so vast through my majesty. O Manyu, together with you on the same chariot, may the Maruts—exulting, thrilled, and possessing sharp-pointed arrows—come forward, sharpening their weapons, these men who take the form of Agni.
Like Agni, O Manyu, blazing with splendor, be our victorious leader when invoked; having slain the enemies, distribute their wealth, measuring out your power and driving away the adversaries.

Overpower the adversary, O Manyu; breaking, crushing, and utterly destroying, go forth against the enemies! Your fierce array has indeed been irresistible; as a subduer, you shall bring them under your control, O Sole-Born One.
You alone are the one praised by many; sharpen every tribe for battle! With you as our ally, O Unconquered Splendor, we raise a brilliant shout for victory.
Like Indra, the victor who speaks no falsehood, O Manyu, be our sovereign protector here. We celebrate your beloved name, O Conqueror; we know that source from which you have arisen.

By your inherent power, O thunderbolt-wielder, O arrow, you possess supreme conquering strength, being ever victorious. O Manyu, through your wisdom, be our ally in the fray for great wealth, O you who are invoked by many!
May Varuṇa and Manyu bestow upon us the combined wealth gathered from both sides. Let our enemies, harboring fear in their hearts, lie prostrate, utterly defeated.

O Manyu, wielder of the thunderbolt and arrow, you who nourish all-encompassing power and might; with you as our ally—powerful, created by strength, and full of force—may we overcome both the Dāsa and the Ārya foe.

Manyu is Indra; Manyu indeed was the god. Manyu is the Hotṛ, Varuṇa, and Jātavedas. The human tribes worship Manyu. O Manyu, come to us, united with our fervor (tapas). Advance, O Manyu, you who are stronger than the strong; with fervor as your ally, strike down the enemies. Slayer of foes, slayer of Vṛtra, and slayer of Dasyus, bring all treasures to us.

For you, O Manyu, possess overwhelming power; you are self-existent, a radiant force that overcomes adversaries. Belonging to all people, victorious, and more powerful—bestow strength upon us in battles.

Being a portion [of you], I have gone away from you, O wise one, by the will of you, the powerful. I, lacking resolve, have provoked you to anger, O Manyu; come to us as the giver of strength in our own person. I am here for you;
come toward us, O conqueror, all-bestowing one, facing us. O Manyu, wielder of the thunderbolt, turn toward us; let us two slay the Dasyus, and remember your kinship.
Come forward, be on our right side, and then let us two strike down many enemies. I offer you the foundation, the summit of the honeyed [soma]; let us both drink first in silence.
May our evil be burned away; O Agni, shine forth wealth upon us. May our evil be burned away.
For the sake of good fields, for the sake of a good path, and for the sake of riches, we sacrifice. May our evil be burned away.
When he is the most glorious among these, and our patrons are preeminent, may he burn away our evil.
When, O Agni, the wise patrons [approach] thee, may we be born through thee; may we ourselves [be born] through thee. May he burn away our evil.
When the rays of the powerful Agni go forth in all directions, may he burn away our evil with his light.

For you, O you who face in every direction, are the one who encompasses all from every side. Blazing away our evil, carry us across our enemies, O you who face in every direction, as if by a boat. Blazing away our evil, carry us across like a river by boat for our well-being. Blazing away our evil.
The *Brahman* is its head; the *Bṛhat* is its back; the *Vāmadevya* is the belly of this Odana. The meters are its wings; Truth is its mouth. Born from austerity, the sacrifice has spread itself out.
Boneless, purified by the wind, cleansed and bright, they go to the world of purity. Jātavedas does not burn their penis; in the heavenly world, there is much company of women for them.
Those who cook the spreading Odana—misfortune never comes near them. Yama sits [waiting]; he approaches the gods and rejoices with the Gandharvas and those worthy of Soma.
Yama does not steal away the seed of those who cook the *viṣṭārin* rice-porridge. Having become a charioteer, he travels on his chariot; having become a bird, he flies beyond the sky.

This is the most excellent of sacrifices, spread out wide; having cooked the *viṣṭārin*, it has entered heaven. The *āṇḍīka*, the *kumuda*, the *bisa*, the *śālūka*, the *śaphaka*, and the *mulālī*—may all these streams come to you, swelling with sweetness in the heavenly world. May lotus-ponds stand around you on every side.

Pools of ghee with honeyed banks, filled with wine for water, full of milk, water, and curds—may all these streams approach you, swelling with sweetness in the heavenly world; may lotus-pools stand around you on every side.

I give four jars, divided into four parts, full of milk, water, and curds. May all these streams approach you, swelling with sweetness in the heavenly world; may lotus-pools stand around you on every side.

I offer this rice-food among the Brāhmaṇas, which spreads abroad, conquers the world, and leads to heaven. May it not fail me, swelling with the *svadhā* offering; may it be for me a cow of all forms, yielding every desire. That rice-food which Prajāpati, the first-born of Cosmic Order (*ṛta*), cooked for the Brāhmaṇa through austerity—that which is the support of the worlds and their central navel—by means of that rice-food may I overcome death.

By that very rice-mess with which those who created living beings crossed beyond death—which they discovered through austerity and exertion, and which they cooked as the primordial Brahman for the sake of Brahman—by that rice-mess may I cross beyond death.
He who supported the earth that nourishes all, who filled the mid-air with moisture, and who propped up the sky aloft by his greatness—by means of that rice-offering, may I overcome death.

Since the months were fashioned from it as its thirty spokes, and the year was fashioned from it as its twelve spokes; since days and nights, though circling it, did not reach it—by means of that rice-offering, may we overcome death.

He who is the giver of life, who has become the possessor of life, for whom the worlds flow with clarified butter—he whose all directions are full of light—by means of that rice-offering, may I overcome death. From which cooked [food] immortality was produced, who became the sovereign lord of the Gāyatrī, in whom the Vedas of every form are deposited—by means of that rice-offering, may I overcome death.

O God, strike down the hater, the scorner of the gods; let those who are my rivals be far away from me. I cook this *brahmaudana* (the rice-mess of sacred power), which conquers all; may the gods listen to me as I have faith.

May Agni Vaiśvānara, the bull of true might, consume them. Whoever would harm us or seek to deceive us, and whoever would act with hostility toward us—whosoever seeks to deceive those who do not wish to deceive, and whosoever himself desires to deceive—I place him within the two jaws of Agni Vaiśvānara.
Those who seek him out in the house, or at the cry of opposition on the new moon night—those flesh-eaters and others who wish to harm, may I overcome them all with might.

With might I subdue the Piśācas; by my might I take away their wealth. I slay all those who plot evil against me; may my intention be fulfilled. Those gods who laugh with him, who measure their speed with the sun, and those who dwell in rivers and mountains—with those cattle may I find [him].
I am the scorcher of the Piśācas, like a tiger among cattle; seeing me, they find no way to escape, just as dogs do not find a way out when they see a lion.

I have no power over the Piśācas, nor over thieves, nor over forest-dwellers; therefore, the Piśācas perish in whatever village I enter. In whatever village I enter, by this my fierce might, the Piśācas perish and do not even conceive of evil.
Those who provoke me with their prattle, like gnats provoking an elephant—I consider them ill-disposed toward people, like those who sleep in small beds.

May Destruction seize him as a horse is caught by its halter—the wretch who rages against me; he shall not escape from the snare. By you, O Herb, the Atharvans first slew the Rākṣasas; by you Kaśyapa slew them, by you Kaṇva, and by you Agastya.
Through you, we drive away the Apsarases and the Gandharvas; O Ajashringi, drive away the Rakshasas and all [enemies] by your fragrance.

Let the Apsarases go to the river, the crossing of the waters, to Avaśvasa; to Gulgulu, Pīlā, Naladī, Auksagandhi, and Pramandanī. Go thither, O Apsarases; you have awakened. Where there are Aśvattha trees, Nyagrodhas, great trees, and crested ones; go thither, O Apsarases; you have awakened. Where your swings are green and white, and where the Āghātas and Karkaryas converse together; go thither, O Apsarases; you have awakened.
This one has come, the most potent among herbs and plants; may the *ajaśṛṅgī*, the *arāṭakī*, and the *tīkṣṇaśṛṅgī* cause [the flow] to gush forth.
I split the testicles even of the dancing Gandharva Śikhaṇḍin, the lord of Apsarases; I go [to him] as to his penis.
Terrible are Indra’s weapons; a hundred are his iron spears. With them, may he scatter the Gandharvas who consume the oblation and devour the lotus-stalks.
Terrible are Indra’s weapons; there are a hundred golden spears. With these, may he strike down the Gandharvas who consume the oblation and devour the lotuses.
Burn up the *avakā* plants, the consuming ones; make my own lights shine within the waters. O Herb, crush all the *piśācas* and overcome them!

One is like a dog, one is like a monkey, and the youth has hair on his whole body. Having become as pleasing to the sight as a lover, the *gandharva* haunts women. We drive him away from here by means of powerful sacred knowledge (*brahman*).
O Apsarases, you are indeed the wives; O *gandharvas*, you are the husbands. Run away, O immortals; do not consort with mortals!
I invoke here that Apsaras who pierces through, who conquers, who is skilled at playing, and who makes the stakes her winnings.

I invoke here that Apsaras who sifts and scatters, the skilled goddess of the game, who takes the stakes won at the throw. She who dances around, gathering what has been won from the stake—may she, desiring our winnings, secure the prize for us through her magic power. May she, rich in milk, come to us; may they not win this wealth from us.
I invoke here that Apsaras who delights in the dice, who bears both sorrow and anger—the joyful and exultant one.

Those who move along with the rays of the sun, or those who move along with the beams of light; he whose bull, rich in vigor, swiftly traverses all the worlds from afar while guarding them—may he come to this our oblation, delighting in it, together with the mid-air, O possessor of vigor!

Together with the mid-air, O possessor of vigor, protect the young female calf here, O vigorous one! These abundant drops are for you; come hither, O steed! This young female calf is yours; may your mind be directed here.

O possessor of vigor, together with the mid-air, protect the dappled calf here, O vigorous one! Here is the fodder, here is the stall; here we bind the calf. As we have mastery over you by name, Svāhā!
On the earth, [the people] bowed down to Agni, and he prospered. Just as they bowed down to Agni on the earth, so may they bow down in submission to me.

The earth is the cow; Agni is her calf. May she, with Agni as her calf, milk for me food, vigor, and my desire—firstly, long life, offspring, prosperity, and wealth. Svāhā! In the atmosphere they bowed down to Vāyu; he prospered. Just as in the atmosphere they bowed down to Vāyu, even so may all bow down in submission to me.
The atmosphere is the cow; [Vāyu] is her calf. May she, with Vāyu as her calf, milk for me food, vigor, and my desire—firstly, long life, offspring, prosperity, and wealth. Svāhā!
The celestial ones bowed down to the Āditya; he prospered. Just as the celestial ones bowed down to the Āditya, so may they bow down in submission to me.

The sky is the milch-cow; its calf is the Sun. May she, with the Sun as her calf, milk for me food, strength, and desire—first long life, then offspring, prosperity, and wealth. Svāhā! To the Moon in the quarters they bowed down; he prospered. Just as they bowed down to the Moon in the quarters, so may they bow down in submission to me.

The quarters are the milch-cows; of them, the moon is the calf. May they, with the moon as their calf, milk for me food, vigor, desire, life—first of all—progeny, nourishment, and wealth. Svāhā! Agni has entered into Agni; he is the son of the seers, the protector against curses. With salutation and reverence I offer to you; may I not, through error, miss the portion of the gods.
O Jātavedas, purified by the heart and by the mind, O God who knowest all ways, I offer this oblation into thy seven mouths; do thou graciously accept the offering.

O Jātavedas, those who offer oblations from the east and who seek to harm us from the eastern quarter—having encountered Agni, let them be turned back and distressed; with this *pratisara* (protective amulet), I strike them down.

Those who offer oblations from the south, O Jātavedas, and who attack us from the southern quarter—having encountered Yama, may they turn back and tremble; with this counter-spell, I strike them down.

O Jātavedas, those who offer oblations from behind and who attack us from the western quarter—having encountered Varuṇa, may they be turned back and distressed; with this *pratisara* (protective amulet), I strike them down facing westward.

O Jātavedas, those who offer from the north and who assail us from the northern quarter—having encountered Soma, let them turn back and tremble; with this *pratisara* (protective amulet), I strike them down facing me.

O Jātavedas, those who offer oblations from below and those who attack us from the northern direction—having reached the earth, may they be struck down and distressed; facing westward, I strike them back with this protective amulet.

O Jātavedas, those who offer oblations from the intermediate space, and those who attack us from the cross-quarter directions—having encountered Vāyu, may they be turned back and distressed; with this *pratisara* (protective amulet), I strike them down facing us.

O Jātavedas, those who offer from above and those who assail us from the upward direction—having encountered the Sun, may they be turned back and distressed; with this *pratisara* (protective amulet), I strike them down facing me.

Those who from the cardinal and intermediate directions offer [oblations] against us, O Jātavedas, from all quarters—they who seek to harm us—let them be turned back and shaken by the power of the sacred word (brahman). Facing them with this protective amulet, I strike them down.

Distinct is the mantra which has occupied its source, increasing with immortal life, well-born; he of unassailable life, radiant like the days, Trita, the supporter, has upheld the three. He who, as the first, established the cosmic laws, from him you manifest many forms; desiring to bestow, the first entered the womb—he who perceived the word before it was uttered.
He who surrendered his body for your sake, for him pure gold flowed according to his own [will]. Herein they two establish immortal names; let the people bring forth garments for us.

When these [rays] have gone further forth toward the ancient [seat], occupying every dwelling that is ageless; O Seer, you two who lick the mother of the dry [grass], do you two urge on the yoke-mate of the kin. And so, O broad-striding one, I, the seer, offer this great homage to you with my poetic wisdom: when you two, moving together, advance toward the earth, there you have established the two great barriers, and they grow strong.

The seers have fashioned seven boundaries; of these, the distressed man may pass only one. He stands as the pillar of Āyu in the nest of the highest, at the parting of the paths, upon the foundations.

And indeed, with immortal life, I go forth performing my duty; as the vital breath, I am the soul of the body, moving gracefully therein. Or rather, the Mighty One bestows treasure, or he who grants the oblation accompanies it with strengthening power.

Or the son praises the father for his sovereignty; they have called upon the eldest boundary-setter for well-being. Now, O Varuṇa, let us behold those stations of yours; from your own ordinances, you create wondrous forms.

With half you fill [the world] with milk; with the other half, O unassailable one, you increase your vital strength. We have magnified the powerful Varuṇa, the helpful friend and son of Aditi. We have proclaimed for him these wondrous forms, which are praised by seers, to Heaven and Earth whose speech is truth.
That indeed was the eldest among all beings, from whom the fierce sacrifice of brilliant manly power arose. As soon as he is born, he overcomes his enemies, when all his helpers rejoice in him.

Increasing in might and possessing abundant strength, you, as an adversary, instill fear in the Dāsa. Both the silent and the vocal [enemies] have been won by you; they cry out together at your exhilarations.
They bestow much mental power upon you when these helpers become twice or thrice [in number]. Mix that which is sweeter than sweet with sweetness; fight well against that with honey through honey.

If indeed the sages now rejoice after you as you win the spoils in battle after battle, O mighty one, exert yourself with greater strength and steadfastness; let not the evil-minded Kaśoka-slayers deceive you.
Through you we prevail in battles, beholding many things worthy of combat. I urge on your weapons with my words; I sharpen your vital powers with my prayer (*brahman*).
You bestow that [strength] both upon the lower and the higher, in which house you have protected us with your aid. Establish the swift Mother; from there, set in motion many heroic deeds.

Praise him, the one of many paths, the preeminent, the most powerful, the Aptya among the Aptyas. He of abundant might displays his power through his strength; he shall overcome every rival of the earth.

May Bṛhaddiva offer these prayers as an exultant hymn for Indra, the foremost winner of light. As the self-ruling king, he governs the great stall of cattle; swift and fervent, he encompasses all like the ocean.
Thus has the great Bṛhaddiva Atharvan spoken: his own body is none other than Indra. The two stainless sisters, dwelling in the mother, impel him and strengthen him with their power.
O Agni, let there be splendor for me in our invocations; kindling you, may we nourish our bodies. Let the four quarters bow down to me; with you as our overseer, may we conquer the hostile armies.

O Agni, repelling the fury of our enemies, do you, as our protector, guard us on every side. Let those who seek to harm us go away headlong into the depths; let the resolve of those who wake against us perish at home.

May all the gods be present at my invocation—Indra, the Maruts, Viṣṇu, and Agni. May the wide expanse of the intermediate space be mine; may Vāta blow for this desire of mine. May they offer sacrifice for me, and may whatever offerings I have made be successful; may the intention of my mind be realized. May I not fall into any sin whatsoever; may all the gods protect me here.

May the gods bestow wealth upon me through sacrifice; may the blessing be mine, and mine the invocation of the gods. May the divine Hotṛ-priests grant us this; may we remain unharmed in body, blessed with brave sons.
O six divine expanses, make wide room for us; O all-gods, rejoice here. Let not overwhelming power find us, nor let ill-will find us; let no crooked, hateful thing find us.

O three goddesses, grant us great protection for our offspring, for our bodies, and for our prosperity. May we not be abandoned by our offspring nor by our bodies; O King Soma, may we not fall into the power of the enemy.

May the wide-striding buffalo grant us protection in this invocation, he who is much-invoked and rich in food. O Indra, Lord of the bay horses, be gracious toward our progeny; do not harm us, nor deliver us over.
May Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and the Lord of the world, the divine Savitṛ who overcomes adversaries, the Ādityas, the Rudras, and both Aśvins—may these gods protect the sacrificer from destruction.
May those who are our rivals depart from us; with Indra and Agni we drive them away. The Ādityas and Rudras have made us their high king, the one who touches the heights and the fierce observer.
From afar we call Indra hitherward—he who wins cattle, wins wealth, and wins horses. May he hear this sacrifice of ours at our invocation; O Lord of the bay steeds, be our friend.
You who were born among the mountains as the most powerful of plants—O Kuṣṭha, destroyer of *takman*, come here and destroy the *takman*!
Born on the mountain that produces beautiful birds, from the Himalayas, they come hither with riches; for they know well how to consume the fever-disease.
The Aśvattha tree, the abode of the gods, is in the third heaven from here. There the gods found Kuṣṭha, the manifestation of immortality.

A golden ship, with golden moorings, moved in the sky; there the gods found Kuṣṭha, the flower of immortality. Golden were the paths, golden the oars; the ships were golden by which they carried Kuṣṭha away.
O Kuṣṭha, bring this man of mine here; drive that [disease] out. Make him free from disease for me.
You are born from the gods; you are the established friend of Soma. As such, be gracious to this breath, to the diffused breath, and to my sight.
Born in the north from the Himalayas, you are led eastward to the people. There they have distributed the most excellent names for Kuṣṭha.
You are Kuṣṭha by name, the most excellent; your father is named the most excellent. Destroy every consumption and render the fever powerless.
Having struck away disease of the head, the affliction of the eyes, and the infirmity of the body—may Kuṣṭha drive all that out, together with divine virility.
Night is your mother, the sky is your father, and Aryaman is your grandfather. You are indeed named Silācī; you are the sister of the gods.
Whoever drinks you lives, for you protect that person. For you are the supporter of all beings and the one who brings them down [to rest].

Tree after tree you climb, like a maiden longing for a man; victorious, standing firm, you are indeed named "The Overcomer. Whatever has been done with a staff, whatever with an arrow, or whatever with the heat of a weapon—you are the remedy for that; as such, heal this man.
You emerge from the auspicious *plakṣa*, from the *aśvattha*, the *khadira*, and the *dhava*; from the auspicious *nyagrodha* and the *parṇa*—come to us, O Arundhatī!
O golden-hued one, fortunate one, sun-colored one, most beautiful of form! You go to the prepared place; indeed, your name is "Preparation.
O golden-hued one, fortunate one, powerful one, with woolly breast! You are the sister of the waters, O Lakṣā; the wind has become your soul.
Silācī by name, the maiden’s son, Aja-babhru is your father. You are moistened by the saliva of that dark horse of Yama.
That which fell from the horse's jaw flowed down upon the tree; having become a winged stream, come to us, O Arundhatī.

Brahman was born first in the east; from the horizon, Vena, the radiant one, revealed him. He has disclosed its highest stations near the foundation, the womb of both the existent and the non-existent.
Those who were unattainable and performed your first deeds—may they not deceive our heroes here; I place this before you.
In the thousand-streamed vault of heaven, they have resounded together, honey-tongued and unfailing. His watchful spies do not close their eyes; at every step there are nooses for the fetter.
Flow forth for the winning of booty, you who overcome all obstacles; you pass over the enemies by means of the ocean. You are named Sanisrasas, the thirteenth month, the house of Indra.
Now, with this [oblation], may you have succeeded, O Asu, Svāhā! O Soma and Rudra, armed with sharp weapons and sharp missiles, most gracious ones, be merciful to us here.
With this [oblation], may you have succeeded, O Asu, Svāhā! O Soma and Rudra, armed with sharp weapons and sharp missiles, most gracious ones, be merciful to us here.
Have you succeeded with this? *Asau*! *Svāhā*! O Soma and Rudra, armed with sharp weapons and sharp missiles, most gracious, be merciful to us here!
Release us from misfortune and from reproach; accept our sacrifice and bestow immortality upon us!

O missile of the eye, missile of the mind, missile of the sacred word (*brahman*), and missile of ascetic heat (*tapas*)—you are a missile against the missile; let those who plot against us become harmless!

Whoever should assail us with his eye, with his mind, with thought, or with intention—whosoever is malevolent—he, O Agni, do thou render powerless by thy power; Svāhā! Thou art the house of Indra. To thee I go for refuge; into thee I enter—with all my senses, with all my persons, with my whole self, with my whole body, together with whatever belongs to me. Thou art the protection of Indra. To thee I go for refuge; into thee I enter—with all my senses, with all my persons, with my whole self, with my whole body, together with whatever belongs to me.

You are the armor of Indra. To you I resort; into you I enter—with all my movement, all my men, all my self, and all my body, together with whatever is mine. You are the protection of Indra. To you I resort; into you I enter—with all my movement, all my men, all my self, and all my body, together with whatever is mine.
Bring it to us! Do not obstruct us, O Arāti! Do not hinder our sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) as it is being led away. Homage to the one who seeks to frustrate, to failure, and homage be to Arāti!
O Arāti, the man whom you place before you as one who reviles—homage we pay to him; do not disturb my acquisition.
May the gain bestowed by the gods be prepared for us by day and by night. May we not fall into enmity; let there be homage to the enemy.

Going forth, we invoke Sarasvatī, Anumati, and Bhaga. I have uttered the beloved and honey-sweet speech at the invocations of the gods. That which I request with my voice, joined with the mind of Sarasvatī—may faith find it today, granted by the tawny Soma.
