Do not obstruct our gain or our speech; may both Indra and Agni bring us riches. May all who desire to give to us today turn away from hostility.
Depart, O failure! We lead away your weapon, O unsuccessful one. I know you, O Arāti, as you shrink away and pierce;
appearing naked, you haunt people with sleep. O Arāti, they seek to destroy the thought and the intention of man.

To her who is great, of vast measure, who has pervaded all the quarters—to that Nirṛti with golden hair, I have paid homage. Golden-hued, fortunate, with a golden seat, the mighty one; to that Arāti with a golden garment, I have paid homage.
Carry the clarified butter to the gods with fuel-sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood; O Agni, delight them here, and let all come to my invocation.

O Indra, come to my invocation; I shall perform this rite, so hear it! May these *atisara* offerings dedicated to Indra incline my intention toward success. Through them, O Jātavedas, may we be able to achieve heroic power, O Lord of our own bodies.
O gods, whatever godless man over there seeks to do harm from that place, let not his oblation reach Agni; O gods, let him not come near our invocation—come only to my own call!
Run past the transgressors; slay them by the word of Indra! Tear them apart like a wolf a sheep! Let no one of you escape alive; seize his very breath!
That priest whom those men have set before them for their own destruction—that man, O Indra, I cast beneath your foot; I hurl him toward death.
If they have gone before the gods and made for themselves the Brahma-shields, fashioning them as body-protectors and defenses—whatever they have uttered, make all that sapless.
Those transgressions that he has committed and those that he shall commit—O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, turn them back again, so that they become like that grass-consuming folk.
Just as Indra, having obtained the cry of victory, cast them beneath his feet, so do I cast those men down for all future years.
O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, pierce them here in their vital organs; right here, O Indra, trample them down, for I am your ally. We take hold of you, O Indra; may we abide in your favor.
To the day, svāhā!
Svāhā to the Earth!
Svāhā to the intermediate space!
Svāhā to the intermediate space!
To the day, svāhā!
Svāhā to the Earth!
The sun is my eye, the wind my breath, the atmosphere my soul, and the earth my body. I am this one named "Unassailable"; I establish myself for the protection of heaven and earth.

Upward [may] life, upward strength, upward the deed, upward the ritual act, upward the inspired thought, upward the sensory power! O you two who grant long life, O lords of long life, you who possess the *svadhā* offering, be my guardians; protect me! Be seated within my very self; do not harm me!

You are my stone armor against whoever, seeking evil, should attack me from the eastern quarter—let him meet with this [consequence]. You are my stone armor against whoever, seeking evil, should attack me from the southern quarter—let him meet with this [consequence].

You are my stone armor; whoever, seeking evil, should attack me from the western quarter, let him meet with this fate. You are my stone armor; whoever, seeking evil, should attack me from the northern quarter, let him meet with this fate. You are my stone armor; whoever, seeking evil, should attack me from the fixed (zenith) quarter, let him meet with this fate.

Thou art my stone armor; may he who, seeking evil, would assail me from the upward direction, meet with this [consequence]. Thou art my stone armor; may he who, seeking evil, would assail me from the intermediate points of the directions, meet with this [consequence].

With the great [breath], I invoke the mind through Mātariśvan; the out-breath and in-breath from the Sun; the eye from the atmosphere; the ear from the sky; and the body from the earth. From Sarasvatī, we invoke speech, joined with the mind.
How did you speak here to the great Asura? How to your father Hari, O you of brilliant manly power? Having given Pṛśni as a sacrificial fee, O Varuṇa, you, O bounteous one, reflected in your mind:

"I shall not become a bounteous giver again out of mere desire; I have looked upon this Pṛśni to assist her. By what poetic wisdom (*kāvyena*), O Atharvan, and by what birth (*jātena*) are you Jātavedas?
Truly, I am profound in poetic wisdom; truly, by my birth I am Jātavedas. Neither a Dāsa nor an Ārya has violated my vow through its greatness, which I shall maintain.

There is no one other than you who is a better poet, nor any more steadfast in wisdom than you, O Varuṇa, possessor of self-sovereignty. You know all these worlds; even that person, though possessed of creative power, stands in awe of you.

For you indeed, O Varuṇa, self-dependent one, know all generations, O excellent leader. Is there anything else beyond this realm? Is there anything lower than this, O Immortal One? There is one thing beyond this realm; by one [step] beyond that, it is difficult even for the wicked to reach. Knowing this, O Varuṇa, I declare it to you: let the Paṇis be beneath our speech; let the Dāsas creep lowly into the earth.

For you indeed, O Varuṇa, speak of many faults among those who bestow wealth again; do not let the Paṇis remain so numerous for me, nor let people call you one who gives no gifts, nor let people call me one who gives no gifts. O singer, I give back to you the spotted cow; come to my entire hymn with your powers, among all the human quarters.
Let my offered hymns reach you, among all the human quarters. Give now to me that which is not yet given to me; you are my companion, my seven-step friend.
Our kinship is the same, O Varuṇa; our birth is the same. I know this which is our common origin. I give to you that which has not yet been given; I am your companion, your seven-step friend.

A god bestowing vigor upon the god who praises him, a wise seer upon the seer who lauds him—O self-dependent Varuṇa, you have indeed begotten Atharvan, the father and kinsman of the gods. For him, grant a most glorious gift; you are our friend and our highest kin.
Kindled today in the dwelling of Manu, O God Jātavedas, you sacrifice to the gods. Bring them hither, O great Mitra-like one, for you are the perceptive messenger, the seer, and the wise one.

O Tanūnapāt, anointing the paths that lead along the course of Ṛta with honey, make them sweet, O fair-tongued one! Accomplishing our prayers through our thoughts and the sacrifice, perform our ritual among the gods.

Being invoked, worthy of praise, and to be celebrated, come hither, O Agni, in harmony with the Vasus! You are the youthful Hotṛ of the gods; as such, being impelled, sacrifice to them as the most skilled sacrificer.

The sacrificial grass is strewn eastward according to the direction of the earth; at the break of this dawn, it is gathered at the beginning of the days. It spreads itself out further and wider, a pleasant seat for the gods and for Aditi.
Let the spacious doors open wide, like wives adorning themselves for their husbands. O divine, lofty, all-encompassing doors, be easy of access for the gods.

Let the two holy ones, Dawn and Night, swelling with moisture and dwelling close together, sit down upon the sacrificial seat—the two celestial maidens, lofty and adorned with gold, wearing brilliant and radiant beauty.

The two divine Hotṛ-priests, the first, eloquent ones, measuring out the sacrifice for man to worship; the two poets who impel [the rites] in the assemblies, pointing toward the eastern light with their direction.

Let Bhāratī come quickly to our sacrifice, and Iḷā, manifesting here like Manu. Let the three goddesses—Sarasvatī and the others—skilled in their work, sit upon this pleasant sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
O Hotṛ, you who are more skilled in sacrifice, being impelled today, worship here as a knower the god Tvaṣṭṛ, who fashioned these two parents, Heaven and Earth, and all beings with their forms.
Release [the oblation] by thyself, anointing the path of the gods in due season with the offerings. Let Vanaspati, the divine immolator Agni, sweeten the oblation with honey and ghee.
As soon as he was born, Agni measured out the sacrifice; he became the leader of the gods. By the command of this Hotṛ, in the speech of *ṛta*, let the gods eat the oblation consecrated with *svāhā*.

For Varuṇa, the seer of heaven, has given it to me. With my powerful words, I cause thy poison to flow away. I have seized the poison that was dug up, that was not dug up, and that which clung [to thee]. Like moisture in a desert, thy poison shall perish.

That poison of yours which is waterless, that very thing I have seized from these [plants]. I seize your middle, your highest, and even your lowest essence; let it perish through fear. And indeed, your roar is like a bull, like thunder from the clouds; with your fierce word, O serpent, you are struck down. And indeed, I have seized that essence of yours with my men, as light emerges from darkness. May the sun rise! With my sight I strike out your sight; with poison I strike your poison. O serpent, die; do not live! Let the poison turn back and come upon you.
O Kirātas, Pṛśnis, Upatṛṇyas, Babhrus, Asitas, and Alīkas, listen to me! Do not stand in the way of my friendship; having made yourselves heard, rest here for the sake of poison.

Of the Asita, the Taimāta, the Babhru, the Apodaka, and of the Sātrāsāha—of this Manyu, I unloose [the powers] like the string from a bow, like chariots. Āligī and Viligī, father and mother—we know your kinship from every side; being powerless, what will you do?
The daughter of Urugūlā was born a slave-girl from Asiknī. The poison of all those who have contracted *pratanka* and *dadru* is rendered powerless.
Karṇā Śvāvidh spoke this while descending from the mountain: "Whatever these dug-out [holes] may be, their poison is most powerless.
It is not *tābuva*, it is not *tābuva*; indeed, you are not *tābuva*. By means of *tābuva*, the poison is rendered powerless.
I have not praised you, nor indeed are you one to be praised; with praise, [I consume] the sapless poison.
The fair-winged bird found you; the boar dug you up with his snout. O Herb, you who desire to harm, strike down the one who desires to harm, and destroy the sorcery performed against us.
Strike down the sorcerers; strike down the one who has fashioned the spell. And furthermore, O Herb, slay him who seeks to harm us!

Like the butcher’s knife for a deer, having cut around the skin, O Gods, fasten the spell back onto the spell-maker like a necklace. Having seized the spell by the hand, lead it away back to the spell-maker. Deliver it right before his eyes, so that the spell may destroy its own creator.

Let sorceries be for the one who performs sorcery; let the curse be for the one who utters a curse. May the sorcery performed by sorcery turn back like a comfortable chariot. Whether it was a woman or a man who performed the sorcery for evil, that very sorcery we lead back to him, as one leads a horse with a halter. Whether you were made by the gods or made by men, you, that sorcery, we lead back again, with Indra as our ally.
O Agni, conqueror of armies, overcome the hostile forces! We take back the magic spell cast by the sorcerer by means of this counter-spell.
Pierce him who has performed the piercing; strike down the one who did it. We shall not sharpen our weapons for your slaughter when you have done no wrong.

Go to him like a son to his father; go, having mounted him like a brother-in-law. Step upon him as one treading on a trap; go back to the doer of the *kṛtyā*, O *kṛtyā*. Like a doe leaping toward a female elephant, let the *kṛtyā* seize her maker.
Let a straight-flying arrow fall upon him from heaven and earth. Let that *kṛtyā* catch him like a deer; let the *kṛtyā* return to the doer of the *kṛtyā*.

Like fire, let it go against the current; like water, let it flow with the current. Let the *kṛtyā* turn back like a comfortable chariot, returning the *kṛtyā* to its maker. One and ten are my protectors, O Herb; born of *ṛta*, O observer of *ṛta*, make me sweet, O Sweet One. Two and twenty are my protectors, O Herb; born of *ṛta*, O observer of *ṛta*, make me sweet, O Sweet One.

Three and thirty are my healers, O herb, born of Truth, rich in Truth; do thou, full of sweetness, make honey for me. Four and forty are my healers, O herb, born of Truth, rich in Truth; do thou, full of sweetness, make honey for me.
Five and fifty are my healers, O herb, born of Truth, rich in Truth; do thou, full of sweetness, make honey for me.
Six and sixty are my expellers, O herb, born of *ṛta*, observer of *ṛta*: make honey for me, O honeyed one.

Seven and seventy are my expellers, O herb, born of *ṛta*, observer of *ṛta*: make honey for me, O honeyed one. Eight and eighty are my expellers, O herb, born of *ṛta*, observer of *ṛta*: make honey for me, O honeyed one.

Nine and ninety are my healers, O herb, born of Truth, rich in Truth; make honey for me, O honeyed one! Ten and a hundred are my healers, O herb, born of Truth, rich in Truth; make honey for me, O honeyed one!
A hundred and a thousand are my healers, O herb, born of *ṛta*, rich in *ṛta*. Make honey for me, O honeyed one! If you are a single bull, let loose; if you are sapless, [let loose].
If you are a double-tongued one, let loose; you are powerless.
If you are full of sap, let loose; if you are sapless, you are sapless.
If you are fourfold, let loose; you are sapless.
If you are the fivefold bull, let loose; you are powerless.
If you are the sixth bull, let loose; if you are sapless, let loose.
If you are the sevenfold bull, let loose; you are powerless.
If you are the eightfold bull, let loose; you are powerless.
If you are a new bull, let loose; you are powerless.
If you are ten bulls, let them loose; you are powerless.
If you are the eleventh, you are one who has cast off water.
They spoke first regarding the sin against the Brahman: the boundless ocean, Mātariśvan, Vīḷuhara, Tapas, Ugra, Mayobhū, and the divine Waters, the first-born of Cosmic Order (Ṛta).
King Soma was the first to restore the wife of the Brahman, returning her without resentment. Varuṇa and Mitra were the attendants; Agni, the Hotṛ-priest, took her by the hand and led her away.
The pledge of this woman must be taken with the hand alone, if one has declared, "She is the wife of a Brahmin. She is not to be sent to a messenger; thus is the kingdom of a Kṣatriya guarded.

Her whom they call Tārakā, the disheveled one, who descends upon the village as a portent of evil—she, the wife of a Brahmin, consumes the kingdom wherever the hare-marked moon has fallen like a torch.

The Vedic student wanders about, performing his various duties; he becomes a single limb of the gods. By him Bṛhaspati recovered his wife, who had been led away by Soma, just as the gods [recovered] the *juhū* ladle.

In this very place, the gods and the seven ancient seers spoke, who sat down through their ascetic fervor. Terrible is the wife of a Brahmin when she is led away; she establishes evil in the highest heaven.

Those embryos that fall away, and that which is torn from the world, and those heroes who are slaughtered by one another—these it is the slayer of the Brahmin’s wife who destroys. Even if ten husbands, other than a Brahmin, were previously with a woman, if a Brahmin has taken her hand, he alone is the husband in every way.

Only a Brāhmaṇa is a husband, not a Rājanya, nor a Vaiśya. Proclaiming this, Sūrya moves toward the five classes of men. Indeed, the gods gave her back; indeed, men gave her back. Kings, upholding the truth, have given back the wife of a Brāhmaṇa.
Having restored the wife of a Brāhmaṇa and having been cleared of sin by the gods, they enjoy the nourishment of the earth and worship the wide-striding one (Viṣṇu).

In that kingdom where the wife of a Brahmin is detained through lack of understanding, there is no auspicious, hundred-vehicled wife who lies upon his bed; nor is a son born in that house with deformed ears or a broad head. In that kingdom where the wife of a Brahmin is detained through lack of understanding, there is no steward with a golden necklace who goes at the head of the sacrificial animals.
The white horse with black ears, yoked to the pole, does not find honor in that kingdom where the wife of a Brahmin is detained through thoughtlessness.

In his field, no lotus pond arises, nor is the *nāṇḍīka* lily or the lotus stalk produced, in that kingdom where the wife of a Brahmin is detained through thoughtlessness. Those who wait upon her milking do not milk the dappled cow for him, in that kingdom where the wife of a Brahmin is detained through thoughtlessness.

Neither does his auspicious cow yield milk, nor does his ox bear the yoke, where a man of ill-repute dwells for a night with a Brahmin. O King, the gods did not give this [cow] to you to eat; O Kshatriya, do not covet the cow of a Brahmin that is not fit to be eaten.
A wicked Kshatriya, malicious in his dice-play and defeated by his own self, might eat the cow of a Brahmin today, but let him live today and not tomorrow.
Like a female viper covered with its skin, O Kṣatriya, this cow of the Brāhmaṇa is harsh and unfit to be eaten.
She indeed leads away the ruling power and destroys splendor; like a fire that has been grasped, she consumes everything. He who regards the Brāhmaṇa as mere food drinks the poison of the blind one.

He who kills him, thinking him to be weak, is a scorner of the gods, desiring wealth and not from his heart. Indra kindles a fire within his heart; he hates both [worlds] as they move through the two skies.

A Brahmin must not be harmed, for he is like the sacred fire of one’s own dear body. Soma is his heir, and Indra is his protector against curses. He swallows the hundred-jawed [serpent], yet it is unable to extract him. The wicked man who thinks, "I shall eat the sweet food of the Brahmins," finds that his tongue becomes the bowstring, his palate the bow-tip, and his teeth the arrows, smeared with the heat of his own ascetic power. With these, the Brahmin pierces those who revile the gods—using the heart as strength, the bow drawn by the gods, and arrows impelled by the divine.
The sharp arrows of the Brahmins are possessed of a deadly point; the shaft they discharge is never in vain. Pursuing him with ascetic fervor and wrath, they shatter him from afar.
Those Vaitahavyas, who were formerly ten hundred and a thousand in number, perished after devouring the cow of a Brahmin.
The cow herself, as she was being slaughtered, struck down those descendants of Vitahavya who had looked upon the last-born calf of Kesara-prabandha.
One hundred and one were those communities whom the earth shook off; having harmed the Brahmin offspring, they perished utterly and beyond recovery.
The devourer of gods wanders among mortals; swallowed by poison, he becomes a mere heap of bones. He who harms a Brahmin, a kinsman of the gods, does not even reach the world of the ancestors.

Agni is indeed our protector; Soma is called our heir; Indra is the slayer of the accuser—thus do the wise know it. Like a poisoned arrow, O Lord of Men, like a viper, O Lord of Cattle, is that terrible arrow of the Brāhmaṇa; with it he pierces the one who reviles him.
They grew beyond measure, as if they would touch the very heavens; but having harmed Bhṛgu, the Sṛñjayas, the descendants of Vitahavya, were utterly defeated.
Those people who harmed the Brāhmaṇa Bṛhatsāman, the descendant of Aṅgiras—for them the ram, the ewe that eats both kinds of food, has devoured their offspring.

Those who spat upon a Brahmin, or those who sought to extort a fee from him—those sit in the middle of the stream, gnawing at their own entrails and hair. As long as the Brahmin-cow is being cooked and she tosses about, she destroys the vital luster of the kingdom; no heroic son is born there. Cruel is her slaughter-knife; coarse flesh is served up. When her milk is drunk, that indeed is an offense against the ancestors.

The kingdom of that fierce king who, thinking himself powerful, seeks to devour a Brahmin, is utterly poured away where the Brahmin is oppressed. Having become eight-footed, four-eyed, four-eared, four-jawed, two-mouthed, and two-tongued, she shakes down the kingdom of the oppressor of Brahmins.

That kingdom indeed flows away like water from a broken boat; wherever they harm a Brahmin, misfortune destroys that kingdom. The trees drive him away, saying, "Do not come into our shade. O Nārada, he who covets the true wealth of a Brahmin—King Varuṇa has declared this to be a divinely ordained poison. Having eaten the cow of a Brahmin, no one at all remains awake in the kingdom.
Nine times ninety were those very regions which the earth shook off; having harmed the Brahmin progeny, they perished in an impossible manner.
That wooden block with a foot-socket which they fasten behind the dead—O oppressor of Brahmins, the gods have declared that to be your bed.
Those tears which rolled from the grieving man as he was being led away—O oppressor of Brahmins, the gods have ordained that to be your portion of the waters.
That with which they bathe the dead, and that with which one moistens the beard—O oppressor of Brahmins, the gods have indeed ordained that as your portion of the waters.
The rain of Mitra and Varuṇa does not fall upon the one who seeks to overpower the Brahman; neither does the assembly favor him, nor does he bring a friend under his control.
A loud-sounding drum, made of wood, fashioned together with the products of the cow; making your voice heard and subduing your rivals, roar against them like a lion about to conquer.

Like a lion, he has roared, firmly bound to the wooden posts, bellowing like a bull toward a cow in heat. You are the bull; your rivals are emasculated. O Indra, your vigor overcomes those who seek to harm us.

Like a bull known for his might among the herd, you who seek cattle, roar as a conqueror of wealth. Pierce the hearts of our enemies with your flame! Let the foes depart, abandoned and driven away from their villages.
Conquering the armies, prolonging our life, grasping what is to be grasped, look out in many directions! O drum, utter the divine speech; as a creator, bring forth the wealth of the enemies!
Hearing the drum’s voice as it speaks with effort, may the woman, distressed and awakened by the sound, run toward her son by the hand—the enemy woman, terrified in the midst of weapons.
O drum, you shall speak first; speaking upon the back of the earth, shine forth! Crushing the army of the enemies, speak with splendor, O drum, with words full of truth and joy.

Let there be a sound between these two skies; let your various noises go forth quickly. Roar toward us, thunder like one who has drunk his fill; create a hymn, O Mitra, for the sake of victory, you who possess heavenly light.
Made manifest by inspired thoughts, he shall utter his voice; rouse up the weapons of the warriors. Gladdening Indra, summon the heroes; with your allies, strike down the enemies.

The one who causes the battle-cry, the loud-voiced, the bold in army, the maker of the way known, the one who roars through the villages; winning glory, knowing the sacred ordinances, distribute fame among the many in the double kingdom.

You are the seeker of excellence, the winner of wealth, the more powerful, the conqueror in battle, sharpened by the sacred word (*brahman*). Like a pressing-stone upon the stones for the stalks, O drum, dance over the booty, seeking cattle!

Subduer of enemies, subduer of those who attack from afar, seeker of cattle, victorious, the breaker-through; like a skilled singer bringing forth a hymn, bring forth your voice for victory in battle! Utter here a cry for nourishment.
You who shake the unshakable, most swift to go to the fray, conqueror of the hostile, invincible leader; protected by Indra, observing the assemblies, illuminating the hearts of enemies—go swiftly!
O drum, utter heart-rending discord among the foes! We instill hatred, dejection, and fear in the enemies; strike them down, O drum!

Trembling in mind, eye, and heart, let the enemies run away in fear when the clarified butter is offered. Born of the tree, gathered with the products of the cow, belonging to all clans—speak terror to the enemies, you who are anointed with clarified butter! Just as wild animals are terrified by a man, so do you, O drum, cry out against the enemies and strike them with fear; furthermore, bewilder their minds.
Just as goats and sheep run away from a wolf, greatly terrified, even so, O drum, roar out against our enemies; strike them with fear and utterly bewilder their minds.
Just as birds are scattered at every dawn by the hawk, and just as [creatures flee] at the roar of a lion, even so, O drum, cry out against our enemies; terrify them and utterly confound their minds.

With the drum and with the skin of a spotted deer, drive away our enemies. All the gods who flee from the onset of battle trembled in fear. With those foot-steps and with their shadow, with which Indra sports, let our enemies tremble—those who advance in military ranks.
Let the twang of bowstrings and the drums resound toward every quarter. May the armies of our enemies, as they retreat in flight, be utterly defeated in their ranks.
O Āditya, take back the eye; O Marīcīs, run after it! Let the foot-clasping snares seize it when the strength of his arms has departed.

You, the fierce Maruts, sons of Pṛśni, with Indra as your ally, crush the enemies! King Soma, King Varuṇa, Mahādeva, and Death, and Indra—let these divine armies, whose banners are the sun and who are of one mind, conquer our foes. Svāhā!

May Agni drive the fever away from here; may Soma, the pressing-stones, Varuṇa of pure strength, the altar, the sacred grass, and the brightly flaming fuel-drifts drive it away. May all hostilities vanish into nothingness. This Agni, who makes all things yellowish-green, burning and consuming like fire—therefore, O Fever, become sapless; then, turn downward or go away below. That which is knotty, knotted, crumbling, and ruddy—O Fever, possessing all power, send that downcast force far away.

Having paid homage, I send Takman downward; may the Fist-seizer of Śakambhara return from the Mahāvṛṣas. The Mūjavants are his home, the Mahāvṛṣas are his home. As far as you have been born, O Takman, so far you have dwelt among the Balhikas. O Takman, serpent, go away! O disease, go away! O cripple-maker, depart far! Seek out the Dāsa woman Niṣṭakvarī and strike her down with your thunderbolt.
O Takman, go to the Mūjavats or to the Balhikas, or even further away; seek out a Śūdra woman who is a wanton, and shake her off, O Takman.

Having gone away from Mahāvṛṣa and Mūjavat to the land of Bandhu, we declare these things to Takman: "These are indeed other fields; you do not delight in another’s field. Being self-controlled, show us mercy. Takman has become an object of longing; he shall go to the Balhikas.
Since you, being cold and then burning, have caused us to tremble with coughing, O Takman, your darts are terrible; with them, spare us!
Do not make these your friends: consumption, cough, and fever. Do not come back again from there; I speak thus to you, O Takman.

O Takman, go away with your brother Consumption, with your sister Cough, and with your rival, Evil, to that other, alien people. Destroy the fever that recurs every third day, that which occurs every fourth day, the daily one, and the autumnal; destroy the cold, the burning, the summer, and the rainy fever.
From the Gandhāris, from the Mūjavats, from the Aṅgas, and from the Magadhas—we entrust the fever-disease (takman) to them, as one would entrust a treasure when departing for a people.
Woven into me are Heaven and Earth; woven into me is the goddess Sarasvatī. Woven into me are both Indra and Agni; may they crush the worm!
O Indra, Lord of Wealth, slay the worms of this child! All enemies are slain by my formidable word.
That which crawls around the eyes, that which crawls around the nostrils, that which goes into the midst of the teeth—that worm we crush!

The two of like form and the two of unlike form, the two black ones and the two red ones, the tawny one and the tawny-eared one, the vulture and the cuckoo—these have been slain. Those worms that are white-bellied, those that are black with white forelegs, and whatever others are of every form—all those worms we crush.
The sun rises in the east, seen by all, the destroyer of the unseen. Striking down both the seen and the unseen, he crushes all worms.
Whether they be *yevāṣas*, *kṣkaṣās*, *ejatkās*, or *śipavitnukas*—let the seen worm be struck down, and let the unseen worm be struck down.
The *yevāṣa* of the worms is slain, and the *nadanimā* is slain. I have ground them all to powder, like *khalva* seeds with a millstone.

The three-headed, three-peaked worm, the brindled and the white—I crush its ribs and I cut off its head. Like Atri, like Kaṇva, like Jamadagni, I slay you worms; with the sacred spell of Agastya, I grind the worms to powder.
Slain is the king of the worms, and their chieftain is slain. Slain is the worm whose mother is slain, slain its brother, and slain its sister.

Slain are his attendants, slain are his followers; and those who are like small insects—all of them are slain. Of all worms and of all kinds of parasites, I split the head with a stone and burn the mouth with fire.

Savitṛ is the lord of instigations; may he protect me in this sacred formulation (*brahman*), in this rite, in this office of the domestic priest, in this foundation, in this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, and in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*! Agni is the lord of the trees; may he protect me in this sacred formulation, in this rite, in this office of the domestic priest, in this foundation, in this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, and in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*!

Heaven and Earth are the sovereign lords of givers; may they protect me in this sacred word (*brahman*), in this rite, in this office of the domestic priest, in this foundation, in this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, and in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*! Varuṇa is the sovereign lord of the waters; may he protect me in this sacred word, in this rite, in this office of the domestic priest, in this foundation, in this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, and in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*!

Mitra and Varuṇa are the lords of rain; may they protect me in this sacred formulation (*brahman*), in this rite, in this office of the domestic priest, in this foundation, in this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, and in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*!

The Maruts are the lords of the mountains; may they protect me in this sacred formulation, in this rite, in this office of the domestic priest, in this foundation, in this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, and in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*!

Soma is the sovereign lord of plants; may he protect me in this sacred formulation, in this rite, in this leadership, in this foundation, in this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, and in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*! Vāyu is the sovereign lord of the intermediate space; may he protect me in this sacred formulation, in this rite, in this leadership, in this foundation, in this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, and in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*!

Sūrya is the lord of eyes; may he protect me in this sacred word (*brahman*), in this rite, in this office of the domestic priest, in this foundation, in this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, and in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*! Candramas is the lord of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*); may he protect me in this sacred word, in this rite, in this office of the domestic priest, in this foundation, in this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, and in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*!

Indra, the overlord of heaven—may he protect me in this sacred word (*brahman*), in this rite, in this office of the domestic priest, in this foundation, in this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, and in this invocation of the gods; *svāhā*! The father of the Maruts, the overlord of cattle—may he protect me in this sacred word, in this rite, in this office of the domestic priest, in this foundation, in this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, and in this invocation of the gods; *svāhā*!

Death is the lord of creatures; may he protect me in this sacred word (*brahman*), in this rite, in this office of the domestic priest, in this foundation, in this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, and in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*! Yama is the lord of the ancestors; may he protect me in this sacred word, in this rite, in this office of the domestic priest, in this foundation, in this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, and in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*!

May those ancestors who are beyond protect me in this sacred formulation (*brahman*), in this rite, in this office of the domestic priest, in this foundation, in this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, and in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*! May those who are below them protect me in this sacred formulation, in this rite, in this office of the domestic priest, in this foundation, in this thought, in this intention, in this blessing, and in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*!

May those great-grandfathers protect me in this sacred word (*brahman*), in this rite, in this priesthood, in this foundation, in this thought, in this intention, in this prayer, and in this invocation of the gods—*svāhā*!
Gathered from the mountain, from the womb of heaven, from every limb, may the seed-placer deposit the embryo into the womb like a leaf upon a branch.
Just as this great earth receives the embryo of all beings, so do I deposit the embryo within you; for that purpose, I call upon you for protection.
Bestow a fetus, O Sinīvālī; bestow a fetus, O Sarasvatī. May both the Aśvins, adorned with lotus-garlands, place a fetus within you.

May Mitra and Varuṇa grant you a fetus; may the god Bṛhaspati grant you a fetus. May both Indra and Agni grant you a fetus; may Dhātṛ grant you a fetus. May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms. May Prajāpati pour [the seed]; may Dhātṛ place a fetus within you.
That which King Varuṇa knows, or that which the goddess Sarasvatī knows, or that which Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, knows—that which produces offspring, drink it.
You are the embryo of the plants, the embryo of the trees; you are the embryo of all that exists. O Agni, bestow the embryo here.
Leap forth, show your heroism; place the embryo in the womb. You are a bull, possessed of virility; we lead you here for the sake of progeny.
Open wide, O Bṛhatsāman; let your embryo lie within your womb. The gods have granted you a son who drinks Soma and possesses both [natures].

O Dhātṛ, with the most excellent form, place a male child within the two labia of this woman so that he may be born in the tenth month. O Tvaṣṭṛ, with the most excellent form, place a male child within the two labia of this woman so that he may be born in the tenth month.
O Savitṛ, with the most excellent form, place a male child within the womb-veins of this woman, so that he may be born in the tenth month.
O Prajāpati, with the most excellent form, place a male child within the womb-veins of this woman, so that he may be born in the tenth month.
May the Yajus-formulas, the sacrificial fuel-sticks, and the *svāhā*-utterances—may Agni, the all-knowing, unite these for you here.
May the god Savitṛ, the great one, knowing [the way], join [us] at this sacrifice; svāhā!
May Indra, the wise one, yoke his well-yoked steeds at this sacrifice for the sake of the hymns and songs of praise; Svāhā!
May these invocations (nivids) go forth in the sacrifice; Svāhā! O remaining ones, come here harnessed together with the wives.
O Maruts, you are the Vedic hymns at the sacrifice; Svāhā! Like a mother her son, carry us across here, being well-yoked.
Hither has come this Aditi with the sacrificial grass and the sprinkling waters, performing the sacrifice; Svāhā!
May Viṣṇu yoke manifold heats; in this sacrifice, may he yoke them well-yoked—Svāhā! May Tvaṣṭṛ yoke manifold forms; in this sacrifice, may he yoke them well-yoked—Svāhā!
May Bhaga yoke blessings for him; in this sacrifice, may he, the wise one, yoke them well-yoked—Svāhā!
May Soma yoke the many streams of milk; well-yoked, at this sacrifice, Svāhā!
May Indra yoke the many streams of milk; well-yoked, at this sacrifice, Svāhā!

O Aśvins, come hither by means of the sacred word (*brahman*), increasing the sacrifice with the *vaṣaṭ*-call! O Bṛhaspati, come hither by means of the sacred word; this sacrifice is light for the sacrificer—Svāhā!
Upward rise his fuel-sticks, upward the bright, glowing flames of Agni. Most radiant, with a beautiful countenance, he is the Son, Tanūnapāt, the Asura with many hands.
A god among the gods, he anoints the paths with honey and ghee.
Approaching the sacrifice with sweetness, the god Narāśaṃsa Agni is the impeller; he is the doer of good deeds, the bestower of all boons.
Behold, he comes with power, being praised with oblations of ghee by the priest who brings worship with reverence.
May Agni worship at the ladles during the preliminary rites; may he worship the majesty of this Agni.
Then, in the low-toned prayers, the Vasus and the bestowers of wealth took their stand at the offerings.
The goddesses, the doors, always guard his ordinance according to all his laws.
O Dawn and Night, you who are wide-extending through the domain of Agni, flowing with sweetness and worthy of worship, being close at hand, protect this sacrifice and our ritual service.

O divine Hotṛs, with the tongue of Agni, celebrate our lofty ritual; sing for us so that there may be a good sacrifice. Let the three goddesses—Iḷā, Sarasvatī, and the great Bhāratī—being praised, sit upon this sacred grass (barhis).
O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, release for us that wonderful, abundant seed, the increase of wealth, and the central source of this [offering].
O Lord of the Forest, release [the victim], being gracious; may Agni himself, as the immolator, make the oblation palatable for the gods.
O Agni Jātavedas, perform the *svāhā* invocation for Indra; may all the gods enjoy this oblation of the sacrifice.

He measures out the nine vital breaths with nine [threads] for the sake of long life lasting a hundred autumns: three in the yellow [thread], three in the silver, and three in the iron, all enveloped by ascetic heat (*tapas*).

Agni, Sūrya, Candramas, Earth, Waters, Heaven, the intermediate space, and the quarters and sub-quarters; may the seasonal deities, in harmony with the seasons, carry me across by means of this threefold [sacrifice].

May the three nourishments rest upon the threefold [sacrifice]; may Pūṣan anoint [us] with milk and ghee. May the abundance of food, the abundance of men, and the abundance of cattle rest here for you.
O Ādityas, sprinkle him with wealth; O Agni, being yourself strengthened, cause him to grow. O Indra, endow him with heroic power; may the threefold nourishing [sacrifice] take its place within him.

May the Earth protect you with her greenery, she who sustains all; may Agni, in harmony with her, fulfill your needs with his iron. May he, together with the plants, bestow upon you the white [gold], which is in accord with you, granting skill and a well-disposed mind. This gold, born in three ways by its very origin: one part became the most beloved of Agni; one part flew away from Soma when he was struck; one part they call the seed of the Waters, the ordainers. May that gold of yours be threefold for the sake of long life. The triple life-span of Jamadagni, the triple life-span of Kaśyapa—the threefold manifestation of immortality—I have prepared these three life-spans for you.
When the three birds went forth with the threefold [sacrifice], the powerful ones, having united in the single syllable, drove away death along with immortality, warding off all misfortunes.
May the golden one protect you from heaven; may the silver one protect you from the mid-region; may the iron one protect you from the earth. This god has gone before the fortresses.
O God, may these three fortresses protect you on every side. Bearing them, may you be radiant and superior to your enemies.
The city of the gods, the immortal, the golden—one who first as a god pierced it in the beginning; to him I pay homage with ten eastern [fingers]. May he grant his approval for my threefold binding.
May Aryaman, Pūṣan, and Bṛhaspati fasten you on. With that name which belongs to one born by day, we fasten you on.
With the seasons and the seasonal periods for the sake of life and splendor; with the brilliance of the year, by that we make your jaw strong.
Drawn from clarified butter, anointed with honey, firming the earth, unshakable, and victorious—splitting your rivals and casting them down, ascend for great good fortune!
Yoked from the front, carry [the oblation], O Jātavedas; O Agni, know this which is being performed. You are the physician, the maker of medicine. Through you, may we win cattle, horses, and men.
Make it so, O Agni Jātavedas, acting in harmony with all the gods. May he who has played against us, whoever has swallowed [our wealth]—may his enclosing-stone fall down.

O Agni Jātavedas, act so that his enclosing-stick shall fall; being in agreement with all the gods, pierce his two eyes, pierce his heart, cut out his tongue, and crush his teeth. O Agni, youngest one, crush back whichever Piśāca has devoured him.

Whatever of his has been taken away, scattered, or carried off from himself, and whatever has been devoured by the *piśācas*—O Agni, you who are wise, bring that back; we shall infuse flesh and life-breath into this body.

Whatever Piśāca has harmed me while eating raw food, cooked food, mixed food, or fully digested food—let those Piśācas depart from this person by means of their own bodies and offspring; let this one be free from disease. Whatever [Piśāca] has harmed me while eating milk or churned curds, or whatever [has harmed me] while eating grain that ripens after being pulled up—let those Piśācas depart from this person by means of their own bodies and offspring; let this one be free from disease.

Whatever [Piśāca] has harmed me while drinking water, or the flesh-eater among the Yātudhānas while I was lying down on my bed—let those Piśācas depart from this person by means of their own bodies and offspring; let this one be free from disease.

Whether by day or by night, whichever one among the flesh-eating sorcerers has harmed me while I lay upon my bed—let those Piśācas be separated from themselves and from their offspring; let this man be free from disease.

O Agni, eat the raw flesh; O Jātavedas, slay the blood-drinking Piśāca who steals the mind! May Indra, the prize-winner, strike him with his thunderbolt; may Soma, the bold, cut off his head. From of old, O Agni, you have crushed the sorcerers; the Rākṣasas have never conquered you in battles. Burn up the flesh-eaters along with their delusions; let none escape your divine weapon.

Gather together, O Jātavedas, that which has been taken away and that which has been carried off; let his limbs increase, and let this man swell like a stalk of Soma. O Jātavedas, let this man swell like a stalk of Soma; O Agni, make him vigorous, pure, and free from disease, so that he may live.
These, O Agni, are thy fuel-sticks, destroyers of Piśācas; do thou accept them and take them up, O Jātavedas.
O Agni, accept with thy flame these fuel-sticks of Tārṣṭāghī; let the flesh-eater abandon his form, he who seeks to seize his flesh.
From nearby you have come; from afar you have come; from the distance you have come. Be right here; do not go away! Do not follow after the ancestors of old. I bind your life-force firmly.
Whatever spell a man of one's own kin or a stranger has cast upon you—with both the unloosing and the releasing, I declare them for you with my voice.
Whatever harm you have done or sworn falsely against a woman or a man through thoughtlessness—with both the unloosing and the releasing, I declare them for you with my voice.
Whatever sin you lie under committed against your mother or whatever against your father—with both the unloosing and the releasing, I declare them for you with my voice.
Whatever your mother, whatever your father, your sister, and your brother have brought upon you—receive this remedy in return; I make you one who reaches old age.
Be here, O man, with your whole mind. Do not go to the two messengers of Yama; live on, come hither before that time!
Summoned back again, O wise one, come! Ascend the rising of the path, the ascent, the stepping forth, the way of every living being.
Do not fear; you shall not die. I make you one who reaches old age. I have driven the consumption from your limbs, the fever of your members.

The breaking of your limbs and the fever of your members, and whatever malady is in your heart—the consumption has flown away like a hawk, overcome by my word, far beyond. O Ṛṣi Bodha and Pratibodha, you who are sleepless and ever-watchful—may those two be the guardians of your breath, remaining awake by day and by night.
This fire is to be approached; here let the sun rise for you. Rise up from the deep death, even from the black darkness.

Homage to Yama, homage be to Death, homage to the Fathers and those who lead [the dead]. I place that Agni in front, he who knows the crossing over, for his safety. Let breath come back, let mind come back, let sight and likewise strength come back. May his body be restored; may it stand firm again upon its feet.
O Agni, unite this man with breath and sight; quicken him with body and with strength. You know the path of immortality; let him not go to death, let him not become one whose home is the earth.

Let not your out-breath fail him, nor let your in-breath be withheld from him. May Sūrya, as your overlord, lift you up from death with his rays. This tongue speaks within, bound and silent; through you, I have cast out the consumption and the hundred fevers of the plague.
This world is most dear to the gods and unconquered; O man, for this death you were ordained when you were born here. We call after you: do not die before old age!
The spell they have wrought for you in an unbaked vessel, the spell they have wrought in mixed grain, the magic they have wrought in raw meat—that I drive back again.

The spell they have wrought for you against the cock, or that which they have wrought against the goat with its tufted ears, the magic they have wrought against the ewe—that I drive back again. The spell they have wrought against you in a single-hoofed animal, the magic they have wrought against the ass with its two rows of teeth—that I drive back again.

The sorcery (*valaga*) which they have wrought for you in the *amūlā* or in the *narācī*, the sorcery which they have wrought in your field—that I drive back again to them. The sorcery which the malevolent ones have wrought for you at the *gārhapatya* fire or at the *pūrvāgni*, the sorcery which they have wrought in the hall—that I drive back again to them.

The sorcery which they have wrought for you in the assembly hall, the sorcery which they have wrought at the gambling place, the sorcery which they have wrought with the dice—that I drive back again to them.

The spell which they wrought for you in the army, which they wrought in the weaponry, the spell which they wrought upon the drum—that I drive back again to you. The spell which they buried for you in a well, or which they dug up in a cemetery, the spell which they wrought in your dwelling—that I drive back again to you. The spell which they wrought for you in the human remains, and that which they placed in the fire and the crumbling ruin, the devourer of raw flesh, the burning heat, the consuming glow—that I drive back again to you.
He brought her by a wrong path; we send her back from here by the right path. The foolish man, O youths, has gathered her together with the foolish through lack of understanding.
He who committed this deed was unable to undo it; he has broken his foot and his toe. May he, though unfortunate, do us a good turn for those who are fortunate.
The sorcery, the spell-weaver, the root-caster, the one bound by oaths—may Indra slay him with a great weapon; may Agni pierce him with his missile.
Sing a fault-finding song, sing a lofty song; bestow splendor! O Atharvan, praise the god Savitar!
Praise him who is the son within the ocean—the youthful one, whose speech is truthful and free from guile, the most gracious.
May that god Savitṛ impel for us many immortal things, so that both our fair praises may go well. O priests, press out the Soma and wash it for Indra; may he hear the word and my call of the praiser.
Into him the drops enter as birds into a tree, into the juice. O Virapśin, strike down the malicious ones who possess the nature of Rākṣasas.
Listen, O Soma-drinker, [prepare] the Soma for Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt—he who is the youthful victor, the sovereign lord, and the one praised by many.
May Indra and Pūṣan protect us; may Aditi and the Maruts protect us. May Apām Napāt and the Seven Rivers protect us; may Viṣṇu and Heaven protect us.

May Heaven and Earth protect us for our assistance; may the pressing-stone and Soma protect us from distress. May the auspicious goddess Sarasvatī protect us, and may Agni protect us with his auspicious guardians.

May the divine Aśvins, lords of splendor, protect us; may Dawn and Night also grant us wide space. O divine Apām Napāt, ward off injury to our household; O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, increase us for complete well-being.
May Tvaṣṭṛ, Parjanya, and Brahmaṇaspati, as well as Aditi with her sons and brothers, protect us now with invincible, rescuing power.

May Aṃśa, Bhaga, Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, Aditi, and the Maruts protect us. May the malice of that oppressor depart; may he drive away the enemy who is near at hand. O Aśvins, favor our prayer; O wide-striding one, protect us with unfailing care. O Father Heaven, ward off whatever misfortune there may be. O Agni, invoked with clarified butter, lead him upward to a higher state; endow him with splendor and increase his progeny manifold.
O Indra, make this man preeminent; may he be the controller of his kinsmen. Endow him with the increase of wealth, and lead him to life and old age.
O Agni, cause him to prosper in whose house we prepare the oblation; for him may Soma speak in favor, and this Brahmaṇaspati as well.
O Brahmaṇaspati, whoever, being godless, seeks to harm us—subject him entirely to my will for the sake of the sacrificer who presses the juice.
O Soma, if a malicious man threatens us who are well-spoken, strike him on the mouth with your thunderbolt; crushed, let him perish.

O Soma, whoever assails us—whether he be a kinsman or a stranger—diminish his strength, as the vast heaven does by its own power. O Soma, come to us with that aid by which Aditi and the guileless Mitra go upon their path.

O Soma, with that power by which you bring the Asuras under our control, with that speak in our favor. With that power by which the gods overcame the might of the Asuras, with that grant us protection.
Just as the creeper entwines a tree on all sides, so do you embrace me; so that you may be loving toward me, and so that you may never depart from me.

Just as a bird, when swooping down, strikes its wings against the earth, so do I strike down your mind, so that you shall be loving toward me, so that you shall not turn away from me like rivers. Just as the sun instantly traverses these two, heaven and earth, so do I traverse your mind, so that you shall be loving toward me, so that you shall not turn away from me like rivers.
Long for my body; long for my feet; long for my eyes; long for my thighs. May the eyes of you who desire a man, and your hair, wither through longing for me.
I cause you to cling to my arms, I cause you to cling to my heart, so that you may abide by my will and follow my thought.
May those cows, whose navel is the means of approach and whose heart is the charm of conciliation, the mothers of clarified butter, bring that woman into harmony with me.
To the earth, to the sense of hearing, to the trees, to Agni the overlord—svāhā!
To the vital breath, to the intermediate space, to the birds, to Vāyu the overlord—svāhā!
To the eye of heaven, to the stars, to Sūrya the sovereign lord, Svāhā!
Mounted upon the *aśvattha* tree at the *śamī*, there the rite for producing a male was performed. That indeed is the means of obtaining a son; that we bring now unto these women.
In the man indeed there is semen; that is infused into the woman. That is the means of obtaining a son; so Prajāpati declared.

Prajāpati, Anumati, and Sinīvālī have fashioned this; they have placed the female seed elsewhere and have placed the male here. Like the sun around the sky, I have gone to the birthplace of the serpents; like the night [surrounding] the world, I ward off your poison with that which is other than destruction.
With that which was known of old by the Brahmans, by the Ṛṣis, and by the gods; with that which has been, that which is to be, and that which exists—by all that I ward off your poison.

May the rivers, the mountains, and the hills be mixed with honey; may the Paruṣṇī and Śīpālā be honey-sweet. May there be well-being for my mouth, may there be well-being for my heart. Homage to the slayers of the gods, homage to the slayers of kings; and to those who are the slayers of commoners—to them, O Death, let there be homage.
Homage to your loud proclamation, homage to your distant proclamation; homage to your goodwill, O Death, and homage to your ill-will—this homage to you.
Homage to you, O Yātudhānas; homage to you, O Bheṣajas! Homage to you, O Mṛtyus; homage to the roots and to the Brāhmaṇas!
Destroy the loosening of the bones, the loosening of the joints, the disease seated in the heart, and all consumption (balāsa) that resides in the limbs and in the joints.
I destroy the phlegm of the one afflicted by phlegm, even as I emasculate him; I cut his bond, his very root, like the *urvārū* plant.
O phlegm, fly away from here like a wingless youngling! And like a year-old calf, run away from here—you who do not slay heroes!
You are the highest of plants; the trees are your attendants. May he be our attendant who assails us!
Whether he be a kinsman or a stranger who assails us—may I rise above them all like the highest of trees.

Just as Soma is made the best of herbs and the best of oblations, so may I be the highest of the *talāśa* trees. Your consuming power, O fierce one, is both devouring and non-devouring; we eat your *karambha* offering; we eat your *karambha* offering.
Vihvala is the name of your father, Madāvatī is the name of your mother; you are indeed he who has brought himself to ruin.
O *tauvilika*, do not delay; let this *ailaba* go away, let it depart. Both the tawny one and the tawny-eared one—go away, O *niḥāla*.
You are the sluggish one, O *alasāla*; you are the former *silāñjāla*, the latter, and the blue-necked *sāla*.

Just as this great earth receives the germ of living beings, so may your embryo be sustained for birth and delivery. Just as this great earth supports these lords of the forest, so may your embryo be sustained for birth and delivery.
Just as this great earth supports the mountains and hills, so may your embryo be sustained for birth and delivery.

Just as this great earth supports the world that stands upon it, so let your embryo be sustained for easy delivery. We blow out from you the first onset of envy, and the subsequent one; we extinguish that heart-born fire and its anguish.

Just as the earth is dead, more dead than the dead, and just as the mind of one who has died, even so is the mind of the envious one dead. That flickering thought of yours which rests within your heart—from that I release your envy, like steam from a leather bag. May the divine folk purify me; may men purify me with their wisdom; may all beings purify me; may the self-purifying one purify me.
May Pavamāna purify me for wisdom, for skill, and for life, and also for safety. O God Savitṛ, with both means—with the filter and with your impulsion—purify us so that we may see clearly.

Like the burning of this fierce Agni, he departs; like one intoxicated, he goes away lamenting. Let him, the lawless one, seek someone other than us; let there be homage to the fever for his deadly weapon.
Homage to Rudra; homage be to Takman; homage to King Varuṇa, the radiant one. Homage to Heaven; homage to Earth; homage to the plants.
You who are the consumer by heat, you who turn all forms yellow—homage I pay to you, that ruddy, brown, forest-born Takman.
Of these three earths, this ground is the highest; from their very skin, I have gathered the remedy.
You are the best of medicines, the most excellent of plants. Like Soma, like Bhaga in his journeys, like Varuṇa among the gods;
you are wealthy, invincible, and desirous of winning—do you win! You are indeed strengtheners of the hair and increasers of the hair.

The tawny, well-winged ones, clothed in the waters, fly up to heaven along a black path. They have returned from the seat of Order (ṛta), and then they have moistened the earth with clarified butter (ghṛta).

Make the waters full of milk and the plants auspicious when you stir, O Maruts with golden ornaments upon your breasts; pour forth nourishment and favor there where, O heroic Maruts, you sprinkle the honey.

O Maruts, send forth that rain, swelling with water, which shall fill all the hollows. It moves like a maiden with loosened hair, like a wife who has been embraced by her husband. Having flowed, those waters, performing their work, flow day and night. I, whose will is most excellent, invoke the divine waters.
May the waters, woven into our ritual acts, release us from here for our guidance; may they instantly enable us to move forward.
Under the impulse of the divine Savitṛ, let men perform their work. May the waters and the plants be auspicious and bring us peace.

From the Himavat they flow forth; there is a great confluence in the Sindhu. Truly, those goddesses, the waters, have granted me this healing medicine for the heart’s glow—that which has shone upon my eyes, and that which is in my heels and the foreparts of my feet. May the waters, the most excellent of physicians, drive all that away.
O Sindhu, you whose wives are the rivers and whose queen is the Sindhu—ye who are all the rivers that exist—grant us the remedy for that; through it may we enjoy your favor.

And those fifty-five [veins] which converge upon the necks—from here let all those utterances of the revilers perish, like the curses of the contemptuous. And those seventy-seven [veins] which converge upon the necks—from here let all those utterances of the revilers perish, like the curses of the contemptuous.
The ninety-nine shoulder-joints that come together—let all those vanish from here like the spells of those who have been humbled.
Release me from evil, O Evil One; being self-controlled, be merciful to us. Place me, unharmed, in the world of the auspicious.
O Evil One, we abandon you whom you do not leave behind. At the turning point of the paths, let the evil fall upon another.
Let the immortal, thousand-eyed one proclaim us elsewhere; let him strike down whom we hate, and slay specifically him whom we loathe.

O Gods, the dove, sent as a messenger by Nirṛti, has come here seeking what it desires. To him let us offer reverence and perform atonement; may there be well-being for our bipeds and well-being for our quadrupeds.
May the sent dove be auspicious to us; O Gods, may this bird come to our house sinless. May Agni, the sage, accept our oblation; may the winged missile pass us by.

The winged missile does not deceive us; the female owl makes her home in the fire-chamber. May he be auspicious to our cattle and to our men; O gods, let not the dove harm us here. Drive away the dove with a verse, expelling it; rejoicing in food, we lead the cow around. Alluring away misfortunes, may it leave behind its tracks and, as one most skilled on the path, step forward toward strength for us.
These have flowed around Agni; these have led the cow around. They have established glory among the gods—who would dare to attack them?
He who first reached the precipice, spying out the path for many; he who rules over his two-footed and four-footed creatures—to that Yama, to Death, let there be homage.
May the winged missile go down upon these; what the owl cries out, let that be in vain, as well as whatever footprint the dove makes in the fire.

Those two messengers of yours, O Nirṛti, who have come here to our house—whether sent or unsent—let that footstep be [erased] by the dove and the owl. Let this [bird] fly hither for freedom from enmity; let it settle here for the sake of heroic sons. Speak away, speak far away, following the distant year! So that in the house of Yama you may behold one who is sapless, behold one who is worthless.

The gods ploughed this barley, mixed with honey, upon the Sarasvatī at the Maṇi-stone. Indra, the lord of a hundred powers, was the master of the plough; the Maruts, the givers of good gifts, were the ploughmen.

That exhilaration of yours which is hairless or dishevelled, by which you make a man an object of ridicule—far from you I cut down other woods; do you, O Śamī tree, grow forth with a hundred branches.
O you of broad leaves, fortunate one, grown great by rain, observer of the cosmic order (ṛtāvarī)! Like a mother to her sons, be gracious toward my hair, O Śamī.

This spotted bull has stepped forth; he has settled before his mother, and as he moves toward the light, he approaches his father. He moves between the two luminous realms, breathing out from his breath. The mighty one has looked out across the sun. He rules over thirty stations; the winged bird of speech has taken his stand, facing each day at the break of dawn.
Offer this into the inner fire with clarified butter; it is the destroyer of sorcerers. Burn away the demons from afar, O Agni; do not let them scorch our homes.
O Piśācas, may Rudra shatter your necks; O Yātudhānas, may he crush your ribs. May the plant of universal power, sent by Yama, overcome you.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, let there be safety for us here; with your flame, drive the devourers away. Let them find neither a kinsman nor a refuge; striking one another down, let them go unto death.
For whom this vast, delightful realm of light belongs—reaching to the very edge of the sky, yoked for his impetuous assault, and ever new—for that Indra it is.
The bold one, having been made bold, does not yield his power to an assailant; as of old, the fame and the power of Indra are such that no one can assail them.
May he grant us that wealth, vast and golden-hued; Indra, the most powerful lord among men.
Send forth your speech to Agni, the bull of the peoples; may he carry us across our enemies.
Agni, who utterly consumes the demons with his sharp flame—may he carry us across our enemies.
He who shines forth from the furthest distance across the desert wastes—may he carry us beyond our enemies.
He who gazes upon all beings and beholds them together—may he carry us beyond our enemies.
He, the radiant Agni, who was born on the further shore of this realm—may he carry us beyond our enemies.
May Vaiśvānara come forth from afar for our protection; may Agni attend to our well-spoken hymns.
May Vaiśvānara come to this sacrifice of ours in unison; may Agni [attend] to our recitations when we are in distress.
Vaiśvānara has fashioned the hymn and the chant of the Aṅgirases; may he bestow splendor and heavenly light upon them.
We implore Vaiśvānara, the observer of cosmic order, the lord of the light of truth, the imperishable heat.
He has fashioned all things; he, the controller, sends forth the seasons, promoting the vigor of the sacrifice.
Agni, in the highest abodes, is the desire of what has been and what is to be; as the sole sovereign ruler, he shines forth.

The thousand-eyed Curse has come near, having yoked his chariot; like a wolf seeking its prey, he seeks out my curser and goes to his house. O Curse, avoid our home, passing us by like fire burning a lake; strike down our curser here like a thunderbolt from heaven striking a tree.
Whether he be one who curses us though we do not curse, or one who curses us while we are cursing—him I cast toward death, like a piece of meat thrown to a dog.

The splendor that is in the lion, in the tiger, or in the adder; that which is in fire, in the Brahmin, and in the sun—the auspicious goddess who gave birth to Indra as her son, may she come to us, in harmony with our luster.

The splendor that is in the elephant, in the leopard, and in gold; that which is in the waters, in the cattle, and in men—the auspicious goddess who gave birth to Indra as her son, may she come to us, in harmony with our luster.

That which is in the chariot, in the axles, in the strength of the bull, in the wind, in Parjanya, and in the vigor of Varuṇa—the auspicious goddess who gave birth to Indra as her son, may she come to us, in harmony with our luster.

In the kingly drum, in the extension, in the vigor of the horse, in the creative power of man—may that auspicious goddess who gave birth to Indra come to us, in harmony with our splendor. May the glorious oblation, impelled by Indra, increase—a thousandfold in heroism, well-sustained, and produced by strength. As it spreads forth for far-reaching vision, cause me, the possessor of the oblation, to grow toward preeminence. With reverence, let us worship the glorious Indra, who is glorious through glories. O Indra, grant us a kingdom impelled by you; may we abide in the bounty of you, the glorious one.
Glorious is Indra, glorious is Agni, glorious was Soma born. Glorious among all that exists, may I be the most glorious.
May Heaven and Earth grant us fearlessness here; may Soma and Savitṛ grant us fearlessness. May the wide mid-air and the oblation to the Seven Seers grant us fearlessness.

For this village, may the four quarters grant strength, prosperity, and well-being; may Savitṛ grant us well-being. May Indra, who has no enemy, grant us fearlessness; let the wrath of kings fall elsewhere.
Make us friendless from below, O Indra; make us friendless from above; make us friendless from behind, and make us friendless from the front.
To mind, to consciousness, to thoughts, to intention, and to perception; to memory, to hearing, and to sight—may we worship these with our oblation.
To the out-breath, the diffused breath, and the vital breath that provides abundant nourishment; to Sarasvatī of the wide expanse—may we worship her with our oblation.
May the divine seers who protect our bodies, those who are born of our own bodies, not abandon us. O immortals, attend upon us mortals; grant us long life that we may live.
Like the string from a bow, I loosen the anger from your heart, so that we two, becoming of one mind, may move together like two friends.

Like two friends, let us be together; I cast down your fury. We bind your heavy fury beneath a stone. I trample upon your fury with my heel and my forefoot, so that you may speak no more against your will, but shall follow my mind.

This *darbha* grass is free from anger, for oneself and for one’s own conduct; it is called the pacifier of wrath, the wrath of the wrathful. This *darbha*, which has many roots and stands firm reaching toward the ocean, having risen from the earth, is called the pacifier of wrath.
We loosen your jaw-joint and we loosen your jaw; so that you may not speak against your will, you shall come under the sway of my mind.
The sky has stood firm; the earth has stood firm; this entire world has stood firm. The trees have stood with their tops erect; let this disease of yours stand still.
Of the hundred remedies that are yours, and the thousand gathered together, the most excellent is the remedy for discharge—the best, the destroyer of disease.

You are the urine of Rudra, the navel of immortality. You are indeed named Viṣāṇakā; you have arisen from the root of the Fathers, the destroyer of the Vātīkṛta disease. Go away, O evil-minded one! Why do you utter imprecations? Depart! I do not desire you. Wander among the trees and the forests. My mind is fixed on my houses and my cattle.
Whatever we have committed through cursing, through reviling, or through imprecation—whether awake or asleep—may Agni cast all those evil deeds and all that is disagreeable far away from us.
O Indra, O Brahmaṇaspati, whatever we do in vain, may the wise Aṅgirasa protect us from misfortune and from distress.

You who are neither living nor dead, you are the immortal germ of the gods, O Sleep. Varuṇānī is your mother, Yama is your father; Araru is your name. We know your origin, O Sleep: you are the son of the divine sisters, the agent of Yama. You are the Ender, you are Death; as such we know you, O Sleep. Protect us, O Sleep, from evil dreaming.
Just as they collect a sixteenth part, just as a half-share, just as a debt, even so do we collect all evil dreams and deliver them to our enemy.

May Agni Vaiśvānara, the maker of all, the source of all well-being, protect us at the morning pressing. May he, the purifier, bestow wealth upon us; may we be long-lived, sharing the draught together.
May the All-Gods, the Maruts, and Indra not forsake us at this second pressing. Long-lived and speaking what is pleasing to them, may we abide in the good favor of the gods.

This is the third pressing of the sages, those who by means of Truth set the chalice in motion. May those sons of Sudhanvan, having attained the light of heaven, lead our well-performed sacrifice toward greater prosperity.
You are the falcon, having the *gāyatrī* meter; I take hold of you. Carry me safely to the conclusion of this sacrifice, *svāhā*!
You are the *ṛbhu*, having the *jagatī* meter; I take hold of you. Carry me safely to the conclusion of this sacrifice, *svāhā*!
You are the bull, having the *triṣṭubh* meter; I take hold of you. Carry me safely to the conclusion of this sacrifice, *svāhā*!
O Agni, no mortal has ever reached the core of your body; the monkey devours his own sharpness, as a cow her own afterbirth.

Like a ram, you spread yourself out and draw yourself together across the wide space when the upper and lower stones chew upon you. Crushing head with head and jaw with jaw, he devours the stalks with his golden jaws.

The fair-winged ones have raised their voice toward heaven; the dark, vigorous ones have danced in the lair. When they descend to the appointed place of the lower stone, those who rest in the sun have deposited abundant seed.

O Aśvins, slay the *tarda*, the *samaṅka*, and the *ākhu*; split the head and crush the vertebrae! Bind their mouths as if with barley-grain, and then grant safety to the grain. O *tarda*! O *pataṅga*! O *jabhya*! O *upakvasa*! Like a sacrificial oblation that has not been properly prepared, depart without eating these barley-grains, without doing harm!

O Lord of the *tarda*s, O Lord of the *vaghā*s, you who have sharp jaws, listen to me! Those forest-dwellers who are devourers, and whoever else you are who are devourers—all of them we cause to be crushed.
Purified by the filter of the wind, Soma has flowed across toward us, the ally and friend of Indra.
May the Waters, our mothers, prepare us; may they who purify with ghee cleanse us with ghee. For the goddesses carry away every impurity; from them I emerge bright and purified.
Whatever offense against the divine host, O Varuṇa, men commit here, whether through lack of awareness or by violating your law, O God, do not harm us for that sin.
Sūrya rises from the sky in front, consuming the demons; Āditya, seen by all, comes from the mountains, the slayer of the unseen.
The cows have settled in their stall; the wild beasts have entered their lairs; the waves of the rivers have subsided; and the unseen [demons] have been struck down.

I have brought this wise, famous plant of Kaṇva, which bestows life and possesses all healing powers; may it destroy his unseen affliction. May both Heaven and Earth, the two wise ones, and the great, bright one fulfill this through the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). May Svadhā take notice, and may Soma, Agni, Vāyu, Savitṛ, and Bhaga protect us. Let breath return to us, let the self return, let sight return, and let the vital spirit return. May Vaiśvānara, the undeceivable protector of our bodies, stand within us against all misfortunes.
We have come together with splendor, with milk, with our bodies, and with a gracious mind. May Tvaṣṭṛ grant us wide space here; may he smooth over whatever in our bodies is injured.
This is that superior bond; I adorn Indra for his success. Increase his sovereignty and great glory, as rain increases the grass.

O Agni and Soma, uphold for him sovereign power and for him wealth; establish him as the superior ally in the conquest of this kingdom. Whether he be a kinsman or a stranger who assails us, subject all of them to my will for the sake of the sacrificer who presses the soma.
The many paths leading to the gods that traverse the space between heaven and earth—whichever of these carries one without loss, to him may all the gods deliver me here.
May summer, winter, the cool season, spring, autumn, and the rains establish us in well-being. Grant us a share in cattle and in progeny; may we abide in your shelter, protected from the wind.
Pay great homage to Idāvatsara, Parivatsara, and Saṃvatsara. May we remain within the benevolence and auspicious goodwill of those worthy of sacrifice.

O gods, let not the serpent slay us along with our children and our men. Let him not release his grip upon what is bound, nor close his gaping jaws. Homage to the divine hosts! Homage be to the Black One; homage to the one with transverse stripes; homage to the self-born, tawny one; homage to the divine hosts!
I join together your tooth with the tooth, and your jaw with the jaw; I join your tongue with the tongue, and your mouth with the mouth.
This indeed is the remedy, this is the remedy of Rudra, by which he drove away the arrow with its single shaft and hundred points.
Sprinkle us with *jālāṣa*, sprinkle us with *jālāṣa*. *Jālāṣa* is a powerful medicine; through it, be gracious to us so that we may live.
May there be peace for us and joy for us, and may nothing whatsoever afflict us. May our sin be laid low; may everything be a medicine for us—may everything be a medicine for us.
May Indra, the Maghavan, make me glorious; may both these, Heaven and Earth, make me glorious. May the god Savitṛ make me glorious; may I be dear here to the giver of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

As Indra is glorious among Heaven and Earth, as the waters are glorious among the plants, even so may we be glorious among all the gods. Glorious is Indra, glorious is Agni; glorious Soma was born. May I be the most glorious of all that exists.
To the oxen you first, to the milch-cows you, O Arundhatī! Grant protection to the non-milch cow and her offspring, and to the four-footed.

May the herb Arundhatī, together with the goddesses, grant us protection. May she make our cow-pen full of milk and our men free from disease. I invoke the all-formed, auspicious, and life-giving one; may she drive away the missile of Rudra far from our cattle.
Aryaman comes here from the east with his top-knot loosened, seeking for this young woman a husband and a wife for the one who seeks them.
She has grown weary, O Aryaman, as she goes to the gathering of others. Truly, O Aryaman, other women now go to her own gathering.
The Ordainer has supported the earth; the Ordainer [has supported] the sky and the sun. May the Ordainer bestow upon this maiden a husband according to her desire.
May the waters send sweetness to me; for me the Sun has brought forth light. To me have all the gods and those born of fervor [given their gifts]; may the god Savitar grant me wide space.
I have separated the earth and the sky; I generated the seven seasons at once. I declare what is truth and what is falsehood; I encompass the divine speech and the tribes of men.
I gave birth to the earth and the sky; I generated the seven seasons and the rivers. I declare what is truth and what is falsehood—I who have delighted in Agni and Soma as friends.

May Vaiśvānara purify us with his rays; may the vitalizing Wind purify us with his breath through the firmaments. May Heaven and Earth, rich in milk, observers of Truth and worthy of sacrifice, purify us with their milk.
Seize upon the gracious speech of Vaiśvānara, whose regions and bodies have smooth backs. Praising him with that [speech] at our communal feasts, may we be masters of riches.
Seize upon the splendor of Vaiśvānara, becoming pure, bright, and purifying. Rejoicing here in the communal feast with the sacred food (*iḍā*), may we long behold the rising sun.

The bond that the goddess Nirṛti fastened upon your necks, which was impossible to unloose—that I loosen for you, for long life, for splendor, and for strength. Eat food that causes no disease, being impelled [by me].

Homage be to you, O Nirṛti of sharp brilliance; loosen these iron fetters. Yama gives you back to me; homage be to that Yama, to Death. You were bound here to an iron post by thousands of deaths. In harmony with Yama and the Fathers, cause this man to ascend to the highest heaven.

O Bull Agni, you gather together all the riches of the noble one. Kindled at the place of *iḍ*, bring us wealth. Agree with one another; be united; let your minds be in harmony, just as the ancient gods, being in accord, attend to their portion. The counsel is common, the assembly is common, the vow is common, and their thought is shared. With this common oblation I sacrifice for you; enter into a common consciousness.
United be your intention, united be your hearts; may your mind be one, so that you may be in perfect harmony.
May wrath be appeased; may the two arms, yoked with the mind, be stilled. O Parāśara, crush their forward-moving vigor, and then bestow wealth upon us.

The handless weapon that you gods hurl against those who are handless—by means of this oblation, I sever the arms of my enemies. Indra first performed this hand-slaying act against the Asuras. May my warriors be victorious with Indra as their steadfast ally.
Handless shall be the enemy who assails us with his armies when they come to fight. O Indra, strike them down with your great weapon; let the plunderer of evil flee, pierced through.
Whether you are stretching [the bow], drawing it back, or rushing forward while discharging arrows—your enemies are rendered handless; Indra has struck them down for you today.
Handless shall be the enemies; we cause their limbs to wither away. Then, O Indra, let us divide their possessions among ourselves by the hundreds.
Indra and Pūṣan have traversed the paths on all sides. May those armies of the enemies be confounded today, far beyond our reach.
Foolish enemies, move about like headless serpents! May Indra slay the best among you, you fools, with his fire!
Bind a deer-skin upon these; strike terror into the antelope! Let the enemy flee away, while the cow comes toward us.
