O divine Agni, send those longing gods whom you bring hither to their own dwelling place; having eaten and drunk the sweet draughts, O Vasus, bestow riches upon this man.
O Gods, we have prepared easy seats for you who have come to this libation with pleasure; carrying and bringing your own treasures, ascend to heaven following the wealthy Gharma.
O sacrifice, go to the sacrifice; go to the lord of the sacrifice; go to your own source, svāhā!
This is your sacrifice, O lord of the sacrifice, accompanied by the hymn of praise (sūktavāka); may it be rich in heroic power, svāhā!
Vaṣaṭ to those for whom the offering has been made, vaṣaṭ to those for whom it has not been made! O gods who know the way, having found the way, go upon the way.
O Lord of the Mind, carry this sacrifice of ours to the gods in heaven; *svāhā*! To heaven, *svāhā*! To earth, *svāhā*! To the intermediate space, *svāhā*! To the wind, in its abode, *svāhā*!

The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is sprinkled with the oblation of clarified butter; may it be united with Indra, the Vasus, and the Maruts; may it be united with the gods, with all the Viśvedevas. Let the oblation go to Indra; *svāhā*! Strew around, enclose the altar; do not steal the kinswoman lying there. This golden, green seat for the Hotṛ-priest—these are the neck-ornaments (*niṣkas*) in the world of the sacrificer.
I turn away from evil dreams, from bad dreams, and from misfortune. I make the sacred word (*brahman*) my protection; may the sorrows that have dreams as their mouth be driven far away.

Whatever food I eat in a dream that is not found in the morning—may all that be auspicious for me, for it is not seen by day. Having paid homage to Heaven and Earth, to the Intermediate Space, and to Death, I look upward; standing erect, may the lords not harm me.
Which Kṣatriya, seeking welfare, shall lead us out from this blameless malice? Who, desiring sacrifice, or who desiring fulfillment, or who among the gods wins long life?
Who, delighting in friendship with Bṛhaspati, shall fashion his body at will, [receiving] the speckled cow, well-milking and ever-calfed, given by Varuṇa to Atharvan?
Departing from what is human and choosing the divine word, turn toward our guidance together with all your friends.

Whatever we have done through forgetfulness, O Agni, or whatever we have failed in our conduct, O Jātavedas—protect us from that, O wise one; for the welfare of our friends, let there be immortality for us.
From heaven, the seven rays of the sun bring them down; the waters of the ocean, those flowing streams, have caused the barb to fall away.

Whether he who seeks to harm us lurks in secret or openly, whether he be a stranger or one of our own kin, O Agni—let him turn back with his teeth as a devouring wolf; let there be neither his wealth nor his offspring remaining, O Agni.

O Jātavedas, whoever should assail us while we sleep or wake, whether we stand still or move about—with Vaiśvānara as your companion and in harmony with him, burn them down, O Jātavedas, turning them back. Homage to this fierce, tawny one who holds dominion over the dice. With clarified butter I propitiate Kali; may he be gracious to us in such a state.
O Agni, carry ghee for the Apsarases; carry dust, sand, and water for the dice. May the gods, enjoying the offering according to their respective portions, rejoice in both kinds of oblations.
The Apsarases revel in the communal feast between the sun and the oblation-holder. May they sprinkle my hands with ghee; may they deliver my rival, the gambler, into my power.
Bring misfortune upon the one who plays against us; flow toward us with ghee! Strike down like a tree with a thunderbolt him who plays against us.
He who has made this wealth for us to win, he who [made] the seizing and the leaving of the dice—may that god, enjoying this our oblation, rejoice with the Gandharvas in common revelry.
"O Dwellers Together," such is your name; for the dice are fierce-looking sustainers of the kingdom. To you, those drops of Soma, we shall pay worship with an oblation; may we be masters of riches.
Since I call upon the gods in need, since we have lived the life of sacred study (*brahmacarya*), and since I seize the brown dice—may they be gracious to us in such a state.
O Agni and Indra, you two have irresistibly struck down the Vṛtras for the donor; for you both are the greatest slayers of Vṛtra.

You two who first conquered the light of heaven and who have taken their stand over all beings—those two bulls, the leaders of men, with the thunderbolt in their arms, Agni and Indra, the slayers of Vṛtra, I invoke.
Bṛhaspati, the god, has approached you with the cup; O Indra, enter us with our songs for the sake of the sacrificer who presses the soma.

You are the belly of Indra, the receptacle for Soma, the self of the gods and of men. Procreate here those offspring of yours which are in these [women] and those which are elsewhere; let them find delight here.

Adorning heaven and earth, who are near with their benevolence and possess great vows, the seven divine waters have flowed forth; may they deliver us from distress. May they release me from the curse, and also from that which pertains to Varuṇa, and also from Yama’s fetter, and from every offense against the gods.
O *tṛṣṭika*, O *tṛṣṭa*, you who are the *vandana* plant, cut that one up, O *tṛṣṭika*! Just as those who have been made hateful [are treated] for the sake of this man who possesses a phallus.
You are *tṛṣṭā*, you are *tṛṣṭikā*; you are poison, you are the poison-destroyer (*viṣātakī*). Just as you are rejected, like a barren cow of a bull.
I take from your flanks; I take from your heart. I take from the appearance of your mouth; I take all your splendor (*varcas*).
Let the diseases depart from here, let the ill-wills and the curses depart! May Agni slay the demoniac ones; may Soma slay those who seek to harm us.
Fly away from here, O evil Fortune; perish from here and fly away to yonder place! With an iron hook, we fasten you to our enemy.
That ill-favored fortune which, like a creeper clinging to a tree, has fallen away from me—O Savitṛ, bestow that elsewhere than upon us, O golden-handed one, granting us wealth!
A hundred and one fortunes are born together with the body at the birth of a mortal; of these, we cast out the most evil ones from here; O Jātavedas, grant us those that are auspicious.
I have separated these [fortunes] like cattle standing in a byre: may the meritorious fortunes remain, and those that are evil I have destroyed.
Homage to Rūru, to Cyavana, to Nodana, to Dhṛṣṇu; homage to Śīta, who fulfills former desires. May he who comes upon this frog on one day or on two days—may that lawless one come upon him.
Come, O Indra, with your joyful bay horses whose manes are like peacock feathers. Let no one hold you back, as fowlers do a bird; pass over them as if across a desert.

I cover your vital organs with armor; may King Soma clothe you with immortality. May Varuṇa make for you a space wider than the wide; may the gods rejoice after you as you conquer. Homage to the Ender, to Death! May your out-breaths and in-breaths rest here. May this man remain here together with his life-force, in the portion of the Sun, in the world of immortality.
Bhaga has lifted him up; Soma, rich in stalks, has lifted him up. The Maruts, the gods, have lifted him up; Indra and Agni have lifted him up for his well-being.
Here is your breath, here your vital force, here your life, here your mind. We lift you up from the snares of Destruction with a divine word.
Step forth from here, O man; do not fall down, casting off the snare of death. Do not be cut off from this world, from the sight of Agni and the Sun.
For you let Vāta Mātariśvan blow; for you let the immortal waters rain down. Let the Sun heat his rays for the well-being of your body; let Death spare you—do not perish!
This garden is not for you to depart from, O man; I grant you life and skillfulness. Ascend this immortal, comfortable chariot, and then, having grown old, you shall speak at the assembly.
Let not your mind go there; let it not pass away; do not abandon the living, nor follow after the fathers. May all the gods protect you here.
Do not long for those who have gone, who lead one to the far distance. Ascend from darkness to the light; come! We take hold of your hands.
Both Śyāma and Śabala, the two dogs sent by Yama who guard the path, have been dispatched; come hither, do not hesitate, and do not stand here with your mind turned away.

Do not follow this path; it is terrible, that by which you were led before. I tell you this: O man, do not step into this darkness. Fear lies beyond; safety is here before you. Let not the flesh-eater, the prowler from afar, harm you. May the sky protect you; may the earth and the sun protect you; and may the moon protect you. May the intermediate space protect you from the missiles of the gods.

May they protect you, may they guard you; homage to them, svāhā to them! May they protect you
May Vāyu, Indra, Dhātṛ, and the protecting Savitṛ place you among the living beings for the sake of the ocean. May breath and strength not abandon you; we call back your life-force after you.

Let not the jaw with its teeth, nor darkness, find you; let not the tongue perish upon the sacrificial grass. How might you be? May the Ādityas and the Vasus lift you up; may Indra and Agni lift you up for your well-being.
May Heaven lift you up, may Earth lift you up, may Prajāpati have grasped you up. May the plants, whose king is Soma, have delivered you up from death.
O gods, let this man remain right here; let him not go from here to yonder world. With a thousandfold power, we cause him to cross over from death.
I have rescued you from death; may those who bestow vigor kindle you. Let not women with disheveled hair, let not weeping mourners wail for you.
I have brought you back; I have found you. You have returned, renewed. O you whose every limb is whole, I have found your entire sight and your full span of life.
Light has emerged for you; darkness has departed from you. We cast away from you death, destruction, and consumption.

Take hold of this attainment of immortality; may your life-span be unbroken until old age. I bring back your vital breath and your life-force; do not go to the realm of dust or darkness, do not perish.
Come hither toward the light of the living; I bring you back for a hundred autumns. Loosen the bonds of death and ill-fortune; I bestow upon you a further, more extended lifespan.
From the wind I have found your breath; from the sun, I [have found] your eye. That mind of yours which is in you, I maintain for you. Be conscious with your limbs; speak with your tongue, talking.

With the breath of bipeds and quadrupeds, I blow upon you like a fire that has been kindled. Homage to your eye, O Death; homage to your breath have I paid. Let this man live, let him not die; we cause him to rise up again. I prepare a remedy for him; O Death, do not slay this man.
I invoke here for his safety the life-giving, unaging, living herb—the protecting, conquering, and powerful one.

Speak for him; do not seize him; release him! Let him remain here, possessing all his life-force. O Bhava and Aśarva, be gracious, grant us protection, ward off misfortune, and bestow long life upon him.

O Death, speak on his behalf; have mercy on him! Let him go forth from here unharmed, with all his limbs intact, hearing well, reaching old age at a hundred years, and may he enjoy happiness through his own self.

May the weapon of the gods spare you; I carry you across. I have delivered you from the dust, I have saved you from death. Far away I drive the flesh-eating Agni; for the sake of your life, I place this boundary around you.
O Death, that path of yours which leads through the dust-strewn realm and is unassailable—protecting this man from it, we make the sacred word (*brahman*) his armor.

I bestow upon you, O Prāṇa and Apāna, old age, death, long life, and well-being. I drive away all the messengers of Yama who roam about, sent by Vaivasvata. From afar, I repel ill-will, Destruction, the Seizer from beyond, the flesh-eating Piśācas, and every demon—whatever is evil; we strike it down like darkness.

From the immortal, life-giving Agni, the Knower of Beings, I win for you his breath, so that you may not perish and may live in harmony with the immortals; this I do for you, and may it be fulfilled for you. May Heaven and Earth be auspicious to you, free from heat and full of splendor. May the Sun shine warmly upon you, and may the Wind blow gently to your heart. May the celestial waters, rich in milk, flow auspiciously over you. May the plants be auspicious to you. I have lifted you up from the lower earth toward the higher earth; there, may both Ādityas, Sūrya and Candramas, protect you.

That garment which is your covering, that girdle which you fasten—may we make that auspicious for your body; may it be non-rough to your touch. When the barber shaves your hair and beard with a well-sharpened, keen-edged razor, do not steal away our life, making our face beautiful.
May rice and barley be auspicious for you, free from disease and not causing emaciation; these two drive away consumption and release one from distress.
Whatever you eat, whatever you drink—the milk of the ploughed field, what is edible and what is inedible—I make all that food for you free from poison.
For the day and for the night, for both together we entrust you. From the stingy spirits who desire to devour, protect this one for me.
A hundred, ten thousand, and two ages—three and four—we allot for you. May Indra, Agni, and all the gods grant their approval to you, being free from anger.
For the autumn, for the winter, for the spring, and for the summer, we entrust you. Pleasant are the rains for you, in which the plants flourish.
Death rules over bipeds; Death rules over quadrupeds. Therefore, I lift you up from Death, the Lord of Cattle; do not be afraid.
Unharmed, you shall not die; you shall not die. Do not fear. Truly, they do not die there, nor do they go to the lowest darkness.

Everyone indeed lives there—the cow, the horse, the man, and the beast—where this *brahman* is performed as a protective enclosure for the sake of life. May it protect you from those of equal kin, from sorcery, and from your own kinsmen. Be free from death, immortal, and long-lived; let not your vital breaths abandon your body. From the one hundred and one deaths and the destructive powers that must be overcome, may the gods release you from them, and from Agni Vaiśvānara.

Thou art the body of Agni, the deliverer; thou art the slayer of demons, the slayer of rivals, and the dispeller of disease. Pūtudru by name is the healing medicine. {5} I anoint the demon-slaying, powerful one; I approach the Friend for his most extensive protection. May Agni, sharpened and kindled by our rites, protect us from harm by day and by night.
O Jātavedas, kindled with thy flame, touch the sorcerers with thy iron teeth. Seize the foolish worshippers of idols with thy tongue; having devoured the flesh-eaters, cast them into thy mouth.
Apply both your jaws, O you who possess both [powers], as a fierce predator sharpening its lower and upper fangs. And traverse the mid-air, O Agni; seize the sorcerers with your jaws.
O Agni, split open the skin of the sorcerer; let the fierce thunderbolt strike him down with its heat. O Jātavedas, crush his joints; let the flesh-eating, flesh-craving [fire] tear him apart.

Wherever you now see him, O Agni Jātavedas—whether he stands still or moves about, or whether he flies through the mid-air—pierce that sorcerer with your arrow, O sharp-shooter, as you sharpen your bolt.

Bending your arrows with sacrifices, O Agni, like one fashioning shafts with fire, and smearing them with thunderbolts—pierce the sorcerers (*yātudhāna*) to the heart with these; break their arms back against them. And seize those who have already seized [us], O Jātavedas; seize the sorcerers with your spears. O Agni, blazing forth, strike them down first; let the ravening, spotted vultures devour him who eats raw flesh. Speak here, O Agni, which one is that sorcerer who does this? Seize him with your fuel, O youngest one; deliver him into the eye of the one who watches over men.

With your sharp eye, O Agni, protect the sacrifice; lead it forward toward the Vasus, O wise one. Let not the sorcerers deceive you as you burn against the murderous Rākṣasas, O you who watch over men.

Three times let the sorcerer go toward your snare, O Agni, he who strikes with falsehood against the Truth. O Jātavedas, thundering with your flame, bind him down in the very presence of the singer.

O Agni, whatever curse the pair utters today, or whatever harshness of speech the singers produce—whatever arrow is born from the fury of the mind—with that pierce the sorcerers in their hearts! Destroy the sorcerers with your heat; O Agni, destroy the *rakṣas* with your flame! Destroy the fools who worship false gods with your radiance; destroy those who feed on life-breath while they blaze with malice!
May the gods today destroy the wicked man; may the curses released strike him back. May the arrows of the voice pierce the thief in his vital parts. May the sorcerer fall into the snare of everyone!

The sorcerer who smears himself with human flesh, the sorcerer who [smears himself] with the flesh of horses or cattle, or he who carries off the milk of the cow—O Agni, shatter their heads with your fiery heat!
Let the sorcerers take poison from the cows; let those of evil intent be cut down for Aditi. May the god Savitar cast them away; may they lose their share of the plants. May they perish!

The milk of the cow belongs to the year; may no sorcerer, O watcher of men, consume it from me. O Agni, whichever one seeks to satisfy himself with the first-milked cream, pierce him in his vital organ with your flame as he turns toward you.
From of old, O Agni, you have crushed the sorcerers; the *rakṣas* have never conquered you in battles. Burn up the flesh-eaters along with their delusions; let none escape your divine missile.
O Agni, protect us from below and from above; protect us from behind and from the front. May those ageless and most scorching flames of yours, glowing against the one who utters evil, consume him.

O Agni, bestow that vision upon the singer by which you behold the hoof-striking sorcerers; like Atharvan, with divine light, consume the mindless one who violates the truth. O victorious Agni, we place you around us as a fortress, you the inspired sage, day after day—bold in appearance, the slayer of the treacherous.
With poison, strike down the demons, the treacherous ones; O Agni, with your sharp flame and with your blazing rays whose tips are glowing hot.
Agni shines forth with lofty light; he makes all things manifest by his greatness. He overcomes the godless, evil-plotting deceits; he sharpens his two horns to gore the Rākṣasas.

O Jātavedas, with those two horns of yours which are ageless, keen-edged, and sharpened by prayer—with them, O Jātavedas, strike back with your flame against the Kimīdin who, with an evil heart, assails us. Pierce him through with your radiance.

O Indra and Soma, burn the *rakṣas*, subdue it, and cast it down, O Bulls; strike down those who increase the darkness. Crush the senseless ones, consume them with fire, slay them, drive them away, and pierce the devourers.

O Indra and Soma, let the evil-plotting one be scorched by his own evil, like a heated cauldron placed upon the fire. Against the hater of prayer, the flesh-eater with his terrible eye, the *kimīdin*—bestow upon him unyielding hatred.

O Indra and Soma, cast the evildoers into the bottomless pit, into the darkness from which not even one of them may rise again; let that wrathful power of yours be for our victory. O Indra and Soma, hurl down the weapon from heaven and from earth, the crusher of the one who speaks evil. Fashion from the mountains a celestial bolt wherewith you burn up the waxing demon.

O Indra and Soma, hurl [your weapons] down from heaven; with your stone-hurling bolts heated by fire, with your unaging, burning blows, pierce the devourers into the abyss so that they go forth voiceless.

O Indra and Soma, let this prayer encompass you on every side, like a girth around two spirited horses. This oblation which I present to you with wisdom—quicken these sacred hymns, O Lords of men, as if quickening two kings.

Remember us with your impetuous ways; strike down the deceivers, the crooked-minded Rākṣasas. O Indra and Soma, let there be no easy path for the evil-doer who ever seeks to harm me, the deceiver. May he who, with a simple mind, walks uprightly, be called a liar by those who revile him with false words—may that speaker of untruth be like water held in the hollow of one's hand, caught and lost, O Indra!

Those who, through their own ways, scatter the simple-minded, or who, by their own natures, corrupt what is auspicious—may Soma deliver them over to the serpent, or may he place them in the lap of Destruction (Nirṛti).

May he be defeated in his own person and his offspring; may he lie beneath all the three earths! O Gods, may the glory of him who seeks to harm me by day and by night wither away.

For the discerning person, truth and falsehood are easily distinguished; these two words contend with one another. Of these two, that which is true, whichever is more upright—that indeed Soma protects; he strikes down the false.
Truly, Soma does not further the crooked man, nor the warrior who holds office falsely. He slays the *rakṣas* and slays the one who speaks untruth; both lie ensnared in Indra’s grasp.

Whether I am a false god, O Agni, or whether I have invoked the gods in vain, why, O Jātavedas, are you angry with us? May those of deceitful speech meet their destruction! May I die this very day if I am a sorcerer, or if I have consumed the life-force of a man. Then may he be separated from his ten sons—he who falsely says of me, "He is a sorcerer.
May Indra slay with a mighty weapon him who calls me a sorcerer though I am no sorcerer, or the *rakṣas* who says, "I am a seer. May he fall as the lowest of all living beings.
She who goes forth like an owl at night, hiding her body from the malicious one—may she fall into the endless pit. May the pressing-stones strike down the *rakṣas* with their clattering sounds.

Spread out, O Maruts, search among the people; seize the *rakṣas* and grind them to pieces—those who fly about by night having become birds, or those who have placed obstacles in the divine sacrifice.
Cast down the stone from heaven, O Indra; O Maghavan, sharpen it, whetted as it is by Soma. From the east, from the west, from below, and from above, strike down the demons with the mountain.

These indeed fly about as dog-demons; seeking to harm, they desire to deceive Indra, the undeceivable. Śakra sharpens his weapon for the treacherous; let him now hurl his thunderbolt at the sorcerers. Śakra sharpens his weapon for the treacherous; let him now hurl his thunderbolt at the sorcerers. Indra became the destroyer of the sorcerers who steal the oblation as they seek to attack. Let the mighty Śakra go forth against the existing demons, shattering them like an axe through a forest or like one breaking vessels.
Slay the owl-sorcerer, the screech-owl sorcerer, the dog-sorcerer, and the cuckoo-sorcerer; slay the eagle-sorcerer and the vulture-sorcerer—crush the demon, O Indra, like a grinding stone!
Let no demon, possessed of sorcery, strike us down; let the pairs of *kimīdin*s flee away. May the Earth protect us from earthly distress, and may the Atmosphere protect us from celestial distress.
O Indra, slay the male sorcerer and also the woman who exults in her magic power. Let the fools who worship false gods perish with their necks broken; let them not behold the rising sun.
Look back! Look forth! O Indra and Soma, remain awake! Cast your weapon at the Rākṣasas; hurl your thunderbolt at the sorcerers!

This amulet, this hero-gem, is bound upon the hero; it is powerful, a slayer of rivals, a brave hero, a protection, and most auspicious. This gem is a slayer of rivals, a possessor of great heroes, victorious, swift, overcoming, and fierce. As a hero, it goes forth counteracting and destroying sorcery. With this gem Indra slew Vṛtra; with this the wise one overcame the Asuras. With this he conquered both these, heaven and earth; with this he conquered the four quarters.
This amulet of Srāktya is a counter-turning, a protective amulet; it is powerful, subduing adversaries, and self-controlled. May it protect us from every side.
This Agni has said, this Soma has said, Bṛhaspati, Savitṛ, and Indra have said: "These gods, acting as my domestic priests, shall drive away hostile sorceries with these counter-protective amulets."
I have hidden myself from heaven and earth, as well as from day and the sun. O gods, acting as my high priests, may you drive away the hostile sorceries with these counter-spells.
Those people who make the *srāktya* amulet their armor—having ascended to heaven like the sun—he, the controller, drives away sorcery (*kṛtyā*).

With the *srāktya* amulet, like a wise seer, I have conquered all hostile armies; I strike down the demons and the sorceries. Whatever sorceries are of the *Āṅgirases*, whatever sorceries are of the *Asuras*, whatever sorceries are self-made, and whatever have been brought by others—let both kinds go far away to the distant realms, beyond ninety navigable rivers.

May the gods—Indra, Viṣṇu, Savitṛ, Rudra, Agni, Prajāpati, Parameṣṭhin, Virāj, Vaiśvānara, and all the seers—bind this amulet as armor for him. You are the best of herbs, like the ox among beasts of burden, and like the tiger among beasts of prey. That protective amulet which we sought and found, it is indeed a tiger, and also a lion, and also a bull; it is the crusher of rivals for whoever wears this amulet.
Neither the Apsarases, nor the Gandharvas, nor mortals slay him; he who wears this amulet shines forth in all directions.

Kaśyapa created you; Kaśyapa brought you forth. Indra bore you among men, and bearing you, he conquered his adversaries. The gods made this amulet a thousandfold power and a protective armor. Whoever seeks to harm you with sorcery, with consecrations, or with sacrifices—O Indra, strike him down with your hundred-knotted thunderbolt. This indeed is the *pratīvarta* amulet, powerful and victorious; may it protect our offspring and wealth, a secure defense and a source of great auspiciousness.
Without rivals for us from below, without rivals for us from above; O Indra, O Hero, place light before us so that we have no rivals from behind.
May Heaven and Earth be my armor; may the Day be my armor, and the Sun my armor. May Indra and Agni be my armor; may Dhātṛ bestow armor upon me.
May that thick, formidable armor belonging to Indra and Agni—which none of all the gods can pierce—protect my body on every side with its great might, so that I may be long-lived and reach old age.
The divine amulet has ascended for me from the earth for my safety. Enter this pillar, which is a protector of the body, providing triple protection for the sake of vigor.
May Indra bestow manly strength upon it. O gods, enter into this [pillar] so that there may be long life for a hundred autumns, and that he may be long-lived and reach old age.

Bestower of well-being, Lord of the people, slayer of Vṛtra, dispeller of enemies, the self-controlled Indra—the victorious, the unconquered, the drinker of Soma, the bringer of fearlessness, the bull—let him bind this amulet for you. Those two which your mother wiped clean when you were born, the finders of a husband: let not the ill-named one covet them there, nor the *aliṃśa*, nor the *vatsapa*. [Drive away] the *palāla* and *anupalāla*, the *śarku*, the *koka*, the *malimluca*, the *palījaka*, the *āśreṣa*, the *vavrivāsas*, the *ṛkṣagrīva*, and the *pramīlin*.
Do not enclose her; do not creep upon her; do not creep between her thighs. I prepare for her a remedy, a spell that drives away the one of ill-repute.
Both the one of ill-repute and the one of fair name desire her embrace. We strike away the stingy spirits; let the one of fair name seek after womanhood.
That black, hairy demon who springs from a clump of grass and has a snout—we drive him away from her, from her testicles and from her pubic region.

The brown *baja* has destroyed the flesh-eater who sniffs, feels about, and licks; he has destroyed the *arāya* and the dog-scurrying parasite. May the *baja* drive away from here those who lie upon you in sleep, appearing as a brother or like a father—those eunuchs with shaven heads (*tirīṭin*).
He who creeps toward you while you sleep, he who seeks to harm you while you are awake—the sun, moving around them like a shadow, has destroyed them.
O herb, destroy that man who makes this woman barren and whose children have died; make him blind and devoid of splendor.

Those who are ill-formed, who have ugly testicles, who wear skins and rags, who dance like eunuchs, and who make a clamor in the forest—those we cause to perish from here.
Those who cannot endure yonder sun as it blazes from the sky—those stingy ones, clothed in goat-skins, foul-smelling, with red mouths, the *makakas*—we cause them to perish.
O Indra, destroy the demons who carry their own bodies excessively upon their shoulders, and who goad the hips of women.
Those who go forward as bonds, carrying horns in their hands, who stand at the oven, laughing aloud, and who produce light within a thicket—those we cause to perish from here.

Those whose heels are in the rear and their heels are in the front, whose faces are in the front; those born of the threshing floor, born of dung-smoke, the *uruṇḍas*, and those who are *maṭmaṭas*; those with testicles like jars and lacking virility—O Brahmaṇaspati, destroy them by means of this awakening spell.
Let those with upturned eyes, who lack a guide, be without women and become eunuchs. O Herb, strike down him who seeks to violate this woman, who has no husband, against her own husband.

The *uddharṣin*, the *muni-keśa*, the *jambhayan*, the *marīmṛśa*, the approaching *udumbara*, the *tuṇḍela*, and the *śāluḍa*—pierce them with your foot and your heel, as a cow kicks over a cooking pot. Whoever touches your embryo, or kills your newborn child—let the tawny one (*piṅga*), armed with a fierce bow, pierce his heart through.
May the wind drive away like a cloud those female spirits who kill newborns as they are born and lie in wait; may it drive away the tawny Gandharvas who claim their share of women.

From Pavīnasa, from Taṅgalva, from Chāyaka, and even from Nagnaka—may Piṅga protect you on every side from the Kimīdin for the sake of offspring and the husband.
From the two-faced, the four-eyed, the five-footed, and the fingerless; from the one who creeps along the stalk, protect us from the one who rolls about repeatedly.
Those who eat raw flesh and those who eat the bloody meat of men; those long-haired ones who devour embryos—those we cause to perish from here.
Those who creep away from the sun like daughters-in-law from their father-in-law—let both *baja* and *piṅga* pierce them through the heart.
*Piṅga*, protect the one being born; let them not make a man into a woman. Let the egg-eaters not harm the embryo; drive the *kimīdin*s away from here!

Those plants that are brown and those that are bright, those that are ruddy and those that are speckled, those that are dark-grey and those that are black—all these herbs we address.
May they protect this man from consumption sent by the gods—those plants of which Heaven is the father, Earth the mother, and the ocean the root;
whose tip is the celestial waters, the herbs. May they destroy from limb after limb the consumption born of sin that afflicts you.

I invoke the spreading, the clumping, the single-stemmed, and the far-reaching herbs. I call upon those that are fibrous, those with joints, and those with many branches—these plants belonging to all the gods, powerful, and life-giving to man.
O conquering plants, with that power of yours which overcomes, and with that heroic strength and might which you possess—by these, deliver this man from this consumption. And so, I prepare a remedy:
I call hither for his safety the life-giving, unharmed, living plant—the Arundhatī, the upholding, the flowering, the honey-sweet.
May the wise ones who delight in my speech come hither, so that we may carry this man across from distress.
The fodder of Agni, the embryo of the waters, those plants that grow ever anew—may these healing herbs, firm and bearing a thousand names, be brought hither.
The *avakā* plants, whose womb is the water, whose very essence is moisture—may these sharp-horned herbs sweep away our misfortune.

Those fierce ones who do not release their hold, who have loosened Varuṇa’s bonds, and those who corrupt poison; moreover, those that are the devourers of consumption (balāsa) and the destroyers of magic spells (kṛtyā)—let those plants come here.
May the most powerful plants that have been purchased and praised protect the cow, the horse, the man, and the livestock in this village.

May these plants have honeyed roots, honeyed tips, and honeyed middles; may their leaves be honeyed and their flowers honeyed. May they, partakers of sweetness and consumers of nectar, yield clarified butter as food, with the cow as their leader. As many as there are, however many these herbs are upon the earth—may those thousand-leaved ones release me from death and from distress.

The Vaiyāghra gem, the protector of plants, the guardian against curses—may it drive away all diseases and demons far from us. They tremble at its roar like that of a lion; they flee from it as if from a fire brought near. May the consumption of cattle and men, driven away by these plants, pass into the navigable rivers.
The plants have released themselves from Agni Vaiśvānara; they have come, spreading over the earth—those of whom the Lord of the Forest is king.

Those Aṅgirasa plants that grow upon the mountains and upon the level plains: may those plants be full of sap and auspicious for us, bringing peace to our hearts. Those herbs which I know, and those which I see with my eyes, those unknown ones that we recognize, and those among whom we know nourishment is gathered.
May all the herbs together heed my word, so that we may carry this man across beyond misfortune.

We cause this person to drink this strength of that nectar; and thus I prepare a remedy so that he may live for a hundred years.
The boar knows the plant, the mongoose knows the healing herb; those which the serpents and the Gandharvas know, I invoke them for his protection.

Those which the fair-winged ones of Aṅgiras know, the celestial ones, and those which the swift ones know; those which the birds, the swans, and all winged creatures know; those herbs which the wild beasts know—I invoke them for his protection.
As many herbs as the inviolable cows eat, as many as goats and sheep [eat], so many herbs, brought hither, shall grant you shelter.
As many medicinal herbs as physicians know among men, so many all-healing ones do I bring unto you.
May those who bear flowers, those who bring forth fruit, those with fruit, and even those without fruit—may they all yield for him, like mothers, for his safety and well-being.

Exhaustion, fierce failure, and incurable affliction; fatigue, lassitude, and delusion—with these I overwhelm all those enemies.

From where were those two born? Which is that half? From which world, from which earth [did they come]? O calves of Virāj, you have risen up from the waters; I ask you, by which [means] were you milked?

He who, with his greatness, made the waters roar, lying upon a threefold womb—he the calf, the wish-fulfilling cow of Virāj, made his bodies secret in the cave. Those three great things, of which he joins speech as the fourth—one should know this through austerity as the Brahman, the wise one, in whom the one is yoked, in whom the one is yoked.

From the *bṛhat* [meter], the *sāmans* were fashioned; from the sixth, five were produced. The *bṛhat* was fashioned from the *bṛhatī*; from what was the *bṛhatī* measured? The *bṛhatī* was measured from its own measure (*mātrā*); the mother’s measure was fashioned from the measure. Indeed, *māyā* was born from *māyā*; from *māyā*, *Mātalī* was born.

The image of Vaiśvānara is above the sky, as far as Agni has extended across the two worlds (*rodasī*). From that sixth [place] from there, the hymns (*stoma*) go; from here they go toward the sixth day of the ritual cycle.

We six Ṛṣis, these Kaśyapas, ask you: for you indeed desire to yoke that which is yoked and that which is fit to be yoked. They call Virāj the father of Brahman; explain her to us, your friends, in her various forms—her who, when she moves forth, the sacrifices follow after her, and who, as she is being approached, they approach; in whose ordinance and impulse the sacrifice stirs—that is Virāj, O Ṛṣis, in the highest heaven.
One breath follows after the breaths of those who breathe, following the Virāj and the Svarāj. Some behold this beautiful Virāj who touches all; others do not behold her.
Who knows the state of union of Virāj? Who knows her seasons, and who her ritual order? Who knows her steps, how many times they have been milked, what her abode is, and how many dawns she possesses?
This is indeed she who first shone forth; she moves, having entered into these other [dawns]. Within her are great majesties; the bride, the mother of the ninefold, has prevailed.

Adorning themselves with the meters as their wings, the two Dawns move together along a common womb. Knowing the way, the two wives of Sūrya move together—the conscious, the radiant, the ageless, possessing abundant seed.
Following the path of *ṛta*, three have come; three heats have followed the seed. One quickens progeny, one nourishment, and one protects the kingdom of those who seek the gods.

Thinking this to be better, I have come here; I am auspicious in your friendship. Your holy *kratu* is of common origin; knowing all, it moves among you all. She stepped forth; she stepped down into the assembly hall. He who knows this goes to his assembly hall and becomes a member of the assembly. She stepped forth; she stepped down into the council. He who knows this goes to his council and becomes a member of the council.
She stepped forth; she stepped down into the invitation. He who knows this goes to his invitation and becomes worthy of invitation.
She rose up; she stood in the intermediate space, having stepped out in four directions.
The gods and humans said to her, "She alone knows that by which we both may live; let us invoke her."
They called her to them.
"Come, O Strength! Come, O Svadhā! Come, O Sūnṛtā! Come, O Irāvatī! Thus [he says].
Indra was her calf; the Gāyatrī was the tethering rope; the cloud was the udder.
The Bṛhat and the Rathantara were two breasts; the Yajñāyajñiya and the Vāmadevya were the other two.
By means of the Rathantara, the gods milked the plants; by means of the Bṛhat, they milked the wide expanse.

He who knows this becomes one whose success lies in cultivation and who is worthy of being supported by others.

King Soma was her calf, and the meter was her vessel. Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa milked her; he milked both sacred knowledge and ascetic heat (*tapas*). The seven seers subsist upon that sacred knowledge and ascetic heat. He who knows this becomes possessed of the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasin*) and one who is to be subsisted upon.

She rose up; she went to the gods. The gods called out to her: "O Urj, come! Indra was her calf, and the *camasa* cup was her vessel. The god Savitṛ milked her; he milked her as Urj (Nourishment) herself. The gods subsist upon that Urj; he who knows this becomes one who is to be subsisted upon.

She went forth; she came to the Gandharvas and Apsarases. The Gandharvas and Apsarases called out to her, "O you of holy fragrance, come! Citraratha Sauryavarcas was her calf, and a lotus leaf was her vessel. Vasuruci Sauryavarcas milked her; he milked out nothing but holy fragrance. The Gandharvas and Apsarases subsist upon that holy fragrance. He who knows this becomes one of holy fragrance, fit to be subsisted upon by others.

She stepped forth; she came to the *itarajanāḥ* (the other people). The *itarajanāḥ* called out to her, "O Tirodhāḥ, come! Kubera Vaiśravaṇa was her calf, and an unbaked earthen vessel was her drinking bowl. Rajatanābhi Kaberaka milked her; he milked her as Tirodhāḥ. The *pitaraḥ* (fathers) who are not *itarajanāḥ* subsist upon that Tirodhāḥ. He who knows this veils all evil and becomes one who is to be subsisted upon.

She rose up; she came to the serpents. The serpents called out to her, "Come, you who possess poison! Takṣaka Vaiśaleya was her calf, and a gourd-vessel was her vessel. Dhṛtarāṣṭra Airāvata milked her; he milked out nothing but poison. All beings subsist upon that poison; he who knows this becomes one upon whom all beings must subsist. All beings subsist upon that poison; he who knows this becomes one upon whom all beings must subsist. Therefore, one should strike back at whoever, knowing thus, sprinkles [him] with a gourd.
And one should not strike back; however, one may strike back [mentally] with the thought, "I strike you with my mind."
Whatever one strikes back, that is indeed poison which one strikes back.

From heaven, from earth, from the intermediate space, from the ocean, from Agni, and from Vāta, the Madhūka-plant was indeed born. Having honored her who is clothed in immortality, all creatures rejoice in her with their hearts. Great is her milk, possessing every form; they say her seed is that of the ocean. From whence the Madhūka-plant comes bestowing gifts, there the breath and there the immortal is established. Men on earth, reflecting in many ways, behold her movement separately. From Agni and from Vāta, the Madhūka-plant was indeed born, the fierce granddaughter of the Maruts.

The Mother of the Ādityas, the Daughter of the Vasus, the breath of creatures, the navel of immortality—golden-hued, honey-whipped, dripping with clarity, she, the great splendor, moves among mortals. The gods generated the whip from honey; her embryo became the one of all forms. The Mother nourishes him when he is born and young; once born, he gazes upon all worlds. Who knows him? Who has truly perceived him—he who is the inexhaustible jar, the vessel of Soma, within her heart? May the wise Brahman rejoice in him.
He knows them both; he indeed perceives those two inexhaustible breasts of hers that yield a thousand streams. They milk out nourishment without faltering.
Making the sound *hiṅ*, the lofty one, bestowing vital strength, she approaches her vow with a loud roar. Crying out toward the three heats, she utters her lowing; she yields milk with her milks.
To her, full of milk, the waters draw near—the mighty bulls who are self-ruling. They rain down; they cause it to rain. He who knows this finds his desire, nourishment, and the waters.
The thundering voice is yours, O Prajāpati; as a bull, you cast forth your vigor upon the earth. From Agni and Vāta, the whip was born as honey; for she is the fierce granddaughter of the Maruts.

Just as Soma is dear to the Aśvins at the morning pressing, so may splendor be established within my own self, O Aśvins. Just as Soma is dear to Indra and Agni at the second pressing, so may splendor be established within my own self, O Indra and Agni.

Just as Soma is dear to the Ṛbhus at the third pressing, so may the Ṛbhus bestow splendor upon my self. May I be born of honey; may I win honey. Rich in milk, O Agni, have I come; unite me with splendor. Unite me, O Agni, with splendor, with progeny, and with long life. May the gods take note of this of mine; may Indra, together with the seers, take note.

Just as honey-makers collect honey within the honeycomb, so may splendor be established within my own self, O Aśvins. Just as bees smear this honey upon the honeycomb, so may splendor, brilliance, strength, and vital power be established in me, O Aśvins.
Whatever sweetness is in the mountains, in the hills, in cows, and in horses; whatever sweetness is in the flowing wine—may that sweetness be in me.
O Aśvins, lords of splendor, anoint me with the honey of the bee, so that I may utter speech full of luster among the people.
O Prajāpati, your voice is the thunder; as a bull, you cast forth vigor upon the earth and in the sky. All creatures depend upon it for life; by means of it, he nourishes the residual strength.
The earth is the staff, the intermediate space is the womb, the sky is the whip, lightning is the lash-tip, and gold is the drop.

Whoever knows the seven honeys of the whip becomes possessed of honey: the Brahmin, the king, the cow, the ox, rice, barley, and honey as the seventh. He becomes possessed of honey; his food becomes honeyed; he wins honeyed worlds, who knows thus.

When it thunders in a cloudless sky, Prajāpati himself manifests for his creatures. I gratify with ghee, oblation, and clarified butter the Bull who slays rivals. O thou who art praised, humble my rivals with great heroic power.

Whatever is not dear to my mind, whatever my eye does not delight in, and whatever consumes me without welcoming me—that evil dream I cast upon my rival; having offered this prayer, may I rise up and shatter him.
O Kāma, cast upon him the evil dream, the misfortune, childlessness, misfortune, and distress—O fierce Lord, hurl these back at him who seeks to harm us with affliction.
Drive them away, O Kāma, drive them away, O Kāma! Let those who are my rivals go to ruin. When they have been driven down into the lowest darkness, do you, O Agni, burn up their dwellings.
This daughter of yours, O Kāma, is called the Cow; the sages call her Speech, the Sovereign Radiance (Virāj). With her, exclude my rivals; let breath, cattle, and life itself desert them.

By the power of Kāma, Indra, King Varuṇa, Viṣṇu, and by the impulse of Savitṛ, and by the office of Agni as Hotṛ, may I drive away my rivals, as a skillful steersman pushes a boat through the waters. May my fierce and powerful desire, acting as my overseer, make me truly free from rivals. May all the gods be my protection; may all the gods come to this my invocation.
Enjoying this clarified butter mixed with ghee, O you for whom Kāma is the eldest, rejoice here, making me indeed free from rivals.
O Indra and Agni, having mounted the same chariot out of desire, cast my rivals down; when they have fallen into the lowest darkness, O Agni, burn their dwellings down after them.

O Kāma, strike down those who are my rivals; cast them into blinding darkness. Let them all be deprived of their senses and rendered powerless; may not even a single day of their lives remain. May they all perish; may not even a single day of their lives remain.
Kāma has slain those who were my rivals; he has made for me a wide space to prosper. Let the four quarters bow down to me; let the six expanses bring me abundance of ghee.
Let them float downward, like a ship severed from its mooring; for those driven away by the arrow, there is no returning.
Agni is the repeller, Indra is the repeller, Soma is the repeller. May the gods, as repellers, drive him away.
Let him wander, driven off, lacking all heroes—hated by his friends and shunned by his own kin. And may the lightnings cast him down upon the earth; may the fierce god crush your enemies.
This Bṛhatī has fallen away, yet it is unfallen; it bears all lightnings and thunders. May the rising Sun, powerful with wealth and splendor, drive my rivals low.

O Kāma, that protection of yours which is threefold and uplifted, that impenetrable armor of *brahman* which has been spread out—by means of that, exclude my rivals; let breath, cattle, and life itself avoid them.

With that by which the gods drove away the Asuras, with which Indra led the Dasyus into the lowest darkness—with that, O Kāma, drive far from this world those who are my rivals. Just as the gods drove away the Asuras, just as Indra crushed the Dasyus into the lowest darkness, so you, O Kāma, drive far from this world those who are my rivals.
Kāma was born first; neither the gods, nor the ancestors, nor mortals have attained him. Therefore, you are superior and ever great; to you, O Kāma, I offer this homage.

As many as are the quarters and the intermediate directions, as many as are the regions visible from heaven—from all those you are greater and ever more vast; to you, O Kāma, I offer this homage.
As many bees, bats, and *kurūru* insects as there are, and as many tree-serpents as there have been—greater than all those you are, forever great; to you, O Kāma, I offer this homage.
O Kāma, O Manyu, you are greater than that which blinks and stands; you are greater than the ocean. Therefore, you are greater and forever great; to you, O Kāma, I offer this homage.
Neither indeed does the wind attain its desire, nor Agni, nor Sūrya, nor even Candramas; you are greater than they, forever great. To you, O Kāma, I offer this homage.

Those auspicious forms of yours, O Kāma, which are blessed, by which that which you choose becomes true—with those do you enter into us; drive away evil thoughts elsewhere. Whether they be comparable, similar, or even measured, we unfasten the bindings of the hall that contains all treasures.

That which is bound upon you, O possessor of all boons—that girdle and whatever knot has been made—I loosen that with my voice, as Bṛhaspati [loosened] the strength. He stretched it out, he drew it tight; he made your knots firm. Knowing the joints like a skilled butcher, we unloose them, as they were loosened by Indra.
O Viśvavārī, we loosen for you the bindings of the bamboo poles, the fastenings of the leather thongs, the grass of the frame, and the lashings of the side-pieces.
Of the tongs, the iron pincers, and the embrace—these fetters of Māna’s wife we now unbind.
Those internal thongs which they bound upon thee for the sake of sport—those we now loosen for thee. O Lady of the House, be auspicious and beneficial to our bodies.
Thou art the oblation-holder, the fire-hall, the dwelling of the wives, and the seat; O divine hall, thou art the seat of the gods.
The eyeless head-band, spread out with a thousand eyes, fastened and bound upon the central beam—we loosen it by means of sacred prayer (*brahman*).
O House, may both he who receives you and he by whom you were measured—both of them, O Mistress of the Measuring-Cord, live to reach old age.

O House, he who built you and gathered together the trees of the forest—Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati made you for the sake of progeny.

Homage to him, homage to the giver and to the Lord of the House! Homage to Agni as he moves forth, and homage to you, O Person! Homage to the cows and to the horses, and to whatever is born within the house! O you who are rich in offspring and rich in progeny, we loosen your fetters.
You conceal the fire within, along with men and cattle; O you who possess offspring and progeny, we loosen your snares.

With that expanse which lies between heaven and earth, with that I enclose this hall for you. That which is the intermediate space, the measurer of the region—that I make into a womb for my treasures; with that I enclose the hall for him. Rich in vigor, rich in milk, fixed and measured upon the earth, bearing all food—O Hall, do not harm those who receive you.
Covered with grass, clothed in straw-bundles, like the night, the Hall is the resting place of the moving world. Measured out, you stand upon the earth like a female elephant with feet.
I untie for you what is tied fast, uncovering that which was bound; may Mitra unbind at dawn what has been pressed down by Varuṇa.
The hall built by Brahmā, built and measured out by the seers—O Indra and Agni, protect this hall, you two immortals, this Soma-dwelling seat.

The hall that is being built with two sides, four sides, or six sides—with eight sides or ten sides—Agni lies within it like an embryo, the lord of the measuring.
Facing you, O Hall, I, facing inward, approach you who are non-violent; for Agni and the Waters are within, the first doors of Cosmic Order (*ṛta*).
These waters I bring forth, free from disease and destroyers of disease; I settle into the house together with immortality and Agni.
Do not cast us into the snare; you are a heavy burden, so become light for us. O House, we carry you wherever we desire, as if you were a bride.
Homage to the eastern direction of the hall; Svāhā to Greatness, Svāhā to the gods who are to be honored with Svāhā!
Homage to the greatness of the hall from the southern direction; Svāhā to the gods who are to be invoked with Svāhā!
To the western direction, to the hall, homage to the Greatness; Svāhā to the gods who are to be invoked with Svāhā!
From the northern direction of the hall, homage to the Greatness; Svāhā! To the gods who are to be invoked with Svāhā!
To the fixed quarter, to the hall, homage to its greatness; Svāhā to the gods who are to be invoked with Svāhā!
To the upward direction, to the hall, homage to its greatness! Svāhā to the gods who are to be invoked with svāhā!

A thousandfold, brilliant, a bull rich in milk, bearing all forms within his flanks; bestowing prosperity upon the liberal sacrificer, the ruddy steed of Bṛhaspati has stretched out the thread of sacrifice.

O Agni, he who has become the counterpart of the waters, preeminent for all like the goddess Earth—the father of calves, the lord of the cows—may he grant us prosperity even in a thousandfold abundance.
The man, pregnant, ancient, and full of milk, the bull bears the vessel of wealth. May Agni Jātavedas carry that offering to Indra by the paths traveled by the gods.

He is the father of calves, the lord of the inviolable cows; he is also the father of the great jars. The calf, the afterbirth, the fresh milk, the colostrum, the curdled milk, and the clarified butter—these indeed are his seed.
This bundle is the portion of the gods, the essence of the waters, of the plants, and of the clarified butter. Śakra chose the draught of Soma when his body became the great pressing-stone.

You carry a jar filled with Soma; you are Tvaṣṭṛ, the progenitor of forms and of cattle. May those who bring forth here be auspicious to you; bestow upon us those [cattle] which are these, O Svadhiti!
It carries goat’s milk; its seed is ghee; they call that thousandfold nourishment a sacrifice. The bull, wearing the form of Indra—may he, given by the gods, come to us as something auspicious.

The vigor of Indra, the two arms of Varuṇa, the shoulders of the Aśvins, and this hump of the Maruts—this [bull] they call Bṛhaspati when he is fully prepared. Those who are wise seers and those who are possessed of insight say so.

O you who are rich in milk, you extend yourself as the divine clans; they call you Indra, they call you Sarasvant. He who, being a Brāhmaṇa, offers up the bull, bestows a thousand [cows] with a single mouth.

Bṛhaspati and Savitṛ have bestowed vital strength upon you; from Tvaṣṭṛ and Vāyu, your self has been brought hither. With my mind, I offer you into the intermediate space; may both Heaven and Earth be your sacrificial grass (barhis). He who goes among the cattle lowing loudly like Indra among the gods—let the Brahman praise the limbs of that bull with auspicious speech. His two sides were from Anumati; his two thighs were from Bhaga. Mitra spoke of the two knee-bones, saying, "These two are mine alone. The cleft was from the Ādityas; the two hips were from Bṛhaspati. The tail belongs to the god Vāta; with it he shakes the plants.

The buttocks belonged to Sinīvālī; they said the skin belonged to Sūryā. They said the feet belonged to Utthātṛ, when they fashioned the bull. The chest was that of Jāmiśaṃsa; the vessel of Soma was held firm. When all the gods had gathered together, they fashioned the bull.
Those lepers gave their hooves to Saramā and to the tortoises; they set aside his undigested food for the worms and the dog-lice.
With his two horns he pierces the Rakṣas; with his eye he destroys misfortune; with his two ears he hears what is auspicious—he who is the inviolable lord of the cows.
He who performs a hundred sacrifices, him the fires do not consume; all the gods quicken that brahmin who offers the bull as an oblation.

Having given a bull to the Brahmins, he makes his mind most excellent; he beholds the prosperity of his cows within his own pen. May there be cattle, may there be offspring, and may there be strength for our bodies. May the gods grant all this to the giver of the bull. This Indra, having drunk deeply, shall bestow conscious wealth. He [bestows] the well-yielding cow, whose calf is ever-present, who yields her desire, and who is wise beyond the heavens.
Tawny-hued, bestowing vital strength from the sky, the all-formed might of Indra has come to us. Granting us long life and progeny, may he attend us with the increase of wealth.
O Upaparcana, mingle [your essence] here in this cow-pen; mingle it with the seed of the bull and with your own heroic power, O Indra.

We entrust this youth to you; sporting with him here, move according to your will. Do not abandon us, O fortunate ones, by birth; prosper us with the increase of wealth! Do not abandon us, O fortunate ones, by birth; prosper us with the increase of wealth! Do not abandon us, O fortunate ones, by birth; prosper us with the increase of wealth! Do not abandon us, O fortunate ones, by birth; prosper us with the increase of wealth! Do not abandon us, O fortunate ones, by birth... [and so on].
Lead him here; take hold of him! Let him go to the world of the righteous, knowing the way. Having crossed through the many great darknesses, let the unborn goat ascend to the third heaven.
I lead you around as a portion for Indra, for the patron at this sacrifice, a wise leader. Seize those who hate us; let the heroes of the sinless sacrificer be unharmed. Wipe away his footprints;
whatever evil deed he has committed, let him tread with pure hooves, knowing the way. Having crossed through the many darknesses, seeing clearly, let the unborn goat ascend to the third heaven.
Having recited over this dark skin, O dissector, do not strike it with the knife according to the joints; do not harm it. Arrange it joint by joint and place it upon the third heaven.
With a verse, I set the cauldron upon the fire; pour in the water and place it therein. Envelop it with fire, O immolators; once cooked, let it go to the world where the doers of good deeds dwell.

Step forth from here, if you are unheated, from the heated cauldron toward the third heaven. You have become fire from the fire; conquer this world of light. They say the goat is Agni, and they say the goat is light; they say the goat is to be given by the living for the sake of the *brahman*. The goat drives away the darkness far away when it is given in this world by one who has faith.
Let the five-fold rice-offering stride out in five ways, as it is about to ascend, toward the three lights. Go to the midst of those who have sacrificed well; take your station upon the third heaven.

O goat, ascend to the world of those who have performed good deeds, where the Śarabha crosses over even the most difficult obstacles. This five-fold rice-offering, when given to the Brahman, shall satisfy the giver with full contentment.

The Unborn One places the giver upon the back of the firmament, in the triple vault, the triple heaven, the triple-backed [vault]. The five-fold rice-offering, being given to the Brahman, you are a cow of all forms, a wish-fulfilling cow; you are the one. The five-fold rice-offering, being given to the Brahman, you are a cow of all forms, a wish-fulfilling cow; you are the one. The five-fold rice-offering, being given to the Brahman, you are a cow of all forms, a wish-fulfilling cow; you are the one. Being given three times, you are a cow of all forms, a wish-fulfilling cow.
O ancestors, this is your third light; he gives a goat with five portions of rice to the Brahman. The goat, when given by one who has faith in this world, drives away the darkness far away.

Desiring the world of those who have sacrificed and performed good deeds, he gives a goat with five portions of rice to the Brahman. May he attain pervasiveness and conquer that world; may it be auspicious for us when accepted.

For the Unborn was born from the flame of Agni—the inspired singer from the inspired singer, the wise one from strength. May the gods arrange that according to the seasons: the sacrifice, the gift, the fulfillment, and the consecrated offering.
One should give a seamless garment and gold as a sacrificial fee; thus one attains those worlds which are celestial and those which are earthly.
May these goat-streams come unto you—divine, Soma-rich, with ghee upon their backs, dripping with honey. Support the earth and the sky upon the back of the firmament, on the seven-rayed [vault].

You are the Unborn; you are the Unborn Heaven. Through you, the Aṅgirases came to know the world. May I recognize that holy world, by which you carry a thousand [gifts], O Agni, and by which you carry all wealth. With that, carry this sacrifice of ours to the light, so that it may go among the gods.
The Unborn, when cooked, establishes one in the heavenly world; the five-fold rice-oblation drives away Destruction. By means of it, may we conquer the worlds possessed of the sun.

Whatever [portion] you placed with the Brahmins and whatever with the common people, and whatever drops of the cooked rice of the goat there may be—O Agni, recognize all that of us in the world of the well-performed deed at the meeting-place of our paths.

The Unborn, O Agni, indeed strode forth across this [world]. His chest became this earth; the sky became his back; the intermediate space was his middle; the quarters were his sides; and the two oceans were his two flanks. Truth and Order are his two eyes; the universe is Truth; Faith is his breath; the Virāj is his head. This indeed is the immeasurable sacrifice, namely the goat with five portions of rice.
He who gives a goat with five portions of rice, having the sacrificial fee as its light, attains the immeasurable sacrifice and wins the immeasurable world.
One should not break his bones, nor should one extract the marrow; taking him whole, one should cause him to enter this and that.
This very form belongs to him; by it he unites with him. He milks out food, greatness, and vigor for that man who gives a goat, the five-rice-dish, whose light is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

Five gold ornaments, five new garments, and five cows that yield every desire become his, who gives a goat, the five-rice-dish, whose light is the sacrificial fee. Five gold ornaments become his light; garments become armor for his body. He attains the heavenly world, who gives a goat, the five-rice-dish, whose light is the sacrificial fee.

She who, having first found a husband, then finds another later—let those two give a goat and five-measure rice; they shall not be separated. The later husband becomes one who shares the same world with the remarried woman, he who gives a goat, five-measure rice, and a light for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Having given a cow with calves in succession, an ox, a pillow, a garment, and gold, they go to the highest heaven.

He who knows the season named Naidāgha—this goat with five portions of rice is indeed the season named Naidāgha—he burns away the prosperity of his hostile rival and prospers himself. He who knows the season named Kurvat—he takes away the prosperity of his hostile rival as it is being performed, for this goat with five portions of rice is indeed the season named Kurvat. He who knows the season named Saṃyat—he takes away the prosperity of his hostile rival as it is being restrained, for this goat with five portions of rice is indeed the season named Saṃyat.

He who knows Brahman as manifest— whose joints are the sacrificial requisites, whose backbone is the *ṛc*-verses, whose body-hairs are the *sāmans*, and whose heart is said to be the *yajus*— for him this sacrificial strewing is indeed the oblation.
When the host of guests looks upon the guests, he gazes upon the place of sacrifice to the gods.
When he speaks out, he enters the consecration; when he asks for water, he leads forward the waters.
Those very waters which are brought forward at the sacrifice are indeed those same ones.
That libation which they offer is indeed that very animal dedicated to Agni and Soma which is bound for sacrifice.
When they prepare the dwellings, they are indeed preparing the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds.
That which they spread out as the sacrificial grass (barhis), that indeed is it.
In that they bring a bed for him above, he thereby wins the world of heaven itself.
Whatever they bring as a coverlet and a pillow, those indeed are the enclosing-sticks.
Whatever ointment and unguent they bring, that is indeed clarified butter.
Those two which they take as a taste before the serving [of the food] are indeed the two sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśau).
That which they call "prepared by eating" (aśanakṛta), they indeed call "prepared by the oblation" (haviṣkṛta).
Those rice grains and barley grains which are poured out are indeed mere stalks.
Those which are the mortars and pestles are indeed the pressing-stones.
The winnowing basket is the filter; the chaff and the dregs are the waters used for pressing.

The *sruc* ladle, the *darvī* spoon, the *īkṣaṇa* probe, the *āyavana* stirring-stick, the *droṇakalaśas*, the *kumbhīs*, the *vāyavya* cups, and this very black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*)—this is indeed what the host of guests (the *atithipati*) prepares for the sacrificer's *Brāhmaṇa*: when he looks at the items to be brought forward, saying, "This is more; this [is more]."
When he says, "Lift it up further," he thereby makes his vital breath more extensive.
He brings the oblations and sets them down.
When they have approached, he offers them as a guest into his own self.
With the *sruc* in his hand, he offers into the *prāṇa* as the sacrificial post, with the *sruk* at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*.
Indeed, these guests—whether dear or even unpleasant—are the officiating priests who cause one to go to the heavenly world.
He who, knowing this, does not eat while feeling hatred, nor eats the food of one who hates him, nor of one who is being scrutinized, nor of one who is scrutinizing—[he prospers].
Indeed, everyone who eats his food has truly consumed all evil.
Indeed, he whose food others do not eat has his evil entirely undevoured.
Truly, he who offers [the oblation] is always joined with the pressing-stones, possessing a moist filter, having the sacrifice spread out, and having brought forth the sacrificial rite.
The sacrifice of him who offers the *upahāra* is indeed extended to Prajāpati.
He who offers the oblation indeed strides after the strides of Prajāpati.
That which is in the dwelling is the Āhavanīya; that which is [the fire] in which they cook is the Gārhapatya; and that [fire] is the Dakṣiṇāgni.
He who eats before the guest eats indeed of the merit of sacrifices and the merit of public works belonging to his household.
Indeed, he who eats before the guest consumes the milk and the essence of the household.
He who eats before the guest indeed consumes the vigor and the prosperity of his house.
He who eats before the guest indeed consumes the offspring, the cattle, and the household of the householder.
He who eats before the guest indeed consumes the fame and the glory of his household.
He who eats before the guest indeed consumes the prosperity and the communal harmony of the household.
This indeed is the guest: one who is learned in the Vedas; therefore, one should not eat before him.
When a guest has eaten, one should eat for the sake of the self-nature of the sacrifice and for the non-interruption of the sacrifice; that is the vow.
This indeed is more delicious than beef—either milk or meat—and one should not eat that [ordinary food].

He who, knowing this, offers it after pouring milk over it, wins as much as one wins by performing a well-succeeded Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; with this [offering], he wins just as much. He who, knowing this, offers it after pouring clarified butter over it, wins as much as one wins by performing a well-succeeded Atirātra sacrifice; with this [offering], he wins just as much.

He who, knowing this, offers honey after pouring it out, wins as much as one wins by performing a well-succeeded *sattra* sacrifice lasting a single day; so much does he win by this means. He who, knowing this, offers meat after pouring it out, wins as much as one wins by performing a well-succeeded twelve-day (*dvādaśāha*) sacrifice; so much does he win by this means.

He who, knowing this, pours out water and offers it, goes for the procreation of offspring and attains a firm foundation; he becomes dear to his offspring—whosoever, knowing this, pours it out and offers it.

For him, Dawn makes the sound *hiṃ*; Savitṛ chants the prelude; Bṛhaspati sings the *udgītha* with vigor; Tvaṣṭṛ performs the response with nourishment; and the All-Gods constitute the finale. He who knows this becomes the finale of prosperity, of progeny, and of cattle.

For him, as the sun rises, it makes the sound *hiṅ*; at the time of gathering [the cows], it chants the *pra-stāva*; at midday, it chants the *ud-gītha*; in the afternoon, it performs the *pratihāra*; and as it sets, it is the *nidhana*. He who knows this becomes the *nidhana* of prosperity, progeny, and cattle. For him, as the cloud forms, it makes the sound *hiṅ*; when thundering, it chants the *pra-stāva*; when lightning flashes, it performs the *pratihāra*; when raining, it chants the *ud-gītha*; and when the rain ceases, it is the *nidhana*. He who knows this becomes the *nidhana* of prosperity, progeny, and cattle.

In that he calls for the Kṣattṛ, he thereby causes [the announcement] to be heard.
Whatever one promises, that indeed is what one causes to be heard in response.
Those who surround him with vessels in their hands, both those in front and those behind, are indeed the *camasādhvaryu* priests.
Among them, there is no one who is not a Hotṛ.
When the host of guests, having served the guests, goes up to his house, he thereby performs the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
In that he distributes the sacrificial gifts, he distributes the fees; in that he performs the concluding rites, he indeed brings the sacrifice to its completion.
Invited, he consumes [the portion] on the earth; invited, he consumes whatever universal form exists upon that earth.
Invited, he partakes in the intermediate space; invited, he partakes in that which possesses all forms in heaven.
Invited, he partakes in heaven; invited, he partakes in that which is multiform in heaven.
Invited among the gods, he partakes; invited, he partakes in that which is of manifold form in heaven.
Invoked among the worlds, he partakes; invoked therein is that which possesses every form in heaven.
He is invited; he is invited.
He attains this world; he attains that world.
He who knows thus conquers the luminous worlds.
Prajāpati and Parameṣṭhin are the two horns; Indra is the head; Agni is the forehead; Yama is the nape of the neck;
King Soma is the brain; the sky is the upper jaw; and the earth is the lower jaw.
Lightning is the tongue, the Maruts are the teeth, Revatī is the neck, the Kṛttikās are the shoulders, and the Gharma is the carriage-pole.
Vāyu is the universe, the heavenly world; he is the dark tree, the supporter, the one to be entered.
The hawk is the purchased price; the atmosphere is the breast-bone; Bṛhaspati is the hump; the *bṛhatī* meters are the vertebrae;
the wives of the gods are the ribs; the *upasad* offerings are the side-flesh.
Mitra and Varuṇa are his shoulders; Tvaṣṭṛ and Aryaman are his forearms; Mahādeva is his two arms.
Indrāṇī is the buttocks, Vāyu the tail, and Pavamāna the hair.
The priesthood and the nobility are the hips; strength is the thighs.
Dhātṛ and Savitṛ are the two knee-bones; the Gandharvas are the shanks; the Apsarases are the ankles; and Aditi is the hooves.
The mind, the heart, the liver, the intellect, the vow, and the pericardium.
Hunger is the belly; food is the rectum; the mountains are the entrails.
Anger is the two kidneys; fury is the testicles; progeny is the penis.
The rivers are the strings, the lords of the rain are the breasts, and the thunder is the udder.
The skin is the all-pervading expanse, the herbs are the body hair, and the stars are the form.
The gods are the testicles, humans are the intestines, and the atras are the belly.
The *rakṣas* eat the blood; other people eat the undigested contents of the stomach.
The cloud is the drink; the marrow is the Nidhana.
Agni was seated; the Aśvins were risen.
Indra stands facing the east; Yama stands facing the south.
Dhātṛ stands facing west; Savitṛ stands facing north.
King Soma has reached the grasses.
Mitra is looking on; bliss has returned.
When being yoked, he is Vaiśvadeva; when yoked, he is Prajāpati; when released, he is the All.

This indeed is the omniform, the all-form, the cow-form. The pain in the head, the affliction of the head, the ear-ache, the blood-red inflammation—all the disease of your head, we charm it out. From your ears, from the hollows of your ears, the ear-ache and the neuralgic pain—all the disease of your head, we charm it out.

From whatever cause the wasting disease (*yakṣma*) falls away from the ear or from the mouth—from all head-disease of yours we drive it out with our spells. That which makes a man blind or causes him to lose his senses—from all head-disease of yours we drive it out with our spells. The breaking of the limbs, the fever of the limbs, the creeping paralysis that pervades every member—from all head-disease of yours we drive it out with our spells.
We drive out by means of mantras the *takman* fever, which resembles Bhīma and causes a person to tremble, that which lasts for all autumns.
That which creeps along the thighs and likewise goes to the groins—we drive the consumption (yakṣman) out from within your limbs to the outside.

If it arises from desire, from lack of desire, or from the heart—balāsa from the heart and from the limbs, we drive it out to the outside. Jaundice (harimāṇam) from your limbs, swelling (apvām) from within the belly, and the seat of consumption within the self—we drive it all out to the outside.

Let the *kāhā-bāha* flow out from your belly; I have spoken the poison of all consumptive diseases (*yakṣman*) out from you—from your belly, from your lungs, from your navel, and from your heart. I have spoken the poison of all consumptive diseases out from you. Those [diseases] which break down the boundaries and flow toward the head—let them flow out through the external opening, harmless and free from disease.
Those that pierce the heart and spread through the ribs—harmless and disease-free, let them flow out through the external opening.
Those that pierce the sides and penetrate the vertebrae—harmless and disease-free, let them flow out through the external opening.
Those that pierce transversely and flow through your flanks—harmless and disease-free, let them flow out through the external opening.
Those worms that crawl along the rectum and delude the intestines—harmless and free from disease, let them flow out through the external opening!

Those that suck out the marrow and break apart the joints—harmless and free from disease, let them flow out through the external opening! Those wasting diseases of yours that cause the limbs to swell and fester—I have driven out the poison of all these wasting diseases from you.

I have spoken the poison out from you for every kind of erysipelas, abscess, rheumatic swelling, and scorpion sting, and for all forms of consumption. From your feet, your knees, your hips, and from your loins; from your spine, your channels, and your neck-tendons—from the head, I have destroyed the disease.
Of this lovely, grey-haired Hotṛ-priest, his middle brother is Ashna; the third brother has ghee upon his back. Here I beheld the Lord of the People, who has seven sons.
Seven yoke the chariot that has a single wheel; a single horse draws it, having seven names. Its wheel has three naves, is ageless, and is irresistible, upon which all these worlds stand.
Those seven who have mounted this chariot—the seven-wheeled one—seven horses draw it. Seven sisters sing together toward it, where the seven names of the cows are deposited.

Who has seen him first being born, when the boneless one supports that which has bones? Where indeed is the life-breath, the blood, and the self of the earth? Who, being wise, has approached to ask this?
Let him who truly knows it speak here: the hidden footstep of this lovely bird. From his head the cows milk forth milk; wearing his covering, they have drunk the water with their feet.
As one simple-minded and lacking understanding, I ask in my mind about these hidden footsteps of the gods. Over the young calf, the seven threads have been stretched out by the seers to be woven.
Unaware, I ask here of those who are aware, of the wise seers, like one ignorant asking those who know: "What indeed is that One, in the form of the Unborn, who has propped apart these six worlds?

The Mother bestowed her portion upon the Father; for in the beginning, she united with him in spirit. She, shrinking back, was pierced by the essence of the embryo. Those full of reverence approached her with their prayer.
The Mother was yoked to the pole of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); the embryo stood within the enclosures. The calf lowed; he beheld the Cow of manifold forms in her three unions.
