As the five-spoked wheel revolves, upon which all worlds are established, its axle does not grow hot despite bearing a heavy burden; from of old its nave has never been severed.

They say that the five-footed father, of twelve forms, dwells in the upper half of heaven, rich in moisture. But these others say he is fixed upon another wheel below, one with seven spokes and six fellies.
That wheel of *Ṛta* (Cosmic Order) revolves around the sky; it has twelve spokes and does not decay. O Agni, here stand the sons, paired together—seven hundred and twenty.

The wheel, with its rim, rolls on undecaying; ten yoked ones draw it upon the outstretched [earth]. The eye of the Sun moves, veiled by the realm of space (*rajas*), in which all beings have taken their stand.

They say those who are women are men; behold, the one with eyes perceives, while the blind man does not. The son who is a seer has understood them; he who truly knows them shall be the father of his father.

Of those born together, they call the seventh the single-born; the six are twins, seers born of the gods. Their desired offerings are established according to their stations; for the Sustainer, they tremble, transformed according to their forms.

Beyond this [world], beyond these, by means of a lower step, the Cow has risen up, bearing her calf. Whitherward has she gone? To what region has she departed? Where indeed will she bring forth, for she is not in this herd?
He who knows his father beyond this—beyond this, beyond these, by means of a lower [step]—who here, acting as a seer, can declare from where divine mind was born?

Those which they call downward, those they call upward; those which they call upward, those they call downward. O Indra and Soma, those things which you two have created, they carry them like yoked horses at the pole through the mid-air.
Two birds, united as companions, cling to the same tree; of these two, one eats the sweet fruit of the fig-tree, while the other looks on without eating.

On that tree whereon all the fair-winged ones settle and from which they all bring forth their young—the sweet fig at its summit, they say, no one reaches who does not know the Father. Where the fair-winged ones, without blinking, sing together for their share of the nectar—there has the wise Guardian of the entire world entered me, the simple-minded. That which is the Gāyatra placed upon the Gāyatra, or the Triṣṭubh which they fashioned from the Triṣṭubh, or the Jagat-foot placed upon the Jagat—those who know this have attained immortality.

With the *gāyatrī* he measures out the *arka*; with the *arka*, the *sāman*; with the *triṣṭubh*, the *vāka*. With the *vāka*, the *vāka*—the two-footed and the four-footed; by means of the syllable (*akṣara*), they measure the seven voices.

With the *jagatī*, he propped up the ocean in heaven; in the *rathantara*, he beheld the sun. They say there are three kindling-sticks (*samidh*) of the *gāyatrī*; therefore it has surpassed [all others] in greatness and majesty.
I call hither this well-milking cow; may the skillful milker milk her. May Savitṛ impel for us the most excellent impulsion. The *gharma* vessel is heated; proclaim that clearly!
Muttering "hiṅ," the mistress of treasures has come hither, seeking her calf with her mind; may this inviolable cow yield milk for the Aśvins, and may she prosper for our great good fortune.

The cow has lowed toward her blinking calf; she has made the "hiṅ" sound at his head so that he may suckle. Lowing toward the warm milk in her mouth, she utters her cry and nourishes him with her milk.

This is he who bellows, by whom the cow is encompassed; resting upon the dark cloud, she utters her cry. By her insights she has indeed surpassed mortals; becoming lightning, she has cast off her covering.

The breath lies within the horse, the living soul moves; firm in the midst of the dwellings is the living one. By means of funeral offerings (*svadhā*), the immortal moves through the dead, sharing a common womb with the mortal.
The gray-haired man has swallowed the young moon as it hastens upon the surface of the waters. Behold the poetic wisdom of the god in its greatness: today he has died, yet yesterday he was alive.

He who made it does not know it; he who saw it is indeed far removed from it. Enveloped within his mother’s womb, Nirṛti has entered among the many offspring. I have seen the Herdsman, who never rests, moving hither and thither upon his paths. He, clothing himself in converging and diverging rays, revolves repeatedly within the worlds.

Heaven is our father, our begetter; there is our kinship. This great earth is our mother. Within the two upturned bowls (heaven and earth) lies the womb; therein the Father has placed the germ of the Daughter.
I ask you about the furthest limit of the earth; I ask about the seed of the virile horse. I ask about the navel of the entire world; I ask about the highest heaven of speech.
This altar is beyond the interior of the earth; this Soma is the seed of the virile horse. This sacrifice is the navel of the entire world; this Brahman is the supreme heaven of speech.
I do not truly know what this is that I am; hidden and armored, I move about with my mind. When the first-born of *ṛta* came to me, then for the first time I attained a share of this speech.

Backward and forward he goes, held by his own nature; the immortal has a common womb with the mortal. These two, eternal and moving in opposite directions, pass along; men perceive one, but they do not perceive the other.

Seven half-embryos, the seed of the world, abide by the command of Viṣṇu in the supporting law. Through their insights and their mind, they are wise; as encompassers, they encompass all on every side.
Upon the syllable of the Ṛgveda, in the highest heaven, whereon all the gods have taken their seat—what will he do with the Ṛgveda who does not know that? Those who know it, they sit together here.

Fashioning the word of the *ṛc* by means of its measure, they fashioned with the half-verse all that moves. The three-footed Brahman, assuming many forms, has spread itself out; by it the four quarters of space live.

May you be blessed with good pasture; may we also be blessed. Eat grass, O inviolable one, at all times; drink pure water as you wander. The Cow has lowed, fashioning the waters; she is one-footed, two-footed, four-footed, eight-footed, nine-footed, having become thousand-syllabled, the fivefold array of the world. From her the oceans flow forth on high.
The dark path, the golden-winged birds, clothed in the waters, fly up to heaven. They have turned back from the seat of Cosmic Order; then indeed they have moistened the earth with ghee.

The footless one goes forth, the first among those that have feet; who, O Mitra and Varuṇa, has understood this of yours? The embryo bears the burden of her; he fulfills the *ṛta* and guards against the *anṛta*.

Virāj is speech, Virāj is the earth, Virāj is the mid-air, Virāj is Prajāpati. Virāj became Death, the sovereign ruler of the Sādhyas; in his power are the past and the future. May he bring the past and the future under my control.
I saw from afar the smoke of the Śaka, spreading sideways across that which is beyond and that which is below. The heroes cooked the speckled bull; these were the first ordinances.

Three long-haired ones appear in due season: one of them shears his hair within the year; the other beholds the universe with his powers; of the third, only his speed is seen, not his form. Speech has been measured out in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them. Three, hidden in secret, they do not set in motion; of speech, mortals speak only the fourth quarter.
They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni; and he is the divine, fair-winged Garuḍa. Being one, the sages speak of him as many; they call him Agni, Yama, and Mātariśvan.
That which the healers fashion like a bride on her bridal procession, multiform and fashioned by their hands—may it depart from its core; we drive it away.
This *kṛtyā*, fashioned with a head, with a nose, and with ears, assembled and multiform—may it depart from its core; we drive it away.
Made by a Śūdra, made by a king, made by a woman, or made by Brahmins—like a wife driven away by her husband, may it afflict the one who made it.

By means of this herb, I have corrupted all sorceries (*kṛtyā*). Whether they were cast upon your field, upon your cattle, or upon your men—let there be evil upon the evildoer; let the curse fall upon the one who curses. We send it back again, so that the sorcery may strike the one who performed it. Facing westward, may the descendant of Aṅgiras, our overseer and domestic priest, turn the sorceries back and slay those who practice them.
He who said to you, "Go away," speaking what was contrary to *udāyya*—turn back toward that *kṛtyā*; do not seek us, for we are innocent.
He who joined together your limbs with his wisdom, like a *ṛbhu* to a chariot—to him go; there is your path. This person here is unknown to you.
Those wise practitioners of sorcery who, having fashioned you, seized you—this *kṛtyā*-destroyer, *śambhu*, which flows back along its own course, with it we bathe you.

Whatever name they took for you when giving [offerings] to the ancestors at the sacrifice—from all that curse, from every evil, may these plants release you. From the offense against the gods, from that against the ancestors, from the taking of names, from the curse, and from the retaliatory spell, may the plants release you by their power, by the sacred word (*brahman*), by the *ṛc*-verses, and by the milk of the seers. Just as the wind sweeps away the dust from the earth and the cloud from the atmosphere, even so let all that which is ill-fated, driven away by the sacred word, depart from me.

Go away, crying out like a bound she-ass! Go toward the makers; driven from here by powerful sacred prayer (*brahman*), we lead you along this path, saying, "This is the way for the sorcery. We send you forth against that which has been sent against us. Go there, breaking up like a wagon-train with its carts—multiform and crafty. Your light is turned away; make your path not toward us, but elsewhere. Go beyond the ninety navigable rivers, past the difficult streams; do not linger, go away!
Like the wind crushing trees, strike them down and bring them low; let not a cow, a horse, or a man remain among them. Turning back the doers from here, awaken the ritual act for their childlessness.

The spell (*kṛtyā*) or the sorcery (*valaga*) which they have buried for you upon the sacrificial grass, in the cemetery, or in the field; or those who, being more cunning, have practiced sorcery against you with the *gārhapatya* fire—you who are simple and innocent;

the enmity that was brought near, discovered, and buried—we have found the treacherous agent. Let it go back to where it was brought from! There let it turn back like a horse! Let it destroy the offspring of the spell-maker.

I shall cut off your necks and your feet, O Kṛtyā; run away! May Indra and Agni protect us, they who are the guardians of progeny.
May King Soma, the sovereign lord, and the lords of all beings be gracious to us.
O Bhava and Śarva, let the magical spell (*kṛtyā*) cast against the evildoer be hurled back at him; O God, hurl the lightning-bolt weapon at the one who performs evil deeds.

Whether it be two-footed or four-footed, the spell that has been fashioned and prepared in every form—having become eight-footed from here, go back again, O bringer of misfortune! Anointed, smeared, beautifully adorned, and carrying all his wickedness, go away! Know, O Spell, your maker, as a daughter knows her own father!
Do not stand by while others perform their duty; lead them as one leads the track of a wounded [animal]. He is the deer and you are the hunter; he is not fit to treat you with contempt.

Indeed, one slays the first archer who has taken up his bow, while another strikes back against him; even as the first is striking, another strikes him down in return. Listen to these words of mine, and then go back to where you came from—to him who made you!
For you are a terrible instrument of innocent bloodshed; do not kill our cow, our horse, or our man! Wherever you have been laid down, from there we raise you up: become lighter than a leaf!
If you are enveloped in darkness, as if caught in a net—having torn all these magical spells (*kṛtyā*) apart from here, we send them back to their maker.
O witchcraft, crush the offspring of those who have practiced witchcraft, the deceivers, and the secret plotters! Do not let them remain, O witchcraft; slay those practitioners of witchcraft!

By whom were the heels of the person brought together? By whom was the flesh gathered? By whom the two ankles? By whom the well-formed fingers? By whom the cavities? By whom the two collarbones? Who established the foundation in the middle?

From what did they fashion the two lower ankles and the two upper kneecaps of the person? Having carved out the shanks, where indeed did they place them? Who has understood that—the joints of the two knees?
Four things are joined at the end of the body: the torso above the knees is loose, yet the hips and thighs are firm; who indeed created those by which the trunk became so well-supported?

How many gods were there, and who were they, who fashioned the chest and the neck of Puruṣa? How many assigned the two breasts, who [assigned] the two shoulders, how many built the shoulder-blades, and how many the ribs?
Who brought together his two arms, saying, "Let them be for heroic deeds"? And which god placed those two shoulders upon his breast?

Who pierced the seven openings in the head—these two ears, the two nostrils, the two eyes, and the mouth—through which the four-footed and two-footed creatures go their way according to the greatness of his manifold victory? He placed the wide tongue within the jaws; he established the great voice upon it. He moves repeatedly within the worlds, clothed in the waters. Who indeed has understood that? Which was the first [to place] his brain, his forehead, and his temple, who [placed] the skull? Having piled what was to be piled within the jaws of the Puruṣa, which god ascended to heaven?
Why does a person carry many things pleasant and unpleasant, dreams, distress, and weariness, as well as fierce joys and delights?
Suffering, adversity, destruction—whence indeed do these come to a person? Success, prosperity, failure, thought, and rising inspirations—from whence do they arise?

Who placed the waters within him, flowing in every direction, manifoldly turning, born for the course of the rivers—waters that are sharp, ruddy, crimson, copper-colored, and smoke-hued; flowing upwards, downwards, and transversely within the Puruṣa? Who placed form within him, who [placed] greatness and name? Who [placed] the path within him, who the signal, and who the modes of movement within the Puruṣa?
Which god infused into this Puruṣa the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the in-breath (*apāna*), the diffused breath (*vyāna*), and the equalizing breath (*samāna*)?
Which one god established the sacrifice in this Puruṣa? Who placed truth in him, and who the untruth? Whence came death, and whence immortality?
Who clothed him in a garment? Who ordained his lifespan? Who bestowed strength upon him? Who fashioned his speed?
By whom was the water stretched out? By whom was the day made for the sake of light? By whom was the dawn kindled? By whom was the evening established?
Who deposited seed in this [world], saying, "Let the thread be spun"? Who placed wisdom within it? Who placed the arrow? Who, the dancer, took up his stance?
By whom was this earth covered? By whom was the sky encompassed? By whom were the mountains surpassed in greatness? By whom were the deeds of Puruṣa performed?
By what does one follow Parjanya? By what, the far-seeing Soma? By what, both sacrifice and faith? And by what is the mind established in this [body]?
By what does one obtain the *śrotriya*? By what this *parameṣṭhin*? By what does a person obtain this Agni? By what does one measure the year?
One obtains the *śrotriya* through Brahman; one obtains this *parameṣṭhin* through Brahman. A person obtains this Agni through Brahman; one measures the year through Brahman.

By what does one dwell among the gods? By what the clans of divine origin? By what is this other constellation? By what is true sovereignty said to exist? The *brahman* dwells among the gods; the *brahman* [dwells among] the clans of divine origin. The *brahman* is this other constellation; the *brahman* is said to be true sovereignty.
By whom was this earth laid out? By whom was the sky placed above? By whom was this intermediate space, wide and extending upwards and across, established?

By Brahman the earth was established; by Brahman the sky was placed above. By Brahman this expanse—the intermediate space—was fixed, both upright and across. Having sewn together its head and its heart, Atharvan sent it forth from the brain, upward from the top of the skull. That indeed is the head of Atharvan, the divine vessel turned downward; that the breath protects, as do food and the mind.

Whether created upright or created across, the Puruṣa has pervaded all directions. He who knows that city of Brahman, of which the Puruṣa is said to be the name—he who indeed knows that city of Brahman enveloped in immortality—for him Brahman and the Brāhmaṇas grant sight, breath, and progeny.
Verily, neither sight nor breath abandons him before old age, he who knows that city of Brahman, of which the Puruṣa is said to be the name.
The city of the gods has eight wheels and nine gates; it is impregnable. Within it is a golden treasury, heaven, enveloped in light.
In that golden treasury, upon the three-spoked, triple-supported [chariot], whatever living being exists—that indeed the knowers of Brahman know as Brahman.
Brahmā entered the golden city Aparājitā, which was radiant, fair as a doe, and completely encompassed by glory.

This amulet of *varaṇa* for me is a bull that destroys rivals. With it, seize your enemies; crush those who intend you harm! Crush them, destroy them, and seize them! Let this amulet be your forerunner in front. By means of the *varaṇa*, the gods warded off the incantations of the Asuras day after day. This *varaṇa* amulet possesses all healing powers; it is thousand-eyed, greenish-yellow, and golden. May it cast your enemies down beneath you; first strike down those who hate you!

This *varaṇa* tree shall ward you off from the spell spread out against you, from this human fear, and from every evil. May this divine lord of the forest ward you off; may the gods have warded away the consumption that has entered into him. If, having fallen asleep, you see an evil dream, or if a deer runs along an undesirable path, or from the sneeze of a bird or its evil cry—this *varaṇa* amulet shall ward all that off.

From ill-will, from destruction, from malevolent magic, and likewise from fear—from the deadly blow of more powerful death—Varaṇa shall ward you off. Whatever sin my mother, my father, my brothers, or my own kin have committed, and whatever sin we ourselves have done, from that this divine Lord of the Forest shall ward us off. My rivals and their kinsmen, shaken by Varaṇa, have gone even into the unillumined realm; let them go to the lowest darkness.
May this *varaṇa* amulet protect me from every direction, from every quarter.
This *varaṇa*, the king, the divine lord of the forest, dwells upon my breast; may it drive away my enemies, as Indra drove away the Dasyus and the Asuras.
I wear this *varaṇa* branch, may I be long-lived for a hundred autumns; may it bestow upon me sovereignty, dominion, cattle, and vital strength.

Just as the wind shatters the lords of the forest, the trees, with its might, so do you shatter my rivals—those born before and those born after. May the *varaṇa* protect you. Just as the wind and the fire consume the trees, the lords of the forest, so do you consume my rivals—those born before and those born after. May the *varaṇa* protect you.

Just as trees, worn away by the wind, lie prostrate and cast down, even so do you destroy my rivals and cast them down—those born before as well as those born after. May the Varaṇa tree protect you from all sides.
Cut them down, O Varaṇa, before their appointed time, before the end of their life—those who seek to harm him among his cattle, and those who seek to harm his kingdom.

O Agni, whatever curse the pair utters today, or whatever harshness of speech the chanters produce—whatever arrow is born from fury and the mind—with that pierce the sorcerers in their hearts! I, the wise one, hurl against him the four-edged thunderbolt of the waters to shatter his head. May it crush all his limbs; may all the gods acknowledge this of mine. With my might, I cut off the head of the hostile rival, the evil-hearted hater.
This amulet, born from the plowshare, shall act as my armor. May he come to me full with the stirred drink, together with sap and splendor.

That amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the gods, the dominion of the Asuras—that very amulet has come to me, together with sap and splendor. That amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the gods, the dominion of the Asuras—that very amulet has come to me, together with cattle, goats, sheep, food, and progeny. That amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the gods, the dominion of the Asuras—that very amulet has come to me, together with rice and barley, and with greatness and prosperity.

This amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the gods, the dwelling-place of the Asuras—may it come to me with a stream of honey and clarified butter, together with the *kīlāla* juice. This amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the gods, the dwelling-place of the Asuras—may it come to me with vigor and milk, together with wealth and splendor.
This amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the gods, the dwelling-place of the Asuras—may it come to me with brilliance and luster, together with glory and fame.
That which Bṛhaspati bound for the gods, the Asura-subduing protection—may this amulet come to me together with all prosperities.
May the deities grant me this amulet for nourishment: the victorious one, the increaser of dominion, the amulet that crushes rivals.
Together with the splendor of Brahman, I cast off what is inauspicious for me. Free from rivals, the slayer of rivals, he has made my rival low.

May this jewel, born of the gods, provide me with superiority over my enemies. May he upon whose behalf these three worlds wait for the milked-out milk—may that jewel ascend me from the head for preeminence.
That which the gods, the ancestors, and human beings always depend upon for their livelihood—may that jewel ascend me from the head for preeminence.
Just as seed grows in a fertile field ploughed by the plow, so may offspring, cattle, and food grow upon me, food after food.
O amulet that increases the sacrifice, for whomsoever I have fastened you on as a blessing—do you, O amulet of a hundredfold efficacy, quicken him to preeminence.

In which limb does his austerity abide? In which limb is his cosmic order (ṛta) established? Where does his vow and where does his faith abide? In which limb is his truth firmly rooted?
From which limb does the fire blaze forth? From which limb does Mātariśvan blow? From which limb does the moon measure itself out, measuring the limb of the great Skambha?
On which limb does the earth stand? On which limb is the mid-region established? On which limb is the sky placed? On which limb stands that which is higher than heaven?
Seeking what does Agni blaze upward? Seeking what does Mātariśvan blow? Tell us of that Skambha toward whom they turn when seeking their goal; who indeed is he?

Where do the half-months go? Where do the months go, in harmony with the year? Tell me of that Skambha where the seasons go and where the seasonal periods go; what indeed is he? Where do the two young women of different forms, day and night, hasten together in harmony, seeking their goal? Tell me of that Skambha where the waters, seeking their goal, flow toward; what indeed is he? Tell me of that Skambha on which Prajāpati, having made himself firm, supported all the worlds; what indeed is he?
Whatever supreme, lowest, and middle form Prajāpati created in manifold shapes—by how much did Skambha enter therein, and what was that which he did not enter? How much did it become?
To what extent has Skambha entered into the past, and to what extent does he lie within the future? When he made one limb into a thousand parts, to what extent did Skambha enter therein?

Tell me of that Skambha, who is he indeed? Upon whom austerity, having exerted itself, maintains its supreme vow; upon whom truth and faith, the waters, and the concentrated Brahman rest—tell me of that Skambha, who is he indeed? Upon whom the earth, the intermediate space, and the sky are placed; wherein fire, the moon, the sun, and the wind stand fixed—tell me of that Skambha, who is he indeed? In whose limb all the thirty-three gods are contained—tell me of that Skambha, who is he indeed?

Tell me of that Skambha, upon whom the first-born seers, the great Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus, and the single Seer are all supported; tell me, who indeed is he? Tell me of that Skambha, upon whom both immortality and death are contained within the Puruṣa; tell me, who indeed is he? Tell me of that Skambha, whose channels are the four quarters and whose channels are the oceans, all contained within the Puruṣa; tell me, who indeed is he? Tell me of that Skambha, upon whom the four primary directions stand as his channels, and where the sacrifice has exerted its power; tell me, who indeed is he?

People know that which is non-existent as the supreme, like a branch that does not rest upon anything; yet those who are inferior consider it to be existent, they who worship that branch. Tell me of that Skambha, upon whom the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus are all established, where the past and the future, and all the worlds, are supported—what indeed is he?
Who today knows that treasure which the thirty-three gods always guard? Who knows that treasure which you, O gods, protect?

Where the gods who know Brahman worship Brahman as the eldest—whosoever should know them directly, he would be a knower of Brahman. Those gods are called "The Great" (*bṛhantaḥ*) who were born from the Non-existent (*asat*); people say that one limb of Skambha is that Non-existent beyond [the world]. Where Skambha, generating, turned toward the Ancient—one limb of Skambha, they understand to be the Ancient.
He whose thirty-three gods were distributed as limbs throughout his body—those thirty-three gods indeed some who know Brahman recognize;
people know him as the supreme Hiraṇyagarbha, beyond whom nothing rises. Skambha poured that gold into the world in the intermediate space.
In Skambha are the worlds, in Skambha is austerity, and in Skambha is established the cosmic order (*ṛta*). O Skambha, I know you directly; in you, Indra, everything is contained.

One invokes him by name before the sun and before the dawn; when the Unborn was first brought into being, he attained that sovereignty over which no other being exists.

Homage to that Supreme Brahman, whose measure is the earth and whose belly is the mid-air; who made heaven his head—to that Supreme Brahman, homage! Homage to that Supreme Brahman, whose eye is the sun and the moon ever-renewed; who made fire his mouth—to that Supreme Brahman, homage! Homage to that Supreme Brahman, whose breath is the wind and whose eyes became the Aṅgirasas; who made the quarters of space his perceptions—to that Supreme Brahman, homage!

The Pillar has supported both these, heaven and earth; the Pillar has supported the wide intermediate space. The Pillar has supported the six broad directions; the Pillar has entered this entire world.
To him who, born from toil and fervor, has pervaded all worlds, who made Soma his own alone—to that Supreme Brahman, homage!
Why does the wind not cease? Why does the mind not rest? Why do the waters, seeking the truth, never cease at any time?
A great Yakṣa stands in the midst of the world, pervading the heat upon the surface of the waters; whatever gods there are take refuge in him, just as branches surround the trunk of a tree.

Tell me of that Skambha, to whom the gods always offer tribute with their hands, feet, speech, ears, and eyes, in the measureless [space]—what indeed is he? His darkness has been struck away; he is turned away from evil. All the lights that exist in Prajāpati are in him. He who knows the golden reed standing in the water—he indeed is the secret Prajāpati.
Some say it is a single thread; two women of different forms weave it, drawing out six strands. One extends the threads, the other holds them; they do not drop them, nor do they reach an end.
Of these two, as if dancing around, I cannot distinguish which one is further back. A man weaves this; men sing it forth; a man has lifted it up upon the firmament.
He who presides over all that has been and all that is to be—he who alone belongs to the noble Arya—to that eldest Brahman, homage!

By the Skambha these two are propped apart; heaven and earth stand firm. The Skambha is all this that possesses a self, whatever breathes and whatever blinks. Three generations have passed beyond it; others have settled around the *arka*. The Great One stands as the measurer of the region (*rajas*); he has entered the green, golden-hued [rays]. Twelve are the spokes, one the wheel; three are the naves—who indeed understands that? Therein are fixed three hundred and sixty pegs and stakes that do not waver.
O Savitṛ, discern this: there are six pairs, and one who is born alone. They desire kinship with him who among them is the one born alone.
Being manifest, he is hidden in the secret cave; he is the great, aging Name. Therein all this is placed: whatever moves, breathes, and stands firm.

One wheel revolves with a single rim; it has a thousand syllables, filling the front and following behind. With one half he generated the entire world; where did that other half of his go? A five-horsed chariot carries them at the head; the yoked side-horses follow along. Its coming is seen, but its going is not; the further is not more distant than the nearer. Transversely hollowed is the cup, standing on its bottom; within it is deposited glory of every form. There sit together the seven seers who were the guardians of this great one.

Whatever moves, flies, and whatever stands still; whatever breathes, does not breathe, and whatever blinks its eyes—He has supported that world of all forms. Having come together, it becomes one alone. Endless and spread out in many places, it is both infinite and finite unto its limits. As the guardian of the vault of heaven, he moves about discerning, the knower of what has been and what is to be.
Prajāpati moves within the womb, invisible; he is born manifoldly. With one half he generated the entire world; as for that which is his other half, what sign is it?
All see with their eyes him who carries water upward as if with a jar, yet not all know him with their mind.
He dwells far away with the full; he is lost far away with the deficient. A great Yakṣa is in the midst of the world; to him the Rāṣṭrabhṛts bring tribute.

That from which the sun rises and where it goes to set—that indeed I consider the eldest; nothing whatsoever surpasses it. Those who, whether in the present, in the middle, or in the past, speak around a learned man who knows the Veda—they all speak around the Sun alone, [who is] Agni the second, and the threefold *haṃsa*.
The two wings of this golden *haṃsa* as he flies to heaven extend across a thousand days. Having laid all the gods upon his breast, he goes beholding all the worlds.
By truth he heats upward; by the sacred word (brahman) he looks downward; by vital breath (prāṇa) he breathes crosswise—he in whom the supreme is established.

In the beginning it became footless; in the beginning it brought forth the light. Having become four-footed, it became an object of enjoyment and took all food for its sustenance.
He becomes an object of enjoyment, and moreover, he eats much food—he who shall worship the eternal God who possesses the higher realm.
They call him eternal, yet even today he may be ever-renewed; day and night are born from one another’s forms.

A hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, and an incalculable amount of one’s own wealth is deposited in this [body]. They seize it from him even as he looks on; therefore, this god delights in this.

Smaller than the smallest hair, yet not seen as even one, therefrom arises that more embracing deity who is dear to me. This auspicious, undecaying, immortal [deity] dwells in the house of the mortal; for whomever she is prepared, she lies with him—he who made her, he has grown old.
You are a woman; you are a man; you are a boy, or even a girl.
As the aged, you move with a staff; as the newborn, you become the one whose face is turned in every direction.

Whether he is their father or their son, whether he is their eldest or their youngest—truly, that one God has entered into the mind; born first, he is indeed within the womb. From the full, he draws forth the full; the full is poured by the full. May we today understand that from which it is poured forth.

The deity named Avi indeed dwells encompassed by the Eternal Order (Ṛta). By her form, these trees are green, wearing green garlands.
She does not abandon him who is near; she does not see him who is near. Behold the poetic wisdom of the god: he neither dies nor does he decay.
Impelled by the Unprecedented (Apūrva), those words speak according to their respective functions; that which they reach while speaking, they call the Great Brahman.

Wherein gods and men are centered like spokes in a nave—therein I ask about the flower of the waters, where it is established by creative power (*māyā*). By whom was the wind impelled when it blows forth; who gave the five directions their common orientation? Which were those gods who, as leaders of the waters, disregarded the *āhuti* offering?
One of them clothes himself in this earth; one has encompassed the intermediate space. He who is the distributor gives them heaven; others guard all the quarters.

He who knows the thread stretched out, in which these creatures are woven; he who knows the thread of the thread—he would know the Great Brahman. I know the thread stretched out, in which these creatures are woven; I know the thread of the thread, as well as that which is the Great Brahman. When Agni, all-consuming, went forth burning between heaven and earth, where stood the women with their single husbands—where was Mātariśvan at that time?
Mātariśvan entered into the waters; the gods entered, and they became the floods.
Vast indeed stands he, the measurer of the mid-air; Pavamāna has entered the bay steeds.

As with the *gāyatrī* meter, he has stepped forth upon the immortal realm by the northern path. Where was that Unborn One seen, who through the *sāman* knows the *sāman*, the dwelling-place and gatherer of treasures, whose laws are true like the god Savitṛ? Like Indra, he has taken his stand in the clash for riches.
The lotus with nine gates is enveloped by the three qualities; that conscious being who resides within it, the knowers of Brahman truly know as Brahman.

Bind the faces even of those who intend us harm; hurl this thunderbolt at our rivals! This first hundredfold oblation, given by Indra, is the slayer of enemies and the path for the sacrificer.
Let the altar be your hide, and let the sacrificial grass be the hairs that are yours. This cord has seized you; let this pressing-stone dance upon you.
Let those fools be your sprinkling waters; let the tongue wipe you clean, O inviolable one. Having become pure and worthy of sacrifice, go to heaven, O hundred-porridge!
He who cooks the hundred-porridge is fulfilled by the fulfillment of his desires; for all his priests, being gratified, depart each to their own station.
He ascends to heaven, where that triple-heaven of the sky is located, he who gives a hundred rice-offerings, making the sacrificial cake its center.
He attains those worlds, both celestial and terrestrial, who gives a hundred-fold rice-offering after having prepared it with the radiance of gold.

O Goddess, those who are your pacifiers and those who are your cooks, and all those people—they shall all protect you; do not fear them, O Śataudana. The Vasus shall protect you from the south, the Maruts from the north, and the Ādityas from behind; as such, run past the Agniṣṭoma.
The gods, the ancestors, human beings, and those Gandharvas and Apsarases—they shall all protect you; as such, run past the Atirātra.
Sprinkling ghee, the fortunate goddess shall go to the gods. O inviolable one, do not harm the cooker; go to heaven, O hundredfold rice-offering!
From those gods who dwell in heaven, those who dwell in the intermediate space, and those who are upon this earth—from them, may you always yield milk, clarified butter, and honey.
That which is your head, that which is your mouth, your two ears, and your two jaws—may they yield for the giver curd, milk, clarified butter, and honey.
May your two lips, your two nostrils, your two horns, and your two eyes yield for the giver curd, milk, clarified butter, and honey.
May your lungs, your heart, your pericardium, together with your throat, yield for the giver curd, milk, clarified butter, and honey.
Whatever liver you have, whatever two kidneys, whatever intestines, and whatever bowels you have—let them yield for the giver curd, milk, clarified butter, and honey.
May that which is your bladder, your rectum, your two kidneys, and your skin—may these yield for the giver curds, milk, clarified butter, and also honey.
May your marrow, your bone, your flesh, and your blood yield for the giver curds, milk, clarified butter, and honey.
May those two arms of yours, those two forearms, those two shoulders, and that hump of yours, yield for the giver curd, milk, clarified butter, and honey.

May your necks, your shoulders, your vertebrae, and your ribs yield for the giver curd, milk, ghee, and honey; may they yield for the giver curd, milk, ghee, and honey; may they yield for the giver curd, milk, ghee, and honey; may they yield for the giver curd, milk, ghee, and honey; may they yield for the giver curd, milk, ghee, and honey; may they yield for the giver curd, milk, ghee, and honey; may they yield for the giver curd, milk.
May your two thighs, your two knees, your two hips, and your pubic region yield for the giver curd, milk, clarified butter, and also honey.
May that which is your tail, those which are your hairs, that which is your udder, and those which are your teats, yield for the giver curds, milk, clarified butter, and likewise honey.
May those thighs of yours, those hocks, the sinews, and those hooves of yours, yield for the giver curd, milk, clarified butter, and honey.
May the hide that is yours at the hundredfold oblation, and the hairs upon you, O inviolable cow, yield curd for the giver, as well as milk, clarified butter, and honey.
Let your two forequarters be two sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) sprinkled with clarified butter; making those, O Goddess, your two wings, carry the cooker to heaven.

Whatever grain or husk is in the mortar, in the pestle, on the hide, or in the winnowing basket—whatever the wind, Mātariśvan, the purifier, has scattered—that may Agni, as the Hotṛ, make into a well-offered oblation.

Homage to you as you are being born, and homage to you once born; homage to your young ones, to your hooves, and to your form, O inviolable one! He who knows the seven downward slopes, he who knows the seven distant realms, and he who knows the head of the sacrifice—he alone should receive the cow.
I know the seven downward slopes; I know the seven distant realms. I know the head of the sacrifice, and I know Soma, the far-seeing one, within this [earth].
By whom the sky was protected, by whom the earth, and by whom these waters were guarded—that Cow of a thousand streams, we invoke with a sacred prayer.
A hundred bronze vessels, a hundred milkers, and a hundred guardians are upon her back. Those gods who breathe within her know the cow (*vaśā*) as one.

She is the foot of sacrifice, the milkless, the self-sustaining (*svadhā*), the breaths, and the great world. The cow, the consort of Parjanya, approaches the gods through sacred formulation (*brahman*).
Agni has entered after you; Soma has entered into you, O Cow. Parjanya is your udder, O Blessed One; the lightnings are your teats, O Cow.

You milked the waters first, the fertile fields next, and you milked the third realm—food and milk—at your will. When you, O observer of the cosmic order (*ṛtavarī*), stood near as you were invoked by the Ādityas, Indra caused you to drink a thousand vessels of Soma at your will.

That milk which the Lord of Wealth, when enraged, took away under his control—that very thing Nāka protects today within three vessels.
The divine cow Vaśā brought that Soma from the three vessels to where the consecrated Atharvan sat upon the golden sacrificial grass.
For she has come together with Soma and with every footed creature; Vaśā has reached the ocean along with the Gandharvas and the Kali-spirits.
For she has come together with the wind and with all winged birds; Vaśā danced upon the ocean, bearing the *ṛc* verses and the *sāman* chants.

For she has come together with the sun, together with every eye; the cow has looked across the ocean, bearing auspicious lights. When you stood there, O observer of *ṛta*, enveloped in gold, the ocean became a horse and leaped upon you, O Vaśā.
Then the auspicious ones met together: Vaśā, the Impeller, and likewise Svadhā, where the consecrated Atharvan sat upon the two golden sacrificial grasses.

The barren cow is the mother of the Rājanya; O Svadhā, the barren cow is your mother. From the sacrifice of the barren cow, the sacrificial implement was born, and from that, consciousness (*citta*) arose.
An upward-pointing drop ascended from the summit of the *Brahman*; from that, you were born as the barren cow (*vaśā*), and from that, the Hotṛ priest was born.
From your mouth the *gāthās* came into being; from your lips, strength; in the barren cow, power. From your belly the sacrifice was born; from your breasts, the rays of light.
From the two *īrma*s the path was born, and from the two thighs [the world] was born under your control. From the entrails the *atrā*s were born; from the belly the plants sprang forth.
When you entered the belly of Varuṇa under his control, then the Brahman summoned you upward, for he indeed knew your guide.
All trembled at the embryo being born from the womb; they called her who gave birth to it "the barren cow" (*vaśā*), for she was ordained by the Brahmans—he indeed is her kin.
He alone brings together the battles; he alone is the master of this [earth]. Sacrifices became the crossing-powers; the cow became the eye of the crossing-powers.
The cow accepted the sacrifice; the cow sustained the sun. Within the cow entered the cooked rice (odana) together with the sacred formulation (brahman).
They say the cow is indeed immortality; they worship the cow as death. The cow became all this: gods, humans, asuras, ancestors, and seers.
He who knows thus should accept a cow; for in this way, the sacrifice yields everything to the giver without faltering.

Three tongues of Varuṇa shine within his mouth; of these, that which shines in the middle is the barren cow (*vaśā*), difficult to accept as a gift. The seed of the barren cow became fourfold: one quarter was water, one quarter was immortality, one quarter was sacrifice, and one quarter was cattle. The barren cow is heaven, the barren cow is earth, the barren cow is Viṣṇu, and the barren cow is Prajāpati. The Sādhyas and the Vasus drank the milk of the barren cow.

Having drunk the milk of the barren cow, the Sādhyas and those who are the Vasus indeed wait upon her milk in the realm of the sun. Some milk her for Soma; some wait upon her for clarified butter. Those who gave a barren cow to one who knows thus have gone from heaven to the third heaven.
By giving a barren cow to Brahmins, one attains all the worlds. For in her is established the cosmic order (*ṛta*), and likewise the sacred word (*brahman*) and ascetic heat (*tapas*).

The cow became all this, as far as the sun shines. The cow became all this, as far as the sun shines. The cow became all this, as far as the sun shines. The cow became all this, as far as the sun shines. The cow became all this, as far as the sun shines. The cow became all this, as far as the sun shines. O Agni, be born! This Aditi, seeking protection and desiring a son, cooks this *brahmaudana*. May the seven seers, the creators of beings, churn you forth here together with progeny.
O bulls, O friends, produce smoke; free from guile, let your voice reach the waters. This Agni is the conqueror of armies, the possessor of brave sons, by whom the gods overcame the Dasyus.

O Agni Jātavedas, you have been born for great heroic power and for the cooking of the *brahmaudana*. The seven seers, the creators of beings, have generated you; bestow upon this woman wealth consisting of all-heroic sons.

Kindled with fuel, O Agni, be thou well-kindled; as one who knows, bring hither the gods worthy of sacrifice. Cook the oblation for them, O Jātavedas, and cause this [sacrificer] to ascend to the highest heaven.

Know the threefold portion that was established of old for you—the gods, the ancestors, and mortals. Distinguish their shares; I divide them among you. That which belongs to the gods shall carry him across to this [world].

O Agni, powerful and victorious, you are indeed a conqueror; cast down those who hate us, our rivals. This measuring-line, being measured and now measured out, shall make your kinsmen bringers of tribute.
Be united with your kinsmen and with milk; lift her up for great heroic power. Standing upright, ascend to the vault of the firmament, that which they call the heavenly world.
May this great Earth, the goddess, receive him as a skin, being well-disposed. Then may we go to the world of the righteous.

Yoke these two pressing-stones together; bind the stalks upon the hide for the sake of the sacrificer. Striking them down, destroy those who attack us here; lift up the progeny that bears them aloft, and carry them upward.

Take the two pressing-stones, O hero, held together in your hand; the gods worthy of sacrifice have come to your sacrifice. Three boons you choose while striving—those successes of yours I shall accomplish here. Three boons you choose while striving—those successes of yours I shall accomplish here. Three boons you choose while striving—those successes of yours I shall accomplish here. Three boons you choose while striving—those successes of yours I shall accomplish here. Three boons you choose while striving—those [successes] of yours...

This is your wisdom, and this is your place of origin; may Aditi, whose sons are heroes, accept you. Drive away those who attack us; bestow upon her wealth consisting of all heroic sons. Sit down upon the winnowing basket and the wooden mortar; O worthy ones of sacrifice, separate yourselves from the husks. Through our shared glory, may we surpass all our equals; I cast the hateful ones beneath my feet.

O woman, come back quickly from the others; the stall of waters has mounted you for the sake of bearing. Of those [waters], seize whichever are worthy of sacrifice; having distinguished them, leave behind the others.

These women have come, adorning themselves; arise, O woman, and take hold of the vigorous one. As a good wife with a husband and offspring, may you be prolific; the sacrifice has come to you—take hold of the vessel.

The portion of vigor which was deposited among you of old—bring hither those waters directed by the seers. May this sacrifice be for you the finder of passage, the finder of refuge, the finder of progeny, the fierce one, the finder of cattle, and the finder of heroes. O Agni, the sacrificial vessel has mounted upon thee; pure and most fervent, burn him with thy heat. Let the divine seers, having gathered together, let them, as the most fervent ones, burn this portion with the seasonal rites.

Pure, purified, and worthy of sacrifice, may these bright waters glide over the sacrificial porridge (*caru*). May they grant us abundant offspring and cattle; may the cooker of the rice-mess go to the world of the righteous.

Purified by the sacred word (*brahman*) and cleansed with clarified butter, may these grains of rice, the stalks of Soma, be fit for sacrifice. Enter the waters; let the *caru* receive you. Having cooked this, may he go to the world of the righteous.
Spread wide with great majesty, O thousand-backed one, in the world of well-performed deeds! Grandfathers, fathers, progeny, and descendants—I am your fifteenth, the cooker.

Thousand-backed, hundred-streamed, imperishable, this *brahmaudana* leads to the gods, goes to heaven. I place those [ancestors] there for you; do not harm their offspring. Be gracious to me alone for the sake of the tribute-bearer.
Arise, O altar; cause this one to increase with progeny. Drive away the Rakṣas, place her further forward. May we surpass all our equals in glory; I cast those who hate us beneath my feet.
Turn back with cattle; come toward her with the deities. Let no curse nor sorcery reach you; rule without disease in your own field.

Fashioned by the *ṛta*, placed here with intent mind—this is the prepared altar for the *brahmaudana*. O woman, place upon it the pure shoulder-supporting [ladle]; there, set down the rice-offering for the gods.
This second ladle is the hand of Aditi, which the seven seers, the creators of beings, fashioned. Knowing the limbs of the rice-offering, may that ladle arrange it upon the altar.

May the gods sit down to you as the cooked oblation; having emerged from the fire, sit down with them again. Purified by Soma, sit within the belly of the Brahmins. May those who consume it, the descendants of seers, not suffer harm.

O King Soma, bestow recognition upon them—upon whichever well-versed Brahmins sit near you. I invoke with a good call the Rishis, the descendants of seers, born from ascetic heat, at this *brahmaudana* (the rice-mess for the Veda).

Pure, cleansed, and worthy of sacrifice are these women; I set them down separately in the hands of the Brahmins. With whatever desire I sprinkle this upon you, may Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, grant it to me.
This is my light, my immortal gold; from the field comes this cow of plenty for me. This wealth I deposit among the Brahmins; I prepare the path to heaven that leads to the ancestors.
Scatter the husks into the fire, into Jātavedas; cast the chaff far away! We have heard this to be the portion of the King of the House; and thus we know it to be the allotted share of Nirṛti.

Know him as one who exerts himself, who cooks, and who presses the Soma; cause him to ascend the path to heaven, by which he may reach the highest state, the supreme age, the firmament, and the highest vault of heaven.
O Adhvaryu, cleanse this mouth of Babhri; being wise, prepare a space for the clarified butter. Anoint all his limbs with ghee. I prepare the path leading to heaven among the Fathers.

Cast the *rakṣas* and strife into Babhri! Whichever non-Brahmins have sat down near you—those who are full of soil, those who are foremost in the east, those of seer-lineage—may they, as the partakers, not suffer harm.

I place you among the descendants of the seers, O Odana; here there is a place for the various lineages of the seers. May Agni and all the Maruts be my guardians; may the Viśve Devas protect the cooked offering.
You are the milking sacrifice, ever swelling, the male, the cow, the seat of riches. Through offspring, immortality, and long life, and through the increase of wealth, may we sit near you.
You are the bull; go to the heavenly world of the seers and their descendants. Sit in the world of the doers of good deeds; there let our prepared portion be.
Gather together, follow along, O Agni; prepare the paths that lead to the gods. May we follow these well-performed deeds to the sacrifice standing in the vault of heaven upon the seven-rayed one.

O Bhava and Śarva, be gracious; do not come against us, O Lords of Beings, O Lords of Animals; homage be to you both! Do not let loose your arrows at us as we approach; do not harm our bipeds or our quadrupeds.

Do not deliver our bodies to the dog or the jackal, nor to the *aliklavas*, the vultures, or those black ones that prey upon carrion. O Lord of Animals, let not your flies or your birds find us for their meal. Homage to your roar, to your breath, and to your wrathful darts, O Bhava! We offer homage to you, O Rudra, the thousand-eyed, the immortal one.
We offer homage to you from the front, from above, and from below; from the encompassing heights of heaven and from the intermediate space, homage to you!
To your mouth, O Lord of Beasts, and to those eyes of yours, O Bhava; to your skin, your form, and your appearance, and to that which faces us, homage to you!

Homage to your limbs, to your belly, to your tongue, and to your mouth; homage to your teeth and to your sense of smell! With that Rudra—the archer with the blue crest, the thousand-eyed, the vigorous, the slayer of Ardhaka—may we never come into conflict.
May Bhava spare us on every side; may Bhava spare us as fire spares the waters. Let him not consume us; let there be homage to him.
Four times "namas" to Bhava, eight times; ten times "namas to you, Paśupati. These five classes of animals are distributed for you: cattle, horses, men, goats, and sheep.

The four quarters are yours; yours is the sky, yours the earth, and yours, O Mighty One, is this wide mid-air. All this that has a soul, all that breathes upon the earth, is yours—all this that has a soul, all that breathes upon the earth, is yours—all this that has a soul, all that breathes upon the earth, is yours—all this that has a soul, all that breathes upon the earth, is yours—all this that has a soul, all that breathes upon the earth, is yours—all this that has a soul, all that breathes upon the earth, is yours—all this that has a soul, all that breathes upon the earth, is yours.

This is your broad vessel, the treasury of wealth, within which all these worlds are contained. As such, O Paśupati, be gracious to us; homage be unto you! Let the jackals, the howling dogs, and the evil-voiced, long-haired women go far away.

You bear a golden, green bow, thousand-slaying and hundred-killing, adorned with a crest. The arrow of Rudra, the weapon of the god, moves abroad; homage be to it, wherever in this direction it may be from here.
O Rudra, whoever approaches you seeking to harm you and hides away—him you pursue from behind like the track of a wounded animal.
O Bhava and Rudra, acting in concert and in harmony, both of you, the fierce ones, move together for the sake of heroic power. Homage to them in whichever direction they may be from here!
Homage be to you as you come; homage be to you as you go away. Homage to you, O Rudra, as you stand, and homage also to you as you sit.
Homage in the evening, homage in the morning, homage by night, homage by day! To Bhava and to Śarva—to both of them I have paid homage.
To the thousand-eyed one, the far-seeing, to Rudra who shoots from the front, the wise one who appears in many forms—may we not fail him with our tongue as he moves along.
To the one with dark horses, the black, the dark-hued, the crusher, the terrible one who makes the long-haired ones fall from their chariot—to him, as we face him from the east, let there be homage!
Do not let your divine bolt strike us, O God; do not be angry with us, O Lord of Creatures—homage be to you! Shake your celestial branch elsewhere than upon us.
Do not harm us; speak for us; spare us; do not be angry; may we never come into conflict with you.
Do not covet our cattle, nor our men, nor our goats and sheep; O fierce one, turn away elsewhere and destroy the offspring of those who offer you nothing.

He whose weapon is fever and cough, who goes forth like the neighing of a stallion, who advances step by step and is clearly discerned—homage be to him! He who stands established in the mid-air, crushing those who do not sacrifice and those who revile the gods—to him be homage with the ten *śakvarī* verses!

To you belong the wild animals, the beasts dwelling in the forest, the swans, the fair-winged birds, and all winged creatures. O Lord of Beasts, your spirit dwells within the waters; for your growth, the celestial waters flow.

The *śiṃśumāras*, the pythons, the *purīkayas*, the *jaṣas*, the fish, and the *rajasas* from whom you hurl [your weapons]: for you there is no distance, nor is there any place where you are not present; O Bhava, you behold the entire earth instantly. From the eastern ocean you strike down to the northern one.

O Rudra, do not afflict us with fever, nor with poison, nor let us be consumed by celestial fire. Cast this lightning bolt elsewhere than upon us. Bhava rules over heaven, Bhava rules over the earth, and Bhava has filled the wide mid-air. To him be homage, however far in whatever direction he may be from here.
Be gracious, O King, to the sacrificer; for you have become the Lord of Animals (*paśupati*). Be gracious to his four-footed and two-footed creatures, who has faith that "the gods exist.
Do not harm our great ones, nor our small ones; do not harm those who carry us, nor those who shall carry us. Do not injure our father and mother, O Rudra; do not strike down our own bodies.
To Rudra’s Elabakāras, to those who swallow what is not praised, to these dogs with great mouths—to them I have offered this homage.

Homage to you, the noisy ones; homage to you, the long-haired ones. Homage to those who have been saluted; homage to those who are enjoying themselves. Homage to you, the divine armies! May there be well-being for us, and may there be fearlessness for us. [Repeated: Homage to the divine armies! May there be well-being for us, and may there be fearlessness for us. Homage to the divine armies! May there be well-being for us, and may there be fearlessness for us. Homage to the divine armies! May there be well-being for us, and may there be fearlessness for us.
Of that rice-offering, Bṛhaspati is the head and the sacred word (brahman) is the mouth.
Heaven and Earth are the ears; the sun and moon are the two eyes; the seven seers are the out-breath and the in-breath;
the eye is the pestle, and desire is the mortar.
Diti is the winnowing basket, Aditi is the one who holds the basket; Vāta has winnowed [the grain]:
the horses are the chaff, the cows are the rice grains, and the gadflies are the husks.
The kidneys are the husks; the spleen is the cloud.
Dark is his iron; his flesh is blood, his blood is red.
Tin ash is green in color; its fragrance is like that of the Puṣkara lotus.
The threshing-floor is the sacrificial vessel, the two shoulder-blades are the two shoulder-yokes, and the spine is the two shafts.
The entrails are the collarbones, and the rectums are the leather thongs.
This very earth becomes the cooking-pot for the rice being prepared, and the sky is its lid.
The cool ribs are the sand; the undigested food is the gravel.
The *ṛta* is the water for washing the hands; the streams are the sprinkling.
The pot was placed upon [the fire] with a Ṛg-verse; it was dispatched by means of the office of the officiating priest.
She is embraced by Brahmā and wedded by the Sāman.
The Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans] are the large vessel and the ladle.
The seasons are the cooks; the seasonal offerings kindle them together.
By means of rice-offerings, all the worlds of the sacrificer are to be fully satisfied.
In whom the ocean, the sky, and the earth—the three, both near and far—are supported.
In whose leavings the gods were fashioned—the eighty-six [clans].
I ask you about that rice, what its great majesty is.
He who should know the greatness of this rice-porridge.
One should not say, "It is not small," nor "It is without seasoning," nor "This and that."
As long as the giver intends to give, one should not speak beyond that.
The exponents of Brahman say: "Did you eat the rice facing away, or facing toward us?"
"You ate the rice; you are the rice."
And he said to him, "Since you have eaten this facing away, your vital breaths will desert you."
"And you have eaten him facing inward; the out-breaths will desert you," he said to him.
I am not the rice, nor is the rice me.
He ate rice upon rice alone.

Then he said to him, "You have eaten this with another head than that with which the ancient seers ate it; therefore, your offspring shall die starting from the eldest. "I did not eat it facing downward, nor facing away, nor facing toward me. I ate it with Bṛhaspati as my head. With that I ate it; with that I sent it forth. This porridge indeed has all its limbs, all its joints, and its entire body. He who knows thus becomes possessed of all his limbs, all his joints, and his entire body—yes, he who knows thus, he who knows thus, he who knows thus."

"And then you ate him with other ears than those with which the ancient seers ate him; therefore you will become deaf," he said to him. "Indeed, I did not eat him facing downward, nor facing away, nor facing toward me; I ate him with the two ears belonging to Heaven and Earth. With those two I ate him, with those two I sent him forth. This rice-mess is indeed possessed of all limbs, all joints, and an entire body. He who knows this becomes possessed of all limbs, all joints, and an entire body—yea, he who knows this."

"And then you ate him with those other two eyes with which the ancient seers ate him; you shall become blind," he said to him. "I have not eaten him facing this way, nor facing away, nor facing toward me; rather, I have eaten him with the sun and moon as my two eyes; through them I have eaten him, through them I have sent him forth. This rice-mess (odana) indeed has all its limbs, all its joints, and its entire body. He who knows thus becomes possessed of all his limbs, all his joints, and his entire body."

Then he said to him: "You have eaten this with another mouth than that with which the ancient seers ate it; therefore, your offspring shall die starting from the mouth. [The seer replied: "I have indeed not eaten it facing downward, nor facing away, nor facing toward me, but with the mouth of Brahman. With that I have eaten it; with that I have sent it forth. This rice-mess (odana) is indeed possessed of all limbs, all joints, and all body. He who knows thus becomes possessed of all limbs, all joints, and all body—yea, he who knows thus."

Then he said to him, "You have eaten this with another tongue than that with which the ancient seers ate it; your tongue shall perish. This rice-mess (odana) indeed possesses all limbs, all joints, and an entire body. He who knows thus becomes possessed of all limbs, all joints, and an entire body. "And then you ate him with other teeth, those with which the ancient seers ate him; 'your teeth shall fall out,' he said to him. This rice-mess (*odana*) indeed has all its limbs, all its joints, and all its body. This rice-mess (odana) indeed has all its limbs, all its joints, and its entire body. "And then you ate it with another breadth, with that same breadth by which the ancient seers ate it. 'Consumption shall slay you,' he said to him. This rice-mess is indeed possessed of all limbs, all joints, and an entire body. "And then you ate it with another back—that very one with which the ancient seers ate it. 'Lightning will strike you,' he said to him. This rice-mess is indeed possessed of all limbs, all joints, and an entire body. He who knows this becomes possessed of all limbs, all joints, and an entire body—yes, he who knows this."

This rice-mess is indeed complete in its limbs, complete in its joints, complete in its body. He who knows thus becomes complete in his limbs, complete in his joints, complete in his body. This rice-mess is indeed complete in its limbs—he who knows thus. This rice-mess is indeed complete in its limbs.

And then he said to him, "You have eaten this with another belly than that with which the ancient seers ate it; a tearer of the belly shall kill you. "I did not eat it facing downward, nor facing away, nor facing toward me, but with a belly of truth. With that I have eaten it; with that I have sent it forth. This rice-mess indeed has all its limbs, all its joints, and its entire body. He who knows thus becomes possessed of all his limbs, all his joints, and his entire body—yea, he who knows thus."

"And then you ate him with another bladder, with that by which the ancient seers ate him. [The teacher] said to him: 'You shall die in the waters. "And then you ate him with other two thighs—those with which the ancient seers ate him. 'Your thighs shall perish,' he said to him. 'Indeed, I did not eat him facing this way, nor facing away, nor facing toward me; rather, with the thighs of Mitra and Varuṇa, with those two I ate him, and with those two I sent him forth. This porridge is indeed possessed of all limbs, all joints, and an entire body. He who knows thus becomes possessed of all limbs, all joints, and an entire body—he who knows thus."

"And then you ate it with two other kneecaps—those with which the ancient seers ate it. 'You will become lame,' he said to him. And then he said to him, "Eat from these other two feet, with those same feet by which the ancient seers ate; you shall become one who wanders far. He who knows thus becomes possessed of all his limbs, all his joints, and his entire body—he who knows thus, he who knows thus."

And then he ate it with those two forefeet with which the ancient seers ate it. "A serpent will kill you," he said to him. "I did not eat it facing downward, nor facing away, nor facing toward me; I ate it with the two forefeet of Savitṛ. With those two I ate it; with those two I sent it down. This rice-mess is indeed possessed of all limbs, all joints, and an entire body. He who knows thus becomes possessed of all limbs, all joints, and an entire body. This rice-mess is indeed possessed of all limbs and an entire body for him who knows thus."

And then he said to him, "You have eaten this with other hands than those with which the ancient seers ate it; you shall kill a Brahmin. He who knows thus becomes complete in his limbs, complete in his joints, and complete in his body—yea, he who knows thus."

"And then you ate it with a support other than that with which the ancient seers ate it; you will die without a foundation and without a resting place," he said to him. This rice-mess is indeed complete in its limbs, complete in its joints, and complete in its body. He who knows this becomes complete in his limbs, complete in his joints, and complete in his body—yes, he who knows this, he who knows this, he who knows this, he who knows this."
This rice porridge is indeed the summit of the sun.
He becomes the world of the sun; he rests upon the summit of the sun—he who knows thus.

He who becomes a witness to one who knows thus obstructs his vital breath.
And he does not obstruct his vital breath; he suffers no loss of anything whatsoever.
He is conquered by misfortune even before old age; his vital breath abandons him.

Homage to Prāṇa, under whose control all this exists; who has become the Lord of all, in whom everything is established. Homage to you, O Prāṇa, for your thundering; homage to you for your lightning; homage to you, O Prāṇa, for your raining. When Prāṇa thunders with his roar, the plants are impregnated; they conceive their embryos and then many are born.
When the breath has arrived at its proper season and the plants cry out, then everything that exists upon the earth rejoices.
When Prāṇa has rained down rain upon the great earth, the cattle rejoice, saying, "Great indeed will our prosperity be!"
The plants, drenched by the breath, have conversed together: "Verily, you have prolonged our life; you have made us all fragrant.
Homage be to you as you come, homage be to you as you go away. Homage to you, O Breath, as you stand, and homage to you as you sit.
Homage to you, O Breath, as you breathe out, and homage be to you as you breathe in. Homage to you as you turn away, homage to you as you turn toward us. This homage is to you in your entirety.
O Prāṇa, that body of yours which is dear, and that which is even more beloved to you, and whatever healing power is yours—bestow that upon us so that we may live.
Prāṇa clothes all creatures as a father clothes his beloved son. Prāṇa is indeed the lord of all, both of that which breathes and that which does not.
Prāṇa is death, Prāṇa is fever; the gods worship Prāṇa. Prāṇa indeed establishes the speaker of truth in the highest world.

The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the sovereign ruler (*virāj*); the vital breath is the director (*deṣṭrī*). All worship the vital breath. The vital breath is indeed the sun and the moon; they call the vital breath Prajāpati.

Out-breath and in-breath are rice and barley; the ox is called the vital breath. In barley the vital breath is established, while rice is called the out-breath. Within the womb, a person breathes out and breathes in. When you, O Prāṇa, quicken him, then he is born again.
They call Mātariśvan "Prāṇa"; indeed, Vāta is called Prāṇa. In Prāṇa is both the past and the future; in Prāṇa everything is established.
The plants born of Atharvan, of Aṅgiras, of the gods, and those born of men—all these spring forth when you, O Prāṇa, quicken them.
When Prāṇa has rained down rain upon the great earth, the herbs are born, as well as whatever plants there may be.

O Prāṇa, he who knows this of you, and in whom you are established—for him all shall bring tribute in that highest world. Just as all these creatures bring tribute to you, O Prāṇa, so shall they bring tribute to him who hears you, O you of good fame.

The embryo moves within the deities; having become manifest, he is born again as a being. As a being, he has entered the future through his powers—the father, by his powers, has entered the son. The swan, rising from the waters, does not lift up one foot. If, indeed, it were to lift that foot, there would be neither today nor tomorrow; there would be neither night nor day, and it would never dawn.

The eight-spoked wheel with its single rim revolves; it has a thousand syllables, extending forward and backward. With one half he generated the entire world; what is that banner which is his other half?
To him who rules over this whole birth and all that moves, to him who possesses a swift bow among others—to you, O Prāṇa, let there be homage!
To him who rules over this entire birth and all that moves, may the tireless, wise Prāṇa abide within me through the sacred word (brahman).
Standing upright while others sleep, he indeed does not lie down horizontally; no one at all has ever heard him sleeping while others are asleep.

The celibate student moves, warming both worlds; in him the gods become of one mind. He supports the earth and the sky; he satisfies his teacher through ascetic fervor.

The ancestors, the divine folk, and all the gods individually follow after the one who practices the holy life (*brahmacārin*). The Gandharvas follow him—thirty-three, three hundred, and six thousand. He satisfies all those gods by means of his ascetic heat (*tapas*).

The teacher, initiating him, makes the religious student his embryo within; he bears him in his belly for three nights; when he is born, the gods assemble to behold him. This fuel-stick is the earth, the second is the sky, and it fills the intermediate space with fuel. The religious student, by means of the fuel-stick, the girdle, toil, and austerity, fulfills the worlds.

Born before the Brahman, the student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) arose by means of ascetic heat (*tapas*), clothed in the *gharma* vessel. From him was born the Brāhmaṇa, the highest Brahman, together with all the gods and immortality.

The student of sacred knowledge goes forth, kindled by the fuel-stick, clothed in black, consecrated, with long beard. He immediately goes from the eastern ocean to the northern one, grasping the worlds and repeatedly traversing them.

The Vedic student (brahmacārī), generating the sacred word (brahman), the waters, the world, Prajāpati, Parameṣṭhin, and Virāj—having become an embryo in the womb of immortality and having indeed become Indra, he shattered the Asuras.
The Teacher fashioned both these expansive and deep firmaments, the earth and the sky. The Vedic student protects them through his ascetic fervor (tapas); in him the gods become of one mind.
The first student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) brought forth this earth as alms and the sky; having made these two his fuel-sticks, he worships them, and upon them all beings are established.

One is near, the other is far beyond the back of heaven; these two treasures are deposited in secret within the Brahmin. The student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) guards them through austerity; the knower of Brahman makes that [Brahman] his own entirely. The student of sacred knowledge guards them through austerity; the knower of Brahman makes that [Brahman] his own entirely. The student of sacred knowledge guards them through austerity; the knower of Brahman makes that [Brahman] his own entirely. One is on this side, the other beyond the earth; these two fires have come together within the two skies. Upon them rest their firm rays; the student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) mounts them through austerity.

Roaring, thundering, ruddy, white-horned, with a great phallus, he has spread himself along the earth. The student of sacred knowledge pours his seed upon the ridge of the earth; by that the four quarters of space live.

In fire, in the sun, in the moon, in the wind, and in the waters, the student (brahmacārī) places the fuel-stick. Their flames move separately in the clouds; their clarified butter is man, rain, and the waters. The teacher is Death, Varuṇa, Soma, and the plants; he is milk. The storm-clouds were the warriors; by them this heaven was brought hither. Having become Varuṇa, the teacher makes the clarified butter his own alone. Whatever he desired from Prajāpati, that the student bestowed upon him from his own self as Mitra.
The teacher is the student of sacred knowledge; the student of sacred knowledge is Prajāpati. Prajāpati shines forth as Virāj; Virāj became Indra, the controller.
Through the practice of celibacy and austerity, the king protects his kingdom; through the practice of celibacy, the teacher seeks a student;
through the practice of celibacy, a maiden finds a young husband; and through the practice of celibacy, the ox and the horse strive to win their fodder.
By means of celibacy and austerity, the gods struck down death; indeed, Indra brought back the light of heaven for the gods through celibacy.

The terrestrial, celestial, wild, and domestic animals—both those without wings and those that are birds—all these were born from the Vedic student (*brahmacārin*).
Individually, all these creatures belonging to Prajāpati sustain their vital breaths within themselves. Brahman protects them all, for they are upheld by the Vedic student.
This, which is consecrated for the gods, moves about shining, never overtaken [by decay]. From that was born the Brāhmaṇa, the highest Brahman, together with all the gods and immortality.

The radiant student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) bears the *brahman*; in him all the gods are gathered together. Generating out-breath, in-breath, and diffused breath (*vyāna*), as well as speech, mind, heart, sacred knowledge, and wisdom—bestow upon us sight, hearing, glory, food, seed, blood, and the belly.

Forming them [the worlds], the student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) stood performing austerities upon the surface of the waters in the ocean. We invoke Agni, the lords of the forest, the herbs, and the plants; Indra, Bṛhaspati, and Sūrya—may they deliver us from distress.
We invoke King Varuṇa, Mitra, Viṣṇu, and Bhaga; Aṃśa and Vivasvat—we invoke them—may they deliver us from distress.
We invoke the god Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, and Pūṣan; Tvaṣṭṛ, the foremost—we invoke him—may they deliver us from distress.

We invoke the Gandharvas and Apsarases, the two Aśvins, and Brahmaṇaspati; may that god who is named Aryaman deliver us from distress. We invoke Day and Night, both Sūrya and Candramas; we invoke all the Ādityas; may they deliver us from distress.
We invoke Vāta, Parjanya, the intermediate space, and likewise the quarters; we invoke all the regions of space; may they deliver us from distress.

May Day and Night, and likewise Dawn, release me from the curse; may the divine Soma release me, whom they call the Moon. The domestic animals of the earth, those of heaven, and the wild beasts of the forest—those winged birds we speak of—may they all release us from distress.
We address Bhava and Śarva, and Rudra who is the Lord of Beasts: may those arrows which we know them to possess be ever auspicious toward us.
We indeed address the seven seers; we address the divine waters and Prajāpati. We address the ancestors, with Yama as their chief; may they release us from distress.
Those gods who dwell in heaven and those who dwell in the intermediate space, and those who are established upon the earth, O Mighty Ones—may they release us from distress.
The Ādityas, Rudras, Vasus, the gods in heaven, the Atharvans, and the wise Aṅgirases—may they release us from distress.

We invoke the sacrifice, the sacrificer, the *ṛc* verses, the *sāman* chants, the healing remedies, the *yajus* formulas, and the priestly offices; may they deliver us from distress. We invoke the five kingdoms of plants, of which *soma* is the best—*darbha*, *bhaṅga*, barley, and *saha*; may they deliver us from distress. We invoke the stingy spirits, the *rakṣas* demons, the serpents, the holy folk (*puṇyajana*), and the ancestors; we invoke the one hundred and one deaths; may they deliver us from distress.

We address the seasons, the lords of the seasons, and the seasonal periods; the years, the full years, and the months—may they deliver us from distress. O gods, arise from the south, from behind, and moving forward! O mighty ones, all you gods, having gathered from the east and from the north, may you deliver us from distress. We address all the gods, who are true to their covenant and who increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*); together with all their consorts, may they deliver us from distress.
We address all the gods, who are true to their covenant and who increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*): together with all their wives, may they release us from distress.
We address the Past, the Lord of beings, and he who is the sovereign of creatures: may all beings, having come together, release us from distress.
Those goddesses who are the five directions, those gods who are the twelve seasons, and those who are the fangs of the year—may they ever be auspicious to us.
