In the *ucchiṣṭa* (the Residue) are name and form; in the *ucchiṣṭa* is the world established. Both Indra and Agni are the *ucchiṣṭa*, within which the entire universe is contained. In the *ucchiṣṭa* are heaven and earth; in it is contained all that has come to be. In the *ucchiṣṭa* are the waters and the ocean; in it is established the moon and the wind.
Both being and non-being are in the *ucchiṣṭa*, as are Death, Strength, and Prajāpati. All worldly things depend upon the *ucchiṣṭa*; both Vra and Dra, as well as Prosperity (*śrī*), reside in me.
Firm, strengthening, steadfast, and fixed—the ten creators of the universe [have placed] the *brahman* [there]. Like a wheel around its hub, all the deities are supported within the *ucchiṣṭa*.

The *Ṛc*, *Sāman*, and *Yajus* are the *ucchiṣṭa*; the *Udgītha*, the *Prastuta*, and the *Stuta* are the *ucchiṣṭa*. The *Hiṅkāra*, the tone (*svara*) of the *Sāman*, and the *Meḍi* are in the *ucchiṣṭa*; and that is in me.
The *Aindrāgna*, the *Pāvamāna*, the *Mahānāmnī* verses, and the *Mahāvrata*—the limbs of the sacrifice are in the *ucchiṣṭa*, like an embryo within the mother.

The Rājasūya, the Vājapeya, the Agniṣṭoma, and that sacrifice (adhvara); the Arka and Aśvamedha, the Jīvabarhis, and the most intoxicating (madintama) [Soma]; the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), as well as initiation (dīkṣā), the fulfiller of desires (kāmapra), together with the meters (chandas); the neglected sacrifices and the long sessions (satrāṇi)—all these are established within the Residue (ucchiṣṭa). The fire-oblation (agnihotra), faith (śraddhā), the exclamation Vaṣaṭ, the vow (vrata), austerity (tapas), the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), the desired offering (iṣṭa), and the meritorious work (pūrta)—all these are established within the Residue.
The one-night sacrifice, the two-night sacrifice, the *sadyaḥkrī*, the *prakrī*, and the *ukthya*—these are woven and deposited within the remnant (*ucchiṣṭa*) of the sacrifice through knowledge.

The four-night, the five-night, and the six-night rites—both together; the sixteen-fold, and the seven-night rite—all those sacrifices established in immortality were born from the Residue (*ucchiṣṭa*).

The *pratīhāra*, the *nidhana*, the *viśvajit*, and the *abhijit*; the one-day and the overnight sacrifices—even the twelve-day rite is contained within that Residue. Truthfulness, humility, security, the ancestral offering, vigor, immortality, and power—all desires are directed toward the Residue; they have been satisfied by that Desire.
The nine earths and the oceans rest upon the Residue; from heaven the sun shines in the Residue, and day and night are likewise contained within it—may that also be in me.
He who bears the Upahavya sacrifice, the Viṣūvat, and those sacrifices hidden in the secret place—he, the Residue, the father of the progenitor, sustains all;
he, the father of the progenitor, the Residue, the grandson of Asu, the grandfather, dwells as the sovereign lord of all, the bull upon the earth, transcending all obstacles.

In the remnant (ucchiṣṭa) are *ṛta*, truth, austerity, the kingdom, toil, dharma, and action; the past and the future, vigor, fortune, and strength are in the strength. Prosperity, vital energy, intention, dominion, the kingdom, and the six expanses are there. The year is above the remnant; the *iḍā* invocations, the *praiṣas*, the cups, and the oblation are there. The four *hotṛ*s, the *āprīs*, the four-month sacrifices, and the *nīvids* are there. In the remnant are the sacrifices, the priestly offices, the animal bindings, and those offerings.

Sugar, sand, stones, herbs, creepers, and grasses; clouds, lightning, and rain—these are all dependent upon, resting within, the *ucchiṣṭa*. Success, attainment, completion, pervasion, greatness, and growth; over-attainment and prosperity—these are placed, deposited, and established within the *ucchiṣṭa*. Whatever breathes with the breath and whatever sees with the eye—all these have been born from the *ucchiṣṭa*; all the gods in heaven are supported by heaven.

From the Residue were born all the *ṛc*s, the *sāmans*, the meters, and the *purāṇa* along with the *yajus*; all the gods dwelling in heaven who are supported by heaven were born from the Residue. Inhalation and exhalation, sight and hearing, that which is imperishable and that which is perishable—all these were born from the Residue; all the gods dwelling in heaven who are supported by heaven were born from the Residue. Blisses, delights, rapturous joys, and those intense and ordinary pleasures—all these were born from the Residue; all the gods dwelling in heaven who are supported by heaven were born from the Residue.
The gods, the ancestors, human beings, and the gandharvas and apsaras—all these were born from the remains; they are all the gods in heaven, established in heaven.
When Manyu brought his wife from the house of Saṃkalpa, who were the kinsmen, who were the suitors, and who indeed was the eldest suitor?

Both Tapas and Karma were within the great ocean; they were the kinsmen, they were the suitors, and Brahman became the eldest suitor. Ten gods were born together before the [other] gods; he who indeed knows them directly may truly speak of the Great today.
Inhalation and exhalation, sight and hearing, imperishability and perishability, the pervasive breath, the upward breath, speech, and mind—these indeed bring about intention.
The seasons were born, as well as Dhātṛ and Bṛhaspati; Indra, Agni, and the Aśvins—at that time, whom did they worship as the eldest?

Both austerity (*tapas*) and action (*karman*) existed within the great ocean; from action, indeed, austerity was born—that is what they worshipped as the eldest. That which was the primordial earth, which those who possess true knowledge know—whosoever truly knows it by its name, he may consider himself a knower of antiquity.

From where was Indra born? From where Soma? From where was Agni born? From where did Tvaṣṭṛ come into being? From where was Dhātṛ born? From Indra came Indra; from Soma came Soma; from Agni came Agni. Tvaṣṭṛ was indeed born from Tvaṣṭṛ; from Dhātṛ, Dhātṛ was born.

When he brought together hair, bone, sinew, flesh, and marrow, and having fashioned a body with feet, into which world did he enter?
From where did he bring the hair, from where the sinews, from where the bones? Who brought the limbs, the joints, and the marrow; from where did he bring the flesh?
Those gods named Saṃsic were they who gathered the constituent parts together. Having poured everything together, the gods entered the mortal Puruṣa.
The thighs, the feet, the two kneecaps, the head, the hands, and also the face; the spine, the breasts, and the sides—what seer put these together?

The head, the hands, and also the face, the tongue, the neck-bones, and the vertebrae—the Great One, having covered all that with skin, joined it together by means of a seam. When that great body lay there, joined by a seam, who brought the color to it, by which it shines today?
All the gods learned it; the virtuous bride understood it. She who is the wife of the Lord of Power brought color into this world.
When Tvaṣṭar pierced him—Tvaṣṭar’s father who was superior—the gods, having made a mortal dwelling, entered the Puruṣa.
Sleep, lethargy, destruction, and the deities named evils entered the body as old age, baldness, and graying hair.

Prosperity and adversity, blessings and misfortunes, as well as all forms of hunger and thirst, entered into the body.
Censure and non-censure, as well as "yes" and "no," entered the body along with faith, sacrificial gifts, and lack of faith.
Both sciences and non-sciences, and whatever else is to be taught—the *Ṛg*, the *Sāman*, and the *Yajus* entered the body of Brahman;
likewise, joys, delights, pleasures, intense delights, and rapturous joys, as well as laughter, songs, and dances, entered into the body.
Speeches, outcries, and all forms of talk—whether uttered by those who are united, joined, or yoked—all entered the body.
In-breath and out-breath, sight and hearing, as well as non-destruction and destruction, diffused breath and upward breath, speech and mind—these move together with the body.
Blessings, commands, instructions, and directives—all thoughts and all volitions have entered into the body.
The waters that are flowing from the earth and those from the dwelling, those that are swift and those that are sluggish, those that are secret, bright, and gross—those they deposited in Bībhatsu.
Having made the bone the fuel-stick, they placed those eight waters down; having made the semen the clarified butter, the gods entered into Puruṣa.
The waters and the deities, along with Virāj and Brahman, entered the body; within the body resides Prajāpati.
The Sun assigned the eye and Vāta the breath to the person. Then the gods bestowed his other self upon Agni.
Therefore, the wise man considers this person to be Brahman, for all the deities dwell within him like cows in a pen.
By the first stroke of death, he goes apart in three ways: with one part he goes there, with one part he goes there, and with one part he remains here.

His body has been placed within the swelling waters; the corpse lies within it, and because of that, it is called "corpse" (*śava*). Those which are arms, those which are arrows, and the heroic powers of bows; the swords, the axes, and the weapons; and whatever intention and purpose is in the heart—all that, O Arbudi, do thou turn against our enemies to be seen by them, and show them their own noble [deeds] laid bare.
Arise, bind yourselves together, O you divine folk who are our friends! May you be visible and protected—those who are our friends, O Arbudi!
Arise, seize them with your means of grasping and binding! Overwhelm the armies of our enemies, O Arbudi!

The god named Arbudi, and Nyarbudi who is the lord—by those two by whom the intermediate space and this great earth are encompassed, following that victory of those two Indra-like ones, I go forth with my army.
Arise, O divine being Arbudi, together with your army! Shattering the host of our enemies, surround them with your coils.

Nyarbuda, beholding the seven noble-born ones, arise with them all when the clarified butter has been offered, together with your army! Let her who wipes away tears, whose ears are small, cry out when a man is slain—she with disheveled hair, O Arbuda, at your bite!
Dragging about her hands, longing in her mind for her son, husband, brother, or kin, she cries out, O Arbuda, at your bite!
May the *ali-klava* birds, the *jāṣkamada*, the vultures, the hawks, the winged ones, the crows, and the birds be satisfied upon the enemies as they look on, once you have bitten them, O Arbudi!
Moreover, let every beast of prey, the fly, and the worm be satisfied upon this human corpse gnawed by you, O Arbudi. Upon this human corpse gnawed by you, O Arbudi.
Seize them, O Arbudi! Compress them within their out-breath and in-breath! Let the whistlings and roars fall together upon the enemies, making them look at one another with terror.
At your striking, O Arbudi, let them tremble; let them be utterly scattered in fear. Strike the enemies with wide-reaching grips and arm-clasps, O Arbudi!
Let their arms be confounded, and let the thought and intention in their hearts be bewildered. Let nothing whatsoever remain of them when you have struck them down, O Arbudi!
Let them run together, striking one another, beating their breasts and thighs; let the tearful, disheveled women wail when a man has been slain—this at your bidding, O Arbudi.

O Arbudi, [drive away] the Apsarases who possess dogs, those who assume various forms, she who licks the inside of the vessel, and she who seeks out what is ill-placed. All of them, O Arbudi, make visible to our enemies, and show them their own offspring!

O Khaḍūra, you who walk upon the heights, you who are short and dwell in the lowlands—those noble ones who have vanished, the Gandharvas and Apsarases, the serpents, the common folk, and the Rakṣasas;

those with four tusks, dark-fanged, pot-bellied, and blood-faced; those who are well-attacking and those who attack from afar—O Arbudi, make those enemies tremble! Let the victorious and the conqueror, Indra and Medinī, triumph over the foes.
Collapsed, crushed, and slain upon his bed is the enemy at Nyarbuda. Let the victorious ones, whose tongues are fire and whose crests are smoke, advance with their army.

By her [power], may Indra strike down the best of the best among those driven away by Arbuda; may Śacīpati slay the enemies, so that not one of them escapes. May Śacīpati slay the enemies, so that not one of them escapes. May Śacīpati slay the enemies, so that not one of them escapes.
Let their hearts burst open; let their life-breath rise upward. Let dryness of mouth overcome the enemies, and not those who are our friends.

Whether they be wise or unwise, whether they turn away or are deaf, those who are blinded by darkness, those who are hornless, and those who wear goatskins—O Arbudi, make them all visible to the enemies, and show them forth clearly.

May Arbudi and Triṣandhi pierce our enemies through, so that we may slay these enemies by the thousands, O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, Lord of Might! The lords of the forest, the products of the forest, the herbs, and the creepers; the Gandharvas, Apsarases, serpents, gods, the holy folk (Puṇyajanas), and the ancestors—O Arbudi, make all of them visible to our enemies, and show them forth in their true form!

The divine Āditya, Brahmaṇaspati, and Indra—these are your lords, O Maruts; and Dhātṛ, Mitra, and Prajāpati are your lords. The Ṛṣis have made you lords over those who are unfriendly, so that they may be seen together, O Arbudi, when you have struck them down.
Rulers over all of them, arise and gird yourselves! O friends, you divine folk, having conquered this battle, take your places according to your respective worlds.
Arise! Bind yourselves together with your banners! O serpents, other folk, and demons, pursue the enemies!

I know your sovereignty and your rule over the *triṣandhi* (three-jointed) weapon, along with your ruddy banners. Those who are in the mid-air, those in heaven, those on earth, and those who are human—let all those of evil name wait upon the mind of the *triṣandhi*.
Those with iron faces, needle-faces, and likewise those with *vikaṅkata*-wood faces, the flesh-eaters swift as the wind—let them seize the enemies with the three-jointed thunderbolt!
Place within, O Jātavedas, this corpse, O Āditya, in great abundance! May this army of Triṣandhi be well-disposed under my control.
Arise, O divine being Arbudi, together with the army! This offering is presented for you; may the oblation of Triṣandhi be pleasing.
Let this four-footed arrow, the white-footed one, strike down [the enemy]. O Kṛtyā, become a weapon against the enemies along with the army of Triṣandhi!
Let the smoke-eyed one fall upon him, and let the short-eared one shriek. By the army of Triṣandhi, let the banners be reddened in victory.

Let the birds that fly in the atmosphere and those that roam in heaven be driven away. Let the beasts of prey, the flies, the raw-flesh eaters, the vultures, and the scavengers seize him; let them gnaw at his corpse.
O Bṛhaspati, by that alliance which you have established with Indra and with the *brahman*, by that alliance with Indra, I summon all the gods here. Conquer from this side, not from yonder!

May the earth, clothed in fire and dark-kneed, make me radiant and sharpened.

Upon the earth they present to the gods the sacrifice, the oblation well-prepared; upon the earth mortals live by means of *svadhā*, their food. May that Earth grant us breath and long life; may the Earth make me reach old age.

O Earth, whatever fragrance has arisen from you, which the plants and the waters bear, which the Gandharvas and Apsarases have shared—by that make me fragrant. Let no one at all bear malice toward us.

That fragrance of yours which entered the lotus, which they gathered together at the wedding of Sūryā—O immortal Earth, with that fragrance at the beginning, make me fragrant; let no one whatsoever hate us.

That fragrance of yours which is among men, in women and in men, which is fortune and splendor; that which is in horses, in heroes, in wild beasts, and even in elephants; that luster which is in the maiden, O Earth—with that, unite us as well; let no one whatsoever hate us.
The stone, the earth, the rock, the dust—that earth is firmly held and supported. To that Earth, whose breast is gold, I have paid homage.
Upon her stand the trees, the lords of the forest, fixed for all time. We call upon the Earth, the sustainer of all, who is firmly established.
Whether rising up, or sitting, standing, or stepping forth—with our right and left feet—may we not stumble upon the earth.

I address the wide-spreading Earth, the patient ground, who increases through sacred prayer (*brahman*). O Earth, may we settle down upon you, who bears strength, nourishment, and a portion of food, and who are rich in clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

Those regions of yours that face the east, those that face the north, those of yours, O Earth, that lie below, and those behind—may they be pleasant for me as I move about. Do not fall upon me, you who are established in the world.
Do not push us from behind, nor from the front, nor from above, nor from below. Be a source of well-being for us, O Earth; let not highwaymen find us. Drive far away the weapon of death.
As far as I gaze upon you, O Earth, with the Sun as my companion, so far may my sight not fail me in each succeeding year.
When lying down, I turn over toward my right side, O Earth; when we lie upon you on our backs with our ribs turned upward facing you—do not harm us there, O Earth, you who receive all things.
Whatever of yours I dig up, O Earth, may that grow back quickly. May I not pierce your vital organ, O seeker of forms; may I not strike your heart.
Summer, rains, autumn, winter, the cool season, and spring—these seasons have been ordained for you, O Earth, as your years. May day and night yield us abundance, O Pṛthivī.

She who casts off the serpent as she gives birth, she who is rich in wild beasts, in whom the fires were established—she who, casting out the Dasyus, the revilers of the gods, choosing Indra as she did Vṛtra for the sake of the mighty bull Śakra, has yielded herself to him;

she in whom the sacrificial seat, the oblation-holders, and the sacrificial post are set up; she in whom the Brahmins, knowers of the Yajus, chant with *ṛc* verses and *sāman* hymns; she in whom the officiating priests are joined together to press the Soma for Indra to drink.
In her, the ancient world-creating seers, the wise ones, together with sacrifice and austerity, caused the cows to be brought forth by means of the sevenfold sacrificial session.
May that Earth point out to us whatever wealth we desire; may Bhaga bestow it upon us, and may Indra come as our leader.

Upon that earth where mortals sing and dance, where they fight with various weapons, where there is the cry of battle and the drum resounds—may that earth drive away our rivals; may the earth make me free from enemies.
In whom food, rice, and barley dwell; whose these five tribes are—homage be to that Earth, the wife of Parjanya, who is rich in rain.
She whose cities are built by the gods, in whose field they labor—may Prajāpati make this Earth, the womb of all, delightful for us in every direction.

Bearing treasures in many ways within her secret depths, may the Earth grant me wealth, jewels, and gold. May the Goddess, the giver of riches, bestow wealth upon us as she is propitiated and well-disposed toward us. Bearing people of many voices and diverse customs according to their respective dwellings, may the Earth yield for me a thousand streams of wealth, like a steady cow that does not kick away.

The serpent that is yours—the scorpion with its stinging bite, seized by winter, wandering and lying in its hole; the worm that quickens, O Earth, and whatever moves during the rainy season—let that not crawl upon us; let that which is auspicious be gracious to us. Those many paths of yours frequented by people, the tracks for the chariot to travel, along which both the good and the evil wander—that path may we conquer, free from enemies and robbers; let that which is auspicious be gracious to us.
Bearing the heavy burden of the wicked, enduring the destruction of evil, the Earth, in harmony with the Boar, yields herself for the sake of the wild Sūkara.
Those forest animals, the beasts dwelling in the woods—lions, tigers, and man-eaters that roam there; drive away from us, O Earth, the wolf, the jackal, misfortune, the female bear, and the Rakṣas.
Those Gandharvas and Apsarases, those Ārayas and Kimīdins, all the Piśācas and Rākṣasas—drive them away from us, O Bhūmi!

To which the two-footed winged creatures fly together—the *haṃsas*, the *suparṇas*, the *śakunas*, and the birds; upon which the wind Mātariśvan moves, creating dust and shaking the trees; following the wind’s forward and backward blowing, its flame blows forth;

upon which black and ruddy are joined, day and night are distributed over the earth; with rain the broad earth is covered and encompassed—may she bestow upon us what is auspicious in every beloved abode.

May Heaven and Earth and the mid-air grant me this wide space; may Agni, Sūrya, the Waters, and all the gods bestow wisdom upon me. I am the victorious one, named "The Superior" upon the earth; I am the subduer, the overcomer of all, the conqueror of every quarter.
O Goddess, when you first spread forth in the east, as you were addressed by the gods, you displayed your greatness. At that moment, prosperity entered you; you fashioned the four quarters of space.
Whatever villages, whatever forests, and whatever assemblies exist upon the earth—whatever battles and gatherings there may be—in all of these, may we speak what is pleasing to you.

Like a horse shaking off dust, she has shaken off those people who have occupied the earth since she was born. She is the delightful one who moves at the forefront, the guardian of the world, the seizer of the lords of the forest and of the plants.
What I speak, that I speak as honeyed; what I behold, that they seek after me. I am radiant and impetuous; I strike down others who are turbulent.
Peaceful, fragrant, pleasant, with milk as white as *kīlāla* and full of nourishment—may the Earth, the broad one, speak in my favor along with her milk.

May she who was sought by Viśvakarman with oblation when she had entered the ocean within the intermediate space (*rajas*), that vessel which was hidden in secret, now become manifest for enjoyment to those who possess mothers.

You are the receptacle for all people, Aditi, the fulfiller of desires, spreading far and wide. Whatever is deficient in you, may Prajāpati, the first-born of Cosmic Order (Ṛta), fill that for you. May your laps, O Earth, be free from disease and free from consumption, granted by you to us. Awakening to a long life, may we be those who bring tribute to you.

Climb onto the reed; let this world not be yours. This head of yours is your allotted portion; come! With that consumption which is in cattle and that consumption which is in men, go away, far below, together with it!
From the one who speaks evil and the one who speaks ill, from the hand and the forehand—by that we drive out all consumption and death from here.

They kindle him, the one who brings prosperity, for well-being—becoming pure, bright, and purifying. He leaves behind defilement and passes beyond sin; Agni, once kindled, purifies with his excellent purification.

The divine Agni Saṃkasuka has ascended to the ridges of heaven. Being released from sin, may he free us from the curse. In this Agni Saṃkasuka we wipe away our impurities; we have become pure and worthy of sacrifice. May he prolong our lives.
Saṃkasuka, Vikasuka, Nirṛtha, and Nisvara—may they, together with their knowledge, drive your consumption far, far away.

The flesh-eater whom we drive away from our horses, our heroes, our cattle, and our goats and sheep— That Agni who causes the destruction of people, him we drive away from other men, from your cows, and from your horses; we drive away the flesh-eater.

That Agni who causes the destruction of life, in whom the gods have cleansed themselves and in whom men likewise have cleansed themselves—in him, O Agni, you who are praised with ghee, having been cleansed, ascend to heaven.
Kindled, O Agni, you who are offered oblations, do not depart from us; shine right here in the sky so that we may long behold the sun.

Be gracious toward the *sīsa* plant, be gracious toward the *naḍa* reed, and toward whatever [injury] is in the *saṃkasuka* fire; likewise, [be gracious] toward the headache in the ewe, in the dark night, and in the pillow.
Having been cleansed in the black sheep’s wool, become pure, worthy of sacrifice. Having been cleansed in the black sheep’s wool, become pure, worthy of sacrifice.
O Death, go away along that other path of yours which is distinct from the path of the gods; I speak to you who have eyes and hear: let these many heroes remain here.

These living ones have turned away from the dead; our invocation of the gods has become auspicious today. We have gone forward for dancing and laughter; as men of noble heroes, may we address the assembly.
I set up this boundary for the living, so that no other among them may now go to that goal. May they live a hundred abundant autumns, passing over death by means of this mountain.
Ascend to full life, choosing old age, striving one after another according to your number. May Tvaṣṭṛ, the well-born, being well-disposed toward you, lead you all to a full span of life.

Just as the days come in succession, and as the seasons pass along with the seasons, and just as the later does not abandon the earlier—O Ordainer (*dhātṛ*), fashion the lifespans of these [people] accordingly. The stony river flows; hold fast to one another, show your prowess, and cross over, O friends! Leave behind here those who are evil-minded; may we, free from disease, cross over toward strengths (*vāja*). Arise and cross over, O friends! This stony river flows. Leave behind here those who have been unpropitious; may we, propitious and well-disposed, cross over toward strengths.

Take hold of the Vaiśvadevī with splendor; becoming pure, bright, and purifying, passing over the difficult paths, may we rejoice for a hundred winters, with all our heroes intact. By northerly paths accompanied by Vāyu, passing over those below by means of those above, the seers who have departed have thrice seven times driven away death by treading upon its tracks.
Avoiding the path of death, attaining a longer and further span of life, sitting together in this assembly, drive away death; then, as living beings, may we proclaim our wisdom at the gathering.

May these women, not widows and having good husbands, touch themselves with collyrium and clarified butter. Free from tears, free from disease, and possessing fine jewels, may the wives ascend first to the place of birth. With the oblation I separate these two; by means of the sacred word (*brahman*), I arrange them. I provide for the Fathers an undecaying *svadhā*; with long life, I unite these [living ones].

O fathers, that Agni who has entered into our hearts, the immortal among mortals—I embrace that god within myself; let him not look with hostility upon us, nor we upon him. Having turned away from the *gārhapatya* fire, go forth, O flesh-eater, toward the south! Make yourself dear to the fathers and to the Brahmins. Taking his double share of wealth, he squanders it through misfortune—the flesh-eating Agni who, as the eldest son, has not been properly installed.
Whatever one ploughs, whatever one gathers by hunting, and whatever one acquires through purchase—all that belongs to a mortal ceases to exist if the eater of raw flesh is not driven away.

The one whom the flesh-eater follows becomes unfit for sacrifice, his luster destroyed; he is not permitted to eat the oblation. He cuts off [the fruit] from plowing, cattle, and wealth—whomever the flesh-eater pursues.
That mortal repeatedly cries out in longing, led toward ruin by the flesh-eater. May Agni, the wise one, drive those flesh-eaters far away from our presence.
When a husband dies, the houses that were to be occupied by his wife are joined together; the wise Brahmin alone is to be approached, he who removes the flesh-eating fire.

Turning from the south toward the north, they have returned, knowing the way along the paths traveled by the gods. Upon the back of the mountain, the bull, the ancient rivers flow anew.
O Agni, you who do not eat raw flesh, drive away the flesh-eater and carry [the sacrificer] to the place of sacrifice for the gods.
This flesh-eater has entered here; this one has followed after the flesh-eater. Having made two tigers apart from each other, I carry away that [one] and leave the other auspicious.
Agni Gārhapatya is the concealment of the gods and the enclosure of men; he rests between both.

O Agni, prolong the life of the living; let those who have died go to the world of the ancestors. Being a good householder, burning away hostility, bestow upon him a more auspicious dawn after every dawn.
O Agni, overcoming all rivals, bestow upon us their vigor and wealth.

Take hold of this Indra, the carrier, the protector; may he lead you out from misfortune and from blame. With him, drive away the missile that comes flying; with him, may you be protected from Rudra’s wrath. Take hold of the ox and the raft; may they lead you out from misfortune and from blame. Ascend this ship of Savitṛ; with the six wide expanses, may we cross beyond destitution.

Day and night you follow, bearing [us], dwelling in peace, a furtherer, rich in heroes; bearing us upon your bed, free from sickness and well-disposed, do you remain with us for a long time, O manly-scented one!
They cut off evil from the gods and live forever. Like a horse that shakes off the reed-grass from its side, Agni shakes off those who eat raw flesh.
Those faithless ones who, desiring wealth, sit as flesh-eaters—they indeed always carry away the cooking-pot of others.
He desires to fly away with his mind, yet he turns back again and again; Agni, knowing them well, drives the flesh-eaters far away from his presence.

The black sheep is the portion of cattle; they say the bronze and the bright [metal] are for the flesh-eater. Ground beans are your sacrificial portion; O Araṇyānī, attend to your offering in the deep forest. Having offered an old reed, a piece of hemp, a staff, and a reed-cane—having made these his fuel, Indra extinguished the fire of Yama.

Having restored the sun to its western course, the wise man has indeed entered upon the path. He has sent away the life-breaths of those [enemies]; with long life, I unite these [people]. As a man, mount the man; come to the skin. Summon there whichever of your beloved ones you desire. As far as you two first met in the beginning, so is your common vitality in the realm of Yama.

So great is your vision, so great your heroic powers, so great your splendor, and so manifold your strengths. When Agni attends to the body as its fuel, then you two, as a pair, shall come together from the cooked [oblation].

Be united in this world, and likewise on the path of the gods; may you both meet together in the realms of King Yama. Purified by purifiers, come hither and pour forth whatever seed has been produced within you both.

O Waters, you who are the sons of life and bringers of vitality, come together and enter this living man. Partake of that which they call the immortal; the Cooked Rice (odana) which your progenitor prepares for you—both the one which your father prepares and that which your mother prepares—for release from defilement and from the impurity of speech. That Cooked Rice has a hundred streams; it is heaven, and by its greatness it pervades both the celestial and atmospheric spheres. Both the spheres and the two worlds won by the sacrificers as their heavenly realms—of those, that which is foremost, luminous and honey-sweet—in that, O sons, may you take refuge in your old age.

Grasp the eastern direction, one after another; those who have faith resort to this world. Whatever cooked food has been served for you in the fire, O husband and wife, take refuge together for its protection. Reaching toward the southern direction, turn around toward this vessel. In it, Yama, in harmony with the ancestors, shall grant you abundant shelter for the cooked offering.

This western quarter is indeed excellent, wherein Soma is the sovereign lord and the one who bestows mercy. In that quarter may you two take refuge; may you attend upon those who perform good deeds, and then, as a pair, partake together of the ripened fruit.

Firm is this Virāj; let there be homage to her! May she be auspicious to our sons and also to me. O Goddess Aditi, possessor of all boons, protect our ripened [offering] like a watchful guardian.
Embrace us closely as a father embraces his sons; may auspicious winds blow for us here upon the earth. O two deities, may the austerity and the truth know that rice-mess which you cook here for us.

Whatever the black bird, having come here while hopping, has encountered stuck within the hole; or whatever the female slave with moist hands has smeared—cleanse the mortar, the pestle, and the water!

This stone, broad-based and bestowing vigor, purified by strainers, shall drive away the demon. Ascend the skin; grant great protection! Let not the husband and wife fall into the sin of losing a grandson.
The Lord of the Forest has come to us along with the gods, driving away demons and *piśācas*. May it rise up and let forth its voice; through it, may we conquer all the worlds.
The animals have encompassed seven oblations: that which among them is luminous and that which has grown strong. The thirty-three deities attend upon them; may he lead us toward the heavenly world.

May you lead us toward the heavenly world; may we be united with wife and sons. I take your hand; let it follow me here. Let not Destruction nor Malignity overcome us. May we pass beyond the Seizer and evil; may you dispel the darkness and speak what is beautiful. O wooden vessel, being lifted up, do not harm him, nor shatter the grain of the one who seeks the gods.
Pervading all, with ghee upon your back, becoming one who is of common origin, come to this world; reach out to the winnowing basket increased by rain, and let it separate the chaff and the husks.

The three worlds are encompassed by the Brahmin: yonder sky, this earth, and the intermediate space. The various forms of cattle are manifold, yet you become one through perfect abundance. Push away this red skin; let the pressing-stone polish it like a washerman cleansing garments.

I cause you, who are the earth, to enter into the earth. This body of yours is uniform, though its appearance has been altered. Whatever scar or mark was written upon you by the act of carving, may you not be harmed by it; I heal that even with sacred prayer (*brahman*).
Like a mother, you welcome the son; I establish you, the earth, upon the earth. O cauldron, jar, do not waver upon the altar, firmly joined with the sacrificial implements and the clarified butter.

May Agni, cooking, protect you from the east; may Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, protect you from the south. May Varuṇa make you firm in the western support; may Soma join you together from the north.

Purified by means of purifiers, they flow clear; from the cloud they go to heaven and to earth, to all the worlds. Those life-giving, bestowers of vitality, established as supports, poured into the vessel—may Agni kindle them around.

They come from heaven and attend upon the earth; they attend upon the ground and dwell above in the intermediate space. Being pure, they indeed beautify themselves; may they lead us toward the heavenly world.

Whether they be powerful, or well-measured, or bright and pure and immortal—may those Waters, being thus instructed, prepare the rice-mess for the husband and wife, cooking it well as they provide for their master.

Counted and few, they attend to the earth, commensurate with the out-breath and in-breath, and with the plants. Uncountable, being cast in, the golden ones have pervaded all—the pure ones, their very purity.
They rise up, they leap about when heated; they cast forth foam and many drops. Like a woman seeing her husband for the sake of the season, O Waters, be united with these rice grains.
Lift up those that are sinking into the depths; let them touch their own selves with water. This water is contained in the vessels, as are these measured grains of rice and these quarters of space.
{15} Hand over the knife; let the harrow work quickly. Without harming the plants, let them be cut at the joints. Soma has attained sovereignty over them; may the plants be free from anger toward us.

Strew the new sacred grass for the rice-mess; may it be dear to the heart and beautiful to the eye. Upon it may the gods together with the divine hosts enter; having sat down, may they consume this according to the seasons.

O Lord of the Forest, sit upon the strewn sacrificial grass, measured out by the *agniṣṭoma* chants and the deities; like Tvaṣṭṛ with a well-fashioned form, may we behold these [sacrificial ladles] here within the vessel with the sharp axe.

After sixty autumns, may the guardian of the treasure desire [to take it], and may he obtain it by means of the cooked oblation. May the living fathers and sons come near to him; O Agni, lead him to this heavenly end.

As a sustainer, be established upon the foundation of the earth; may the deities cause you, the steadfast one, to move forth. May the husband and wife, possessing living sons, lift you up from the place of the fire while they themselves live.
Having conquered all the worlds you have come together; you have fully satisfied all desires as many as there are. Plunge into the place of movement and the ladle; draw this up into a single vessel.
Spread it out before you, and sprinkle this vessel with clarified butter. Like lowing cows toward their young calf, O gods, utter the sound of *hiṅ* for this one who seeks the breast.
You have made this world a covering; let the wide, peerless heaven spread out. Upon it shall rest the buffalo, the fair-winged bird; O gods, deliver him over to the deities.

Whatever your wife cooks beyond you, O husband, or whatever you, O husband, [cook] beyond her, O wife—let you two join that together; let it be yours in common, as you bring about a single world together.

As many as dwell upon this earth, our sons who have been born from us—invite them all to this vessel, you two who know the navel, as the children gather together. The streams of the Vasu, swollen with honey, mixed with clarified butter, the very centers of immortality—all these he secures for himself. May the guardian of the treasure seek him out in the sixtieth autumn;

may the guardian of the treasure seek him as his own treasure. May those others who are not masters be on all sides powerless. Bestowed by us, deposited as heaven, it has ascended to the three heavens by means of its three sections.
May Agni burn away the demon that is godless; let the flesh-eating *piśāca* be driven out from here. We thrust him away, we repel him from us; may the Ādityas and the Aṅgirases attend to him.

To the Ādityas and the Aṅgirases, I announce this honey mixed with clarified butter. With pure hands and having not struck down this [offering], the two well-doers have reached the unquenchable heaven.
I have obtained this supreme section, from which Parameṣṭhin attained it from that world. Pour out the clarified butter; anoint it well with fat. This is our portion here for the Aṅgirasas.

For the sake of truth, for ascetic heat, and for the deities, we entrust this treasure, this hoard. Let it not fail us in gambling, nor in the assembly; let it not be surrendered to another before my time.
I cook; I give; upon my own labor and compassion rests the wife. A son has been born to the world of youth; may you both take hold of a later age.

There is no sin here, nor is there any foundation for it, that one goes along with friends who do not honor him. This vessel of ours has been placed whole; the cooked food shall enter back into the cooker.
Let us make him the dearest of the dear ones. May those whom they hate go to their destination. The cow, the ox, and the various birds—may these drive away death that comes from men.

This skin has been placed upon the man; all other animals remain unclothed. Clothe yourselves with sovereignty as your own self, wearing a garment that is not woven of threads.

Whatever you have spoken falsely at the dice-game, whatever you have spoken in the assembly, or whatever falsehood you have uttered out of desire for wealth—having clothed yourselves together over the common thread [of life], deposit all that impurity therein.
Rain down upon us, go unto the gods; fly upward from the smoke of the skin. Becoming all-pervading, with ghee upon your back, go to this world which is your own womb.

The heavenly body has unfolded itself in many ways according to its knowledge; from within itself, it has cast out that which is of another color. Purifying itself, it has driven away the black and the white; that which is red, I offer to you into the fire.

To the eastern quarter, to Agni the overlord, to Asita the protector, and to Āditya who wields the arrow—him we entrust to you. Guard him for us until he returns. May he lead us here to old age; may he deliver us to old age from death. Then may we be united with what is cooked [the ripened reward].

To the southern quarter, to Indra as the overlord, to Tiraścīrāji as the protector, and to Yama accompanied by his arrows—we entrust this [child]. Guard him for us until he returns; may he lead us here to old age. May he deliver us unto old age, not unto death; then may we be united with the ripened [state].

To the western quarter, to Varuṇa the overlord, to the viper as protector, to food accompanied by arrows—this one we entrust to you; guard him for us until his departure. May he lead us here to old age; may he deliver us to old age for death, and then may we be united with the cooked [food].

To the northern quarter, to Soma as overlord, to Svaja as protector, to the thunderbolt-bearing Iṣumatī—we entrust this [child] to you. Guard him for us until his return. May she lead him here to old age; may she deliver him to old age for death. Then may we be united with him once more when he is cooked (mature).

For the fixed quarter, for Viṣṇu the overlord, for Kalmāṣagrīva the protector, for the plants rich in nourishment—we entrust this [child] to you; guard him for us until his return. May he lead us here to old age; may he deliver us unto death through old age, and then may we be united with what is cooked (the funeral offering).

To the upward direction, to Bṛhaspati as overlord, to Śvitra as protector, to Varṣā accompanied by his arrow—we entrust this [child]. Guard him for us until he returns. One should simply say, "I give," and he should acquiesce to her. When one gives a cow to Brahmins who beg for it, that act is endowed with progeny and offspring;
he exchanges it for progeny and is enriched with cattle. But he who does not wish to give the cow of the gods to the descendants of sages when they beg for it—by a hornless cow his [house] collapses;
by a lame one he crushes a pillar; by a tailless one his house is consumed by fire; by a one-eyed cow his own property is lost.
From his stationing upon her, the *vilohita* finds the master of the herd; likewise, from the stationing upon the barren cow (*vaśā*), he finds what is known as *duradabhnā*.
From his stationing upon her feet, he finds the name *viklindu*; through namelessness, those [limbs] wither away which she sniffs at with her mouth.
He who pierces her ears is cut off from the gods. Thinking, "I am making a mark," he makes himself smaller.

When someone cuts the hair of this [cow] for some enjoyment, from that the young colts die and the wolf slays the calves. When a crow has pecked at the hair of this truthful one while her owner is present, from that the young males die and consumption finds them through lack of naming. When a maidservant throws together the cow’s washing-water and dung, from that a deformed child is born; therefore, one should not disregard this sin.

O God, for those who come to her with this desire, she is made subject to their will; they say that the one who treats her with hostility incurs the curse of the Brahmins.

He who does not wish to give a cow to the descendants of seers when they beg for it from the gods cuts himself off from the gods and incurs the wrath of the Brahmins. If he has a barren cow as his means of enjoyment, he should seek another; for if he does not give her away when asked, she harms the man who refuses to part with what was requested.

Just as a treasure-trove deposited with Brahmins [is protected], so too is the barren cow (*vaśā*). They covet her for whatever reason she may be born; they covet what belongs to them when the Brahmins take the barren cow. Just as one might overcome them through another means, such indeed should be the confinement of this cow.
One should certainly keep her until she has reached three years of age and her disease is unknown. And when you know her to be a barren cow, O Nārada, then the Brahmins shall come to you.
Whoever says of this cow, "She is not submissive," regarding her who is the treasure deposited by the gods—for him both Bhava and Śarva, having circled around, discharge their arrow.
He who does not know her udder, nor even her teats—she milks for him with both [teats] only if he was able to give away the submissive cow.
He lies caught by Duradabhna, he who, having been asked, does not wish to give; his desires do not succeed, he who wishes to act without having given her away.

The curse of cattle descends upon him who, being a mortal, acts with hostility toward the gods by failing to give a cow to the Brahmins—that which is the portion deposited for the gods.

When other Brahmins might beg a hundred cows from the master of cattle, the gods then said of this cow: "Such indeed is the cow for one who knows thus. For him who, knowing thus, gives the cow to others without first giving it to [the one who knows], the earth together with its deities becomes a difficult path to traverse upon his standing there. The gods begged for the cow at the very beginning when she was born; Nārada, together with the gods, recognized her and brought her forth.
A barren cow makes a man childless and possess few cattle; moreover, when she is requested by Brahmins, he treats her with hostility.

To Agni and Soma, to Kāma, to Mitra, and to Varuṇa—the Brāhmaṇas make their requests to them; he who does not give to them cuts himself off from them. As long as the master of her [the cow] does not hear these verses for himself, so long may he move among his cattle; but having heard them, he must not dwell in the house of one who does not give.
If one, having heard these verses, nevertheless moves among the cattle of one who does not give, the gods, being provoked, cut short both his life and his prosperity.
The barren cow wanders in many ways, a treasure deposited by the gods; reveal your forms when he seeks to strike down our standing place.
What one intends with the mind, that even reaches the gods; from there, the Brahmins approach her to request [her hand].
Through the utterance of *svadhā* for the ancestors, through sacrifice for the deities, and through giving for the mother cow, the kṣatriya does not incur the mother’s displeasure.

The barren cow (*vaśā*) is the mother of the *rājanya*; thus was she produced in the beginning. They say that the non-offering of her—that which is given to the Brahmins—is like one who might snatch away the clarified butter held in the ladle for Agni. Indeed, he who does not give the barren cow to the Brahmins cuts it off from himself as if for Agni. A well-milking cow, with a sacrificial cake for her calf, stands by him in this world. That barren cow yields all desires to him who has bestowed her.

In the realm of Yama, the barren cow (*vaśā*) yields all desires for one who has offered her; yet they say that for one who withholds her when she is requested, she wanders about in anger like a wrathful cow being driven toward a bull, leading him to the world of hell. Let not the man who considers a barren cow to be a *vehat* (a cow that miscarries) be bound in the snares of Death. Even Bṛhaspati makes him beg for his sons and grandsons who, considering a barren cow to be a *vehat*, cooks her at home.
This great cow, moving among the cattle, shines forth even while she dwells within them; moreover, she yields poison for the bull who gives her to one who desires her.
That which is given to the Brahmins is dear to cattle; moreover, that which is an oblation for the gods is dear to the barren cow.
Those barren cows which the gods fashioned from the sacrifice after emerging from it—of those, Nārada brought forth the terrifying Viliptī.

The gods deliberated over her, wondering whether she was subject to control or not subject to control. Nārada said to them: "She is the most subject to control among those who are subject to control."

"How many barren cows (*vaśā*), O Nārada, do you know that are born of men? I ask you, the wise one: of which may a non-Brahmin not eat? "O Bṛhaspati, there is the cow smeared with [unholy things], and the cow that has recently calved (*sūtavaśā*). Of these, a non-Brahmin who desires prosperity should not eat. Homage be to you, O Nārada, who truly knows the barren cow. Which among them is the most terrible, by not giving which one would suffer defeat?"
The *viliptī*, O Bṛhaspati, and likewise the *sūtavaśā*—these are the *vaśā*. A non-Brāhmaṇa who desires prosperity should not eat of her.
There are indeed three kinds of *vaśā* born: the *viliptī*, the *sūtavaśā*, and the *vaśā* itself. One should bestow these upon the Brāhmaṇas; he incurs no breach toward Prajāpati.

If one is asked, "O Brāhmaṇas, this is the sacrificial offering for you," and they should ask him for a *vaśā*, then those [cows] which are in the house of the one who has taken [the offering] should be given, even if they are formidable.
The gods spoke against Vaśā, saying, "She has not given to us," and thus they were provoked to anger; by means of these verses, Bheda was indeed utterly defeated because of her.
Even when Indra requested her, Bheda did not give up this cow; therefore, for that offense, the gods cut him down from above.

Those wretched men who, as revilers, speak against giving up the cow, cut themselves off through their lack of sense by provoking the wrath of Indra. Those who drive away the lord of the cows and then say, "Do not give her," they go about enveloped by the missile of Rudra through their lack of sense.

she rests in the Ṛgveda, is covered by truth, enveloped by prosperity, and surrounded by glory.
Enveloped by the self-sustaining power (svadhā), encompassed by faith (śraddhā), protected by consecration (dīkṣā), established in sacrifice, the world is the finale (nidhana).
This Brahmin is the sovereign lord of the state of Brahmā.
For a Kṣatriya who seizes that Brahmin’s cow and defeats a Brāhmaṇa.
Truthfulness, heroic power, and auspicious fortune advance.
Vital essence and brilliance, endurance and strength, speech and the senses, fortune and righteousness.
The priesthood and the nobility, the realm and the commoners, brilliance and glory, splendor and wealth.
Life-span and form, name and fame, the out-breath and the in-breath, the eye and the ear.
Milk and juice, food and the eating of food, cosmic order and truth, sacrifice and charitable works, progeny and cattle—
this is that formidable Brahman-cow, whose venom is evil, a manifest *kṛtyā* (sorcery) enveloped in a mass of roots.
In this [night], all terrors and all deaths are present.
In this [night], all cruel acts and all murders of men [are permitted].
That Brahman-slaying, god-drinking cow, being seized, drags [the taker] into the snares of death.
For that host has a hundredfold slaughter; for it is the destruction of the oppressor of the sacred word.
Therefore, indeed, a cow is inviolable by a wise man toward Brahmins.
The thunderbolt is the one that runs; Vaiśvānara is the one who has been raised up.
The weapon, uprooting the hooves, Mahādeva gazes upon it.
Having razor-sharp edges, she bellows as she looks on, flashing forth her thunder.
Death, the fierce god, utters the sound *hiṅ*; she who spreads herself around is the tail.
The bowstring, repeatedly twanging against both ears, causes the consumption that makes one urinate excessively.
The flowing stream is being milked; the head-ache has been milked out.
The seat stands nearby; the combatants have seized one another.
The arrow being fitted to the point of the bow, the weapon being struck down.
Sin falls like poison; darkness has fallen.

O God, the weapon being carried away is a failure; it has been taken away.
When being placed upon, she is evil; when being laid down, she is harshness.
The poison departs; the fever has departed.
Being cooked, she drives away evil and bad dreams.
The earth, being prepared with its roots and vegetation removed, has been fully prepared.
The unconsciousness was cleared away by the pure fragrance, and the venomous snakes were removed.
Non-existence was being offered; defeat was offered.
Śarva is enraged; Piśyamānā and Śimidā are being devoured.
The unaverted one is being eaten; Nirṛti is the one who has eaten.

The Brahman-cow, when eaten by the world, cuts off from this one and from that one the one who treats a Brahmin with contempt. Her slaughter is sorcery, her killing is a malevolent spell; her entrails are secret spells.
Do not abandon those who have not yet arrived.
Agni, having become a consumer of raw flesh, enters and devours the Brahmin’s cow, which belongs to one who has oppressed a Brahmin.
It cuts away all his limbs, joints, and roots.
It cuts off his paternal kin and alienates his maternal kin.
The Brahman-cow, when not returned by a Kṣatriya to the one who deprived her of her Brāhmaṇahood, causes all the kinsmen of the one who took her in marriage to be consumed.
He makes him homeless, without horses, and childless; he becomes one who is left behind by others, and he perishes.
Indeed, at his slaughter, vultures quickly made a feast.
Verily, quickly the long-haired women dance around his cremation pyre, striking their breasts with their hands and uttering the evil *ailaba* cry.
Verily, quickly the wolves make the *ailaba* cry in his dwellings.
They quickly ask him about that which was there: "Father, what is this now?"
Cut it! Cut it down! Cut it completely! Burn it away! Burn it away!
O daughter of Aṅgiras, subdue this oppressor of the Brahmin who seizes [the property].
For you are called Vaiśvadevī, a magical spell (kṛtyā) enveloped in the *kūlbaja* rite.
Burning, fiercely burning, it is the thunderbolt of Brahman.
Becoming death with razor-sharp edges, run forth!
Bestow upon us the splendor of victory, the merit of sacrifices and charitable works, and our desired blessings.
Having taken it from the living, you bestow it upon the deceased in that other world.
O inviolable one, become the track for the Brahmin’s curse;
become a missile, an arrow, a weapon against the evil-doer, and one whose venom is evil.
O Invincible One, strike off the head of the oppressor of the Brahmins, who has committed an offense, who reviles the gods, and who is devoid of generosity!

May Agni burn the evil-minded one crushed and trampled by you; may Agni burn the evil-minded one crushed and trampled by you; may Agni burn the evil-minded one crushed and trampled by you; may Agni burn the evil-minded one crushed and trampled by you; may Agni burn the evil-minded one crushed and trampled by you; may Agni burn the evil-minded one crushed and trampled by you; may Agni burn the evil-minded one crushed and trampled by you; may Agni burn the evil-minded one crushed and trampled by you; may Agni burn the evil-minded one crushed and trampled by you.
Cut it down, cut it away, cut it all to pieces; burn it, burn it up, burn it entirely!
O Goddess, O inviolable one, burn up the oppressor of Brahmins from the very root.
Just as one has come from the abode of Yama, from the worlds of the wicked, from afar.
Thus, O inviolable goddess, [act] against the one who has committed an offense against the Veda, the hater of the gods, and the one who bestows no gifts.
With a hundred-jointed thunderbolt, sharp and with a razor-edged tip.
Strike down the shoulders; strike down the head!
Cut his body hairs; strip away his skin.
Cut away his flesh; tear out his sinews.
Crush his bones; extract his marrow.
Loosen all his limbs and joints.
May Agni, the consumer of raw flesh, drive him away from the earth; may Vāyu burn him up from the great expanse of the intermediate space.
May Sūrya drive him away from heaven; may he burn him down.
Rise up, O steed who art within the waters; enter this prosperous kingdom. He who is Rohita, who begot this entire universe—may he sustain you well for the sake of sovereignty.

May strength come forth, that which is within the waters; ascend to the clans who have their source in you. Holding Soma, cause the waters, the plants, the cattle, and all bipeds and quadrupeds to enter here.
You, the fierce Maruts, sons of Pṛśni, with Indra as your ally, crush the enemies. May your ruddy steed hear us, O bounteous ones—O Maruts, thrice-seven in number, who delight in sweet joy.

Rohita sprang forth; as the embryo of women, he ascended the lap of all living beings. With them, firmly grasped, he was discovered by the six wide expanses; beholding a path, he brought the kingdom here.

For you Rohita has brought sovereignty here; he has cast away adversaries; safety has become yours. May Heaven and Earth, together with the *revatī* verses and the *śakvarī* meters, milk for you here your desire.

Rohita begot Heaven and Earth; there Parameṣṭhin stretched out the thread. There the Unborn One-footed (Aja Ekapād) took his stand; by his strength he made Heaven and Earth firm. Rohita made Heaven and Earth firm; by him the sun was established, by him the vault of heaven. By him the atmosphere and the regions were measured out; by him the gods found immortality.
The red one has grown forth, assuming every form, bringing together both the shoots and the sprouts. Having ascended to heaven with his great majesty, may he anoint your kingdom with milk and ghee.

Those shoots of yours, those sprouts, those upward-growths by which you fill the sky and the mid-air—increasing through the power of the sacred word (*brahman*) and through milk, remain watchful for the clan and the kingdom of the Red One.

Those clans that arose from your heat (*tapas*) have come here following the calf, the *gāyatrī*. May they enter you with a gracious mind; may the mother come together with the red calf. May they enter you with a gracious mind; may the mother come together with the red calf. May they enter you with a gracious mind; may the mother come together with the red calf. May they enter you with a gracious mind; may the mother come together with the red calf. May they enter you with a gracious mind; may the mother come together with the red calf. May they enter you... The red one has risen up to the vault of heaven, generating all forms, the youthful sage. With his sharp light, Agni shines forth; he has made dear things manifest in the third realm.

The thousand-horned bull, Jātavedas, invoked with clarified butter, whose back is Soma, the possessor of noble heroes—may he not abandon me when I am in need, nor may I ever forsake him. Grant me abundance of cattle and abundance of heroes. Rohita is the progenitor of sacrifice and its mouth; for Rohita, I offer with speech, with hearing, and with mind. The gods, being well-disposed, go toward Rohita; may he cause me to ascend through ascents to the assembly.
Rohita distributed the sacrifice for Viśvakarman; from him these splendors have come to me. I shall proclaim your origin within the expanse of the world.

The Bṛhatī and the Paṅkti have mounted you, O Jātavedas, with splendor; the Kakubh has mounted you, the Uṣṇih, the syllable, and the Vaṣaṭ-call have mounted you. The Rohita has mounted you along with the seed. He clothes himself in the womb of the earth; he clothes himself in heaven; he clothes himself in the mid-air. He has pervaded the worlds upon the height of the sun. O Lord of Speech, may the earth be pleasant to us; may our womb and our bed be pleasant and very gracious. May our breath remain right here in this friendship. As such, O Parameṣṭhin, may Agni endow you with long life and splendor.

O Lord of Speech, those five seasons of ours which belong to Viśvakarman and have come into being—let there be vital breath right here in our friendship. May that you, O Parameṣṭhin, endow with life and luster.

O Lord of Speech, produce goodwill and a well-disposed mind; bring cattle to our cow-pen and offspring to our wombs. Let there be vital breath right here in our friendship. May that you, O Parameṣṭhin, endow me with life and luster.

When the spotted deer and the ruddy one draw you as the side-horse at the chariot, you go forth in splendor, releasing the waters.

The follower of Rohitā is Rohiṇī, the wise one, golden-hued, vast, and full of splendor. Through her may we win all forms of strength; through her may we overcome all hostile armies. This is the seat of Rohiṇī, of Rohitā; that is the path upon which the speckled deer goes. The Gandharvas and the Kaśyapas lead her up; the seers protect her with vigilance.
The immortal, golden, banner-bearing horses of the Sun always draw his easy-moving chariot. Drinking the clarified butter, the radiant god Rohitā has entered the speckled sky.
The red bull with sharpened horns who has encompassed both Agni and Sūrya—he who supports the earth and the sky—from him the gods release their creations.

Rohita ascended to heaven from the great ocean; Rohita, the grower, has grown forth as all things. Measure out the milk-laden, ghee-anointed cow of the gods; let her not touch the waters. Let Indra drink the *soma*; let there be peace; let Agni offer praise; drive away our adversaries.
Enkindled by fuel, increased by clarified butter, and offered with clarified butter—may Agni, the subduer of all, destroy my rivals who are hostile. May he strike them down;
may he burn up the enemy who assails us. With the flesh-consuming fire, we utterly consume our rivals.
Strike down those who face downward, O Indra, wielder of the arm with the thunderbolt! And may I consume my rivals with the splendors of Agni.

O Agni, cast our rivals beneath us; O Bṛhaspati, cause the one who seeks to drink us dry among our kinsmen to tremble. O Indra, Agni, Mitra, and Varuṇa, let those whose wrath is unyielding fall low. O divine Sūrya, as you rise, strike down my rivals; strike them down with a stone; let them go to the lowest darkness.
The calf of Virāj, the bull of hymns, has ascended the mid-air with his bright back. With clarified butter they sing their song to the Calf; being the Brahman, they strengthen him with the Brahman.
Ascend to heaven and ascend to earth; ascend to sovereignty and ascend to wealth. Ascend to progeny and ascend to immortality; touch your body with the Rohita.

The gods who, as sustainers of the kingdom, move all around the sun—with them may Rohita, being in harmony and well-disposed, establish the kingdom for you. Sacrifices purified by sacred prayer carry you upward; like travelers on the road, the bay steeds carry you. You shine across the ocean, over the surging flood.

O Rohita, heaven and earth rest upon you, you who conquer wealth, conquer cattle, and conquer booty. I shall proclaim your thousand births and seven [generations]; I shall speak of your navel within the expanse of the world.
Glorious, you go to the intermediate points and the quarters; glorious among cattle and among the people; glorious in the lap of Aditi, the earth—may I be as beautiful as Savitṛ.
Being there, you know what is here; being here, you see those things. From here they behold the light, the wise Sūrya in heaven.

Beyond the further shore, by means of this nearer step, the cow has risen up, bearing her calf. Whitherward has she gone? To what region has she departed? Where indeed will she bring forth, for she is not in this herd?

She who has become one-footed, two-footed, four-footed, eight-footed, and nine-footed—she is the thousand-syllabled array of the world; from her the oceans flow forth in all directions. Ascending to heaven, the Immortal has favored my speech. Purified by sacred prayer (*brahman*), the sacrifices bear you upward; like steeds on their journey, the bay horses carry you.
O Immortal One, I know that ascent of yours which is in heaven, and that dwelling place of yours in the highest firmament.
Sūrya looks beyond the sky, Sūrya looks beyond the earth, Sūrya looks beyond the waters. Sūrya, the sole eye of all that exists, has ascended to the great heaven.
The wide expanses became the enclosing sticks; the earth was fashioned as the altar. Therein Rohita established these two fires: the cold and the heat.

Having brought forth cold and heat and having fashioned the sacrificial posts as mountains, they sacrificed with rain and clarified butter for Agni, the red one who finds the light of heaven. By the sacred word (*brahman*) of the red one who finds the light of heaven, Agni is kindled; from him comes heat, from him comes cold, and from him sacrifice was born. Increasing through the sacred word, nourished by the sacred word, and offered with the sacred word, the two fires, kindled by the sacred word, sacrificed for the red one who finds the light of heaven.

The two Agnis, kindled by prayer, have sacrificed for the ruddy one who finds the light of heaven—he whom Vāta caresses, or whom Indra and Brahmaṇaspati [caress]. The two Agnis, kindled by prayer, have sacrificed for the ruddy one who finds the light of heaven.

Having fashioned the earth as the sacrificial altar (*vedi*) and made heaven the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), having made the heat (*ghr̥ṃsa*) his fire, Rohita created the entire world endowed with a self by means of rain as the clarified butter (*ājya*).
Rain became the clarified butter, heat the fire, and the earth was fashioned as the altar. There, Agni established these mountains upward by means of sacred hymns (*gīrbhiḥ*).
Having fashioned them upward by means of hymns, Rohita spoke to the earth: "In you let all this be born—whatever has been and whatever is yet to be."
That sacrifice, the first, was born as what has been and what is to be. From it was born all this, whatever shines here. It was brought by the seer Rohita.

I cut off the root of him who kicks a cow with his foot and urinates facing the sun; we shall not grant him further shade. I cut off the root of him who passes between me and the fire while casting a shadow over me; we shall not grant him further shade.
O divine Sūrya, whatever person today comes between you and me—from him we wipe away bad dreams, impurity, and misfortunes.
May we not stray from the path, nor from the sacrifice, O Indra, we who possess the Soma; may no enemies stand against us.

May what is dear to you here for your offspring be fulfilled; be watchful in this house for the sake of the household fire. Embrace your body with this husband, and then, long-lived, you shall speak at the assembly.
Stay right here; do not depart. Attain the full span of life, sporting with your sons and grandsons, rejoicing, and secure in your own dwellings.

These two move one after the other by means of their creative power (*māyā*); like two playing children, they traverse the ocean. One of them surveys all beings; the other, ordaining the seasons, is born anew.
Being born, you become ever new again; as the banner of the days, you go at the forefront of the dawns. Arriving, you distribute the portion to the gods; O Moon, you extend a long life.
Give away the *śāmulya* garment; distribute wealth among the Brahmins. This sorcery (*kṛtyā*), having become footed, enters the husband through his wife.
Blue and red becomes the sorcery; the clinging attachment is cast off. Her kinsmen prosper, while the husband is bound in fetters.
Repulsive and pale becomes that body, by means of that evil thing, when the husband wraps his own limb with the garment of the bride.
The carving, the cutting up, and furthermore the slicing—behold these forms of Sūryā; the Brahman adorns them.
This is parched, this is bitter, like a bone, like poison—it is not for eating. Only he who knows the *sūryā* prayer deserves the bride's garment.
He, the Brahman priest, indeed brings that auspicious, pleasant garment, he who knows the expiation by which the wife is not harmed.

May you two bring together abundant fortune; speaking the Truth among those who speak the Truth, O Brahmaṇaspati, make him pleasing as a husband for her. Let the bridegroom utter these words: "Stay right here, do not go away; O cows, increase this man with progeny. Moving toward splendor, the radiant cows, resplendent with Soma—may all the gods turn their minds toward you here.
O cows, enter into this man together with offspring; he shall not fail the portion of the gods. For him, O Pūṣan and all you Maruts, and for him let Dhātṛ and Savitṛ impel you.
May the paths be thornless and straight by which our friends go to choose a bride. May Bhaga, Aryaman, and Dhātṛ unite her with splendor.

Whatever splendor is placed in dice and in wine, whatever splendor is in cows, O Aśvins—with that splendor protect this woman. With that splendor by which, O Aśvins, the great inviolable [cow] was joined at the hindquarters, or by which wine was produced, or by which the dice were consecrated—with that splendor protect this woman.
He who shines within the waters without fuel, whom the sages praise during the sacrifices—O Son of the Waters, grant us the honeyed waters by which Indra, the heroic one, grew strong.
Here I cast away the glowing grasp that corrupts the body; I draw up that which is auspicious and radiant.

Let the Brahmins bring her the waters for the ceremonial bath; let the waters rise up, not slaying the hero. Let Aryaman’s fire pass around her; let Pūṣan attend to her, while the father-in-law and the husband’s brother look on.
