He who with his arrow struck down the many who committed great sin and thought themselves beyond reckoning; he who does not grant success to the arrogant, who is the slayer of the Dasyu—he, O people, is Indra.
He who discovered Śambhara dwelling in the mountains in the fortieth autumn; he who slew the serpent displaying its might, the son of Danu as he lay there—he, O people, is Indra.

He who overcame Śambhara with his weapons; he who drank the unpleasant draught of the pressed soma from the *kāsnā* vessel; he within the mountain who overwhelmed the many people performing sacrifice—he, O people, is Indra. He who, the bull with seven reins, the mighty one, released the seven rivers to flow; he who, thunderbolt-armed, struck down Rauhiṇa as he was scaling heaven—he, O people, is Indra.

Even Heaven and Earth bow down before him; even the mountains tremble at his very breath. He who is the Soma-drinker, the one with the thunderbolt in his arm, the one with the thunderbolt in his hand—he, O people, is Indra.

He who protects with his aid the one who presses the juice, the one who cooks, the one who praises, and the one who exerts himself; he for whom prayer is the strengthener, for whom the Soma is, and for whom this gift is intended—he, O people, is Indra.
Born, he looked out from the lap of his parents; he knows not of a progenitor higher than his own. He who, being praised, observes the laws of the gods for us—he, O people, is Indra.
He who desires the Soma, the lord of tawny steeds, at whose presence all beings tremble, who slew Śambara and Śuṣṇa, who is the sole hero—he, O people, is Indra.

You who bestow booty even upon the one who presses the juice and cooks the offering when it is hard to win—you indeed are the True One. May we, O Indra, ever be dear to you, and with brave sons, may we proclaim our wisdom in the assembly.

To him alone, the powerful and swift one, I offer this hymn like a refreshing draught, to the majestic one who is worthy of praise, the irresistible Indra—to him I present these most excellent prayers.

To him indeed I extend my song of praise like a gift of food; I bring forth this hymn for his protection with perfect skill. For Indra, the ancient lord, they have purified their thoughts with heart, mind, and inspired wisdom.
To him indeed I bring this supreme, light-winning hymn with my mouth; with invocations and well-fashioned prayers, I shall magnify the most generous patron.

To him indeed I send forth this hymn, as a carpenter fashions a chariot for its master; and with well-fashioned songs, I offer praise to Indra, the wise one who bears songs, the one who stirs all things.

For him indeed, like a prize-winning steed, I anoint the hymn with my ladle for Indra, so that the hero may be praised—he who is rich in gifts, whose fame is celebrated, and who is the shatterer of forts. For him indeed, Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned the thunderbolt, most skillfully wrought and resonant for battle, with which he found Vṛtra’s vital spot, striking down the powerful one with his blow, however great his size.

At the libations of his mother, he has quickly drunk the great draught and the pleasant food; the powerful Viṣṇu stole the cooked offering. As an archer, he pierced the boar through the mountain. Even the divine wives, the goddesses, wove a hymn for this Indra, for the slaying of the serpent. He encompassed the two wide worlds, heaven and earth; they do not encompass his greatness. His majesty indeed exceeds that of heaven, earth, and the intermediate space. Praised by all, the self-radiant Indra, the vessel of power, has grown strong for the battle from his own light within the home.

By his very might, Indra shattered Vṛtra who was glowing with fury with his thunderbolt; he released the rivers like penned-up cows, being well-disposed to grant him renown. By his brilliance alone, the rivers were stilled when he hemmed them in with his thunderbolt. Acting as a sovereign lord, bestowing gifts upon the donor, the victorious one made a ford for Turvīti. To him indeed, O powerful one, bring forth the thunderbolt with haste; you who are all-sustaining, cleave Vṛtra as one splits the joints of a cow, piercing through so that the floods of water may flow.

Proclaim now with new hymns the ancient deeds of this swift one: how, brandishing his weapons for battle, he, roaring in his fury, utterly destroys the enemies. Out of fear of him indeed, even the firm mountains and heaven and earth tremble at his very birth. Repeatedly praising the protection of the Friend, Nodhas has instantly become ready for heroic valor.

To him indeed was this gift bestowed by them, since he alone, as the sovereign lord, won much wealth. Indra aided Etaśa, the swift winner of cattle, who contended with Sūrya in the race for the prize of horses.

Thus have the Gotamas fashioned these well-wrought prayers for you, O Indra, to yoke your bay steeds; bestow upon them a thought adorned with every form. May he, rich in wisdom, come quickly at dawn through our prayer.

Him alone who is to be invoked by all people, that Indra, do thou praise with these songs—him who rules as a bull possessed of virile strength, the true hero, full of many wondrous powers, the victorious one; he who rules as a bull possessed of virile strength, the true hero, full of many wondrous powers, the victorious one; he who rules as a bull possessed of virile strength, the true hero, full of many wondrous powers, the victorious one; he who rules as a bull possessed of virile strength, the true hero, full of many wondrous powers, the victorious one; he who rules as a bull possessed of virile strength, the true hero... the true hero.

Him indeed our ancient fathers, the Navagvas—the seven sages—strengthened with their prayers, seeking his aid: him who strikes down the foe, the overcomer, who dwells upon the mountains, whose speech is guileless, and who is most powerful through his thoughts.

We implore that Indra for this wealth which possesses many heroes, is rich in men, and abounds in food—wealth that is unfailing, undecaying, and heavenly. O Lord of Bay Horses, bring that to us so that we may rejoice.

Declare that to us, O Indra, whether your singers of old have indeed attained your favor. What is your portion, what is your strength, O fierce one, you who strike down the oppressor, you who are invoked by many and possess abundant wealth, O slayer of Asuras?

Seeking him, the trembling, eloquent song reaches toward Indra, who holds the thunderbolt in his hand and stands upon his chariot—he who is the mighty grasper, the great achiever, the giver of booty. It finds its way toward the powerful one for the sake of nourishment.

With this very power, O self-strong one, you shattered with your mind-swift mountain even those things that were unshakable and firmly fixed; you, of great might, boldly rent asunder the strongholds, O exuberant hero.
Him, your most powerful one from of old, we seek to honor with a new prayer as of ancient times. May that Indra, the measureless one, the excellent guide, carry us across all difficult passages.

For the sake of the person who acts with malice, you have set ablaze the earthly and celestial realms of the mid-air. O Bull, consume them on every side with your flame; for the hater of sacred prayer, scorch both the earth and the waters.
You have become the king of the divine folk and of the earthly world, O Indra of brilliant aspect. Take the thunderbolt in your right hand, O Indra; O Ageless One, you destroy all magical deceptions.

Grant us, O Indra, enduring well-being for the conquest of enemies—great and unyielding—that by which you, O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, may make the Dāsa and Ārya foes, and the Nahuṣas, easy to overcome.

O much-invoked Ordainer, worthy of sacrifice, come to us with your teams of horses that bring all boons; those which neither god nor non-god can restrain—come swiftly with them, O lover of the pressing-stone.
He who, like a fearsome bull with sharpened horns, alone causes all the peoples to tremble; you who are the giver of wealth to the one who presses the Soma better than the many who do not offer;
you, O Indra, indeed protected Kutsa, listening with your own body in the battle when, bestowing aid upon the son of Arjuni, you brought down the Dāsa Śuṣṇa and Kuyava for him.

O bold one, with your boldness you have protected Sudās, whose offerings were accepted, with all your aids; you protected Trasadasyu, the son of Purukutsa, and Pūru in the winning of land and in the slayings of Vṛtra.

O god of heroic mind, with your steeds of bay hue, you slay many Vṛtras at the feast of heroes through the men. You sent the Dasyus Cumuri and Dhuni to sleep so that they might be easily slain for Dabhīti. These were your mighty deeds, O wielder of the thunderbolt: that you instantly overthrew ninety-nine fortresses and occupied the hundredth as your dwelling; and I too slew Vṛtra and Namuci.

Everlasting are those enjoyments of yours, O Indra, bestowed upon the liberal Sudās who offers oblations. For you, the Bull, I yoke the two vigorous bay steeds; may our prayers reach you, O most powerful one, for the sake of strength.

O Lord of a thousand powers, O possessor of bay horses, let us not fall into misfortune or be cast away in this your encompassing battle. Protect us with your safe defenses, so that we may remain dear to you among the patrons.
O Maghavan, being dear to you, may we men rejoice as friends under your protection and favor. Subdue Turvaśa and Yadva; perform a deed worthy of praise for Atithigva.
Even now, O Maghavan, in your favor, men who recite hymns proclaim their songs of praise. You who, through our invocations, have scattered the Paṇis—choose us for that very alliance!

These hymns of men, O most heroic one, are directed toward you as they bestow riches upon us. For them, O Indra, be auspicious in the slaying of Vṛtra; be the friend, the hero, and the protector of these men.
Now, O heroic Indra, being praised for your aid, impelled by our prayer, grow strong in your body. Mete out to us strengths and dwellings! Do you all protect us evermore with your blessings.
Come, for we have pressed the Soma for you; O Indra, drink this! Sit upon this sacred grass (barhis) of mine.
Let the two long-maned bay horses, yoked by prayer (brahman), carry you here, O Indra; listen to our prayers.
O Indra, we Brahmins, possessing Soma and having pressed the juice, call upon you as our ally, you who drink the Soma.
The singers have sung aloud to Indra; the chanters have praised Indra with hymns; the voices have shouted for Indra.
Indra indeed, joined with his two bay steeds, is mingled with the word-yoked [chariot]. Indra is the wielder of the thunderbolt, the golden one.
Indra raised the sun upon the sky for far-reaching vision; he split the mountain apart with the cattle.
We invoke Indra for you from all sides, away from other people; may he be ours alone.
In the exhilaration of Soma, Indra extended across the mid-air and the luminous realms when he split Vala asunder.
He drove the cows out for the Aṅgirases, making manifest those that were hidden in the cave; he pushed Vala down toward us.
By Indra, the luminous realms of heaven—firmly established and made secure, steadfast and unshakable—were not to be driven away.
Like a joyous wave of waters, O Indra, this hymn of praise hastens toward you; your exhilarating draughts have shone forth.
For you are seen united with Indra, meeting with him who is fearless; both of you are joyful, equal in splendor.
With blameless, heaven-reaching hosts, the sacrifice, powerful as Indra, shines forth with those troops who are dear to him.
Then indeed, according to their own nature, they have again brought forth the state of being embryos, assuming names worthy of sacrifice.
With the bones of Dadhyanc, Indra, irresistible in battle, struck down ninety-nine Vṛtras. Seeking the horse’s head which was hidden away in the mountains, he found it at Śaryaṇāvat.
Regarding this, it is said: They recognized the secret name of Tvaṣṭṛ’s bull here in the dwelling of the moon.

From Indra, I have measured out for myself a body that is eight-footed, nine-cornered, and touches the eternal Order (ṛta). Both worlds, heaven and earth, cried out in response to you as you roared, O Indra, when you became the slayer of the Dasyus.
Rising up with vigor, you shook your jaws after drinking the Soma pressed in the ladle, O Indra.
Shatter all our enemies; drive away the oppressors, strike down the mockers, and bring us that desirable wealth.
O Indra, whatever desirable wealth has been placed within a cleft, within a solid place, or within a hollow, bring that to us.
O you whose gift of abundant wealth all men recognize, bring us that desirable treasure.
Let the praiser extol with new songs Indra, the sovereign lord of the peoples, the hero who conquers men, the most bountiful.

In whom all hymns of praise and all glorious deeds find delight, like the favor of the waters in the ocean—him I seek to win with beautiful praise: the supreme king, the doer of deeds in battle, the great prize-winner for those seeking gain.
This very word of yours you now embrace, as a pigeon enters its nest; indeed, you take heed of this our speech.
O Lord of Rādhā, O you who are borne by songs, O Hero, may your praise be accompanied by prosperity and truthfulness.

Stand upright for our protection in this contest, O Śatakratu; let us converse together regarding other matters. [Be] the leader toward greater wealth, the maker of light in battles, the one who overcomes enemies in combat.
May he, the much-invoked Indra, our protector, carry us safely across all enemies by means of his ship.
O Indra, do you favor us with strengths; grant us a path and lead us toward happiness.

We incite that Indra for the sake of great victory over Vṛtra; may he become the bull, the showerer of blessings. That Indra has been prepared for the giving of gifts; he is the most powerful, established in the exhilaration of the Soma. He is radiant, worthy of praise, and fit for the Soma;
like a thunderbolt fashioned by song, he is mighty and unshakable. Sublime and invincible, he has grown great.
To Indra alone have the singers raised their lofty song; to Indra have the chanters raised their hymns; to Indra have the voices cried out.
Indra indeed, mingled with his two bay steeds, is joined with the word-yoked chariot; Indra is the golden wielder of the thunderbolt.
Indra caused the sun to ascend in heaven for far-reaching vision; he split the mountain apart with the cattle.
Come hither, for we have pressed the Soma for you; O Indra, drink this! Sit upon this sacred grass of mine.
Let the two long-maned bay horses, yoked by prayer, carry you here, O Indra; listen to our prayers.
O Indra, we Brahmins, possessing Soma and having pressed the juice, call upon you as our ally, you who drink the Soma.
Those who stand around harness the ruddy, bright one as he moves; the luminous realms shine in heaven.

They yoke his two beloved bay horses to the chariot on either side—red, bold, and carrying the hero. Creating a signal for the signal-less and a form for the formless, O men, you were born together with the dawns.
His rays bear up that god Jātavedas, Sūrya, so that everyone may behold him.
Those stars go forth with their beams like thieves, before the Sun who beholds all. His heralds have become visible; his rays extend among the people, shining like fires.
Swift, visible to all, you are the maker of light, O Sūrya; you illuminate the entire radiant realm.
Facing the clans of the gods, facing the human tribes, you rise up; facing all, so that the light may be seen.
O Purifier Varuṇa, with that eye wherewith you behold the bustling people, [look upon us].
You rise toward the sky across the broad expanse, measuring out the days with your rays; O Sūrya, you behold all living beings.

Seven bay horses carry you in your chariot, O divine Sūrya, you whose hair is flame, the far-seeing one. The Sun has yoked the seven bright mares, the daughters of his chariot; with them, self-yoked, he goes forth.

The longing songs pour forth splendor upon you, as milch-cows low toward their calf. These beautiful ones flow, blending milk with splendor, like mothers toward their newborn with their hearts. O Vajra, through your purifying power, bring fame to the dying man; bring me long life, ghee, and milk.

This spotted bull has stepped forth; he has sat before his mother, and as he moves toward the light, he goes to his father. He moves between the two luminous realms, from his out-breath and in-breath. The mighty one has looked out upon the sun. He rules over thirty stations; the bird of speech has taken his stand, facing each day at the break of dawn.
When the Śakras have ascended to speech, you two seek to win the mid-air; the gods have rejoiced together with the Bull.
The invincible Śakra has spoken the word of the unassailable one; being most bountiful, he has gladdened us in heaven.
O Śakra, be bold in speech; you rule over the established order according to the Law. Rejoicing, you have spread out the sacred grass.

We praise with songs that Indra of yours—the wondrous one who overcomes the assailants, who delights in the exhilarating juice of wealth—just as cows low toward their calf in the stalls. We implore him, the celestial and bounteous giver, who is encompassed by powers, who is like a mountain rich in many enjoyments, and who swiftly grants us food-filled booty consisting of hundreds and thousands of cattle.
I beg that heroic power from you, that sacred prayer for the sake of first thought, by which you protected the ascetics and Bhr̥gu when wealth was at stake, and by which you aided Praskaṇva.

That by which you released the great waters toward the ocean—that, O Indra, is your virile power. At once that majesty of his cannot be attained, he whom the two worlds have cried out after. What newest of the *atasī* plants shall the swift mortal praise? For even now, while praising his majesty and his Indra-power, they have not reached his celestial light.

When, praising him, shall they attain the divine state? Who is the seer, who the inspired poet, that proclaims it? When, O bounteous Indra, will you come to the call of the one who presses the juice, and when to the one who praises?
Sing forth your praise to Indra, the bounteous giver, as he is known: the Maghavan who possesses abundant wealth bestows gifts upon his singers as if by the thousands.
Like one with a hundred armies, he advances boldly; he slays the Vṛtras for the sake of the donor. Like streams from a mountain, the gifts of him who provides much nourishment overflow.
Sing forth for the sake of aid to Śakra, the renowned one of excellent bounty, who bestows desirable wealth upon the one who presses the Soma and praises him, as if by the thousands.
His weapons are hundredfold, his missiles invincible; the great impetuous powers of Indra swell like a mountain rich in nourishment when the pressed juices have exhilarated him.
We, having pressed the juice and trimmed the sacred grass, sit around you as singers, O Vṛtra-slayer, at the outpourings of the filter, like waters.
O Vasu, the men bearing hymns cry out to you alone when the juice is pressed; when, O Indra, will you come thirsting to the pressed juice in our home, like a bellowing bull?
O bold Kaṇvas, be resolute; strike out thousandfold booty for us! O Maghavan, O far-seeing one, we quickly seek that which is golden-hued, rich in cattle.
Who knows him as he drinks at the pressed juice? What vital strength does he bestow? He who shatters the fortresses with his might, the fair-cheeked one, exhilarated by the soma-plant;
like a wild elephant in rut, he has assumed his course in many places. No one can hold you back; come to the pressed juice! You move as a great one with your power.
He who is fierce, unsubdued, steadfast, and prepared for battle—if Maghavan Indra hears the call of his praiser, he will not stay away but shall come.

For the sake of victory, they have fashioned and begotten Indra, the hero who overcomes all hostile armies, acting in concert with them. By their will, they made him most excellent, the destroyer of enemies in the choice-contest, fierce, strongest, powerful, and swift.

The singers have raised their voices together to praise Indra for the drinking of Soma, so that he, the lord of heaven whose laws are firm, may increase [their strength] through his might and his aids.
The inspired poets, with their songs, bow toward the rim [of the wheel] like rams; they are brilliant, guileless, and swift, even at your ear, together with those who chant the hymns.

That Indra I invoke—the bounteous, the fierce, who truly possesses irresistible powers. May he, the most generous and worthy of sacrifice, turn toward us through our songs; may the wielder of the thunderbolt make all paths easy for us to reach wealth.

O Indra, bring those enjoyments which you, possessing the light of heaven, took from the Asuras. O Maghavan, increase the one who praises this [deed], and those who have trimmed the sacred grass for you.
O Indra, that horse and cow which you have held as your imperishable portion—bestow that upon the sacrificer who presses the soma and gives the sacrificial fee, not upon the miserly dealer.

Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, has grown strong through men for exhilaration and for power. Him indeed we invoke in great battles and in small; may he protect us in the contests for booty. For you, O hero, are the leader of armies; you are the one who bestows much. You are the increaser even of the meager; you grant wealth to the sacrificer who presses the soma—for abundant is your treasure.

When battles arise and wealth is staked for the bold, harness your two bay steeds that flow with exhilaration. Whom will you slay? To whom will you grant riches? O Indra, place us in riches! For at every intoxication, you, the one of upright intent, have given us herds of cattle. Seize with both your hands many hundreds of treasures; sharpen them and bring us wealth!
Rejoice in the pressed juice, O Hero, for the sake of strength and bounty; for we know you as the possessor of many riches, and we have released our desires toward you—therefore, be our protector.
These people of yours, O Indra, nourish every desirable thing; for you, the noble one, look within upon the wealth of the people who do not offer oblations. Bring that wealth to us.
We invoke day by day for our protection the one of beautiful form who accomplishes all deeds, as one calls a good milch-cow for the milker.

Come to our libations; O drinker of Soma, drink of the Soma! This exhilaration of the wealthy one is indeed a giver of cattle. Thus may we find your most intimate favors. Do not overlook us; come to us!
Drink our most powerful, brilliant, and watchful Soma for our protection, O Indra, Lord of a hundred powers!
O Indra, Lord of a hundred powers, those vital energies of yours which exist among the five peoples—those I choose for myself.
O Indra, you have attained great renown; bestow upon us invincible splendor. We cause your strength to swell upward.
Come to us from nearby, or indeed, O Śakra, from afar; O wielder of the thunderbolt, Indra, come here from whatever world is yours.
Indra, indeed, shall drive away great fear; for he is steadfast and all-seeing. May Indra be gracious to us; let no evil reach us from behind, and may there be prosperity before us.
May Indra grant us freedom from fear from all directions; he is the conqueror of enemies and all-seeing.
Who knows him when he drinks beside the pressed juice? What vital strength does he bestow? He who shatters the fortresses with his might, the fair-cheeked one, exhilarated by the soma-plant;
like a wild elephant in rut, he has assumed his course in many places. No one can hold you back; come to the pressed juice! You move as a great one with your power.
He who is fierce, unsubdued, steadfast, and prepared for battle—if Maghavan Indra hears the call of the singer, let him not stay away but come hither.
We, having pressed the soma and trimmed the sacred grass, like waters at the outpourings of a filter, O slayer of Vṛtra, sit around you as your praisers.
At the pressing, O Vasu, the men who recite hymns call upon you in their exclusive devotion. When, O Indra, will you come to our home, thirsty for the pressed juice, like a bellowing bull?
Bold one, through the Kaṇvas, boldly strike out thousandfold booty. O Maghavan, far-seeing one, we quickly seek that wealth which is golden-hued and rich in cattle.
They gaze upon the sun as it were; indeed, they enjoy all the riches of Indra when he is born and being born with might. We look toward our portion as if for a share.
Praise the giver of wealth who is free from harmful intent; auspicious are the gifts of Indra. He does not frustrate the desire of him who serves him, but impels his mind toward giving.

Truly, O Sūrya, you are great; truly, O Āditya, you are great. The greatness of you, who are already great, is celebrated; indeed, O God, you are great. Truly, O Sūrya, you are great in fame; entirely, O God, you are great. By your greatness, you are the divine priest of the gods, a pervasive and invincible light.
Upward now surge these most honey-sweet songs, these hymns of praise, like chariots seeking booty—ever-conquering, winners of wealth, with inexhaustible aid, striving for victory.
Like the Kaṇvas, like the Bhr̥gus, like the sun, they have attained every desire; magnifying Indra with their hymns, the Āyus and Priyamedhas have raised their voices.
His portion indeed exceeds all, like the spoils of a victor; no enemies can harm that Indra who possesses the bay steeds. He bestows skill upon the Soma-presser.
Bestow upon the worshipful ones a mantra that is not meager, well-established, and beautifully formed; even many snares cannot overcome him who stands by Indra through his ritual action.
For thus you are one who seeks heroes, thus you are a hero and steadfast; thus your mind is to be won over.
Thus has your bounty, O possessor of great wealth, been established by all the ordainers. Even evil, O Indra, is with me;
do not be sluggish like a priest, O Lord of spoils! Rejoice in the pressed juice mixed with milk.
For thus is his true speech—abundant, rich in cattle, and great—as a ripe branch for the donor.
For thus are thy manifestations and aids, O Indra, which instantly come to the donor who is like me.
For thus are his desirable things: the hymn and the recitation to be praised for Indra, for the drinking of the Soma.
We celebrate that exhilarating draught of yours, the bull that conquers in battles, the world-maker, O wielder of the stone, who possesses the beauty of gold;
by which you found the lights for Āyu and for Manu. Rejoicing in this sacred grass, you shine forth.
Even now, as of old, those who offer hymns praise you; win for us the waters, the wives of the bull, day after day.
Sing forth unto him, the one invoked by many, the one praised by many; with songs, seek to win over the powerful Indra.
He whose great might is twofold supports both heaven and earth, and by his virility, the mountains, the plains, the waters, and the sun.

O King, praised by many, you alone strike down the Vṛtras, O Indra, so that we may attain victory and glory. We, seeking your aid, call upon you—the wondrous one—as those who bear a heavy burden call for support; we call upon you, the wondrous one, in the battle for booty. We call upon you, the wondrous one, in the battle for booty. For our protection in this rite, let that youthful, fierce, and bold one come to us; for we, as friends, have chosen you, O Indra, the winner of spoils, as our protector.
Him who brought this and that better fortune to us in the past—him I praise for you, O friends, Indra, for our protection.
The lord of bay horses, the protector of the good, the subduer of peoples; for he is indeed the one who has rejoiced. May that Maghavan bestow upon us, his worshippers, hundreds of cattle and horses.
Sing forth a lofty *sāman* to Indra, the inspired sage, the great one—the upholder of the cosmic order (*dharman*), the wise, the one worthy of praise.
O Indra, you are the conqueror; you caused the sun to shine. You are the maker of all, the god of all; you are great.
Radiating with light, you went to the heavenly realm, the luminous sphere of the sky. O gods, they have striven for friendship with you, O Indra.
Sing forth to him who is invoked by many, who is praised by many—Indra. With songs, seek to win over the powerful one.
He whose great power is twofold has sustained the two worlds, the mountains, the plains, the waters, and the sky by his virile might.
As such, O much-praised one, you rule alone; you strike down the Vṛtras, O Indra, so that we may attain victory and glory.
Now, let us bring these worlds to fulfillment, both Indra and all the gods together. May Indra, along with the Ādityas, fashion for us our sacrifice, our bodies, and our progeny.

May Indra, together with his host of Ādityas and Maruts, be the protector of our bodies. When the gods, having slain the Asuras, came forth, guarding their divine status, they brought the sun back with their powers; then indeed they beheld their own vigorous self-sustenance. Through this, may we win the god-ordained prize; may we rejoice for a hundred winters, blessed with heroic sons.
He who alone bestows wealth upon the mortal who offers oblations—the sovereign, the unopposed Indra—verily he is so.
When will he trample with his foot the stingy mortal like a mushroom? When, indeed, will Indra hear our songs?

For he who, having pressed the Soma, seeks to win you over from among many—Indra alone possesses that fierce power. O most powerful Indra, we beg for that exhilaration which is the greatest drinker of Soma, which awakens consciousness, and by which you strike down the devourer.
We implore that [aid] by which you protected Daśagva Adhrigu, who was trembling, and Svarṇara, and by which you protected the ocean.
We pray for that path of Truth by which you impelled the Sindhu and the great waters as if they were chariots;
come to us, O Indra, as our beloved, the ever-conquering one who cannot be hidden, broad on all sides like a mountain, the Lord of Heaven.
For you, O true drinker of Soma, have surpassed both the worlds, heaven and earth; O Indra, you are the strengthener of the one who presses the juice, the Lord of Heaven.
For you, O Indra, are the shatterer of eternal fortresses; you are the slayer of the Dasyu, the prosperer of Manu, and the lord of heaven.

Thus, O Adhvaryu, pour out this most intoxicating of the sweet juices; for thus indeed is the hero praised, he who ever increases [our strength]. O Indra, driver of the bay steeds, no one has ever attained your ancient praise through might or through song of praise. We, seeking glory, have invoked you, the lord of spoils, who is to be magnified by sacrifices that do not fail.
Now let us, as friends, praise Indra, the hero worthy of hymns, who alone surpasses all the tribes.
To him who does not withhold cattle, who seeks kine, the celestial one, speak wondrous speech—more sweet than clarified butter and honey.
His heroic powers are immeasurable; his bounty cannot be surpassed; his sacrificial fee encompasses all like light.
Praise Indra, as Vyaśva did—the waveless, powerful Yama, who bestows the wealth of the enemy upon the donor.
Thus now, O son of Vyaśva, praise him, the tenth and the new one, the well-knowing, the one to be celebrated by those who move.
For you know, O wielder of the thunderbolt, how to avoid the snares of destruction day after day, like one who purifies himself from pitfalls.

For the one who presses the juice wins a dwelling from the abundant; for the one who presses the juice indeed sacrifices away his enemies, the enemies of the gods. The one who presses the juice, like a prize-winning steed unrestrained, seeks to win thousands. To the one who presses the juice, Indra gives enduring wealth; he gives enduring wealth.

May those manly deeds of yours never turn away from us, nor may your glories ever decay—may they not decay before our time! That wondrous, immortal fame of yours which resounds anew in age after age—that, O Maruts, bestow upon us, that which is difficult to attain, that which is difficult to attain!

I honor Agni as the Hotṛ, the munificent Vasu, the Son of Strength, Jātavedas—the wise one, like a sage, Jātavedas—who, a god of perfect sacrifice, with his upright form directed toward the gods, desires the radiant glow of clarified butter with his flame, as the melted fat is poured forth.

Blended with sacrifices, with spotted deer and spears, the bright ones are dear in their ornaments; having sat upon the sacred grass, O sons of Bharata, heroes of heaven, drink the Soma from the Potṛ’s cup!

Bring the gods here, O inspired sage, and sacrifice; O Hotṛ, sit down willingly at the three altars. Accept the Soma-mead that has been set forth; drink from the Āgnīdhra-vessel and satisfy yourself with your portion.

This [Soma] is the increaser of the manly strength of your body; from of old, power and vigor have been placed within your arms. Pressed for you, O Maghavan, it is brought to you; drink of this to your heart's content from the mouth of the Brahman. Him whom I called upon before, him indeed I call upon now; he is the one to be invoked, he who is the master of the name "Giver. O Giver of Wealth, drink the Soma-sweetness set forth by the Adhvaryus; drink the Soma from the Potṛ’s cup according to the seasons.
We invoke day by day for our protection the one of beautiful form who accomplishes all deeds, as one calls a good milch-cow for the milker.

Come to our libations; O drinker of Soma, drink of the Soma! This exhilaration of the wealthy one is indeed a giver of cattle. Thus may we find your most intimate favors. Do not overlook us; come to us!
Ask Indra, the wise one, who is not overcome by his enemies—he who is more excellent than your friends.
Or let our revilers say, "He has gone away elsewhere," while they offer their service only to Indra.
Or let the wondrous tribes call us fortunate, O Master; may we indeed abide in the protection of Indra.
Bring this swift one for the swift, the glory of the sacrifice that delights the men; flying, may he exhilarate his friend.
Having drunk of this, O Śatakratu, you became the slayer of Vṛtras; you protected the victor in the battles for booty.
As such, O Śatakratu, we incite you, the victor in battles, for the winning of riches, O Indra.
To him who is the great channel of wealth, the easy passage for the one who presses the Soma, to that Indra sing ye!
Come here, sit down, and sing forth to Indra, O friends who bring hymns of praise!

To him, the most abundant among many, the lord of all desirable things—Indra—at the pressed soma. May he indeed be with us in our endeavor, may he be with us for wealth and in our wisdom; may he come to us with spoils of war.
Sing for that Indra, at whose side the enemies do not withstand his two bay horses in battles.
These pressed Soma juices, pure and mixed with curds, flow for your enjoyment. O Indra, you were born instantly grown great for the drinking of the pressed juice, for supreme sovereignty, O wise one.
Let the swift Soma drops enter you, O Indra, lover of songs; may they be a source of well-being for you, the perceptive one.
The hymns have magnified you; the songs of praise have magnified you, O Lord of a hundred powers; may our voices magnify you.
May Indra, whose protection is inexhaustible, win this thousandfold booty in which all manly deeds reside.
O Indra, lover of song, let not mortal men do harm to our bodies; as the sovereign lord, ward off the weapon of death from us.
Those who stand around harness the ruddy, bright one as he moves; the luminaries shine in the sky.

They harness his two beloved bay horses, with wings spread wide on the chariot—red, bold, and carrying the hero. Creating a banner for the one without a banner, and a form for the formless, O men, you were born together with the dawns.
Then indeed, according to their own nature, they sent him back again into the state of an embryo, assuming a name worthy of sacrifice.
Even with those who break through the firm, even from the cave, O Indra, you found the ruddy cows by means of your priests.
Like those seeking the gods according to their thought, our songs have sounded toward the famous Great One who finds wealth.
You are indeed seen united with Indra, having come together with him who is fearless—both joyous and equal in splendor.
With blameless, radiant, and desirable throngs, the powerful Indra worships the sacrifice.
From there, O traveler, come hither, or from the luminous realm of heaven; here all our songs of praise are directed toward him.
Or we seek bounty from here, or from heaven, or from the earthly realm, or from the great intermediate space—Indra himself.
To Indra alone have the singers sung aloud; to Indra with hymns have the chanters chanted; to Indra have the voices cried out.
Indra indeed, mingled with the two bay steeds, is joined with the word as his yoke-fellow; Indra is the wielder of the thunderbolt, the golden one.
Indra caused the sun to ascend in heaven for far-reaching vision; he has driven Indra forth with the rays of light.
O Indra, protect us in battles for booty and in contests for thousands; you who are fierce, with your fierce aids.
We invoke Indra in the great contest, Indra in the small; we call upon the wielder of the thunderbolt as our ally against the Vṛtras.
O Bull, you who have granted us all things, open up that vessel for us, being unopposed by any adversary.
At every clash, the hymns of Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, rise higher and higher; I find no end to his perfect praise.
Like a bull among herds, he drives the peoples with his might—the sovereign, the unassailable one. He who alone rules over the people, over riches—Indra, the lord of the five tribes.
We invoke Indra for you from all sides, away from other people; may he be ours alone.
O Indra, bring to us for our protection that most excellent wealth which wins booty, conquers all, and is ever victorious.
May we, aided by thee, smite down the Vṛtras with our fists; may we, aided by thee, strike them down with our horse.

O Indra, aided by thee, may we take up the thunderbolt as a weapon; may we conquer our rivals in battle. With us heroes who are archers, O Indra, and with thee as our ally, may we utterly overcome those who attack us.

Great indeed is Indra, and let his majesty extend even further to the wielder of the thunderbolt; his power is as vast in extent as the sky. Those heroes who have attained their place in the assembly, or the inspired singers seeking to win offspring through their prayer—his belly, the greatest drinker of Soma, swells like the ocean, like the wide waters from the palate of heaven.
For thus his truth is overflowing, rich in cattle, and great—like a branch laden with ripe fruit for the donor.
For thus, O Indra, your manifestations and aids are instantly available to one like me who offers oblations.
For thus, for Indra’s drinking of the Soma, his desirable hymn and recited praise are to be proclaimed.

O Indra, come; exhilarate yourself with the soma-juice through all its stages, you who are great and a protector by your might. Let this gladdening draught be poured for the gladdening Indra; let it be made for him who accomplishes all deeds.
Rejoice, O fair-cheeked one, with these gladdening hymns, O lord of all people, at these libations.
O Indra, songs have been poured forth for you; they have risen up toward you, the unassailable bull and lord.
O Indra, impel toward us wondrous and choice wealth; let it indeed be abundant and sufficient for you.
O Indra, impel us there toward wealth—us who are impetuous, O you of many glories, and full of renown.
O Indra, bestow upon us wide and lofty fame, rich in cattle and wealth, encompassing all life and imperishable.
Grant us great renown and splendor that wins a thousandfold; O Indra, grant us those nourishments borne on chariots.
Praising with hymns the praiseworthy Indra, the lord of wealth and treasure, we call him who comes to our aid.
To the well-born, noble lord, the pious man sings forth a great hymn of strength for the great Indra.

For at all libations, those who desire the bull urge you on—the one common to all—each separately, as they seek to win the light of heaven, each separately. We set you, like a ship that carries us across, at the pole of our strength; like men seeking Indra with sacrifices, the Āyus invoke Indra with hymns—the Āyus invoke Indra.

Couples seeking aid have spread themselves out for you, O Indra, at the winning of the stall of cattle, releasing the captives—releasing them while overcoming the foe. When you, O Indra, bring together two people who seek cattle or who seek the light of heaven, you manifest your power, O Bull, wielding the thunderbolt that is ever with you, O Indra, the companion of your strength.

May he indeed take pleasure in this dawn; be mindful of our hymn and our oblation through our invocations, in the winning of the light through our invocations. Since you, O Indra, the Bull armed with the thunderbolt, intend to slay the demons, listen to the prayer of me, this newest worshipper, listen to the prayer of this newest one.
For you alone, O Hero, are all these libations; for you I compose these strengthening prayers. You are to be invoked by men at all times.
Never indeed do they attain the full extent of your greatness, O Wondrous One, when you are thus mindful; nor, O Indra, can they reach your heroic power or your bounty.
Bring forth [your offerings] for the great one who increases greatness; offer your devotion to the wise one. Move forth to the many clans, O filler of the peoples!

When the golden thunderbolt is ready, then Indra, the lord of the long-renowned strength, mounts his chariot drawn by the two bay steeds, along with the patrons. He, the bounteous one famed from of old, is the master of that strength. Even now, as rain falls upon the herds, Indra sprinkles his golden beard. He goes down to the well-established dwelling when the honeyed juice is pressed; he shakes it like the wind shaking the forest.

He who with his voice struck down many thousands of malevolent, discordant, and insulting speakers—that very manly deed of his we celebrate, he who, like a father, increased his own vigor and might. For even though we are as if unpraised, O true Soma-drinker, do thou, O Indra, grant us hope for cattle, for horses, and for a thousand splendid treasures, O Lord of abundant wealth! O fair-cheeked one, Lord of spoils, O possessor of power, thy wondrous deeds are manifest; do thou, O Indra, grant us hope for cattle, for horses, and for a thousand splendid treasures, O Lord of abundant wealth!
Lay them to sleep, you two of diverse appearance; let them lie down without waking. O Indra, bestow upon us a share of beautiful cattle and horses, in thousands, O possessor of great wealth!
Let those enemies sleep; O Hero, let the givers wake! O Indra, bestow upon us a share of beautiful cattle and horses, in thousands, O possessor of great wealth!
O Indra, crush the braying donkey who mocks us with that [behavior]! O Indra, most wealthy one, grant us a share of beautiful cattle and horses by the thousands!
Let the wind blow far away from the forest with its whirling dust! O Indra, most wealthy one, grant us a share of beautiful cattle and horses by the thousands!
Slay every reviler; crush the Kṛkadāśva! O Indra, most wealthy one, grant us a share of beautiful cattle and horses by the thousands!

Couples seeking aid have spread themselves out for you, O Indra, at the winning of the stall of cattle, releasing the captives—seeking to overcome them, O Indra, they release them. When you, O Indra, bring together two people who seek cattle and who strive for the light of heaven, you manifest your power, O Bull, with your companion, the thunderbolt that is ever-present, O Indra, your companion. The Pūrus know of this heroic deed of yours, when you, O Indra, overthrew the autumnal fortresses, overthrew them by force. Punish that mortal who offers no sacrifice, O Indra, Lord of Might! You stole away the great earth and these waters, rejoicing in these waters.

Then indeed they celebrated this heroic deed of yours during the exhilarations, O Bull, when you, the desiring ones, helped those who sought your friendship; when you helped them, you performed a great deed for them so that they might prevail in battles. They have won various rivers, seeking glory they have won them. Like a bird settled in a tree, the pure hymn has awakened you two, O swift ones. He whose Hotṛ-priest is Indra through many days—the protector of men, the most heroic among heroes, the lord of the night.

May we be present at the dancing of this dawn and of the one to come; may we be the most manly of men. Triśoka brought a hundred heroes after him with his chariot, which, victorious, was accompanied by Kutsa.

What exhilaration is there for you, O Indra, that is delightful? O fierce one, run forth toward our doors and our songs! Why do you not come hither toward me with your wisdom? May I be able to bring you near with gifts and food.

What indeed is the glory of one like you, O Indra, among men? By what thought will you act? When have you come to us? Like a true friend, O wide-striding one, be mindful of our sustenance; for all our thoughts are fixed upon the food of this [sacrifice].

Drive them forward to the goal as the sun drives its rays; let those who desire this go forth like those seeking a wife. And those men, O Indra of many births, who offer many songs to you along with food—[let them prosper].

For you, O Indra, mother heaven is well-measured with her greatness, and earth with her wisdom. For your choice, let the pressed juices mixed with ghee be sweet; let the honeyed draughts be pleasant for your drinking.

They have poured out a full vessel of honeyed mead for this Indra, for he is the one whose gifts are true. He has grown great across the expanse of the earth, preeminent through his wisdom and manly deeds.
The self-strong Indra has shattered the enemy hosts; many strive to win his friendship. Mount upon your chariot as if in battle, which you shall urge on with auspicious favor.

Let the true Maghavan, the consumer of the dregs, come hither; let his bay steeds run toward us. For him we have pressed the soma-juice, well-prepared; being praised, may he grant us his presence here.
Descend, O Hero, from the end of the path, to gladden us today at this libation. May the wise one recite a hymn like Uśanas, a prayer for the sake of the conscious Asura.

Like a seer accomplishing the secret rites of the assembly, may the Bull, drinking deeply of the poured libation, sing his praise. Truly from heaven he brought forth the seven singers; even by day they performed their works while chanting.

When the beautiful light of heaven was found through hymns, they made the great radiance shine at the break of dawn. The most heroic one, in his favor toward men, has dispelled the blinding and turbid darkness so that all may see clearly.
Indra grew to immeasurable size; with his greatness he filled both worlds, heaven and earth. Even beyond that, his majesty extended further, for he has surpassed all existing beings.
Śakra, knowing all manly deeds, released the waters together with his eager friends. Those Uśij who split even the rock with their words have opened the cow-filled stall.
You struck down Vṛtra who had obstructed the waters; the earth, in accord with you, favored your thunderbolt. You sent forth the oceanic floods; O bold hero, by your might you became their lord.

When you, O much-invoked one, shattered the rock for the waters, Saramā appeared before you. As our leader, praised by the Aṅgirases, may you burst open the cow-pens and bring us abundant booty. Sing this song for you while the soma is pressed, for the hero invoked by many, which is as pleasing to the mighty one as it is to a bull.
The Bounteous One does not withhold the gift of wealth consisting of cattle when he hears our songs.
May the slayer of the Dasyus go to Kuvit’s cow-pen; may he open it for us with his powers.
O Indra, bring us wisdom, just as a father provides for his sons; O much-invoked one, grant us aid on this journey so that we, living, may attain the light.
May unknown, malevolent, and inauspicious powers not step upon us; with you as our ally, O Hero, may we cross over the many flowing waters.
O Indra, bring us the highest, most powerful, and fulfilling glory, with which you, O wondrous one with the thunderbolt in hand and beautiful jaws, have filled both these worlds, heaven and earth.
We invoke you, the fierce one who subdues the peoples, O King among the gods, for our protection. O Vasu, make all our wavering things firm; make our enemies easy to overcome.
If there were a hundred heavens for you, O Indra, and a hundred earths as well, O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, neither a thousand suns nor the two worlds could equal you at your birth.

You have filled [all things] with your greatness and your dark power, O Bull; you have pervaded all with your might, O Most Powerful One. Protect us, O Maghavan, in the cattle-pen, O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, with your wondrous aids.
O Indra, if I were the master of as much wealth as you possess, I would surely provide for the singer, O Dispenser of Wealth; I would not abandon him to misery.
May I learn this day by day from the Great One, so that wealth may be found somewhere; for there is no kinship better than yours, O Maghavan, not even a father is more so.

O Indra, grant a triple-layered, triple-protecting, and auspicious refuge as a shelter to the patrons and to me; ward off the lightning-flash from them. Those who, with minds intent on cattle, have overcome the enemy and strike him down boldly—O Maghavan Indra, lover of songs, be our closest protector of our bodies.
O Indra of wondrous luster, come hither! These pressed juices long for you, purified through the fine strainers.
O Indra, come, impelled by our prayer, urged on by the inspired singer to the soma-presser; come to the sacred hymns of the worshipper.
O Indra, come swiftly to the sacred hymns, O Lord of the Bay Steeds; take pleasure in our pressed juice.
O friends, do not praise anything else; do not suffer harm. Praise only Indra, the bull, while the soma is pressed; recite your hymns repeatedly.

Praise him who is like a rushing bull, undecaying, like a cow that conquers the people, the one who causes both enmity and reconciliation, the most bountiful, who provides for both sides. For although these people invoke you in various ways for protection, O Indra, let this our prayer be your means of strengthening through all the days.
The wise ones vie with one another, O Maghavan, regarding the inspired hymns of the noble folk. Come hither; bring us strength in many forms, most near for our protection.

With a prayer joined by prayer, I yoke your two bay steeds, your swift companions who revel together. Ascending your firm and comfortable chariot, O Indra, come to the Soma as one who is discerning and wise.
Adhvaryus, offer the reddish milked stalk to the bull of the people. From the cow, Indra comes every day seeking the place of drinking, desiring the pressed Soma.
The lovely food which you have held from of old, you desire its draught day after day. Rejoicing with heart and mind, O Indra, desiring them, drink the Soma juices that have been set forth.
At your birth, you drank Soma for the sake of conquest; your mother proclaimed your greatness. O Indra, you filled the wide mid-air; through battle, you created space for the gods.

When you fought those who deemed themselves great, we overcame them as they boasted with their arms. Or when, O Indra, surrounded by heroes, you would fight, may we win that glorious battle through you.

I shall proclaim the first deeds of Indra, and those recent ones which the Bounteous Lord has performed. When he overcame the godless illusions, then Soma became his own alone. This entire world of cattle all around belongs to you; whatever you behold with the eye of the Sun, you are the sole lord of the kine, O Indra. May we enjoy the wealth that is offered to you.
O Bṛhaspati and Indra, you two are the masters of celestial and earthly wealth. Bestow riches upon the singer who praises you. Do you ever protect us with your blessings.

Bṛhaspati, who by his might suddenly propped apart the ends of the earth, he who dwells in the three stations with his roar—him the ancient seers, the inspired poets, meditating, have placed at the forefront, he whose tongue is delightful.
Those who, shaking the earth and rejoicing in their clear vision, have overstepped us, O Bṛhaspati—the spotted, gliding, unassailable, wide expanse—O Bṛhaspati, protect its source!
O Bṛhaspati, from that furthest distance, those who touch the Eternal Order have settled down for thee; for thee the dug-out wells, milked by the stones, drip honey on every side in abundance.
Bṛhaspati, being born first from the great light in the highest heaven, seven-mouthed and many-born, blew away the darkness with his roar, having seven rays.
With his well-praising and chanting host, he shattered Vala, the enclosure, with his voice. Bṛhaspati, thundering, drove out the lowing, ruddy cows that provide the sacrificial food.
Thus let us serve the father, the bull of all the gods, with sacrifices, homage, and oblations. O Bṛhaspati, may we, possessing good offspring and heroic sons, become masters of riches.

Like one casting a net far across the water, bring forth this hymn for him like one adorning himself. O sages, cross over the speech of the enemy with your own voice; O singer, cause Indra to rest his mind upon the Soma.
Encourage your friend, the Cow, with your milking; O singer, awaken the lover Indra. Like a full vessel overflowing with wealth, draw forth the Hero to grant us riches.
Why indeed, O Maghavan, do they call you a liberal giver? Sharpen me, for I hear that you are the one who sharpens. O Śakra, let my prayer be effective; O Indra, bring us fortune that finds wealth.

O Indra, people standing together in battle call upon you in their desire for possessions. Here, he who possesses oblations makes you his ally; the hero does not seek friendship with one who presses no Soma. He who, providing nourishment, presses strong Soma juices for him—[for that man] he slays the swift-moving enemies at dawn, subduing them with his power and striking down Vṛtra.

In Indra, in whom we place our praise—Indra Maghavan who has directed his desire toward us—let his enemy tremble even from afar; let all human glories bow down before him. Drive the enemy far away with that fierce *śamba* weapon, O You invoked by many! Bestow upon us wealth in barley and cattle, O Indra; grant the singer a prayer rich in spoils.

Into whom the bull-like Soma-pressers pour during the race—the sharp Somas with their abundant ends—Maghavan does not fail to bestow a gift; he brings much desirable wealth to the one who presses the juice.
Moreover, he who desires the gods wins even a great stake, as a gambler wins at the proper time; he who does not withhold his wealth from them, him the god unites with riches through his own powers.
May we overcome evil-minded poverty with cattle, and all hunger with grain, O much-invoked one! May we, unhurt, be the first among kings to win riches through our communities.
May Bṛhaspati protect us from behind, and from above, and from below against the wicked; may Indra from the front and from the middle grant us, as a friend to friends, a wider space.

He who is the mountain-shatterer, the first-born, the upholder of cosmic order (*ṛtāvā*), Bṛhaspati, the descendant of Aṅgiras, accompanied by oblations; he of double majesty, who dwells at the *pragharma* sacrifice, our father—the bull roars loudly unto the two worlds (*rodasī*).

He, Bṛhaspati, who has created a wide space for the person who approaches him at the invocation of the gods; slaying the Vṛtras, he shatters the fortresses, conquers the enemies, and overcomes his foes in battles.
Bṛhaspati has won all treasures; this god has conquered the great stalls of cattle. Desiring to win the waters and the light, the irresistible Bṛhaspati slays the enemy with his hymns.

Our father discovered this seven-headed, lofty prayer, born of Eternal Order (Ṛta). Indeed, the son of Viśvajanya, Ayāsya, brought it forth while reciting the hymn for Indra. Praising the Truth, meditating with upright thought, the sons of Heaven, the heroes of the Asura, the Aṅgirases, establishing the station of the inspired singer, conceived the first foundation of the sacrifice.
Like swans, with his chattering friends, Bṛhaspati cast apart the stone-made bonds; crying out toward the cattle, he praised them and, as one who knows, sang aloud.

With two [steps] he drove [the cows] from below, with one [step] the cattle that stood hidden behind the bridge of falsehood; Bṛhaspati, seeking light in the darkness, drove the ruddy cows forth, for he disclosed the three [worlds].
Having split it apart, he cut out three things from the western ocean simultaneously: Bṛhaspati discovered the Dawn, the Sun, and the Cow; he found the light, thundering like the sky.
Indra, with his roar, split Vala—the guardian of the milch-cows—as if with a hand; seeking the milk-mixture with sweat-anointed [companions], he made the Paṇi weep and stole the cows away.
With those true, radiant, and booty-seeking friends, he shattered the enclosure of the cows; Brahmanaspati, with those bull-like boars sweating from the heat, attained the wealth.
With truthful minds, seeking the cattle, they impelled the Lord of Cattle with their prayers. Bṛhaspati, through his own companions who avoid mutual reproach, released the ruddy cows.
Strengthening him with auspicious hymns as he roars like a lion in his dwelling, may we rejoice after Bṛhaspati, the bull, the victorious one, in every battle for the sake of heroes.
When he won the prize of all forms and ascended to heaven and the highest dwellings, we, strengthening Bṛhaspati the bull, though being many, bore the light with our mouths.

Make our prayer true for the bestowing of vital strength; for you protect even the humble man with your own ways. Let all enemies be driven away behind us; hear this, O Heaven and Earth, you who pervade all things!
Indra by his greatness split asunder the head of the great ocean-like Arbuda; he slew the serpent and set the seven rivers free. O Heaven and Earth, together with the gods, protect us!
Sing forth with song to Indra, the lord of cattle, as he is known: the begetter of truth, the protector of the good.
The bay steeds have been let loose upon the red sacrificial grass where we raise our voices together in praise.
For Indra, for the wielder of the thunderbolt, the cows have yielded the sweet milk-mixture, since he found it in his vicinity.
When we two, Indra and I, go up to the dwelling-place on the summit of the sun, having drunk of the honeyed draught, let us dwell together in the three-times-seven stations of our friend.
Sing, sing forth, O Priyamedhas, sing! Let the sons also sing; sing boldly as if to a fortress!

The *gargara* lute resounds; the *godhā* lizard croaks all around; the *piṅgā* cricket chirps all around. For Indra, the prayer (*brahman*) is raised up. When the dappled cows, easy to milk and not shrinking back, come flying down—seize the shrinking Soma for Indra to drink! Indra has drunk, Agni has drunk, and all the gods have become exhilarated. Varuṇa indeed dwells here; toward him the waters have lowed, like mother-cows toward their calf.

You are a good god, O Varuṇa, whose throat the seven rivers flow over, as if over a hollowed-out vessel for the sun. He who caused the swift, well-yoked steeds to spring forth for the worshipper—he, the leader, is indeed a marvel, he who was released as the highest of all. Indeed, the mighty Indra holds himself above all enemies; even as a youth, by his song, he split apart the porridge being cooked on the far mountain.
Like a young child, a little boy, he has mounted the lower chariot; he brought the buffalo and the deer, of far-reaching power, for his father and mother.
O fair-jawed lord of the house, mount now upon the golden chariot! Then let us two accompany the heavenly, thousand-footed, ruddy steed that brings well-being and is free from blemish.
To him, the self-radiant one, the worshipful ones sit down in this manner; for his purpose is well-established when they turn him toward them for the sake of giving.
Following the ancient dwelling place of these Priyamedhas, those who have spread the sacrificial grass and prepared the offerings have attained the former gift.
He who is the king of the people, the irresistible mover with chariots, the overcomer of all hostile armies—he is celebrated as the greatest slayer of Vṛtra.
O Puruhanman, glorify that Indra for his aid, in whose hand from of old the beautiful thunderbolt was placed by the Ordainer, like the great Sun set in the sky.
No one can equal him in deed who made him ever-increasing—Indra, praised by all, the skillful, the unassailable, the bold with daring might;
the unconquerable, the fierce, the victor in battles. At his birth, when he won the wide expanses, the great milch-cows lowed together; the heavens and the earths lowed in response.
Even if there were a hundred heavens, O Indra, and a hundred earths belonging to you, not even a thousand suns, O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, nor the two worlds, could equal you at your birth.

You have filled [the universe] with your greatness and manly power, O Bull, most mighty one, by your strength. Protect us, O Maghavan, in the cattle-pen, O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, with your wondrous aids.
May our hymns of praise exhilarate you; bestow bounty, O Lord of the Stone; strike down those who hate our sacred prayer.
With your foot, trample down those who offer no gifts; you are great, for there is no one who can withstand you.

You, O Indra, are the lord of the pressed juices and the lord of the unpressed; you are the king of all people. Swinging themselves to and fro, the active ones wait upon the newly born Indra, having obtained his heroic power.
O Indra, you were born from strength, from power, and from might; O Bull, you are indeed the Bull yourself.
You, O Indra, are the slayer of Vṛtra; you have extended across the mid-air and propped up the heavens with your might.
O Indra, you bear the hymn of praise in your arms in full accord, whetting the thunderbolt with your power.
O Indra, you are the conqueror of all beings by your might; you have pervaded all the worlds.
Let Indra, the lord of heaven, come for exhilaration—he who, impetuous according to his law, is full of power, surpassing all hostile forces with his boundless and great virility.

Firm is your chariot, easy to guide are your two bay steeds; O Lord of men, the thunderbolt is clasped in your hand. Come hither quickly, O King, by a fair path; we shall increase your manly powers as you drink.

May the fierce, powerful, and mighty ones, who carry Indra and delight in the communal feast, bring hither to us this lord of men, whose arm wields the thunderbolt, the fierce one, the bull of true strength, and the one of exceeding vigor.

Thus, you, the wise one, the companion of the Lord who possesses the *droṇakalaśa*, the pillar of vigor, the supporter—you act as a bull. Display your power, gather it within yourself, so that you may be the master for the increase of those who drink the *kenipa* (the pressed soma).

May riches come to us, for I have praised you; come to the bearer of the good blessing, to the one who possesses the soma! You are the lord; sit upon this sacred grass (*barhis*) here. Your vessels are inviolable by law.

The first invocations of the gods went forth separately; they performed deeds for glory that were difficult to surpass. Those who were unable to ascend the ship of sacrifice—those writhing ones entered into the depths.

Thus indeed, let the others, the evil-minded, remain far behind—the horses which have been yoked to a difficult yoke. Truly, those who are here before us are ready for the giving, wherein there are many works and provisions for enjoyment.

He has held firm the mountains and the plains as they shook; Dyaus has roared and made the mid-air regions tremble. He props apart the two converging bowls; having drunk of the strong draught, he utters hymns in his exhilaration.

I carry this well-fashioned goad of yours, O Maghavan, with which you shall break those who strike with their hooves. May there be a welcome for you at this libation; O Maghavan, be a partaker in the pressed juice and the sacrifice.
O Much-invoked One, may we overcome evil-minded poverty with cattle, and all hunger with barley. May we, as the foremost, win riches through the kings and by our own heroic band.
May Bṛhaspati protect us from behind, and from above, and from below against the wicked. May Indra from the front and from the middle grant wide space to us, his friends, as a friend.

At the Trikadruka festivals, the mighty buffalo, possessed of great strength, drank his fill of the Soma mixed with barley, pressed by Viṣṇu according to his desire. It exhilarated him for the sake of performing great deeds—the great and wide one. May that god, the true Indu, attend upon the god Indra, the true one. Sing forth a hymn of power to this Indra, whose chariot is foremost; he is the maker of space even in close combat, the slayer of Vṛtra in the clash of battles. Be our inspirer! Let the bowstrings of our enemies snap upon their bows!

You released the rivers to flow downward; you slew the serpent. O Indra, you were born without a rival; you nourish every desirable thing. We embrace you closely; let the bowstrings of our enemies snap upon their bows.

May all hostilities be scattered; may the pious man’s prayers reach us. You hurl the weapon at the enemy, O Indra, who seeks to slay us. That gift of yours which bestows wealth—may the bowstrings of our adversaries snap upon their bows.

Drink of this sharp, invigorating draught; unyoke both bay steeds here along with the entire chariot. O Indra, let not other sacrificers detain you; these juices pressed for you have been prepared for you alone. For you they were pressed, and for you they shall be pressed; our strengthening songs call upon you. O Indra, enjoying this libation today, you who know all things, drink the Soma here.
To him who, with longing mind and whole heart, desiring the gods, presses the Soma for him—Indra does not withhold his cattle from such a one; rather, he makes him glorious and beautiful.
He remains unperceived by that wealthy man who does not press Soma for him; Maghavan casts him down into his arm-span and slays him, the hater of sacred prayer, without being entreated.
Desiring horses, desiring cattle, and desiring booty, we call upon you to come hither. Standing ready in your new favor, O Indra, may we invoke you for our well-being.
I release you with this oblation so that you may live, from unknown consumption and from royal consumption. If the Seizer has grasped him, O Indra and Agni, release him from her grasp!

Whether his life is exhausted, or he has passed away, or has already been led into the presence of Death—I bring him back from the lap of Destruction, so that he may touch this world for a hundred autumns. With an oblation of a thousand eyes, a hundredfold strength, and a hundredfold lifespan, I have brought him back. May Indra lead him through the autumns to the further shore of all misfortune. Live a hundred autumns, growing in vigor; live a hundred winters and a hundred springs. May Indra, Agni, Savitṛ, and Bṛhaspati—with an oblation of a hundredfold lifespan—bring him back to you.
I have brought you back; you have returned, renewed. O you who are whole in every limb, I have found for you your entire sight and your entire lifespan.
May Agni, in harmony with the *brahman*, as the slayer of demons, drive away from here the disease that, having a foul name, has settled upon your embryo and your womb.
That disease with a foul name which has settled upon your embryo and your womb—Agni, together with the *brahman*, has utterly destroyed that flesh-eater.
He who kills what is flying for you, what is sitting still, or what is crawling; he who seeks to destroy what has been born for you—that one we cause to perish from here.
He who spreads apart your thighs and lies between the husband and wife, he who licks the interior of the womb—him we cause to perish from here.
Him who, having been your brother and husband, now lies with you as a lover; him who seeks to destroy your offspring—him we cause to perish from here.
Him who lies down after deluding you with the darkness of sleep, and him who seeks to destroy your offspring—him we cause to perish from here.
From your two eyes, from your two nostrils, from your two ears, and from your chin— I tear away the disease of the head from your brain and from your tongue.
From your necks, from your occipitals, from your vertebrae, and from your spine— I tear away the disease of the shoulders from your forearms and from your arms.
From your heart, from your lungs, from your liver, and from your ribs— We tear away the disease from your kidneys, from your spleen, and from your liver.

From your intestines, from your bowels, from the large intestine, and from the belly; from your two sides, from the bladder, and from the navel—I tear the disease away from you. From your thighs, from your knees, from your heels, and from your forefeet; from the anus, from the hips, and from the groin—I tear the disease away from you. From the urethra, from the penis, from your body hair, and from your nails; from your entire self—I tear that disease away from you here.
From your bones, from your marrow, from your sinews, and from your vessels—from your two hands, from your fingers, and from your nails—I tear away your consumption.
From every limb, from every hair, and from every joint of yours, we tear apart with the tearing-tool of Kaśyapa the consumption that dwells in your skin, driving it away in all directions.
Depart, O Lord of the Mind; go away, O Kāma, and wander far. Look toward Nirṛti; the mind of the living man turns in many directions.
We have indeed caused this wielder of the thunderbolt to drink here today; therefore, bring him the pressed juice now in equal measure. Pay honor now to the famous one!
Even the wild wolf, the oppressor of sheep, honors him at his appointed times. Accepting this our hymn of praise, O Indra, come hither with wondrous thought.
What manly deed of this Indra remains yet undone? By what glorious fame has the slayer of Vṛtra not been heard of from his very birth?

For it is you alone that we poets invoke for the winning of booty; you, O Indra, the lord of the good, do men invoke in battles against the Vṛtras, and you in the races of the steed. Therefore, O wonderful one, wielder of the thunderbolt, boldly bestow upon us, O great Adrisvan, cattle and chariot-horses, O Indra, like the total prize for a victor.
For the first draught, O Indra, the Āyus with their hymns of praise, the Ṛbhus coming together, and the Rudras have raised their voices in song, extolling you, the ancient one.
Indeed, in the exhilaration of this pressed soma, at Viṣṇu’s [call], Indra increased his manly strength. Today, as in former times, the Āyus sing praises after that majesty of his.
For now, O Indra, lover of songs, we have released our great desires toward you, like those going upward with water.

O Hero, the sacred hymns (*brahmāṇi*) strengthen you as the waters strengthen the reeds; O Hero, the sacred hymns strengthen you as the waters strengthen the reeds. O Lord of the Stone, though you have grown strong day by day, they yoke the two bay steeds of the Impetuous One with song upon the broad chariot with its wide yoke—the steeds that carry Indra, yoked by our word. We choose Agni as the messenger, the invoker (*hotṛ*), the all-knowing, the skillful performer of this sacrifice; the skillful performer of this sacrifice.
