They ever invoke Agni with invocations, the lord of the people, the bearer of oblations, the beloved of many.

O Agni, being born, bring the gods here for him who has trimmed the sacred grass; you are our Hotṛ-priest, worthy of praise. Worthy of laudation, worthy of homage, visible even through the darkness, Agni, the bull, is kindled.
Agni, the bull, is kindled like a horse that carries the gods; him, the bulls, bearing oblations, worship.

O Bull Agni, we who are bulls kindle you, the showerer of blessings, shining mightily. Invoke Agni for protection with songs of praise, him whose flame is fierce; invoke Agni for wealth, O Purumīḷha, and the men invoke the famous Agni for a dwelling of perfect light.
O Agni, come with the fires; we choose you as the Hotṛ-priest. Let the extended ladle, filled with oblation, anoint you, the most excellent sacrificer, to sit upon the sacred grass.
For toward you, O Aṅgiras, Son of Strength, the ladles move at the sacrifice. We seek Agni, the Son of Vital Power, whose hair is ghee, the foremost in sacrifices.
May these songs of mine, O Lord of abundant wealth, increase you—these pure, wise hymns of brilliant luster that have resounded with praises.

He, who was made mighty by a thousand seers, has spread himself out like the ocean; his greatness is true, and his power is celebrated at the sacrifices in the sovereignty of the inspired singer. May Indra, who is to be invoked in all battles, be present for us; may the slayer of Vṛtra, the supreme victor worthy of praise, come to our sacred prayers and libations.
You are the foremost giver of riches; you are the true one who acts as lord. We choose the alliance of the son of great power, the one of abundant splendor.
O Indra, in battles you overcome all rival hosts. You are the destroyer of curses, the progenitor, the conqueror of all. Overcome those who seek to overcome us.
The two worlds follow your surging strength, like two mothers following their child. All rival hosts yield to your wrath when you, O Indra, strike down Vṛtra.
For our aid, we invoke from here the ageless one, the hurler who is never sent forth, the swift victor, the striker, the best of charioteers, the unconquered, the increaser of Tugra’s line;

him who is the king of the peoples, who moves with his chariots irresistible, the overcomer of all hostile armies, the eldest, the slayer of Vṛtra—O Puruhanman, glorify that Indra for protection. In whose hand, the sustainer, the beautiful thunderbolt was placed of old, like the great sun in the sky.
That great power of yours, O Indra, your vigor and your will—the Dhiṣaṇā sharpens your choice-worthy thunderbolt.

O Indra, heaven increases your manly strength, and earth increases your fame; the waters and the mountains urge you on. Viṣṇu, the dweller in the vast expanse, and Mitra and Varuṇa sing your praise; the host of Maruts rejoices after you.
All the tribes and all the peoples bow down before his wrath, as rivers flow toward the ocean.
That power of his shone forth when Indra rolled together both worlds like a hide. With his hundred-jointed thunderbolt, the bull-like god shattered the head of the fiercely trembling Vṛtra.
That indeed was the eldest among all beings, from which the fierce one, of brilliant manly power, was born. As soon as he was born, he overcomes his enemies, when all his helpers rejoice after him.

Increasing in strength, possessing great might, he, as an adversary, strikes fear into the Dāsa. Both the silent and the vocal [enemies] he has won; they cry out to you at the libations when the offerings are presented. They pour forth their mental power into you abundantly, when these helpers become twice or thrice [in number]. Mix that which is sweeter than the sweet with sweetness; win that honey with honey in the contest!
If indeed the sages rejoice after you as you win the spoils in every battle, O mighty one, exert your more powerful and steadfast strength; let not the evil-minded Kaśoka-slayers harm you.
Through you we prevail in battles, beholding many things worthy of war. I urge on your weapons with my words; I sharpen your vital powers with my prayer.
You bestow that [strength] both upon the lower and the higher, in which house you have protected us with your aid. Establish the swift Mother; from here, impel forth many heroic deeds.

Praise him, the one of many paths, the preeminent, the most powerful, the *āptya* among the *āptyas*. He of abundant might reveals himself through his strength; he shall overcome every rival of the earth.

May Bṛhaddiva, the son of Agni, the winner of light, offer these prayers as a hymn of praise to Indra. As great sovereign ruler, he dwells in the vast stall of cattle; impetuous and fervent, he dries up even the entire ocean.
Thus has the great Bṛhaddiva Atharvan spoken to Indra as his own body. The two stainless sisters, dwelling in the mother, incite him and strengthen him with power.
The brilliant banner and face of the gods, the radiant Sūrya rising toward the quarters, the light-maker, has overcome the darknesses and all misfortunes with his splendors—he, the pure one.
The brilliant face of the gods has risen: the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni. Sūrya has filled heaven, earth, and the mid-region; he is the soul of all that moves and stands still.
Sūrya follows after the shining goddess Uṣas as a youth approaches a maiden, where god-seeking men extend their generations for the sake of auspiciousness upon auspiciousness.

O Indra, bring to us strength and manly valor, O Śatakratu, O far-seeing one; bring a hero who conquers in battle! For you, O Vasu, have become our father and our mother, O Śatakratu; therefore, we seek your favor.
To you, O mighty one, much-invoked Śatakratu, do I speak as I seek for strength; grant us excellent heroic power.
Thus do the tawny cows drink of the sweet, central draught; they who, moving together with the bull Indra, rejoice for the sake of splendor.
Rich in their own sovereignty, those dappled cows, longing for his touch, mix the Soma; these dear milch-cows of Indra urge on the thunderbolt, the missile, rich in their own sovereignty.
With reverence, those wise ones worship his conquering power; they follow his many ordinances for the sake of primordial awareness, according to their own sovereignty, as excellent ones.
For Indra, the exhilarating one, let our songs resound around the pressed juice; let the poets sing the hymn of praise.
We invoke Indra at the pressing—the one in whom all glories rejoice and in whom the seven assemblies delight.
At the Trikadruka rites, O Gods, you extended the conscious sacrifice; may our songs of praise increase that very sacrifice for us.
Whether you, O Indra, rejoice in Soma with Viṣṇu, or with Trita Āptya, or whether you delight among the Maruts with the drops;
or whether, O Śakra, you rejoice in the distance beyond the sea—rejoice indeed in this pressed juice of ours, together with the drops.
Or since you, O Lord of the Good, are the strengthener of the one who presses the juice and performs the sacrifice, or since you take delight in his hymn along with the drops;
and whatever you have risen toward today, O Vṛtra-slayer, O Sūrya—all that, O Indra, is under your control.
Or rather, O Lord of the Good, though you have grown great, you do not think, "I shall die. And yet, that thought of yours is indeed true.
Whether the Soma juices are pressed in a distant land or in a nearby place, you, O Indra, go to them all.
May Indra listen to both our voices; may the most powerful Maghavan come hither with his focused mind to drink the Soma.
For the two worlds have fashioned him as their sovereign king, the bull, for the sake of strength. Indeed, you sit as the foremost among those who are exalted, for your mind is set upon the Soma.
O Indra, by your very birth from of old, you are without a rival and without kin; yet through battle alone, you seek to gain kinship.
Never indeed do you find the wealthy man for friendship; your horses of Soma scorn you. When you let out a roar, you gather [the people] together, and then you are invoked like a father.
For I have indeed received from my father the wisdom of the Eternal Order (Ṛta); I was born like the Sun.
With an ancient prayer, I adorn my songs like Kaṇva, by which Indra has indeed assumed his strength.
O Indra, those seers who have not praised you, and those who have praised you—grow great through my excellent praise alone.
Let us not be like strangers to you, O Indra, nor like those who are alien to you. We have thought ourselves like abandoned forests, O wielder of the thunderbolt, difficult to satisfy.

We indeed considered ourselves slow and lacking in strength, O slayer of Vṛtra; yet, O Hero, through your great bounty, we have performed good deeds and shall rejoice in accordance with our hymn of praise.
Drink the Soma, O Indra; let that which the stone has pressed for you exhilarate you, O Lord of the Tawny Steeds, like a well-guided steed urged by the arms of the presser.
That exhilaration of yours which is your dear companion, by which you slay the Vṛtras, O Lord of the Tawny Steeds—that, O Indra, Lord of Abundant Wealth, shall intoxicate you.
Understand well this speech of mine, O Maghavan, this hymn of praise which Vasiṣṭha recites for you. Accept these sacred prayers at our communal feast.
O Indra, Lord of Power, grant us aid with all your protections; for we follow you, O Hero, the glorious one who finds wealth, as we would follow Bhaga.
O God, you are the protector of the horse, the multiplier of cattle, and a golden spring; for no one can exhaust the gift within you. Whatever I ask of you, bring that to me.
Indra alone we invoke for the service of the gods, Indra while the sacrifice proceeds, Indra in the clash of battle—we who long for victory—and Indra for the winning of wealth.

By his greatness Indra has spread out the two worlds, heaven and earth; by his power Indra caused the sun to shine. In Indra all beings have found their support, and in Indra the pressed drops find their rest.
The ancient hymn has been sung; speak the sacred prayer to Indra. Many lofty songs of Truth have resounded, and the inspirations of the praiser have been released.
The swift, inspired singers have sung their hymn, dripping with clarity and rich in sweetness. For us, wealth has spread forth, along with manly strength; for us, the pressed drops of Soma flow.
Whether, O Indra, you are called by men from the east, the west, the north, or the south—you are indeed the one invoked by many heroes among the people, the bold one among the Turvaśas.
Or when you rejoice together with Ruma, Ruśama, Śyāvaka, and Kṛpa, O Indra—the Kaṇvas, bringing hymns of praise through their sacred prayers, draw you toward them; O Indra, come hither!

We praise you, O Hero, like unmilked cows; you who are the lord of this moving world, the beholder of heaven, the lord, O Indra, of all that stands still. No other like you exists—neither celestial nor terrestrial; none has been born, nor will be born. Desiring horses, O Maghavan, and desiring cattle, we, the seekers of booty, call upon you, O Indra.
May there be for us wealthy provisions at the common feast with Indra, providing great strength, so that we may rejoice, possessed of food.
Truly, one such as you, O bold one, when entreated by the singers in person, have fulfilled their desire like the axle of two wheels.
When, O Śatakratu, you fulfill the service and the longing of the chanters, you do so with your powers like the axle [of the chariot].

That is the divinity of Sūrya, that is his greatness: in the midst of his work he has withdrawn what was spread out. As soon as he has unyoked his bay horses from their station, then Night spreads her garment over all.
In the lap of heaven, Sūrya assumes that form for the beholding of Mitra and Varuṇa; one part of him is endless and radiant, while his other part is black, which his bay steeds gather together.
With what aid will the wondrous one, the ever-increasing friend, come to us? With what most powerful host?
Which true exhilaration of the soma-juice, most bountiful, shall intoxicate you so that you may break open even the firmest wealth?
May you, the protector of us who are your friends and singers, come to our aid with a hundred succors.
May we now bring these worlds into subjection, Indra and all the gods together. May Indra, along with the Ādityas, fashion for us the sacrifice, our own bodies, and our progeny.

May Indra, together with his host of Ādityas and Maruts, be the protector of our bodies. When the gods, having slain the Asuras, advanced while guarding their godhead, they brought the sun back with their powers; then indeed they beheld their own vigorous self-sustenance. Through this, may we win the strength bestowed by the gods; may we rejoice for a hundred winters, blessed with brave sons.

O Indra, Maghavan, subduer of all, drive away our enemies to the east, drive them to the west. Drive them to the north, O Hero, and drive them to the south, so that we may rejoice in your wide protection.

Surely, just as those possessing barley reap the grain in due order, separating it [from the chaff], so do you provide here and there the food for those who have not come to the cutting of the sacred grass (*barhis*) with an offering of reverence. For your journey is not in vain at the appointed time, nor has your glory failed to be found in the assemblies. Desiring cattle, seeking horses, and striving for strength, the sages [approach] Indra, the bull, for friendship.
O Aśvins, lords of beauty, drinking together the *surā* liquor from Namuci the Asura, you aided Indra in his deeds.
Like parents for their son, both Aśvins protected you, O Indra, with their poetic wisdom and wondrous deeds. When you drank the *surāma* liquor with your powers, Sarasvatī refreshed you, O Maghavan.

May Indra, the good protector, the possessor of wealth, be very gracious to us with his aids—he who is all-knowing. May he drive away hatred and grant us safety; may we be masters of heroic vigor. May that Indra, the good protector and possessor of wealth, keep our enemies far away from us. May we abide in the favor of that holy one, in his auspicious goodwill.
For they have let loose the presser, yet they did not regard Indra as a god; where Vṛṣākapi, my friend, revels among the wealth of the noble one—Indra is superior to all.
O Indra, you run away, avoiding the distress caused by Vṛṣākapi; indeed, you do not find us anywhere else for the drinking of Soma—Indra is superior to all.
What has this Vṛṣākapi, this tawny beast, done to you, that you now show such envy toward him? Or is it the wealthy property of the noble one?—Indra is superior to all.

O Indra, may the dog that hunts the boar now snap at the ear of this Vṛṣākapi whom you, O Indra, protect as a dear friend; Indra is superior to all. The ape has defiled my dear, well-fashioned, and polished [limbs]; I shall surely rend his head, for I will not be easy prey for the evil-doer; Indra is superior to all. No woman has been more beautiful than I, nor more skilled in dalliance; no one has moved more closely to me, nor raised her thighs more high; Indra is superior to all.
O Mother, it is easy for you to obtain; it will be just like a limb. My buttocks, my thighs, and my head—my heart seems to tremble all over. Indra is superior to all.
O lady with beautiful arms, beautiful fingers, broad chest, and broad hips! O wife of a hero, why do you revile our Vṛṣākapi? Indra is superior to all.
This cruel man regards me as if I were childless, yet I am the mother of heroes, the wife of Indra, and the friend of the Maruts. Indra is superior to all.

In ancient times, the woman used to go to the common sacrifice or the assembly; now, as the wise mistress of the cosmic order (*ṛta*), the consort of Indra is glorified. Indra is supreme over all. Among these women, I have heard that Indrāṇī is most fortunate; for her husband shall never die of old age, not even in the future. Indra is supreme over all. O Indrāṇī, I find no delight apart from my friend Vṛṣākapi, whose beloved oblation of water goes to the gods. Indra is supreme over all.

O wealthy Vṛṣākapāyī, you who have good sons and good daughters-in-law, Indra shall eat your oxen; he shall eat some dear oblation prepared for him. Indra is superior to all. For fifteen oxen and twenty more they cook for me all at once; indeed, I eat the fatness; they fill both my flanks. Indra is superior to all.
Like a sharp-horned bull bellowing within the herds, the stirred drink, O Indra, is pleasant to your heart—what the devotee presses out for you. Indra is superior to all.
He does not have power over him between whose thighs the penis hangs limp; he has power over him whose hairy member expands as he sits. Indra is superior to all.
He does not have power over him whose hairy member expands as he sits; he has power over him between whose thighs the broad penis hangs limp. Indra is superior to all.
O Indra, this Vṛṣākapi found a slain wild animal, a knife, a slaughter-ground, a new cauldron, and a load of firewood piled upon a wagon. Indra is superior to all.
Here I come, looking out, searching for the Dāsa and the Ārya; I drink the soma pressed by the simple-minded one; I have looked upon the wise man. Indra is superior to all.

The desert and the ravine—how many leagues (*yojana*) are there between them? O Vṛṣākapi, go home to your nearest dwelling. Indra is superior to all. Come back again, O Vṛṣākapi; let us two arrange our welfare together. You who are this dispeller of sleep, go back home by the path. Indra is superior to all.

When you went upward, O Indra and Vṛṣākapi, to the house—where was that beast of many sins, who goes about disturbing people? Indra is superior to all. The daughter of Manu, named Parśu, gave birth at once to twenty sons. It was truly a blessing for her, even though her womb was in pain. Indra is superior to all. Listen to this, O people: Narāśaṃsa shall be praised. We, the descendants of Kuru, have given sixty thousand and ninety [cows] among the Ruśamas.
He whose twenty camels, laden with brides, pull the chariot—its height reaching toward the sky, its touch like that of the heavens—rejoices as it speeds along.
He has bestowed for his nourishment a hundred gold coins, ten garlands, three hundred horses, and ten thousand cattle.
O Rebha, speak out! Speak out like a bird on a ripe tree! Like a tongue in a lost place, like a razor between the tongs.

The singers send forth their inspired thoughts like bulls toward the cows; their sons are not held back, nor are the cows kept away. O singer, bring forward your prayer that finds cattle and finds wealth; blend this speech for the gods, as an arrow is fixed upon one who is not a coward.

For the king who is beneficial to all people—the god who transcends mortals—press out the fine hymn of praise for Vaiśvānara, O you who dwell around him. Having established his domain, he brought about security; moving toward his seat, the Kauravya husband, building a nest, speaks with his wife.
"Which shall I bring for you: curd, stirred drink, or the distilled soma? Thus the wife asks her husband in the realm of King Parikṣit.
The ripened barley, facing the sun, slips away from its place on the path. That person prospers in the kingdom of King Parikṣit; he attains what is auspicious.

Indra has awakened the artisan: "Arise, go among the people! Praise me alone as the Mighty One; every enemy shall give you gifts. Here let cattle multiply, here horses, here men; here indeed sits Pūṣan, the giver of a thousand sacrificial fees.
O Indra, let these cows not suffer harm; let no cowherd injure them. Let no hostile person, O Indra, nor any thief have power over them.
You do not take pleasure in us with this well-spoken word—may we be blessed with auspicious speech. May we never suffer harm from the forest or from the road, like songs [that reach you].
That man who is fit for the assembly, fit for the sacrifice, a presser of soma and a worshipper—him, as well as the sun, the gods, O destroyers of enemies, have ordained from of old.

That he would cause his sister to spread [her womb], that he would seek to deceive his friend, and that the eldest, lacking wisdom, acts thus—they call it "the lower" (*adharāk*). That the son of a noble man becomes a bold oppressor—of this the inspired sage has spoken; such is the Gandharva’s desirable word.
And as for him who is a miserly trafficker, who does not worship the gods among the many wise ones—I have heard that they call him "one who turns away" (*apāk*).
Those gods who have sacrificed and those who have bestowed gifts—having risen to heaven like Sūrya, may Maghavan roar for us.

He whose eyes are unanointed, who is unbesmeared, who has no jewel and no gold, who is not a Brahman, yet is the son of a Brahman—a praiser measured by the ritual rules. He whose eyes are anointed, who is well-besmeared, who has a fine jewel and fine gold, who is a true Brahman, the son of a Brahman—a praiser measured by the ritual rules.
The drinking-place is without water, the pool is shallow, the ford is difficult to find; the maiden is unapproachable, though beautiful—she is considered such in the sacred rites.
But the drinking-place has good water, the pool is deep, the ford is easy to find; the maiden is approachable, though beautiful—she is considered such in the sacred rites.
The queen has been set aside, and he goes to battle for his well-being; he is not swift, yet he is enduring—she is considered such in the sacred rites.
The beloved queen and the chief consort, the one who goes to battle with well-being, the father-in-law, and the son-in-law—these are reckoned as equal in their respective roles.
O Indra, when you plunged into that human conflict of the ten kings, Virūpa was for everyone; he was fit for the sacrifice along with the Yakṣas.
You, O Maghavan, the bull, the sun, made the mortal Akṣu free from intoxication. You tore Rauhiṇa apart and split asunder the head of Vṛtra.
He who established the mountains, who plunged into the waters—he who is Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, from him, the Great One, let there be homage to you, O Indra!
They spoke to Uccaiḥśravas as he ran upon the back of the two bay horses: "O auspicious horse, bring Indra here for victory, he who wears the beautiful garland!
Those white steeds of Ajaiśravas who yoke you, the bay horse, to the right side—you, O Indra, bearing them as the first among the gods to be honored, are magnified.
These mares leap forward.
Against the one who flows contrary, against the son of the presser.
Among them, one was Hariknikā.
O Hariknikā, what do you desire?
A virtuous son made of gold.
Where has he gone, having cast aside what was struck?
Where those three *śiṃśapā* trees are.
Three [times] around.
The adders.
They sit blowing upon the horn.
Great indeed are your coursers.
He indeed attains his desire.
He is called "possessor of cows" because he has attained the states of cattle.
O man, you desire what is base.
"Bound by age," so it is said.
"May evil be bound for you."
The female ascetic remained awake.
The bridle of the horse is at the hoof-print of the cow.
She is the mistress of Śyenī.
Anāmayā is the uvula.
O Noble One, what is the abundance of your arrows?
Who is the milk of the stone?
Who [drinks] the milk of the Arjunī?
Who is the milk of Kārṣṇī?
Ask him this; ask Kuha.
Ask about the ripened deception.
The Yavanas with their swift horses and camels.
Not being agitated, they are free from the evil of the defilements.
Āmaṇakaḥ, Maṇatsakaḥ.
O King, you are like a second sun.
The oblation for Enaścipañcika is the *havis*.
They ran toward the Maghās.
A horn has arisen.
May our friends not find you out.
They come to the son of the barren cow.
This one here has given this [gift]. Irāvaḥ. Idaṃ. Ayam. Dadau.
And then [he says], "This one, this one."
And then, "This [earth]," he says.
And then he became a restless dog.
This is a portion of the world.
It is broken with the words "āminon."
Following that, the breaking [of the bonds].
Varuṇa goes forth with his treasures.
Or a hundredfold is the power of speech.
A hundred golden horses; a hundred golden chariots; a hundred golden rugs—O Ahula, Kuśa, Vartaka, he carries them as if on a hoof!
The woman approaches with her braid.
The rectal muscles do not contract.
"This is mine; it is my honey."
Those trees stand together.
The cooked offering.
The Śaka offering.
The Aśvattha, the Khadira, and the Dhava.
Discontent and cessation.
Like a slain serpent.
The Person pervaded [all].
He milked the ewe Pūṣakā.
The *parastva* [formula] follows after each half-verse.
The two leather bags for the elephant-driver's water-flask.
A single bottle-gourd.
A gourd that has been buried.
The *karkarika* is that which is dug in.
The wind churns it up.
"He shall build a nest," so [he thought].
The fierce one has stretched out his bow.
The arrow does not reach the unstrung bow.
Who is scratching this karkarī among them?
Who among them struck the drum?
If this [self] were to kill, how could it kill?
O Goddess, strike! Strike down!
Again and again, he went around the entire house.
There are three names for the camel.
"He is golden," so some have said.
Or there are two, which are the two children.
He whose vehicle is the blue-crested peacock.
"Two rays are stretched out; the person grinds them both. O maiden, it is not at all as you think, O maiden.
Your mother’s two rays have ceased; the person has turned away from falsehood. O maiden, it is not at all as you think, O maiden.
Grasping both ears, you pull them toward the middle. O maiden, it is not at all as you think, O maiden."
While she lies on her back or reclines, you stand over her and conceal [the secret]. O maiden, it is not at all as you think, O maiden.
Upon the smooth, upon the very smooth, you conceal only the smooth. O maiden, it is not at all as you think, O maiden.
As if falling upon the unsmooth, with the hair inside, beyond the pool. O maiden, it is not at all as you think, O maiden.
Here, in this manner, previously, behind, above, below, crookedly, you have reviled [us].
Here, in this place, the calves, moving about, sit facing east, west, north, and south.
Here, in this manner—eastward, westward, northward, and downward—the *sthālīpāka* offering dissolves away.
Here, in this manner—east, west, north, and south—that indeed becomes vast and dissolves away.
Here, thus, eastward, westward, northward, and downward sits Lāhaṇi Līśāthī.
Here, thus, eastward, westward, northward, downward, and upward, one moves about.
"Bhuja" means approached; "śala" means departed; "phali" means established. O singer, by the two beatings of the drum, may we rise up, O divine one!
A treasure-chest, a hole, a turmeric-root, a book, a pair of sandals, a foot; the highest birth, people, the most excellent woman, women on the path;
gourds, speckled butter, the *aśvattha* and *palāśa* leaves; the ant-hill, the well, the horse's hoof, the lightning-stone, the cow's hoof, O singer, and then the divine protection.
These gods have stepped forth; O *adhvaryu*, perform the rite quickly! Truly, you are the essence of cows; you are the one who digs deep.
When the wife is seen—the wife who is about to sacrifice, O singer, *othāmaḥ*! Divine one! The Hotṛ with his stride, O singer, *othāmaḥ*! Divine one!
Indeed, O singer, the Ādityas brought the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Aṅgirases. To that, O singer, they looked back; indeed, O singer, they looked back to it.

O singer, they indeed accepted her for us; O singer, you indeed accepted her for us. Like days, they were not to be distinguished from one another; like sacrifices, they were not to be led by different leaders.
And he is white, swift-footed; and as the youngest, he speeds with his feet; and he fulfills the measure of speed.

O Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus, may you indeed accept this gift, O Aṅgiras. This gift is all-pervading and powerful; this gift is vast and wide. May the gods grant us this divine wealth; may it be well-disposed toward you. May it belong to you day after day; receive it indeed as such.
O Indra, with your protection, bring the oblation from the Pārāvatas to the inspired singer who praises you, the winner of wealth, Duraśravas.
O Indra, for the pigeon that was fleeing with its wings clipped, you provided ripe śyāmāka grain and many pīlu fruits as food.
The Araṅgara bell sounds loudly, bound in three ways with triple cords; it proclaims the nourishment and drives away the lack of nourishment.
What small and thick thing has clung to her, this one who crushes with her thighs? Her testicles quiver like two *śakula* fish in a cow-hoof.
When he struck down the testicles with his thick member, they grew apart on both sides like two donkeys in the sand.
What tiny, very tiny thing is pressed down like a jujube fruit—it goes forth like a spring reed, spreading for the wind.

That which the gods made manifest—the limping, the crippled woman—she, the woman with her kin, is seen clearly, like the eye of the world of truth. The great Agni was not satisfied; he roared aloud; those without standing fled. The forest of power, the skin, the flour, and the footstep were unable to endure.
As she was passing over the great fire and the mortar, Mahānagnī said: "O tree, just as they strike you, so shall it be."

The great Agni speaks to the fallen [seeds]: "O you who have come into being, just as your fruit ripens, O Lord of the Forest, so shall it be. The great Agni speaks to the fallen [seeds]: "O you who have come into being, just as birds, having burned [the husks], are not consumed in heaven.
The great Agni speaks to the sister [the mortar] that has entered the [husked] grain: "In this way, let us divide the winnowing-basket for the fruit of the tree."
The great Mahānagnī runs around the cock with a wooden pin. We do not know what beast this is that carries away the *dhāṇikā* with its head.
The great Mahānagnī runs after the running Mahānagna. Guard these cows of his; mate with me for the sake of eating rice-porridge.
The god-favored Mahānagnī presses you hard; he is truly a great digger-out of the *khodana*. The fat one [eats] the new *kusam*.

O most fierce one, release this burnt finger; O great and auspicious one, mate with me for the sake of rice-porridge. The godless and great Agni oppresses you; it is well that you cook the porridge for the great one. The tawny girl, the daughter of Kardama, runs about in the ashes.
Truly great is the auspicious *bilva* tree; truly great is the auspicious *udumbara* tree. The great one overcomes the unanointed; the carving out of the great is excellent.
She who is a tawny maiden, fat and flourishing in spring—may she draw forth this weeping, pure, thumb-sized vessel of oil.
When you went forward with your chests, O you who carry the dregs of rust, all the enemies of Indra were slain—the swift ones, like bubbles.

O men, bring forth the prize-winning steed; urge him on, rouse him for the winning of the spoil. Bring hither the son of Niṣṭigrī, Indra, with all haste, for our protection and to drink the Soma here.
I have celebrated Dadhikrāvan, the victorious, the spirited horse. May he make our mouths fragrant; may he prolong our lives.
The pressed Somas, most rich in sweetness and exhilarating, have flowed through the filter for Indra. May your intoxications go to the gods.
"The drop flows clear for Indra," thus the gods have declared. The Lord of Speech exerts himself, ruling over all by his might.
With a thousand streams he flows, an ocean that stirs the voice. Soma is the lord of riches, the friend of Indra day by day.
The dark drop, hastening with ten thousand [followers], descended upon the Aṃśumatī river. Indra helped him as he blew [the blast]; the hero-minded one cast off the hostile powers.
I saw the drop moving in the distance, in the secret hiding place of the river Aṃśumatī; like a black cloud, he has taken his stand. O heroes, I urge you: fight in the battle!
Then the Drop, flashing forth, took his station in the lap of Aṃśumatī; with Bṛhaspati as his ally, Indra overcame the godless tribes that were attacking him.
At your birth, O Indra, you became the enemy of those seven who had no enemies; you found Heaven and Earth when they were hidden, and you bestowed joy upon the vast worlds.

O wielder of the thunderbolt, you, bold with courage, struck down that peerless power with your bolt; you shattered Śuṣṇa with your weapons, and by your might, O Indra, you found the cattle. We incite that Indra for the slaying of the great Vṛtra; let him be the bull, the showerer of benefits. That Indra has been made for the giving of gifts; he is the most powerful, established in the exhilaration of the Soma; he is resplendent, worthy of praise, and beloved of the Soma.

Like a thunderbolt forged by speech, he is powerful and unshakable; lofty and invincible, Indra has grown great through his might, like Parjanya rich in rain. He has been magnified by the hymns of Vatsa. When the priests, the bearers of the sacrifice, bring forth the offspring of *ṛta*, the sages advance with the vehicle of *ṛta*.

When the Kaṇvas have fashioned Indra with their hymns as the accomplisher of the sacrifice, they proclaim his kinship as his weapon. O Aśvins, come now for the protection of Vatsa; grant him a broad, secure shelter free from danger, and drive away those who are hostile.
Whatever manly power exists in the mid-air, whatever in heaven, and whatever among the five peoples—bestow all that strength upon us, O Aśvins.
O Aśvins, just as the sages have contemplated your wondrous deeds, even so take heed of Kaṇva.

This hot offering, O Aśvins, is poured out for you with hymns of praise; this is the honeyed Soma, O lords of ample wealth, by which you perceive Vṛtra. Whatever has been wrought by you, O performers of many marvels, in the waters, in the tree, or in the plants—with that, O Aśvins, protect me!
Whether you hasten forth, O Nāsatyas, or whether you practice healing as gods, this calf of yours does not find satisfaction through our prayers alone, for you go to him who possesses the oblation.
Now indeed, the seer has envisioned a hymn for the Aśvins with skill; let him pour out the most honey-sweet Soma and the warm milk-offering (gharma) for Atharvan.

O Aśvins, mount now your chariot of swift course; may these hymns of mine cause you to hasten hither like a cloud. Whether today we cause you, O Nāsatyas, to hasten hither with our recitations, or with our songs, O Aśvins—be mindful of Kaṇva as of yourselves. Just as Kakṣīvān, and as the seer Vyaśva, and as Dīrghatamas invoked you, and as Pṛthī Vainya invoked you at the sacrificial seats—even so, O Aśvins, be mindful of us from this place.
Come as protectors of our dwellings and protectors from afar; be the guardians of our world and the guardians of our bodies. Come to the dwelling for the sake of our children and our descendants.

Whether you travel on the same chariot with Indra, O Aśvins, or whether you share a common abode with Vāyu, or whether you are in harmony with the Ādityas and the Ṛbhus, or whether you stand in the wide strides of Viṣṇu—whether you are in harmony with the Ādityas and the Ṛbhus, or whether you stand in the wide strides of Viṣṇu.
That I may today invoke the Aśvins for the winning of booty, that they may conquer in battles—that is the most excellent aid of the Aśvins.
Come now, O Aśvins; these oblations have been set forth for you. These Soma-draughts are for you among the Turvaśas and Yadus, and these among the Kaṇvas as well.
Whatever medicine, O Nāsatyas, exists in the distance or near at hand—with that, O wise ones, grant protection now to Vimada and to Vatsa.
I have awakened together with the divine Speech, I [the speech] of the Aśvins. The Goddess has disclosed the thought and the bounty for mortals.
O Dawn, awaken the two Aśvins; O great Goddess Sūnṛtā, awaken them. O Hotṛ of the sacrifice, awaken them in due order, and awaken great glory for our exhilaration.
O Uṣas, as you come with your radiance, you shine together with Sūrya; here indeed comes the chariot of the Aśvins, seeking a dwelling-place that protects men.
When the pressed stalks have been milked like cows with their udders, or when the voices of those seeking the gods have sounded forth for you,

O Aśvins— [then] for glory, for power, for protection that overcomes men, for skill, O ye of keen insight! When now, O Aśvins, you sit upon the father’s seat with your prayers, or when you come with blessings, O ye worthy of hymns.

We invoke today that chariot of yours, O Aśvins, which has wide-reaching power and brings the gathering of cattle—the chariot that carries Sūryā on its seat, the life-giving vehicle praised by songs, most abundant, and seeking wealth.
O Aśvins, you two deities win that glory from heaven through your powers; your wondrous forms are accompanied by nourishing foods when the towering steeds draw your chariot.

Who today, having offered oblations, shall turn you toward him with hymns for aid, or for the drinking of the pressed soma? Or who, offering reverence, shall turn you, O Aśvins, toward the ancient lover of the Eternal Order (*ṛta*)?
O Nāsatyas, you who exist in many places, come to this sacrifice with your golden chariot; drink of the sweet Soma juice and bestow treasure upon the person who worships you.
Come toward us from heaven and from earth on your well-rolling golden chariot; let not other seekers of the gods detain you, for your ancient kinship has been established.

O wonder-workers, now measure out for us great wealth consisting of many heroes among both our groups. Since the men have brought praise to you, O Aśvins, the Ājamīḷhas have come to the joint song of celebration.

In this very place, that which I have offered to you both together—this is our benevolence, O you who possess the jewels of strength. Protect the singer; for toward you, O Nāsatyas, my desire is directed.
May the plants be honey-sweet, may the heavens and the waters be so; may the mid-air be honey-sweet for us. May the Lord of the Field be honey-sweet for us; may we follow him unharmed.
That deed of yours, O Aśvins, is worthy of praise: the Bull of heaven, of the mid-region, and of the earth. And those thousand praises in the quest for cattle—to all of them come hither to drink!
